================================================================================
QUESTION-BY-QUESTION ANSWERS
================================================================================

Q1. reCAPTCHA mandatory + fail-closed — works?
  ANSWER: YES. Solid implementation.
  Evidence:
    - route.ts:86-93 — token required: `!recaptchaToken || typeof !== "string" || length < 10` → 400 captcha_required.
    - route.ts:96-103 — POST to https://www.google.com/recaptcha/api/siteverify with `secret: process.env.RECAPTCHA_SECRET || ""` and `response: recaptchaToken`.
    - route.ts:105 — `captchaOk = !!verifyData.success;`
    - route.ts:109-112 — catch block logs the network error and DOES NOT set captchaOk=true. captchaOk stays false → fail-closed.
    - route.ts:113-118 — final `if (!captchaOk) return 400 captcha_failed`.
    - Frontend sends the token: page.tsx:346 `(window as any).grecaptcha?.getResponse()`; page.tsx:361 `recaptchaToken: recaptchaResponse`.
    - Frontend guards: page.tsx:347-351 — empty response → aborts before fetch.
    - If RECAPTCHA_SECRET env var is missing → empty string sent to Google → Google returns success:false → captchaOk=false → 400. Fail-closed on missing env.
  Severity: PASS.

Q2. Honeypot field (website) — actually sent by frontend?
  ANSWER: YES.
  Evidence:
    - page.tsx:764-771 — `<input type="text" name="website" tabIndex={-1} autoComplete="off" aria-hidden="true" style={{ position: "absolute", left: "-9999px", ... }} />` (hidden via off-screen positioning, NOT `display:none` — better, because some bots ignore display:none but still fill off-screen inputs).
    - page.tsx:363 — `website: (e.target as HTMLFormElement).website?.value || ""` included in POST body.
    - Server check: route.ts:69-75 — `if (website)` → log honeypot_triggered → return `{ ok: true }` (silent success to confuse the bot).
  Severity: PASS.
  Minor: honeypot value is logged with slice(0, 50) — OK. Length uncapped (see Q8).

Q3. Time-trap (_t) — actually sent by frontend?
  ANSWER: YES — sent, BUT BYPASSABLE.
  Evidence it's sent:
    - page.tsx:773 — `<input type="hidden" name="_t" value={mounted ? Date.now() : 0} />`
    - page.tsx:365 — `_t: (e.target as HTMLFormElement)._t?.value || Date.now()` in POST body.
    - Server check: route.ts:77-81 — `if (submittedAt && Date.now() - submittedAt < 2000) return 400 too_fast`.
  Finding C-2 (HIGH/MED): Time-trap is fully client-controlled and trivially bypassable:
    - Server trusts whatever `_t` value the client sends. An attacker can:
      (a) Omit `_t` → route.ts:78 `if (submittedAt && ...)` → submittedAt=0 is falsy → check skipped entirely.
      (b) Send `_t: Date.now() - 60000` (60s ago) → `Date.now() - submittedAt = 60000` > 2000 → check passes.
      (c) Send `_t: -1` → `Date.now() - (-1)` = huge → passes.
      (d) Send `_t: "not-a-number"` → `Number("not-a-number") = NaN` → `NaN && ...` is falsy → skipped.
    PoC:
      curl -s -X POST https://victim.com/api/contact \
        -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
        -d '{"name":"x","email":"x@y.z","message":"abcdef ghijk","recaptchaToken":"<valid>","_t":0,"website":""}'
      # → bypasses time-trap entirely.
  Severity: MEDIUM (mitigated by reCAPTCHA — but if reCAPTCHA is bypassed via token-replay or human-solving farms, time-trap provides no defense-in-depth).

Q4. Rate limit (3 per 10min) — works?
  ANSWER: NO — fully bypassable. Two layered rate limits, both broken by the same flaw.
  Evidence (route-level):
    - route.ts:6-7 — `RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_MS = 10*60*1000`, `RATE_LIMIT_MAX = 3`.
    - route.ts:8 — `const hits = new Map<string, number[]>();` (in-memory).
    - route.ts:10-21 — `rateLimit(ip)` filters timestamps in the window; if arr.length >= 3 → false.
    - route.ts:36-39 — IP extraction: `req.headers.get("x-forwarded-for")?.split(",")[0]?.trim() || req.headers.get("x-real-ip") || "unknown"`.
  Finding C-1 (HIGH): X-Forwarded-For trusted blindly (same flaw as F-9 from prior audit):
    - Attacker controls XFF header → supplies a fresh fake IP per request → `hits.get(ip)` always misses → unlimited throughput.
    PoC:
      for i in $(seq 1 50); do
        curl -s -X POST https://victim.com/api/contact \
          -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
          -H "X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.$i" \
          -d '{"name":"x","email":"x@y.z","message":"spam message here","recaptchaToken":"<solved>","_t":0,"website":""}'
      done
      # → all 50 accepted (limited only by reCAPTCHA token-solving rate, not by IP).
  Evidence (middleware-level):
    - middleware.ts:21 — `RATE_LIMIT_PATHS = ["/api/user/login", "/api/contact", "/api/chat"]`.
    - middleware.ts:144-148 — `const ip = req.headers.get("x-forwarded-for")?.split(",")[0]?.trim() || req.headers.get("x-real-ip") || "unknown"`. Same trust flaw. max=8 per 15min.
    - Both layers bypassed by the same XFF spoof.
  Finding C-8 (LOW): In-memory `hits` Map (route.ts:8) is never periodically swept. Each unique spoofed IP leaves an array entry forever → memory growth under attack.
  Severity: HIGH (when combined with a reCAPTCHA-solving service, this enables message-spam floods and DB pollution).

Q5. Bot detection (UA check) — bypassable?
  ANSWER: YES — trivially.
  Evidence: route.ts:43 `if (/bot|crawl|spider|slurp|wget|curl/i.test(userAgent) && userAgent.length < 80) return 403`.
  Finding C-3 (MED): Three bypass paths:
    (a) `&& userAgent.length < 80` — any UA ≥80 chars that contains "bot" (e.g., a long Chrome UA with "About" or "robotics" in a plugin string) is NOT blocked.
    (b) Empty UA: route.ts:40 `userAgent = req.headers.get("user-agent") || ""` → empty string. Regex `/bot.../i.test("")` is false → no block. Bots that omit UA pass.
    (c) Normal browser UA: `Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) ...` → no keyword match → no block.
  PoC:
    curl -s -X POST https://victim.com/api/contact \
      -H "User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36" \
      ...
      # → passes UA check.
    curl -s -X POST https://victim.com/api/contact -H "User-Agent: " ...   # empty UA also passes.
  Severity: MEDIUM (this is defense-in-depth, not primary; reCAPTCHA is the real gate).

Q6. Spam pattern detection — works?
  ANSWER: PARTIAL — catches naive spam, misses sophisticated.
  Evidence: route.ts:23-32 — `isSpammy(text)` checks:
    1. Keywords: `/\b(viagra|cialis|casino|lottery|prize|winner|bitcoin investment)\b/`
    2. 3+ URLs: `/(https?:\/\/[^\s]+){3,}/`
    3. 11+ of same char: `/(.)\1{10,}/`
  Finding C-5 (LOW): Multiple bypasses:
    - (a) Only `message` is checked (route.ts:140). `name` and `email` are NOT checked. Attacker can put spam URL or keyword in `name` (e.g., name="cheap viagra pills") and message="hello world" — passes.
    - (b) URL regex only matches `http://` or `https://` schemes. A message with 5 bare-domain URLs (`www.spam1.com www.spam2.com ...`) does not trigger pattern #2.
    - (c) Keyword list is tiny and English-only. Persian/German spam, misspellings (v1agra, c1alis), or synonyms (pharmacy, RX, dating) bypass.
    - (d) Char-repeat regex `/(.)\1{10,}/` — Unicode multibyte chars may behave oddly; also attacker can just use varied chars.
    - (e) No check for ALL-CAPS shouting, excessive exclamation marks, etc.
  PoC:
    curl ... -d '{"name":"Buy Cheap Meds","email":"x@y.z","message":"hello, please reply"}'  # name-based spam bypasses.
    curl ... -d '{"name":"x","email":"x@y.z","message":"visit spam1.com spam2.com spam3.com"}'  # www-only URLs bypass.
  Severity: LOW (defense-in-depth; not the primary gate).

Q7. Email validation — solid?
  ANSWER: ADEQUATE, not strict.
  Evidence: route.ts:120 `const emailRe = /^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/;`. Also enforced on frontend (page.tsx:327).
  Finding C-6 (LOW):
    - Regex rejects whitespace and missing `@`/`.` — good baseline.
    - But accepts invalid forms: `a@b.c`, `..@x.y`, `a@b.c.d.e.f.g`, `a@b.c` (where b.c is not a real TLD), `john..doe@example.com` (consecutive dots).
    - No DNS MX lookup (acceptable — adds latency and is optional).
    - No length check on local/domain parts beyond the 200-char total cap (route.ts:66).
    - Unicode in email accepted (could be a feature or a vulnerability depending on context).
  Severity: LOW (acceptable for a contact form; would be HIGH for a signup form).

Q8. Length caps on inputs?
  ANSWER: YES for primary fields; NO for control fields.
  Evidence (capped):
    - route.ts:65 — `name = String(body.name||"").trim().slice(0, 100)`
    - route.ts:66 — `email = ...slice(0, 200)`
    - route.ts:67 — `message = ...slice(0, 5000)`
    - page.tsx:776 — `<input maxLength={100}>` (name)
    - page.tsx:780 — `<input maxLength={200}>` (email)
    - page.tsx:784 — `<textarea maxLength={5000}>` (message)
  Finding C-7 (LOW): No length caps on:
    - `recaptchaToken` (route.ts:86) — only checked `length < 10` for minimum. No max. An attacker could send a 1MB token to inflate the Google verify request. Mitigated by middleware body cap of 1MB (middleware.ts:198).
    - `website` honeypot (route.ts:69) — uncapped. Only used in `logSecurityEvent(..., website.slice(0,50))` so DB-safe, but the body itself can be huge.
    - `_t` time-trap (route.ts:77) — uncapped. `Number(body._t)` could be a very long string, but Number() returns NaN for huge strings → check skipped.
  Severity: LOW.

Q9. Is IP stored (privacy)?
  ANSWER: YES — stored indefinitely with no retention policy.
  Evidence:
    - route.ts:36-39 — IP extracted from X-Forwarded-For / x-real-ip / "unknown".
    - route.ts:148 — `data: { name, email, message, ip, userAgent }` — persisted to ContactMessage.
    - prisma/schema.prisma:39 — `ip String?` column on ContactMessage.
    - Also stored in SecurityLog (security.ts:22 — `data: { type, ip, detail }`) on every honeypot/time-trap/captcha event.
  Finding C-4 (MED): Privacy concern.
    - No retention TTL — IP retained for the lifetime of the DB row (ContactMessage has no `expiresAt` field).
    - No GDPR/PII consent banner. The site collects IP silently.
    - "unknown" stored as a string when IP can't be determined — minor.
    - Index on `[email]` (schema.prisma:48) but not on ip — fine for privacy (no easy IP-based search).
  Severity: MEDIUM (privacy/compliance, not security).

Q10. Is UA stored (privacy)?
  ANSWER: YES — same concerns as IP.
  Evidence:
    - route.ts:40 — `userAgent = req.headers.get("user-agent") || ""`.
    - route.ts:148 — stored.
    - prisma/schema.prisma:40 — `userAgent String?`.
  Finding C-4b (MED): UA is a quasi-identifier. Combined with IP, enables fingerprinting. Stored indefinitely.
  Severity: MEDIUM (privacy/compliance).

Q11. Can attacker inject HTML in name/email/message?
  ANSWER: NO XSS in admin UI. Limited Markdown injection in Bale notification. Subject-only risk in forwarded email.
  Evidence (admin UI safe):
    - src/app/user-dashboard/page.tsx:455-462 — renders `{msg.name}`, `{msg.email}`, `{msg.message}` as React children. React escapes text by default. No `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for these fields.
    - src/components/ContentManager.tsx — unrelated; no contact-message rendering.
    - src/app/api/messages/route.ts:36-39 — returns raw message via JSON; consumer (admin UI) escapes.
  Finding C-9 (LOW): Bale notification Markdown injection:
    - bale.ts:55 — `parse_mode: "Markdown"`.
    - bale.ts:76-77 — `*From:* ${msg.name}` and `*Email:* ${msg.email}` — raw interpolation.
    - bale.ts:80 — `${msg.message.slice(0,500)}` — raw interpolation.
    PoC: attacker sends:
      name: "**URGENT** [Click here](https://evil.com/phish) admin"
      email: "x@y.z"
      message: "_Reset your password at http://evil.com/reset_"
    → Admin's Bale notification renders bold text and a clickable phishing link.
  Severity: LOW (admin targeted, not site-wide XSS).

  Finding C-9b (LOW): Email subject header-injection (latent):
    - route.ts:167 — `_subject: \`📨 New message from ${name}\``. name is capped at 100 chars but NOT sanitized for newlines (`\r\n`).
    - Formsubmit.co takes a JSON body, so the responsibility for SMTP-header escaping is theirs. If formsubmit.co naively interpolates the JSON value into a `Subject:` header without stripping CRLF, an attacker could inject `name: "x\r\nBcc: victim@example.com"` to add hidden recipients.
    - Not directly exploitable from this code; depends on formsubmit.co's implementation. Worth noting in audit.
  Severity: LOW (third-party-dependent).

Q12. Does it forward to email via formsubmit.co securely?
  ANSWER: PARTIALLY. Several issues.
  Evidence: route.ts:158-176.
    - Reads `forwardEmail` from SiteSetting (admin-controlled).
    - POSTs to `https://formsubmit.co/ajax/${forwardEmail}` with JSON body.
    - Body includes `_subject`, `_template: "table"`, `_captcha: "false"`, plus name/email/message/submitted_at.
    - Wrapped in `.catch(() => {})` — silent failure.
  Finding C-10 (LOW): Silent error swallowing:
    - route.ts:173 — `.catch(() => {})` on the fetch. If formsubmit returns 4xx/5xx (e.g., email not activated, rate-limited, network down), the error is silently dropped. The contact message IS saved to DB (route.ts:147), so not lost — but admin gets no signal that email forwarding failed.
    - The outer `.catch(() => {})` at route.ts:176 also swallows errors from the dynamic import.
  Severity: LOW.

  Finding C-11 (LOW): URL interpolation of `forwardEmail`:
    - route.ts:163 — `fetch(\`https://formsubmit.co/ajax/${forwardEmail}\`, ...)`. If `forwardEmail` contains URL-special chars (e.g., `a@b.com/../../other-endpoint?x=y` or contains `#`/`?`), the request path is malformed or redirected.
    - `forwardEmail` is admin-set via SiteSetting — so only an admin (or a backdoored admin per F-NEW-2 in prior audit) can weaponize this. SSRF-like risk if admin is compromised.
  Severity: LOW (admin-gated).

  Finding C-12 (INFO): Formsubmit.co security model:
    - No shared secret / HMAC. Anyone who knows `forwardEmail` can POST to formsubmit's `/ajax/<email>` endpoint and trigger an email to that inbox.
    - First-time activation requires clicking a confirmation link sent to that inbox — but after activation, no auth.
    - `_captcha: "false"` disables formsubmit's own captcha — acceptable here because reCAPTCHA was verified server-side (route.ts:113-118).
  Severity: INFO (architectural).

  Finding C-13 (LOW): No fetch timeout:
    - route.ts:163 — `fetch(...)` without `AbortController`/timeout. If formsubmit hangs, the promise stays pending indefinitely. Garbage-collected eventually by V8, but resource leak under high load.
    - Mitigated by being fire-and-forget (route returns before fetch completes).
  Severity: LOW.

## Detailed Findings

### F-CSRF-1 (MED) — Login CSRF possible (no Origin check on /api/user/login)
- File: /home/z/my-project/src/middleware.ts:24-37 (PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES includes "/api/user/login")
- File: /home/z/my-project/src/middleware.ts:159 (`!isPublicApi` skips Origin check)
- File: /home/z/my-project/src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:36-118 (sets `access_session` cookie unconditionally on credential match)
- File: /home/z/my-project/src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:106-112 (Set-Cookie with SameSite=strict)

Analysis: `/api/user/login` is in `PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES`, so the middleware's Origin check is bypassed. The route responds with `Set-Cookie: access_session=<token>; SameSite=strict` regardless of the request's Origin. The SameSite=strict attribute governs when the cookie is SENT on future cross-site requests — it does NOT prevent the cookie from being SET by a cross-site response. The browser honors `Set-Cookie` from any same-site URL response.

PoC (login CSRF — "session fixation via login"):
```html
<!-- Hosted on https://attacker.example.com/csrf.html -->
<form id="f" action="https://victim.example.com/api/user/login" method="POST"
      enctype="text/plain">
  <input name='{"username":"attacker","password":"attacker-pass","x":"'
         value='ignored"}' type="hidden">
</form>
<script>f.submit();</script>
```
- Victim is logged into their own account on victim.example.com.
- Victim visits attacker.example.com/csrf.html.
- Browser submits POST to victim.example.com/api/user/login with attacker's credentials.
- Server validates creds (they match attacker's account) → returns 200 + Set-Cookie.
- Browser stores attacker's `access_session` cookie (overwrites victim's cookie via Object.fromEntries — see F-11).
- Victim now believes they're using their own account but is actually using the attacker's.
- Any sensitive data the victim enters (contact form, chat, dashboard input) is visible to the attacker on next login.

Severity: MED. Limited by the fact that the attacker must already have a valid account on the victim's site (lowers impact), but enables "reverse honeytrap" attacks where attacker tricks victim into entering data they think is private.

### F-CSRF-2 (LOW) — Logout CSRF (already noted as F-24 + F-NEW-6, re-confirmed)
- File: /home/z/my-project/src/middleware.ts:30 (`"/api/user/logout"` in PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES)
- File: /home/z/my-project/src/app/api/user/logout/route.ts:7-11 (POST handler deletes cookie without auth)

Analysis: The logout route:
```ts
export async function POST() {
  const response = NextResponse.json({ ok: true });
  response.cookies.delete("access_session");
  return response;
}
```
does not read the cookie, verify a token, or check Origin. SameSite=strict prevents the victim's `access_session` cookie from being SENT on the cross-site POST, but the server's `Set-Cookie: access_session=; Max-Age=0` response is still honored by the browser, clearing the victim's cookie.

PoC:
```html
<form action="https://victim.example.com/api/user/logout" method="POST">
  <input type="submit" value="Click me">
</form>
```
- Or auto-submit via `<img src="...">`-style trick is NOT possible (POST required); user must click.
- After click, victim's `access_session` cookie is deleted → victim is forced to re-login.
- Severity: LOW (minor DoS — same as previously filed F-NEW-6).

### F-CSRF-3 (MED) — sameSite=strict does NOT fully prevent CSRF
- File: /home/z/my-project/src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:106-112

Analysis: SameSite=strict only blocks cookie INCLUSION on cross-site requests. It does not:
1. Block cookie SETTING on cross-site responses (login CSRF — F-CSRF-1).
2. Block `Set-Cookie: ...=; Max-Age=0` deletion responses (logout CSRF — F-CSRF-2).
3. Protect unauthenticated public endpoints (chat/contact/track — attacker doesn't need victim's cookie).
4. Protect against requests that don't require cookies (CSRF on /api/track, /api/contact).

The login route sets `sameSite: "strict"` on the issued cookie, but this is a defense for FUTURE requests, not for the issuance itself.

### F-CSRF-4 (MED) — No CSRF token anywhere (only Origin + sameSite)
- Files audited: every route under /home/z/my-project/src/app/api/**/route.ts — none issue, store, or verify a CSRF token.
- File: /home/z/my-project/src/middleware.ts:157-177 (Origin check is the only CSRF defense)

Analysis: The codebase has only two CSRF defenses:
1. `Origin === Host` check in middleware (bypassed for 7 PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES routes).
2. `sameSite: "strict"` cookie (bypassed for cookie-set and cookie-delete scenarios — see F-CSRF-3).

No defense-in-depth: no synchronizer-token, no double-submit cookie, no `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin` check, no custom-header check (`X-Requested-With` would force a CORS preflight and let the server reject non-preflightable requests). If either defense is weakened (e.g., admin accidentally changes sameSite to "lax" or "none"), every admin POST/PUT/DELETE becomes CSRF-vulnerable.

Recommendation (advisory only — DO NOT APPLY): add Sec-Fetch-Site check in middleware:
```ts
const fetchSite = req.headers.get("sec-fetch-site");
if ((method === "POST" || method === "PUT" || method === "DELETE") &&
    fetchSite && fetchSite !== "same-origin" && fetchSite !== "none") {
  return NextResponse.json({ ok: false, error: "cross_site" }, { status: 403 });
}
```
This is browser-mediated-only and complements Origin (which can be omitted on same-origin requests).

### F-CSRF-5 (LOW) — State-changing GET: /api/user/verify writes to AccessLog
- File: /home/z/my-project/src/app/api/user/verify/route.ts:27-31

Code:
```ts
const access = await checkAccess(user.id);
if (!access.allowed) {
  // لاگ دسترسی رد شده
  await logAccess(user.id, access.reason, getClientIp(request), request.headers.get("user-agent"));
}
```

`logAccess` writes to `db.accessLog` (CREATE). This is a state-changing GET. The middleware's CSRF check at line 159 only fires for POST/PUT/DELETE — GETs are never CSRF-checked. A cross-site `<img src="https://victim.example.com/api/user/verify">` or `<link rel="prefetch">` would trigger the GET request. If the victim is logged in (cookie sent for same-origin GET — but for cross-origin `<img>`, sameSite=strict blocks the cookie, so logAccess would be skipped because `getSessionFromRequest` returns null without the cookie). So this is largely theoretical, but the pattern is still bad practice.

Severity: LOW. Not directly exploitable due to sameSite=strict blocking the cookie on cross-site GETs, but the GET-mutates-DB pattern is a latent CSRF risk if sameSite is ever weakened.

Also note: GET endpoints that return sensitive data (e.g., /api/messages?password=xxx, /api/admin/security?password=xxx) are read-only at the DB level, but they accept credentials in the URL query string — already noted in prior audits (F-21, F-29). These GETs are CSRF-irrelevant since they require neither cookie nor Origin.

### F-CSRF-6 (INFO) — No OPTIONS handler, no Access-Control-Allow-* headers
- Files audited: grep for `export async function OPTIONS` → 0 results.
- Files audited: grep for `Access-Control-Allow` → 0 results.

Analysis: There is no CORS configuration. The site is same-origin by default. Cross-origin requests behave as follows:

- For "simple" cross-site requests (form POST with `enctype=text/plain`, `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, or `multipart/form-data`): no preflight, request reaches server. Browser blocks the JS-readable response (no ACA-* headers) — but the side-effect on the server still executes. This is the attack surface for F-CSRF-1, F-CSRF-2.
- For "non-simple" cross-site requests (XHR/fetch with `Content-Type: application/json` or custom headers like `X-Requested-With`): browser sends OPTIONS preflight. Middleware runs (matcher doesn't exclude OPTIONS). For OPTIONS to /api/admin/*, the middleware's session check at line 188-193 fires: `hasValidSession(cookieHeader)` — preflight requests don't include cookies → returns 401. Browser sees 401 with no ACA-* headers → blocks actual request. Accidental defense-in-depth: admin endpoints are protected by the missing CORS config + session check.
- For OPTIONS to public endpoints (e.g., /api/user/login, /api/contact, /api/chat): no session check applies → middleware falls through to `NextResponse.next()` with security headers, but no ACA-* headers. Browser sees preflight response without ACA-* → blocks actual request. So XHR/fetch-based CSRF on public endpoints is blocked by missing CORS — only form-based CSRF works (which is what F-CSRF-1 and F-CSRF-2 use).

Severity: INFO. The accidental blocking of CORS preflight is a positive side effect, but it should be made explicit. If a future developer adds an OPTIONS handler that returns `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` with credentials support, the entire CSRF defense for admin endpoints would collapse to just sameSite=strict.

### F-CSRF-7 (LOW) — Content-Type bypass theoretically possible, but blocked in practice
- File: /home/z/my-project/src/middleware.ts:159 (Origin check applies regardless of Content-Type)

Analysis: The middleware does NOT inspect Content-Type. A cross-site form with `enctype="text/plain"` can submit a body shaped like JSON (`{"username":"x","password":"y"}`) which `request.json()` will parse. However:
- For admin endpoints: Origin check fires (admin routes are NOT in PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES), so cross-site forms are blocked at the Origin check. SameSite=strict also blocks the cookie. Content-Type bypass is moot.
- For public endpoints (login, logout, chat, contact, track): no CSRF check applies regardless of Content-Type. Content-Type bypass is irrelevant.
- For preflightable Content-Types (application/json) on cross-origin fetch: preflight triggers, no ACA-* headers returned → blocked at preflight.

Net: Content-Type bypass is not exploitable as a CSRF today. The bypass becomes relevant only if sameSite=strict is weakened AND Origin check is removed. Defense-in-depth would require a custom-header check (e.g., `X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest`) which forces preflight.

### F-CSRF-8 (LOW) — Public POST endpoints (chat, contact, track) exempt from CSRF
- Files:
  - /home/z/my-project/src/middleware.ts:28,30,31,32 (`/api/user/login`, `/api/user/logout`, `/api/contact`, `/api/chat`, `/api/track` in PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES)
  - /home/z/my-project/src/app/api/contact/route.ts:34-190 (creates ContactMessage)
  - /home/z/my-project/src/app/api/chat/route.ts:64-215 (creates ChatSession + ChatMessage)
  - /home/z/my-project/src/app/api/track/route.ts:9-34 (creates PageView)

Analysis: These endpoints have no auth requirement (correctly — they're public services). However, they also have no CSRF check. A malicious page on attacker.com can submit forms to inject spam contact messages, fake chat sessions, or pollute page-view analytics. The mitigations:
- /api/contact: requires reCAPTCHA token (line 86-118) — blocks pure-form CSRF. Attacker would need a valid reCAPTCHA token, which requires user interaction with the reCAPTCHA widget on the attacker's page. Reasonable defense.
- /api/chat: rate-limited per IP at 8/min (route.ts:8-21), but X-Forwarded-For is trusted blindly (F-9) → rate limit bypassable. No reCAPTCHA. Spam injection possible.
- /api/track: NO rate limit at all, NO auth, NO Origin check. Trivial analytics pollution via `<img>`-tag-style auto-POST (no — POST needs form). But cross-site form auto-submit works.

PoC (chat spam injection):
```html
<form id="f" action="https://victim.example.com/api/chat" method="POST"
      enctype="text/plain">
  <input name='{"message":"spam","lang":"en","visitorId":"anon","x":"'
         value='ignored"}'>
</form>
<script>setInterval(() => f.submit(), 1000);</script>
```
Severity: LOW (spam/DoS only, no auth bypass).

### F-CSRF-9 (OK) — Webhook exemption correct
- Files:
  - /home/z/my-project/src/middleware.ts:33-34 (`/api/bale/webhook`, `/api/telegram/webhook` in PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES — exempted from Origin check, correct because webhooks are server-to-server and don't have browser Origin)
  - /home/z/my-project/src/app/api/bale/webhook/route.ts:16-49 (verifies `BALE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` via `crypto.timingSafeEqual` at line 27)
  - /home/z/my-project/src/app/api/telegram/webhook/route.ts:6-28 (verifies `TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` via `crypto.timingSafeEqual` at line 16)

Analysis: Both webhooks correctly rely on a shared secret (not cookies/Origin) because Bale/Telegram servers don't send cookies or browser-mediated Origin headers. The secret is checked with constant-time comparison. The exemption from CSRF is correct.

Caveat (already in prior audit as F-19): the secret is accepted via URL query string (`?secret=XXX`), which may leak in server logs, referrer headers, and browser history. This is a separate issue and out of scope for CSRF.

### F-CSRF-10 (LOW, re-affirms prior F-10/F-NEW-10) — Origin check bypassable by non-browser clients
- File: /home/z/my-project/src/middleware.ts:160-176

Code:
```ts
const origin = req.headers.get("origin");
const host = req.headers.get("host");
// Origin باید مطابق host باشه (همان-origin)
if (!origin || !host) {
  // reject
}
try {
  const originUrl = new URL(origin);
  if (originUrl.host !== host) {
    // reject
  }
} catch { /* reject */ }
```

Analysis: Both `Origin` and `Host` are HTTP headers. Browsers set them automatically and the attacker cannot tamper with them on browser-mediated requests. But scripts (curl, Python requests, Node fetch) can set both `Origin` and `Host` to any value. So:
- Browser-mediated CSRF: BLOCKED (Origin reflects actual script origin).
- Script-mediated CSRF (requires stolen cookie — scripts can't access victim's cookies): the Origin check is bypassable, but the cookie check still holds because scripts can't get the victim's cookie without an XSS.
- If the attacker has a stolen cookie (e.g., via XSS or exfiltration), they can forge both Origin and Host and the middleware will accept it. SameSite=strict doesn't help because the request includes the stolen cookie directly (not via browser-mediated cookie-sending).

Severity: LOW (browser-mediated CSRF is blocked; script-mediated attacks require prior cookie theft, which is a separate vulnerability).

### F-CSRF-11 (OK) — /api/messages correctly removed from PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES (F-20 closed)
- File: /home/z/my-project/src/middleware.ts:24-37 (verified: `/api/messages` NOT listed)
- File: /home/z/my-project/src/middleware.ts:188-193 (explicit session check for `/api/messages`)

The previous F-20 finding ("CSRF check skipped for /api/messages") is now closed for /api/messages. The route still appears in `checkAdminAuth` chain — Origin check fires for POST /api/messages, session cookie required, admin auth required.

Note: F-20 also mentioned `/api/chat` is still in PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES — RE-CONFIRMED here at line 32. The /api/chat exemption is by design (public chat) but has the spam-injection issue noted in F-CSRF-8.

### F-CSRF-12 (LOW) — Origin check missing on `null` Origin
- File: /home/z/my-project/src/middleware.ts:163

Code:
```ts
if (!origin || !host) {
  // reject
}
```

Analysis: The middleware rejects requests with NO Origin header (which is the correct behavior — same-origin browser POSTs always include Origin). However, some non-browser contexts (e.g., `<meta name="referrer" content="no-referrer">` doesn't affect Origin) and privacy-enhanced browsers may send `Origin: null`. The middleware currently treats `null` as a string and `new URL("null")` would throw → caught by the catch → rejected. So `Origin: null` is correctly rejected. Not exploitable.

But: privacy-preserving browser modes (Tor, Safari ITP with strict privacy) sometimes send `Origin: null` for same-origin requests too. This means legitimate same-origin POSTs from these browsers would be rejected. Operational impact, not a security issue.

## Verified-Correct Items (defense holds)

- ✅ All admin POST/PUT/DELETE routes consistently call `checkAdminAuth` or `checkAdminSession` (15+ routes verified).
- ✅ `/api/messages` correctly removed from `PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES` (F-20 closed for messages).
- ✅ Webhook exemptions are correct: server-to-server endpoints use shared-secret HMAC verification, not cookies/Origin.
- ✅ Origin check correctly rejects missing/invalid Origin via try/catch.
- ✅ SameSite=strict cookie blocks browser-mediated CSRF for all admin endpoints (provided cookie isn't stolen — F-6/F-NEW-5 remain).
- ✅ No state-changing GET in admin routes — all admin GETs are pure reads.
- ✅ `form-action 'self'` in CSP (middleware.ts:130) restricts form submissions to same-origin + formsubmit.co (defense-in-depth for native form posts, but doesn't apply to fetch/XHR-based CSRF).

## Fix-Priority Order (advisory only — DO NOT APPLY per task instructions)

1. F-CSRF-1 — Add Origin check (or CSRF token) to /api/user/login to prevent login CSRF. MED.
2. F-CSRF-4 — Add per-session CSRF token (synchronizer pattern) or Sec-Fetch-Site check in middleware for defense-in-depth. MED.
3. F-CSRF-2 — Remove /api/user/logout from PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES OR add Origin check. LOW.
4. F-CSRF-8 — Add Origin check to /api/chat and /api/track (reCAPTCHA already covers /api/contact). LOW.
5. F-CSRF-5 — Convert /api/user/verify GET log write to a POST, or skip the log on GET. LOW.
6. F-CSRF-6 — Add explicit OPTIONS handler that returns 204 with security headers (or 405), to make CORS posture explicit. INFO.
7. F-CSRF-7 — Add custom-header check (X-Requested-With) to force CORS preflight on state-changing endpoints. LOW (defense-in-depth).

   low real-world exploitability but HIGH per advisory.
   Severity: HIGH (per advisory), LOW (per exploitability).

2. Pinned (no ^ or ~)?
   ❌ NO — every single declared dependency uses a caret (`^`) range.
   - dependencies: ALL six use `^`
   - devDependencies: ALL six use `^` (3 of them only major: `^4`, `^4`, `^5`)
   This means `bun install` / `npm install` on a fresh clone silently floats
   to the latest minor/patch. Already observed drift:
     - declared `next ^16.1.1`  → resolved `16.3.6` (3 minors ahead)
     - declared `prisma ^6.11.1` → resolved `6.19.3` (8 minors ahead)
     - declared `react ^19.0.0` → resolved `19.3.0` (3 minors ahead)
   The lockfile (bun.lock) DOES pin resolved versions for installed
   machines, but the declared ranges invite supply-chain drift on any
   `bun update` or fresh install without lockfile. Recommend:
     - Add `.npmrc` with `save-exact=true`
     - Re-write package.json with exact versions (drop `^`)
   Severity: MEDIUM (hygiene / supply-chain).

5. bcryptjs version safe?
   ✅ YES (with caveats).
   - Declared `^3.0.3`, resolved `3.0.3`.
   - Historical bcryptjs vuln (password truncation > 72 bytes allowing
     prefix collisions, fixed in 2.4.3) is NOT present in 3.x.
   - `bun audit` reports no advisory for bcryptjs@3.0.3.
   Caveats:
     (a) Not pinned — `^3.0.3` allows floating to 3.1.x+ silently.
     (b) bcryptjs is pure-JavaScript (no native binding) — ~3× slower
         than node-bcrypt. Under high auth volume this becomes a CPU
         DoS amplification (single bcrypt.compare ≈ 100ms with rounds=10,
         per src/lib/access-auth.ts). Combined with F-5 (no rate limit
         on /api/admin/*) and F-9 (X-Forwarded-For bypass), an attacker
         can saturate the event loop with bcrypt work. Not a CVE but
         an operational concern.
   Severity: LOW (informational).

12. Is sharp actually used (installed but unused)?
    ❌ NO — sharp is installed but UNUSED by application code.
    - `sharp@0.35.4` is installed in node_modules/ (with 19 platform
      binaries: @img/sharp-darwin-arm64, @img/sharp-linux-x64, etc.).
    - It is NOT declared in package.json dependencies or devDependencies.
    - It is declared in package-lock.json:1789 as `"sharp": "^0.35.4"`
      inside `next`'s `optionalDependencies` block (lines 1781-1790):
        "optionalDependencies": {
          "@next/swc-darwin-arm64": "16.3.6",
          ...
          "sharp": "^0.35.4"
        }
      ⇒ sharp is auto-installed as a transitive optional dep of Next.js
        (Next uses it for `next/image` server-side optimization).
    - Application code NEVER imports sharp:
        grep -rn "from ['\"]sharp['\"]" src/      → 0 matches
        grep -rn "require\(['\"]sharp['\"]\)" src/ → 0 matches
    - Application code NEVER uses `next/image`:
        grep -rn "next/image\|<Image" src/ → 2 matches, both in
        src/middleware.ts as a regex pattern string (excluding
        `_next/image` from middleware matching), NOT actual imports.
    - The project uses plain <img> tags (eslint rule
      `@next/next/no-img-element` is disabled in eslint.config.mjs)
      and serves static images from /public directly.
    ⇒ sharp wastes ~25 MB of platform binaries (one per OS/arch
      combo) with zero usage. Harmless at runtime, but bloats the
      Docker image and install time.
    Recommendation: set `images: { unoptimized: true }` in
    next.config.ts and override sharp to a no-op in package.json:
      "overrides": { "sharp": "npm:noop@1.0.0" }
    OR simply accept the bloat (sharp's install is conditional on
    platform and bun/npm will skip if unneeded).
    Severity: LOW (hygiene / image-size).

Weak spots:

    `await res.json()` without type checking (see §10).

Build passes and `tsc --noEmit` is clean against the current tsconfig, so
the project SHIPS without TypeScript errors. However, the type-safety
surface is much weaker than it appears:

  • ESLint is broken (missing dependency) and would be near-useless even if
    installed, because 18 critical rules are disabled in eslint.config.mjs.
  • The 36 unused locals/params/imports are NOT visible without
    `--noUnusedLocals --noUnusedParameters`, so they have accumulated
    silently (5 dead component imports in src/app/page.tsx alone).
  • 53 `any`-typed symbols and 4 `as any` casts defeat type-checking at
    every fetch boundary and every map callback.
  • 0 of 31 API routes declare a return type, so callers in components
    have no compile-time contract on the response shape.
  • Schema/frontend drift is unguarded — components redeclare Prisma
    model shapes manually.

================================================================================
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
================================================================================
- Rate limiting exists at TWO layers (middleware + per-route) for login/contact/chat,
  but ALL of it can be bypassed by spoofing the X-Forwarded-For header.
- Admin API, webhooks, /api/track, /api/chat/messages have ZERO rate limit.
- 1 MB body-size check uses the Content-Length header (bypassable via chunked TE).
- 3 of 4 in-memory rate-limit Maps are NEVER garbage-collected → slow memory leak.
- Several unbounded DB queries and unbounded writes (public /api/track, public
  /api/chat/messages, /api/chat POST session-message load).
- No request timeouts anywhere; LLM / reCAPTCHA / formsubmit fetches can hang.
- bcrypt.compare() is called only when username exists → user enumeration via timing.

Q1. Login brute-force protection (5/15min) — works?
================================================================================
Status: PARTIALLY WORKS — two layers stacked, both bypassable via XFF.
Severity: HIGH (combined with Q8 spoofing → CRITICAL for brute-force).

  File: src/middleware.ts:21
    const RATE_LIMIT_PATHS = ["/api/user/login", "/api/contact", "/api/chat"];
  File: src/middleware.ts:144-155
    if (RATE_LIMIT_PATHS.includes(pathname)) {
      const ip = req.headers.get("x-forwarded-for")?.split(",")[0]?.trim() ||
                 req.headers.get("x-real-ip") || "unknown";
      const max = pathname === "/api/user/login" ? 5 : 8;
      if (!checkRateLimit(`${pathname}:${ip}`, max)) { ... 429 ... }
    }
  File: src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:20-34   (second layer)
    const RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW = 15 * 60 * 1000; const RATE_LIMIT_MAX = 5;
    const loginAttempts = new Map<string, { count, resetAt }>();
    function checkRateLimit(ip: string): boolean { ... }

PoC (bypass): curl with rotating XFF — each request lands on a fresh key:
    for i in $(seq 1 100); do
      curl -X POST https://target/api/user/login \
        -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
        -H "X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.$i" \
        -d '{"username":"admin","password":"guess'$i'"}'
    done
  → 100 attempts in 1 second, never trips either limiter.

Also note: middleware key includes pathname (`${pathname}:${ip}`), route's key
is just ip. They are independent Maps — they don't share state. Two layers but
they don't compose into a stricter limit; the more lenient one applies if XFF
is fixed (5 in 15 min — works), but both share the same XFF-bypass hole.

PoC (CPU/resource DoS even when rate limit holds):

  (src/app/api/contact/route.ts:96-103) on EVERY accepted request before the
  body is even validated. With 3 XFF-rotated IPs in 10 min you can trigger
  3 reCAPTCHA verification calls per IP, but at scale (botnet) you can DoS
  Google reCAPTCHA quota AND trigger an outbound `formsubmit.co` fetch
  (route.ts:163) for each saved message. Both fetches have NO timeout
  (see Q12) — they can be made to hang and tie up the connection pool.

    getSessionFromRequest (parse cookie, HMAC-verify) → db.accessUser.findUnique

  SQLite (file lock contention) will eventually serialize and degrade.
  No 429 returned, no IP block (the middleware ip-block in
  src/lib/security.ts:27-57 is NOT consulted by middleware before admin auth).

  (src/lib/access-auth.ts:91) so the timing-attack surface on the cookie
  itself is OK. The issue is the absence of any failed-attempt throttle.

  File: src/middleware.ts:24-37              webhooks are in PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES
                                             (no CSRF check, no session check)

Secret compared with crypto.timingSafeEqual — good. But:
  - No rate limit on failed-secret responses (403).
  - Each request still parses the JSON body before the secret check returns
    NO — actually secret check happens BEFORE body parse (route.ts:19-29),
    but middleware's body-size check at middleware.ts:196-205 still runs and
    uses Content-Length only (see Q6).
  - timingSafeEqual is short-circuited by length mismatch
    (route.ts:27: `if (secretBuf.length !== expBuf.length || ...)`) — this
    leaks whether the length matches. Minor; acceptable in practice.

PoC: HTTP brute-force the webhook secret (if it's a short/weak secret):
    for s in $(wordlist); do
      curl -X POST "https://target/api/bale/webhook?secret=$s" -d '{}'
    done
  No 429 ever returned. Timing-safe compare means no per-byte timing leak,
  but no rate-limit hedge either.

================================================================================
Q6. Body size limit 1MB — actually enforced?
================================================================================
Status: PARTIALLY — bypassable via chunked transfer encoding.
Severity: HIGH.

  File: src/middleware.ts:196-205
    if (method === "POST" || method === "PUT" || method === "PATCH") {
      const contentLength = parseInt(req.headers.get("content-length") || "0", 10);
      if (contentLength > 1024 * 1024) {
        return NextResponse.json({ ok:false, error:"payload_too_large" }, {status:413});
      }
    }

Defects:
  (a) Header-only check. Attacker sends chunked transfer encoding
      (no Content-Length) → middleware passes → req.json() (undici/Next.js)
      reads up to its default limit (~4 MB for App Router, no .json() body
      size cap by default on `Request.json()`).
  (b) Method coverage incomplete. DELETE handlers also read JSON body:
        src/app/api/admin/clips/route.ts:82  `const body = await req.json();`
      middleware never checks DELETE bodies (line 196 whitelist).
  (c) GET handlers reading query strings are not bounded at all (low-risk
      because query strings have their own server limits).
  (d) No Next.js-level bodyParser.sizeLimit override in next.config.ts
      (file has only `output`, `poweredByHeader`, `typescript`,
      `reactStrictMode`, `headers`, `outputFileTracingIncludes`).

PoC (bypass via chunked):
    curl -X POST https://target/api/chat \
      -H "Transfer-Encoding: chunked" \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      --data-binary @5mb-payload.json
  → middleware sees content-length=null/0 → passes → req.json() reads the
  full 5 MB → JSON.parse runs synchronously on the event loop → CPU spike,
  potential OOM if many concurrent.

Q7. In-memory rate limit Maps — cleaned periodically?
================================================================================
Status: PARTIALLY — 1 of 4 Maps cleaned.
Severity: MEDIUM (slow memory leak → eventual OOM under sustained traffic).

  ✅ src/middleware.ts:42        rateLimitMap
       src/middleware.ts:58-65   setInterval every 5 min, .unref() called,
                                 deletes expired entries.
  ❌ src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:22   loginAttempts
       NO setInterval. Entries persist until the same IP hits again
       with an expired resetAt (then overwritten). IPs that never return

  ❌ src/app/api/contact/route.ts:8      hits (number[] per IP)
       NO setInterval. Same accumulation pattern. Worse: each entry is

  ❌ src/app/api/chat/route.ts:9          hits (number[] per IP)
       Same as contact.

PoC (memory exhaustion):
  Attacker rotates XFF across 10M spoofed IPs, one request each → 10M Map
  entries with stale resetAt/numbers arrays. Each entry ~100 bytes → ~1 GB

  (loginAttempts Map uses object values {count,resetAt} so ~80 B per entry;
   contact/chat Maps use number[] which is larger.)

Q8. X-Forwarded-For spoofing bypass rate limit?
================================================================================
Status: YES — CRITICAL bypass on every IP-based control in the app.
Severity: CRITICAL.

  Trust chain (all read the FIRST comma-separated value of XFF, which the
  client can set arbitrarily):
    src/middleware.ts:145-146         (rate-limit key for login/contact/chat)
    src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:46 → getClientIp() in access-auth.ts
    src/lib/access-auth.ts:175-181   (login, security POST, verify, etc.)
    src/app/api/contact/route.ts:37-39
    src/app/api/chat/route.ts:66-69
    src/app/api/track/route.ts:12

  Proxy config that should sanitize but doesn't:
    nginx-ehsanmorad.conf:24  proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For
                                         $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
      ↑ $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for APPENDS the real client IP to whatever
        the client already sent — does NOT replace. So if client sends
        `X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4`, nginx forwards `1.2.3.4, <real-ip>`.
        The app then takes `1.2.3.4` (split[0]) as the trusted source.
    Caddyfile (no XFF rewrite) — passes whatever client sent.
    docker-compose.yml: NODE_ENV=development — also doesn't sanitize.

  There is no Trusted-Proxy allow-list anywhere in the codebase.

PoC: identical to Q1 PoC — every rate-limit and every IP-based block
(src/lib/security.ts:8 isIpBlocked) can be sidestepped by rotating XFF.
isIpBlocked is NEVER consulted by middleware before rate-limiting or
auth-checking anyway — it's only consulted by recordSuspiciousActivity
which is itself only called from /api/contact (not from login/chat).

================================================================================
Q9. Expensive sync operations (bcrypt in hot path)?
================================================================================
Status: YES — bcrypt.compare() on every login attempt; user enumeration
        via timing; CPU DoS via parallel logins.
Severity: HIGH.

  File: src/lib/access-auth.ts:50-52  hashPassword — bcrypt.genSalt(10) + hash
  File: src/lib/access-auth.ts:58-60  verifyPassword — bcrypt.compare()
        saltRounds = 10 → ~50–100 ms CPU per call (libuv threadpool, default
        size 4 → 4 concurrent bcrypts saturate the pool).
  File: src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:58-66
    const user = await db.accessUser.findUnique({ where: { username } });
    if (!user) return 401;             // ← returns IMMEDIATELY, no bcrypt
    const passwordOk = await verifyPassword(password, user.passwordHash);
    if (!passwordOk) return 401;

Defect A — user enumeration via timing:
  Existing username → 50–100 ms (bcrypt runs).
  Non-existing username → <1 ms (early return).
  Attacker measures response time per username → enumerates valid usernames.
  Mitigation that should be present: always run bcrypt against a dummy hash
  when user is missing, so timing is constant.

Defect B — CPU DoS via parallel login attempts:
  Combined with Q1 (XFF bypass) + Q8: an attacker can fire many concurrent
  login attempts for an existing username. Each attempt hogs a libuv thread
  for ~100 ms. With default UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=4, ~40 req/s of CPU-bound
  work saturates the pool and slows the entire Node process (including
  unrelated requests — DB queries, static API routes, etc.).
  PoC:
    for i in $(seq 1 100); do
      curl .../api/user/login -H "X-Forwarded-For: $RANDOM.$RANDOM.$RANDOM.$RANDOM" \
        -d '{"username":"admin","password":"x'$i'"}' &
    done; wait
  No 429 (rate-limit bypassed by XFF). UV threadpool saturated for ~10 s.

Other CPU-heavy operations in hot path:
  - JSON.parse of every request body — bounded by Q6 if it held, but Q6 is
    bypassable.
  - db.accessUser.findUnique on every admin/* request (Q4 amplification).

Q11. Can attacker crash Node via huge body?
================================================================================
Status: POTENTIAL — needs Q6 bypass; combined attack is realistic.
Severity: HIGH.

  Chain:
    1. Bypass Q6 1 MB check via chunked transfer encoding (no Content-Length).
    2. Hit any route that does `await req.json()` and JSON.parses the body:
       - src/app/api/contact/route.ts:57       (public, but rate-limited —
                                                  XFF bypass restores the
                                                  attack)
       - src/app/api/chat/route.ts:79           (same)
       - src/app/api/track/route.ts:11         (public, NO rate limit)
       - src/app/api/admin/clips/route.ts:82   (DELETE body — not covered
                                                  by middleware size check)
       - src/app/api/admin/* POSTs (auth-gated but Q4 has no rate limit)
    3. `req.json()` calls `JSON.parse` synchronously on the event loop.
       A 50 MB malformed JSON string ≈ seconds of single-threaded CPU,
       blocking every other request. Concurrent attackers (or one with
       many sockets) can pin the event loop indefinitely.

  Secondary crash vector — OOM via Q7 (Map growth) + Q10 (DB growth):
    - Rate-limit Maps grow with XFF rotation (Q7).
    - /api/track inserts DB rows unbounded (Q10).
    - /api/chat/messages dumps unbounded rows into a single response.
    Heap memory grows → V8 OOM → process killed by kernel or `--max-old-
    space-size` abort.

================================================================================
Q12. Is there a request timeout?
================================================================================
Status: NONE — no per-request timeout anywhere.
Severity: HIGH (slow-loris-style amplification; hung outbound fetches).

  - No `export const maxDuration` on any route (grep found none).
  - No `AbortController` / `AbortSignal` passed to any fetch call (grep
    found only client-side setTimeout in components, none server-side).
  - No `next.config.ts` server-actions timeout config.

  Specific unbounded outbound fetches (every one can hang the request and
  consume a connection slot indefinitely):
    src/lib/providers.ts:100-112   callOpenAI       — fetch OpenAI, no timeout
    src/lib/providers.ts:127-140    callAnthropic    — fetch Claude, no timeout
    src/lib/providers.ts:152-160    callOllama       — fetch local, no timeout
    src/lib/providers.ts:172-184    callGroq         — fetch Groq, no timeout
    src/app/api/contact/route.ts:96-103  fetch reCAPTCHA siteverify, no timeout
    src/app/api/contact/route.ts:163      fetch formsubmit.co, no timeout
    src/app/api/admin/email/route.ts:75   fetch formsubmit.co, no timeout
    src/lib/bale.ts:49                    sendBaleMessage → fetch Bale, no timeout
    src/lib/telegram.ts                  (sendTelegramMessage, similar pattern)

  Inbound: no Next.js route handler enforces a deadline. A slow LLM
  provider can keep a single request open for the platform's default
  (Next.js standalone on Node has NO default request timeout — request
  lives as long as the handler runs).

  PoC (connection-pool exhaustion):
    - Configure an AI provider pointing at a slow/hanging endpoint
      (e.g., a tcp listener that accepts but never responds).
    - Hit /api/chat 8 times (within rate limit) — all 8 requests hang
      forever. Subsequent /api/chat calls also hang. Node's default
      agent maxSockets (Infinity per host) means no socket reuse limit,
      but file-descriptor limit (default 1024) is reached quickly.
    - Process keeps running but is functionally dead for /api/chat.

#3 — DB file path secure — PARTIAL PASS — MEDIUM
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
GOOD:
- install.sh:95 — `chmod 700 db` (before any DB writes)
- install.sh:128 — `chmod 700 db` (re-affirmed after chown)

GAPS:
(a) src/lib/db.ts:6 — `const dbPath = path.join(process.cwd(), 'db', 'custom.db')`
    - Hardcodes path relative to `process.cwd()`. In Next.js standalone mode
      (`node .next/standalone/server.js`), `process.cwd()` is the directory from
      which `node` was invoked, NOT necessarily SITE_DIR.
    - If systemd `WorkingDirectory=` is misconfigured (e.g., `/`), the app will
      silently create/use a NEW empty database at `/db/custom.db` instead of the
      seeded `$SITE_DIR/db/custom.db`. This is a "data-loss silent failure"
      pattern, not a security vuln per se, but it causes auth bypass (empty
      AccessUser table → no admin → if checkAdminAuth falls back to password,
      default admin/admin123 from #7 may be re-seeded → fresh compromise).
    - OVERRIDES `DATABASE_URL` from env (prisma/schema.prisma:13 declares
      `url = env("DATABASE_URL")` but db.ts:14-20 overrides the datasource
      URL with `file:${dbPath}`). The `.env` file's `DATABASE_URL` is dead
      at runtime — two sources of truth, the hardcoded one wins.
    - Not a path-traversal/injection vuln (process.cwd() is server-controlled).

(b) No `umask 077` at top of install.sh — verified (grep `umask` in install.sh and
    docker-entrypoint.sh returned no matches). Means SQLite-created sidecar files
    (`db/custom.db-wal`, `db/custom.db-shm`, `db/custom.db-journal`) inherit the
    process umask (typically 022 → world-readable). install.sh:131 removes stale
    sidecars before first run but does NOT prevent SQLite from recreating them
    with default perms at runtime. WAL file contains committed transaction data
    (including plaintext API keys / bot tokens per #2) → world-readable.

(c) docker-entrypoint.sh:20 — `touch /app/db/custom.db` — no explicit `chmod`
    after touch (verified: no `chmod` line follows in docker-entrypoint.sh).
    Container inherits umask.

(d) scripts/list_messages.py:5 — `DB = Path("/home/z/my-project/db/custom.db")`
    Hardcoded dev-machine absolute path (also noted in worklog line 13159, 13220).

SEVERITY: MEDIUM (gaps in WAL/SHM perms + brittle cwd-based path resolution).

- All DB access uses Prisma's typed/parameterized API (findMany, findUnique,

- src/lib/db.ts:1-22 — standard PrismaClient singleton pattern with globalThis
  caching; no raw SQL anywhere.
- scripts/seed_access_users.py:91, 104 — uses Python sqlite3 with `?` parameter
  placeholders (`cur.execute("SELECT ... WHERE username = ?", ("admin",))`).
  Parameterized, no injection.
- ONLY caveat: scripts/reset-admin-password.sh:50 —
  `sqlite3 db/custom.db "UPDATE AccessUser SET passwordHash = '$HASH', ..."`
  Bash string interpolation of `$HASH` into SQL. Bcrypt hashes (`$2a$10$...`)
  contain no `'` characters so it's safe IN PRACTICE, but the pattern is
  SQL-injection-shaped if the hash function ever changes. Already noted as
  F-22 in worklog. This is a shell script, not Prisma — out of audit scope
  for "Prisma client init" but flagged for completeness.

VERDICT: No Prisma-level SQL injection risk.

#9 — Transactions for multi-step operations — FAIL — MEDIUM
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
- grep for `$transaction` across /home/z/my-project/src → NO MATCHES. Verified.
  Zero Prisma transactions in the entire codebase.

Multi-step operations performed WITHOUT transactional integrity:

(a) src/app/api/admin/clear/route.ts:43-46 — destructive cascade done manually:
      await db.messageReply.deleteMany({ where: { messageId: id } });
      await db.messageNote.deleteMany({ where: { messageId: id } });
      await db.messageTagRelation.deleteMany({ where: { messageId: id } });
      await db.contactMessage.delete({ where: { id } });
    Schema declares `onDelete: Cascade` on these relations (schema.prisma:83,
    125, 137), so the manual deleteMany is redundant AND non-transactional.
    If `contactMessage.delete` fails (e.g., race with another request), the
    child rows are already deleted → orphaned/inconsistent state.
    Same pattern at lines 28-29 (chatMessage → chatSession) and 35-36 (bulk).

(b) src/app/api/admin/settings/route.ts:45-49 — setSetting three keys via
    Promise.all (parallel, NOT transactional). If `telegramBotToken` save
    succeeds but `telegramEnabled` save fails, the bot is enabled with a stale
    token (or vice versa).
    Same pattern at lines 75-81 (bulk settings update).

(c) src/app/api/admin/chat-reply/route.ts:42-46 — create message + update
    session.updatedAt. If session.update fails, the ChatMessage is orphaned
    (still queryable via sessionId but session.updatedAt is stale → frontend
    "latest message" sort may break).

(d) TOCTOU race on every "toggle" pattern (read-then-write without transaction):
    - src/app/api/admin/providers/route.ts:111-118 (findUnique → update enabled).
    - src/app/api/admin/themes/route.ts:93-99 (findUnique → update visible).
    - src/app/api/admin/nav/route.ts:58-60 (findUnique → update visible).
    - src/app/api/admin/equipment/route.ts:78-81 (findUnique → update visible).
    Two concurrent toggle requests can both read `enabled=true`, both write
    `enabled=false`, leaving the row disabled when the user expected enabled.

(e) src/lib/providers.ts:202-248 — `seedDefaultProviders()` loops over 4 providers
    with sequential `db.aiProvider.create()` calls (line 246). If the loop fails
    midway (DB error, disk full), partial providers exist with priority gaps.

SEVERITY: MEDIUM (data-integrity / consistency risk; no direct security exploit,
but corrupts state under concurrent access or partial failure).

LOW  | No circuit breaker                                  | If upstream is down, every request still hits it. No backoff.

QUESTION-BY-QUESTION VERDICT
================================================================================

■ Q1. Is personal.css complete and beautiful?
  Verdict: ⚠️ MOSTLY COMPLETE, but contains bugs and inconsistencies.
  Complete coverage:
    - 3,478 lines covering: layout, hero, terminal, about, skills, books,
      articles, tutorials, contact, footer, admin modal, RF elements
      (oscilloscope, smith chart, signal bars, wave divider, chat,
      admin tabs/reply/settings, theme switcher, signal lab, lab
      visualizer, equipment rack, spectrum analyzer), 7 color themes
      (terminal default + clean + midnight + amber + cyan + purple +
      solar), 5 font selectors (vazirmatn/inter/lora/fira-code/geist-mono),
      user-dashboard layout (shell/container/header/tabs/info-cards/
      messages/reply/empty-state), settings panel (cards/inputs/toast/
      providers), RTL adjustments, a11y (focus-visible, sr-only, reduced
      motion), responsive breakpoints (480/600/720/768/900 px).
  Beauty strengths:
    - Coherent green-on-black palette with 3-tier text contrast
      (--text/--text-dim/--text-faint).
    - Terminal aesthetic preserved via $ / // / > / ## / ./ prefixes on
      labels, hero-title text-shadow glow, CRT scanline overlay.
    - Theme variants are well-tuned (each has matching shadow-glow,
      scanlines flag, semantic color mapping).
    - Logical-properties usage in dashboard (margin-inline-start,
      border-inline-start) for RTL friendliness — lines 2805, 3377, 3396.
  Beauty weaknesses (see TOP-10 below):
    - Undefined `--font-vazir` referenced 24× — falls back to `monospace`.
    - Duplicate `@keyframes blink` (line 385 vs 3336) — second overrides
      first; terminal cursor and loading cursor have different rhythms.
    - Hardcoded border-radius values 1/4/6/8/10/12 px scattered (no token).
    - No spacing scale (4/6/8/10/12/14/16/20/24/40/80 used ad-hoc).
    - No real loading skeleton class — only text + blink cursor.
    - `text-transform: uppercase` applied to Persian labels in
      `.dashboard-title`, `.dashboard-tab`, `.settings-card-title`,
      `.settings-label` — Persian has no uppercase; visually ignored
      but indicates design assumed Latin script.

■ Q2. Does user-dashboard/page.tsx use CSS classes (not inline styles)?
  Verdict: ⚠️ ALMOST — 1 inline style remains.
  Total inline `style={{}}` count in file: 1.
  - Line 438: `<div className="dashboard-access-warning" role="alert"
      style={{ background: "rgba(255,0,64,0.1)", borderColor:
      "var(--red)", color: "var(--red)" }}>Error: {error}</div>`
  Should be replaced with a dedicated `.dashboard-error` class
  (variant of `.dashboard-access-warning` with red palette).
  Everything else uses semantic class names:
    - `.dashboard-shell`, `.dashboard-container`, `.dashboard-header`,
      `.dashboard-title`, `.dashboard-subtitle`, `.dashboard-actions`,
      `.dashboard-btn`, `.dashboard-btn.danger`, `.dashboard-select`,
      `.dashboard-access-warning`, `.dashboard-tabs`, `.dashboard-tab`,
      `.dashboard-tab.active`, `.dashboard-content`, `.dashboard-help-box`,
      `.dashboard-info-grid`, `.dashboard-info-card`, `.dashboard-info-label`,
      `.dashboard-info-value`, `.dashboard-loading`, `.dashboard-messages-list`,
      `.dashboard-message-card`, `.dashboard-message-header`,
      `.dashboard-message-name`, `.dashboard-message-email`,
      `.dashboard-message-date`, `.dashboard-message-text`,
      `.dashboard-message-replies`, `.dashboard-message-reply-text`,
      `.dashboard-message-actions`, `.dashboard-reply-form`,
      `.dashboard-reply-textarea`, `.dashboard-empty-state`.
  Aria: `role="tablist"`, `role="tab"`, `aria-selected`, `role="alert"`,
  `aria-live="polite"` on loading screen — a11y is solid.

■ Q3. Is SettingsPanel.tsx beautiful?
  Verdict: ✅ MOST BEAUTIFUL — best of the 4 components.
  Strengths:
    - Zero inline styles (verified via grep).
    - Uses semantic classes consistently (settings-root, settings-card,
      settings-card-title, settings-field, settings-label, settings-input,
      settings-select, settings-btn, settings-btn-small, settings-btn-icon,
      settings-checkbox-row, settings-checkbox-label, settings-hint,
      settings-toast, settings-providers-list, settings-provider-item,
      settings-provider-info, settings-provider-status, settings-empty,
      settings-provider-editor, settings-actions, settings-help-card,
      settings-help-list).
    - Per-field `dir="ltr"` on technical inputs (token, chat ID, email)
      and `dir="rtl"` on Persian name inputs — correct for mixed-script.
    - Loading state via `.settings-loading` (centered text).
    - Toast via `.settings-toast` with success/error variants.
    - Help section visually de-emphasized (`.settings-help-card`).
    - Password show/hide via icon button (👁/🙈).
  Weaknesses:
    - Toast `position: sticky; top: 0` scrolls out of view in long lists.
    - `message.startsWith("✅")` for success detection (line 568) — brittle.
    - No per-action loading spinner on Save buttons (FEAT-01-L1).
    - "No providers configured." (line 845), "Disable"/"Enable" (833),
      "Edit"/"New Provider" (867) — hardcoded English, not localized
      (FEAT-01-U1/U2/U3, already logged).

■ Q4. Is ContentManager.tsx beautiful?
  Verdict: ❌ NO — 17 inline `style={{}}` blocks; reuses public-site
  classes (admin-reply-box, admin-message, admin-tabs) instead of
  dedicated content-manager classes.
  Issues:
    - Line 193: `<div style={{ display: "flex", gap: 8, marginBottom: 16,
      flexWrap: "wrap" }}>` — should be `.content-manager-toolbar`.
    - Line 196: `<span style={{ color: "var(--text-dim)", fontSize:

    - Line 200: `<div className="admin-reply-box" style={{ marginBottom: 16 }}>`
      — overrides class margin inline.
    - Line 204: textarea inline style duplicates `.settings-input`
      aesthetics but with different padding/font-size.
    - Lines 211, 216, 219, 221, 223, 227, 235, 237, 246, 253, 256: every
      label, input, textarea, button-group uses inline styles.
    - Line 256: delete button overrides `.btn-ghost` color to `var(--red)`
      via inline style — should be `.btn-danger`.
    - No empty-state class; uses `<p style={{...}}>No items yet.</p>`.
    - No toast; uses native `alert()` / `confirm()` (lines 84, 107, 116,
      119) — breaks terminal aesthetic.
    - `confirm("Delete?")` is English-only (no `lang` parameter respected).
    - Active "type tab" underline animation defined (`.admin-tab.active`)
      is reused — good. But the `.content-manager-type-tab` class defined
      in CSS (lines 2490-2513) is NEVER USED by ContentManager.tsx.
    - Tabs use Object.keys(typeLabels) iteration order — equipment is
      last; no icon for each type, just text labels.
    - Bulk-import textarea has no JSON syntax help, no example, no

■ Q5. Is AccessUserManager.tsx beautiful?
  Verdict: ❌ NO — 49 inline `style={{}}` blocks; 4 module-level style
  constants (labelStyle, inputStyle, thStyle, tdStyle) defined as JS
  objects; uses undefined CSS variables.
  Critical bugs (will render incorrectly):
    - `var(--primary)` referenced 4× (lines 237, 275, 454, 548 implicit
      via labelStyle textTransform... actually labelStyle uses
      `var(--text-dim)` — OK). Actual --primary refs: lines 237, 275,
      454 in h3 headings.
    - `var(--primary-bright)` referenced 3× (lines 255, 468, 548 input
      color, 572 action color).
    - `var(--bg-panel2)` referenced 2× (lines 243, 477 in `<tr>` bg).
    - NONE of these variables are defined in personal.css. The correct
      names are `--green` / `--green-bright` / `--bg-panel-2`. Result:
      all h3 headings inherit the body text color (off-green #c8ffc8,
      not bright #39ff14), inputs render in default text color, and the
      table header rows have transparent background.
    - `<tr style={{ background: "var(--bg-panel2)" }}>` (line 243, 477)
      — `var(--bg-panel2)` is undefined → background is `transparent`,
      making the sticky table header overlap scroll content with no
      contrast.
  Other issues:
    - Uses native `confirm()` (line 201) and `alert()` (lines 213, 216)
      for delete confirmation and errors.
    - Day-picker buttons use `.signal-waveform-btn` class (defined for
      oscilloscope waveform selection) — semantically wrong; visual
      style is for a 4-column waveform grid, not a 7-day picker.
    - Permission-picker buttons also use `.signal-waveform-btn` —
      same wrong-class issue.
    - Table has 9 columns at fontSize: 11px — overflows on tablet;
      the `overflowX: auto` wrapper helps but rows are cramped.
    - No empty-state illustration; just `<td colSpan={9}>هیچ کاربری
      وجود ندارد...</td>` (line 525).
    - No toast; errors shown as red box (line 282-284, 464-466) that
      is never auto-cleared.
    - Logs view (lines 233-268): table with sticky thead, but column
      widths not constrained; "Details" column can be very long
      (log.details), no truncation.
    - Edit/New form has no `<form>` semantic structure on outer div
      (it does use `<form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>` at line 287 — good).
    - RTL: `textAlign: "right"` on Users table thead (line 477) is
      hardcoded; doesn't flip with `dir`. Should be `textAlign: "start"`.

■ Q6. Is ThemeBuilder.tsx beautiful?
  Verdict: ❌ NO — 38 inline `style={{}}` blocks; no dedicated CSS
  classes at all (grep finds 0 `.theme-builder-*` rules in personal.css).
  Issues:
    - Editor grid (line 136-140): `gridTemplateColumns: "1fr 1fr"` with
      no `@media (max-width: 720px)` breakpoint — on mobile, color inputs
      and live preview are squished side-by-side, unusable.
    - Color picker row (line 155): fixed `width: 80` for label — long
      labels like "Primary Bright" overflow and clip.
    - Live preview container (line 195-198) has NO `position: relative`;
      the scanlines overlay (line 199-203) uses `position: absolute;
      inset: 0` — overlay escapes the preview box and covers the entire
      admin panel. Confirmed bug.
    - Theme card grid (line 245): `grid-template-columns:
      repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr))` — fine, but cards use
      inline `border`/`padding`/`background` instead of a class.
    - Color dot row (line 270-273): tiny 12px squares with no tooltip;
      user can't tell which color is which without opening the editor.
    - Action buttons (lines 277-288): inline `fontSize: "0.68rem",
      padding: "3px 6px"` — smaller than `.btn-sm` standard.
    - No empty-state class; uses `<p style={{...}}>No custom themes
      yet...</p>` (line 241).
    - No toast; uses native `confirm("Delete this theme?")` (line 102).
    - The "name" input (line 147) has no validation; the same name can
      be used twice.
    - No "duplicate theme" action — admin must recreate from scratch.
    - No way to set a theme as the site default from this panel;
      the admin must manually edit `localStorage` or use a different
      mechanism.
    - COLOR_FIELDS array (line 42) lists 15 colors but no grouping
      (Background / Primary / Text / Border / Status) — flat list is
      hard to scan.

■ Q7. Color consistency (green-on-black terminal theme)
  Verdict: ⚠️ INCONSISTENT in admin area.
  Public site (hero, sections, cards): ✅ consistent green-on-black.
  Admin panel:
    - Dashboard (user-dashboard/page.tsx + .dashboard-* classes): ✅
      uses --green / --green-bright / --text-dim correctly.
    - SettingsPanel: ✅ uses --green / --green-bright / --red correctly.
    - AccessUserManager: ❌ uses undefined --primary / --primary-bright
      / --bg-panel2 (see Q5). Headings render in body text color, not
      bright green. Inputs render in default color, not green-bright.
      Table headers have transparent background.
    - ThemeBuilder: ✅ uses --green-bright / --text-dim / --border
      correctly (verified at lines 137, 144, 150, 162, 166, 192, 239,
      241, 248, 285).
    - AparatClipManager (not in scope but noticed): ❌ also uses
      --primary / --primary-bright (lines 130, 224, 250, 288).
    - FontSelector (not in scope): ❌ uses --primary (line 38).
  Conclusion: 3 components (AccessUserManager, AparatClipManager,
  FontSelector) reference an old variable naming scheme (`--primary`
  family) that was renamed to `--green` family but never updated.
  These should be migrated.

■ Q8. Spacing consistency
  Verdict: ❌ NO spacing scale defined.
  Ad-hoc values used: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 24, 28, 32, 40,
  48, 60, 80 px. No `--space-1`...`--space-8` tokens.
  Examples of inconsistency (same conceptual gap, different values):
    - Card padding: 20px (`.about-card`), 24px (`.contact-form`,
      `.dashboard-container`), 14px (`.osc-controls`), 16px (`.signal-
      controls`, `.lab-visualizer` bar), 10px (`.settings-provider-item`).
    - Field gap: 14px (`.settings-row`), 12px (`.dashboard-info-grid`),
      16px (`.settings-root`), 8px (`.settings-providers-list`).
    - Section margin-bottom: 16px (most), 20px (`.admin-settings-section`),
      24px (`.dashboard-header`), 48px (`.section-head`).
  Recommendation: define `--space-1: 4px; --space-2: 8px; --space-3:
  12px; --space-4: 16px; --space-5: 24px; --space-6: 32px; --space-7:
  48px; --space-8: 64px` and migrate.

■ Q9. Typography hierarchy
  Verdict: ⚠️ WEAK in admin area.
  Public site has a clean scale:
    - hero-title: clamp(2.4rem, 6vw, 4.5rem) — H1
    - section-title: clamp(1.8rem, 3.5vw, 2.8rem) — H2
    - about-stats strong: 1.6rem — H3 numeric
    - skill-card h3: 1rem — H3 card title
    - book-body h3: 1rem — H3 card title
    - body: 15px
    - small: 0.78rem (12.5px)
    - micro: 0.72rem (11.5px)
  Admin panel typography is ad-hoc and too small:
    - dashboard-title: 18px (H1)
    - dashboard-info-label: 9px (cap label)
    - dashboard-info-value: 13px (data)
    - settings-card-title: 15px (H4)
    - settings-label: 11px (form label)
    - settings-input: 13px (form value)
    - settings-hint: 11px
    - settings-help-list: 12px
    - dashboard-message-name: 13px
    - dashboard-message-text: 12px
    - dashboard-message-date: 10px
    - dashboard-message-reply-text: 11px
    - dashboard-empty-state: 13px
    - dashboard-tab: 11px
    - dashboard-btn: 11px
    - AccessUserManager th: 10px (uppercase)
    - AccessUserManager td: 11px
    - AccessUserManager labelStyle: 10px (uppercase)
    - AccessUserManager inputStyle: 12px
    - AccessUserManager small: 10px
    - ThemeBuilder labels: 0.72rem (11.5px)
    - ThemeBuilder inputs: 0.8rem / 0.72rem
    - ThemeBuilder preview body: 0.7rem (11.2px) — too small
  Persian text below 12px is hard to read; 9-10px (dashboard-info-label,
  AccessUserManager labels) is illegible for Persian script.
  Recommendation: enforce minimum 12px for Persian; use clamp() for
  fluid type; establish explicit H1/H2/H3/H4/body/small scale tokens.

  Verdict: ❌ NO real skeletons — only text + blink cursor.

    - ContentManager: `<p style={{...}}>loading...</p>` (line 235) —

    - ThemeBuilder: `<p style={{...}}>loading...</p>` (line 239) —

    - AccessUserManager: `<div style={{...}}>در حال بارگذاری

    - MessagesPanel: `<div className="dashboard-empty-state">در حال
