============================================================
1. RATE LIMIT LOGIC CORRECTNESS
============================================================

[R1-LOW] middleware.ts:45-55 — Fixed-window algorithm allows burst at window boundary.
  checkRateLimit() uses `entry.resetAt < now` to reset. An attacker can fire `max`
  requests at T-1s (just before window end) and another `max` at T+1s (new window),
  yielding 2*max requests within ~2 seconds. Sliding-window or token-bucket would
  prevent this. Currently login max=5 (line 147) → 10 logins in 2s possible.

[R2-LOW] middleware.ts:52 — When count >= max, returns false but does NOT extend
  resetAt. Correct (no lockout-extension attack), but also does NOT decay the
  counter, so a legitimate user who hit the limit must wait full 15 min. Acceptable
  trade-off, documented here for completeness.

[R3-INFO] middleware.ts:147 — `max = pathname === "/api/user/login" ? 5 : 8`.
  Magic numbers inline; should be a per-route config map. Login 5/15min is OK.
  Contact/chat 8/15min — chat may be too strict for legitimate usage, contact OK.

[R4-INFO] middleware.ts:21 + login/route.ts:20-22 — Double rate-limit on /api/user/login.
  Both middleware and the route handler independently rate-limit the same endpoint
  with the same params (5/15min) but DIFFERENT Maps. Effective limit is 5 (whichever
  fires first). Not a bug, but redundant. If middleware's Map is cleared (restart),
  the route-level Map still applies. Acceptable defense-in-depth, but the two
  implementations should be unified to avoid drift.

[R5-MED] middleware.ts:148 — Rate-limit key is `${pathname}:${ip}`. If `ip === "unknown"
  (line 146 fallback), ALL anonymous clients share a single bucket keyed `pathname:unknown`.
  On a corporate NAT / Tor exit, legitimate users would block each other. Also makes
  the rate-limit trivially DoS-able: send 5 requests with no XFF header to lock out
  every "unknown" IP user.

  Verdict on correctness: LOGIC IS CORRECT (counter, boundary, return values).
  Algorithm choice is the weakness, not the implementation.

============================================================
2. CSRF ORIGIN CHECK
============================================================

[C1-MED] middleware.ts:159 — Only POST / PUT / DELETE are CSRF-checked. PATCH is
  NOT covered. Any state-changing PATCH route (e.g. /api/admin/users partial update)
  is CSRF-exempt. Next.js API routes commonly use PATCH for partial updates.

[C2-HIGH] middleware.ts:158-176 — PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES bypass CSRF entirely. This
  includes `/api/user/logout` (line 29). Logout CSRF is a known attack vector —
  an attacker can log the victim out via cross-site POST. Logout should require
  CSRF token or same-origin check. (Cross-ref: prior F-24/F-NEW-6, still open.)

[C3-MED] middleware.ts:169 — `originUrl.host !== host` is case-sensitive.
  `URL.host` is normalized to lowercase, but the `Host` header is case-insensitive
  per HTTP/1.1 spec. If a client sends `Host: EXAMPLE.com` and `Origin: https://example.com`,
  comparison fails → false-positive 403. Not a bypass, but a correctness bug that
  could break legitimate clients whose proxies upper-case the Host header.
  Should be: `originUrl.host.toLowerCase() !== host.toLowerCase()`.

[C4-LOW] middleware.ts:163-176 — Missing Origin is rejected (line 163). Some
  privacy-focused browsers strip Origin on same-origin requests. Strict but
  defensible. Not a bug; documenting trade-off.

[C5-LOW] middleware.ts:157-177 — Does not check `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin`
  header as additional defense. Modern browsers send this; would catch XSS-driven
  CSRF even when Origin is spoofable via plugin (e.g. flash, though deprecated).

[C6-INFO] middleware.ts:169 — Origin host comparison does NOT consider port.
  `URL.host` includes port when non-default (e.g. `localhost:3000`), and so does
  the `Host` header. So the comparison is actually port-aware — correct behavior.
  Documenting that this is NOT a bug.

============================================================
3. BODY SIZE LIMIT (1MB)
============================================================

[B1-HIGH] middleware.ts:196 — Only POST / PUT / PATCH are size-checked. DELETE
  is NOT covered. DELETE requests can carry a body (RFC 7231 §4.3.5 allows it).
  If any DELETE route reads body, no size limit applies. Defense gap.

[B2-CRITICAL] middleware.ts:197-204 — Trusts `Content-Length` header. A client
  using `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` sends NO Content-Length, so the check at
  line 198 evaluates `0 > 1MB` → false → middleware lets it through. The actual
  body can be arbitrarily large and will be buffered by Next.js / route handler
  until OOM. This is a real DoS vector. Mitigation requires either rejecting
  chunked encoding or relying on Next.js's route-level `maxBodySize` config
  (which is NOT set in next.config.ts).

[B3-LOW] middleware.ts:197 — `parseInt(..., 10)` returns NaN for malformed
  values. `NaN > 1024*1024` is false, so a malformed Content-Length bypasses
  the check. In practice Next.js rejects malformed Content-Length earlier, but
  the middleware does not defensively handle this case.

[B4-INFO] middleware.ts:198 — Boundary `> 1024*1024` allows exactly 1048576 bytes
  (1 MiB). Comment says "1MB limit" — correct.

  that the app does NOT use youtube-nocookie embeds, so no current gap. If the app

[P4-MED] middleware.ts:114 — script-src contains BOTH `'unsafe-inline'` AND
  `'unsafe-eval'`. `'unsafe-eval'` is needed only for Next.js dev mode (HMR,
  eval-based source maps). In production builds, `'unsafe-eval'` should be removed.
  `'unsafe-inline'` should be replaced with per-request nonces (Next.js 13.4+
  supports nonce-based CSP via `request.headers.get('x-nonce')`). Current setup
  allows inline event handlers and `eval()` from any same-origin script — a
  significant XSS amplification surface. (Cross-ref: prior F-18, still open.)

[P5-MED] middleware.ts:111-133 — Missing `upgrade-insecure-requests` directive.
  Without it, any legacy `http://` URL in HTML (e.g. `<img src="http://...">`)
  will be fetched over HTTP, breaking the HTTPS-only guarantee and enabling
  mixed-content passive sniffing.

[P6-MED] middleware.ts:111-133 — Missing `report-uri` / `report-to` directive.
  CSP violations are silently dropped — no visibility into attacks or accidental
  misconfigurations. Should point to a logging endpoint (e.g. /api/csp-report).

[P7-LOW] middleware.ts:111-133 — Missing `media-src` (defaults to default-src
  'self'). If the app ever embeds external `<audio>` / `<video>` (e.g. podcast
  hosting), it will be blocked. No current usage detected, so latent only.

[P8-LOW] middleware.ts:111-133 — Missing `worker-src` (defaults to script-src,
  which includes 'unsafe-eval'). Web Workers can be created from eval'd code —
  not great. Should be `worker-src 'self'`.

[P9-MED] middleware.ts:209 — **CSP is set ONLY on the final pass-through
  NextResponse.next()**. The 6 early-return error responses (429 at line 153,
  403 at lines 165/171/175, 401 at line 191, 413 at line 203) and the redirect
  at line 183 all return WITHOUT CSP. An attacker who triggers an error response
  can read it inside an `<iframe>` (frame-ancestors is in CSP, but without CSP
  set, only X-Frame-Options: DENY at line 100 protects — and that header IS set
  via addSecurityHeaders, so clickjacking is still blocked). However, script
  injection into error JSON is still possible if the JSON is rendered as HTML
  by a downstream proxy. **HIGH severity in principle, MED in practice** because
  the error responses are JSON not HTML. (Cross-ref: prior audit Q12, still
  open.)

============================================================
5. HSTS ON HTTPS ONLY
============================================================

[H1-HIGH] middleware.ts:211 — `req.url.startsWith("https://")` is fragile.
  In Next.js middleware running behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy, `req.url`
  reflects the proxy→origin connection scheme, NOT the client→proxy scheme.
  If the proxy speaks HTTP to Next.js (common for nginx → Next.js on port 3000),
  `req.url` starts with `http://` and HSTS is NEVER set, even on HTTPS requests.
  Correct approach: `req.nextUrl.protocol === "https:"` (which respects
  X-Forwarded-Proto when `trustProxyHeader` is enabled) or explicitly check
  `req.headers.get("x-forwarded-proto") === "https"`. (Cross-ref: prior F-27,
  marked PARTIAL — still open.)

[H2-LOW] middleware.ts:212 — `includeSubDomains` is set. If any subdomain
  (e.g. dev.example.com, staging.example.com) serves HTTP-only content, HSTS
  will force-HTTPS it and break. Verify all subdomains support HTTPS before
  keeping this flag. (No subdomain inventory available — flag for review.)

[H3-INFO] middleware.ts:212 — `preload` directive present. This signals consent
  to be added to browser HSTS preload lists (hstspreload.org). Site must be
  submitted to actually be preloaded. Harmless if not submitted, but the
  max-age=63072000 (2 years) meets the preload requirement.

============================================================
6. SECURITY HEADERS
============================================================

[S1-MED] middleware.ts:98-106 — Missing `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` (COOP).
  Should be `same-origin` to prevent cross-origin window attacks (Spectre-class
  side-channel, window.open cross-origin reference).

[S2-MED] middleware.ts:98-106 — Missing `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy` (COEP).
  Should be `require-corp` (with CORP headers on cross-origin resources) to
  enable cross-origin isolation and SharedArrayBuffer. Without it, advanced
  isolation features unavailable.

[S3-MED] middleware.ts:98-106 — Missing `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy` (CORP).
  Should be `same-origin` to prevent cross-origin reads of resources.

[S4-LOW] middleware.ts:104 — `res.headers.set("X-Powered-By", "")` sets the
  header to an empty string instead of deleting it. Most browsers/proxies will
  still transmit an empty header. Better: `res.headers.delete("X-Powered-By")`.
  Additionally, next.config.ts already sets `poweredByHeader: false`, so this
  line is redundant defense. Not a bug, but a no-op that may give false
  confidence.

[S5-MED] middleware.ts:208-214 — Same gap as P9: security headers from
  addSecurityHeaders ARE applied to error responses (good), but the CSP and
  HSTS at lines 209/212 are ONLY applied to the final NextResponse.next(). The
  401/403/413/429 responses and the /user-dashboard redirect (line 183) all
  miss CSP and HSTS. The redirect (NextResponse.redirect) is the worst case —
  it returns NEITHER addSecurityHeaders NOR CSP/HSTS, because it returns
  directly without wrapping in addSecurityHeaders. **HIGH severity for the
  redirect path.**

[S6-LOW] middleware.ts:98-106 — Missing `Cache-Control` for sensitive
  responses. API responses containing user data could be cached by intermediate
  proxies. Should add `Cache-Control: no-store` to /api/admin/* and
  /api/messages responses. Per-route handling may exist; not enforced at
  middleware level.

[S7-INFO] middleware.ts:99-103 — The 5 headers set (nosniff, DENY, referrer,
  permissions-policy, X-XSS-Protection:0) are all correct and modern.
  X-XSS-Protection:0 is the right choice (disables the buggy IE XSS auditor
  that could be turned into an XSS vector). X-Frame-Options:DENY is redundant
  with CSP frame-ancestors:none — defense in depth, OK.

[S8-INFO] next.config.ts:18-25 — next.config.ts also sets these 5 headers
  via the `headers()` block. Redundant with middleware. Not harmful; if
  middleware is bypassed (matcher exclusion) the next.config.ts headers
  still apply. Good defense-in-depth.

============================================================
7. RATE LIMIT MAP MEMORY LEAK
============================================================

[M1-CRITICAL] middleware.ts:42 + 58-65 — **setInterval cleanup is a no-op in
  Edge Runtime.** Next.js middleware runs in Edge Runtime by default (no
  `runtime: 'nodejs'` in config object at line 220-228). In Edge Runtime:
    - `setInterval` is UNDEFINED → the guard `typeof setInterval !== "undefined"`
      evaluates false → cleanup block never executes.
    - `Buffer.from(...)` at line 81 is also UNDEFINED → caught by try/catch →
      hasValidSession always returns false → all session-protected routes
      return 401 and all dashboard access redirects to /user-login.
  The worklog's V17.3-FINAL test results ("Login (admin/admin123): موفق",
  "/api/admin/settings: HTTP 200") imply middleware IS working, which means
  either (a) the runtime is actually Node.js (configured elsewhere not found
  in this audit) or (b) Next.js polyfills Buffer in Edge for this version.
  Either way, the setInterval cleanup is silently skipped in Edge →
  rateLimitMap grows unbounded with each unique IP. **Verify runtime
  explicitly by adding `export const config = { runtime: 'nodejs',
  matcher: [...] }`.**

[M2-HIGH] middleware.ts:42 — No maximum size cap on `rateLimitMap`. An attacker
  rotating `X-Forwarded-For` values (trivial — see finding X1 below) creates one
  entry per unique value per rate-limited path. At 3 rate-limited paths
  (line 21) × N spoofed IPs, the Map grows linearly with attacker effort.
  Combined with M1 (no cleanup in Edge), this is unbounded memory growth → OOM.
  Should cap at e.g. 10000 entries with LRU eviction.

[M3-LOW] middleware.ts:59-64 — Cleanup interval is 5 minutes, but the rate-limit
  window is 15 minutes (line 43). An expired entry can persist up to 5 minutes
  past its window before cleanup. Acceptable memory overhead (~33% above steady
  state), not a bug.

[M4-LOW] middleware.ts:64 — `.unref?.()` is Node.js-only (Timeout.unref). In
  browser/Edge it's a no-op (optional chaining skips). Without unref, the timer
  keeps the process alive — but in serverless/Edge this is moot. OK.

============================================================
8. X-FORWARDED-FOR SPOOFING
============================================================

[X1-HIGH] middleware.ts:145-146 — **X-Forwarded-For is trusted blindly.**
  `req.headers.get("x-forwarded-for")?.split(",")[0]?.trim()` takes the
  leftmost value, which is the ORIGINAL client value — but if the app is
  not behind a proxy that OVERWRITES (not appends to) XFF, an attacker
  controls this value entirely. Setting `X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4` per request
  gives the attacker a fresh rate-limit bucket each time → unlimited login
  attempts → credential stuffing. (Cross-ref: prior F-9, still open.)

[X2-HIGH] middleware.ts:146 — `x-real-ip` fallback is ALSO client-controllable.
  If the deployment does not set x-real-ip at the proxy layer (or strips it
  from client requests), an attacker can set `X-Real-IP: <random>` per request
  to bypass the rate limit even when XFF is properly stripped by the proxy.

[X3-MED] middleware.ts:145 — Same pattern duplicated in
  src/lib/access-auth.ts:175-181 (getClientIp) and src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:46.
  Three independent IP-extraction implementations, all with the same spoofing
  flaw. Should be unified into a single trusted-proxy-aware helper.

[X4-LOW] middleware.ts:145 — `split(",")[0]` does not validate the IP format.
  An attacker could set `X-Forwarded-For: <long string>` (up to header size
  limit) to bloat the Map key. Combined with M2 (no cap), this accelerates OOM.
  Should validate IPv4/IPv6 format before using as key.

[X5-INFO] middleware.ts:145-146 — No use of `req.ip` (Next.js does not expose
  socket IP in middleware). In API routes, `request.socket.remoteAddress` would
  be authoritative but is not used. Mitigation requires proxy-level enforcement
  (Cloudflare, nginx) of XFF overwrite.

============================================================
9. PATH TRAVERSAL BYPASS
============================================================

[T1-INFO] middleware.ts:138,158,180,188 — Path traversal analysis: NO DIRECT
  BYPASS FOUND. The middleware does not perform file I/O. All prefix checks use
  `pathname === p || pathname.startsWith(p + "/")` (lines 158, 180), which
  correctly prevents prefix confusion (e.g. `/api/content-foo` does NOT match
  the public prefix `/api/content`). Next.js normalizes `req.nextUrl.pathname`
  (URL-decodes, collapses `..`), so `/api/admin/../admin/foo` resolves to
  `/api/admin/foo` before the check at line 188.

[T2-LOW] middleware.ts:18 + 188 — `ADMIN_API_PREFIX = "/api/admin/"` includes a
  trailing slash. The check `pathname.startsWith(ADMIN_API_PREFIX)` (line 188)
  means `/api/admin` (no trailing slash) is NOT matched and falls through
  without session check. If a route exists at exactly `/api/admin` (no trailing
  slash), it bypasses the session check. Verify no such route is registered.
  Recommended: also handle `pathname === "/api/admin"` explicitly or strip the
  trailing slash from the constant.

[T3-LOW] middleware.ts:227 — **Matcher regex extension-exclusion footgun.**
  The matcher `/((?!_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|.*\.(?:png|jpg|jpeg|
  gif|webp|svg|ico|txt|xml|css|js|woff|woff2|ttf|eot)$).*)` excludes any path
  ending in `.js`, `.txt`, `.xml`, etc. from middleware. If a future sensitive
  route is added at e.g. `/api/admin/export.csv` or `/api/admin/logs.txt`, it
  will BYPASS the middleware entirely (no session check, no CSP, no rate limit).
  No such route currently exists (verified via grep), but the matcher is a
  latent security footgun. Recommended: scope the extension exclusion to
  specific paths (e.g. `/_next/static/.*\.(js|css)$`) rather than any path.

[T4-LOW] middleware.ts:158 — `pathname.startsWith(p + "/")` for PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES
  means `/api/content/` (with trailing slash) matches but `/api/content` (exact)
  ALSO matches via the first clause. Both are public. OK. But note that
  `/api/content` and `/api/content/` are treated identically — Next.js may serve
  both, redirect, or 308. No security impact.

[T5-INFO] middleware.ts:138-139 — `req.nextUrl.pathname` is used (good). URL-
  encoded slashes (`%2F`) are preserved by Next.js (NOT decoded into `/`), so
  `/api/admin%2Ffoo` does NOT match `startsWith("/api/admin/")` and would 404.
  No bypass via encoded slashes.

============================================================
10. PUBLIC API PREFIXES CORRECTNESS
============================================================

[A1-MED] middleware.ts:24-37 — `/api/user/verify` (line 29) is public but NOT in
  RATE_LIMIT_PATHS (line 21). If verify is OTP-based (e.g. SMS code, TOTP), an
  attacker can brute-force the OTP without rate limit. Verify the route's
  implementation in /api/user/verify/route.ts — if it accepts a code, add it to
  RATE_LIMIT_PATHS with max ~5/15min.

[A2-LOW] middleware.ts:24-37 — `/api/user/logout` (line 30) is public, bypassing
  CSRF (see C2). Logout CSRF is a known attack — an attacker can log the victim
  out by embedding `<form action="https://victim/api/user/logout" method="POST">`
  in any page. Should require CSRF token OR same-origin check.

[A3-INFO] middleware.ts:24-37 — `/api/bale/webhook` and `/api/telegram/webhook`
  (lines 33-34) are public (correct — external services don't send Origin header)
  and NOT rate-limited (correct — webhook senders shouldn't be throttled).
  However, they SHOULD verify webhook signatures (HMAC) at the route level.
  Not a middleware concern; flagging for defense-in-depth.

[A4-INFO] middleware.ts:24-37 — `/api/rss` and `/api/sitemap` (lines 35-36) are
  public GET endpoints. Correctly exempt from CSRF (CSRF only applies to
  mutating methods). OK.

[A5-LOW] middleware.ts:24-37 — Public prefixes use a MIX of "exact paths" and
  "directory prefixes". For example, `/api/user/login` is treated as a prefix
  (line 158 `pathname.startsWith(p + "/")`), so `/api/user/login/anything` would
  also be public. If `/api/user/login/foobar` ever becomes a sensitive route,
  it inherits the public exemption. Recommended: distinguish exact paths from
  prefixes explicitly (e.g. separate arrays).

[A6-MED] middleware.ts:158 vs 188 — `/api/messages` is NOT in PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES
  (correctly), but is checked separately at line 188 with `pathname ===
  "/api/messages"` (exact match only). This means `/api/messages/foo` (sub-paths)
  does NOT require session. If sub-routes exist (e.g. /api/messages/send,
  /api/messages/delete), they bypass session check. Verify no sub-routes exist,
  OR change to `pathname === "/api/messages" || pathname.startsWith("/api/messages/")`.

[A7-INFO] middleware.ts:24-37 — All public prefixes are under `/api/`. No public
  page routes (e.g. /, /clips, /contact) are listed — those don't need CSRF
  exemption because they're GET-only. OK.

============================================================
CROSS-CUTTING / DEFENSE-IN-DEPTH NOTES
============================================================

[N1-HIGH] middleware.ts:70-93 — `hasValidSession` is FORMAT-ONLY. It checks that
  the cookie decodes to `userId.expiresAt.signature` (3 parts), the expiry is in
  the future, and userId is non-empty. It does NOT verify the HMAC signature —
  the comment at lines 87-88 admits this. An attacker who knows the cookie
  format can forge a cookie with any userId and a future expiry, bypassing the
  middleware session check at lines 181 and 189. Defense-in-depth holds ONLY
  because each admin API route independently calls `checkAdminAuth` /
  `checkAdminSession` (which DO verify HMAC). But the `/user-dashboard` page
  gate (line 180-185) is fully bypassable — an attacker can load the dashboard
  HTML, though API calls from there will 401. (Cross-ref: prior F-1, still open.)
  Recommended: import the HMAC verification into middleware (SESSION_SECRET
  access requires Node.js runtime — see M1).

[N2-MED] middleware.ts:81 — `Buffer.from(decodeURIComponent(token), "base64")`.
  Buffer is a Node.js global. In Edge Runtime it's undefined → caught by the
  try/catch at line 80 → hasValidSession returns false → all session-protected
  routes 401. Confirms M1's runtime concern. If middleware is genuinely running
  in Node.js, this is fine. Verify with `console.log(typeof Buffer)` in dev.

[N3-LOW] middleware.ts:138 — `export function middleware(req: NextRequest)`.
  Function is NOT async. This is fine for the current synchronous logic, but if
  HMAC verification is added (N1), the function must become async to use `crypto`
  APIs in some runtimes.

Q7. Contact form with honeypot + time-trap?
================================================================================
  ⚠️ HONEYPOT ✅ WORKS / TIME-TRAP ❌ CRITICAL SELF-DEFEAT
  ---- Honeypot (WORKS) ----
    - page.tsx:764-771: hidden `<input type="text" name="website"
      tabIndex={-1} autoComplete="off" style={{position:absolute;
      left:-9999px;width:1;height:1;overflow:hidden}} aria-hidden="true" />`.
    - page.tsx:363: sends `website` field to /api/contact:
      `website: (e.target as HTMLFormElement).website?.value || ""`.
    - route.ts:69-75: if non-empty, logs `honeypot_triggered` security
      event + returns fake `{ok:true}` (bot doesn't know it was rejected).
    ✓ Correctly implemented.
  ---- Time-trap (CRITICAL — DEFEATS ITSELF) ----
    - page.tsx:773: `<input type="hidden" name="_t" value={mounted ? Date.now() : 0} />`.
    - The `value={mounted ? Date.now() : 0}` expression is RE-EVALUATED on
      EVERY React render. React updates the DOM `value` of this hidden
      input on each render (hidden inputs are controlled by `value`).
    - The live-clock effect at page.tsx:216-264 calls `setUtcTime`/
      `setLocalTime` via `setInterval(tick, 1000)` every 1 second →
      triggers a re-render every second.
    - Therefore the hidden `_t` DOM value is refreshed to the CURRENT
      `Date.now()` every second.
    - Submit handler at page.tsx:365 reads:
      `_t: (e.target as HTMLFormElement)._t?.value || Date.now()`
      — returns the LATEST DOM value (at most ~1 second old).
    - Server check at route.ts:77-78:
      `if (submittedAt && Date.now() - submittedAt < 2000) → reject as "too_fast"`.
    - Result: for ANY human submission, `Date.now() - submittedAt` is
      between 0 and ~1000ms < 2000ms → **EVERY legitimate submission is
      rejected as "too_fast"** with HTTP 400.
    - Client error mapping at page.tsx:383-390 handles "rate_limit",
      "spam_detected", "missing_fields", "invalid_email",
      "message_too_short" — but NOT "too_fast" → falls through to generic
      `errs.server` message → user sees a generic "server error" and
      their message is LOST.
    - The contact form is effectively UNUSABLE for real users.
    - Root cause: the time-trap timestamp must be captured ONCE (e.g., in
      a useState initialized on mount, or defaultValue on a one-time
      render) — NOT re-evaluated on every render.
  ---- Other defenses (working) ----
    - reCAPTCHA: page.tsx:346-351 (client checks getResponse) + route.ts:
      86-118 (server siteverify, fail-closed). ✓
    - Rate limit: route.ts:6-21 (3 per IP per 10 min). ✓
      (prior SEC-02 audit notes X-Forwarded-For spoofing breaks this)
    - Spam pattern detection: route.ts:23-32,140-145. ✓
    - Field validation: route.ts:120-138 (email regex, min length 10). ✓
  Severity: CRITICAL (contact form broken for all legitimate users)

  const saveItem = async (item: Item) => {
    const isNew = !item.id;
    const action = isNew ? "create" : "update";
    const endpoint = activeType === "equipment" ? "equipment" : "content";
    const payload: any = { type: activeType, action };
    if (!isNew) payload.id = item.id;
    payload.data = { ...item };
    delete payload.data.id; delete payload.data.createdAt; delete payload.data.updatedAt;
    if (payload.data.specs && typeof payload.data.specs === "object") {
      payload.data.specs = JSON.stringify(payload.data.specs);
    }
    try {
      await fetch(`/api/admin/${endpoint}`, {
        method: "POST", headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
        credentials: "include",
        body: JSON.stringify(payload),
      });
      setEditing(null); loadItems();
    } catch {}
  };

Findings — PAYLOAD CHECK (create+update):
  ✅ PASS (line 63-64): `isNew = !item.id; action = isNew ? "create" : "update"`
       — correctly branches create vs update on presence of `item.id`.
  ✅ PASS (line 65): Endpoint dispatch same as loadItems.
  ✅ PASS (line 66): `payload.type = activeType` — required by
       content/route.ts:61,72 (used to select model). For equipment,
       `type` is ignored by backend but harmless extra field.
  ✅ PASS (line 67): `if (!isNew) payload.id = item.id` — `id` only
       included on update, never on create. Matches content/route.ts:88-89
       (`update` requires `body.id`) and equipment/route.ts:63-65.
  ✅ PASS (line 76): `credentials: "include"` (see §10).
  ✅ PASS (line 75): `method: "POST"` + `Content-Type: application/json`.
  ✅ PASS (no password): Backend admin-auth.ts:17-18 ignores password
       param. Frontend correctly omits it — auth relies on session cookie.
  ✅ PASS (line 69): `delete payload.data.id; createdAt; updatedAt`
       — defensive strip on the data sub-object (backend content/route.ts:92
       and equipment/route.ts:70 do the same; belt-and-braces).

Findings — ROBUSTNESS of saveItem:
  ❌ NEG (HIGH, line 73-80): saveItem does NOT check `res.ok` or
       `data.ok`. The response body is NEVER consumed — no
       `await res.json()`. If save fails (validation 400 from
       content/route.ts:74 `invalid_type`, auth 401, server 500),
       the edit panel still closes (`setEditing(null)` line 79) and
       `loadItems()` reloads — user has NO idea their edit failed.
       This is the worst UX outcome in the file.
  ❌ NEG (MED, line 80): `catch {}` swallows all errors silently.
       Network/CORS errors → form closes silently, no feedback.
  ❌ NEG (MED, line 70-72 + line 218-219): specs JSON double-handling.
       Backend equipment GET returns `specs` as a PARSED OBJECT
       (equipment/route.ts:22-30: `specs: JSON.parse(e.specs)`).
       When admin clicks "edit" (line 254 `setEditing({ ...item })`),
       `editing.specs` is an object. The textarea binding at line 218
       (`value={editing[f.key] || ""}`) calls `.toString()` on the
       object → renders `[object Object]` in the textarea. User sees
       garbage and may overwrite. SAVE PATH STILL WORKS (line 70-72
       re-stringifies the object before POST, and equipment/route.ts:67-69
       no-ops because the value is already a string), but the EDIT
       DISPLAY IS BROKEN for existing equipment items with non-null specs.
  ❌ NEG (INFO, line 73-78): response body never read. Server-returned
       `{ ok, item }` (content/route.ts:85, 97; equipment/route.ts:61, 72)
       is discarded.

Verdict: PAYLOAD IS CORRECT — create/update payload shape matches both
        backends. But saveItem has NO error handling and NO res.ok check,
        so a failed save is indistinguishable from a successful one.
        Existing-equipment specs edit display is broken ([object Object]).

7) Error handling
------------------------------------------------------------
Location: throughout — loadItems:51-53, saveItem:80, deleteItem:86-91,
          toggleItem:96-101, bulkImport:104-120.

Findings:
  ❌ NEG (HIGH — NO UNIFIED STRATEGY): Error handling is wildly inconsistent:
       - loadItems  (line 51-53): catch{} → setItems([]) silently
       - saveItem   (line 80):    catch{} → swallows everything silently
       - deleteItem (line 86-91): NO try/catch AT ALL — rejects unhandled
       - toggleItem (line 96-101): NO try/catch AT ALL — rejects unhandled
       - bulkImport (line 119):   catch → alert("Invalid JSON") (wrong msg
                                  for non-JSON errors)
     deleteItem and toggleItem have ZERO error handling — any fetch
     failure becomes an UnhandledPromiseRejection visible only in console.

  ❌ NEG (HIGH — NO 401 HANDLING ANYWHERE): If the session cookie expires:
       - loadItems:  silently shows "No items yet." (line 237)
       - saveItem:   silently closes the edit form (line 79 setEditing(null))
       - deleteItem: silently calls loadItems() as if success (line 91)
       - toggleItem: silently calls loadItems() as if success (line 101)
       - bulkImport: silently does nothing (line 115 if(data.ok) is false)
     User is NEVER redirected to /user-login. User sees stale UI and
     has no idea their session expired. Compare to TextEditor.tsx which
     has the same flaw (PANEL-08 audit, worklog.md:35954).

  ❌ NEG (HIGH — NO res.ok CHECK ON 4/5 FUNCTIONS): Only bulkImport reads
       `data.ok` (line 115). The other 4 (loadItems, saveItem, deleteItem,
       toggleItem) don't check `res.ok` OR `data.ok`. Server errors
       (400/401/500) propagate silently or are swallowed by empty catch.

  ❌ NEG (MED — MISLEADING ERROR MESSAGE): bulkImport line 119 shows
       "Invalid JSON" for ANY caught error, including network failures
       and HTTP 500s. The message is only correct for JSON.parse failure
       at line 106.

  ❌ NEG (LOW — NO ERROR STATE): There is no `useState<string | null>`
       for an error message anywhere in the file. Therefore there is
       NO mechanism to display any error to the user even if one were
       caught. (Same flaw as TextEditor — PANEL-08 audit, worklog.md:35974.)

Verdict: FAIL — error handling is inconsistent, incomplete, and
        misleading. deleteItem/toggleItem have none; loadItems/saveItem
        swallow silently; bulkImport shows wrong messages; no 401 handling.

9) Loading state
------------------------------------------------------------
Location:
  State decl: src/components/ContentManager.tsx:12
    `const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);`
  Set true:  src/components/ContentManager.tsx:27  `setLoading(true)`  (loadItems only)
  Set false: src/components/ContentManager.tsx:54  `setLoading(false)` (loadItems only)
  UI gate:   src/components/ContentManager.tsx:234-237
    `if (loading) { return <p ...>loading...</p> }`

Findings:
  ✅ POS (line 12): Initial state is `true` — UI shows loading on first
       paint, before fetch resolves. Avoids flash of "No items yet."
  ✅ POS (line 27 + 54): setLoading(true) before fetch; setLoading(false)
       OUTSIDE the try/catch → always runs even on error.
  ✅ POS (line 234-235): Loading UI is shown when `loading` is true,
       gating the items list. Prevents interaction with stale data
       during reload.

  ❌ NEG (HIGH — NO MUTATION LOADING STATE): `setLoading(true)` is only
       called inside `loadItems` (line 27). The 4 mutating functions
       (saveItem line 62-81, deleteItem line 83-92, toggleItem line
       94-102, bulkImport line 104-120) do NOT set loading=true during
       their fetches. User can:
         - Click "save" multiple times → duplicate POSTs (line 228
           onClick fires saveItem which has no debounce/guard).
         - Click "delete" multiple times → multiple delete requests
           (line 256 onClick fires deleteItem).
         - Click "show/hide" multiple times → multiple toggle POSTs
           (line 255 onClick fires toggleItem).
         - Click "import" multiple times → duplicate bulk_imports
           (line 205 onClick fires bulkImport).
       No button-level disabled state, no spinner, no "saving..." label.

  ❌ NEG (MED — FULL-SCREEN GATE ON RELOAD): After every mutation,
       `loadItems()` is called (lines 79, 91, 101, 117). This sets
       `loading=true` (line 27) → the items list disappears and shows
       "loading..." (line 234-235) for the duration of the reload.
       For a single-item save, the entire list reflows. Could be
       avoided with optimistic updates or a per-row loading state.

  ❌ NEG (LOW — UNTRANSLATED): "loading..." (line 235) and "No items
       yet." (line 237) are English-only — ignores `lang` prop.
       Persian/German users see English. (Mirrors PANEL-08 §5 LOW
       finding at worklog.md:35938.)

  ❌ NEG (LOW): No spinner component, no skeleton loader — just plain
       text. Other admin components (e.g., MessagesPanel) use the
       same pattern.

Verdict: PARTIAL — initial-load loading state WORKS correctly. NO
        loading state for any mutation (save/delete/toggle/bulkImport).
        User can double-submit; full-screen gate on every reload is jarring.

Q1. Chat end-to-end works?
================================================================================
  ⚠️ PARTIAL — flow works but contains a duplicate-message race
  src/components/ChatSection.tsx:80-129 (send), :58-78 (poll)

  Happy path (verified by code reading):
    1. Visitor types message → POST /api/chat  (ChatSection.tsx:90-99)
    2. Server: rate-limit → apiEnabled → upsert session → save user msg
       → notify Bale → callLLMWithFallback → save assistant reply
       → return { ok, sessionId, reply, messageId }  (route.ts:64-207)
    3. Client appends user msg (line 87) and assistant reply (lines 103-106)
    4. Client sets sessionId (line 102) → poll effect activates (line 59)
    5. Poll hits /api/chat/messages?sessionId=…&since=ts every 3s
       (ChatSection.tsx:60-78) → fetches any NEW assistant messages
       (e.g. admin reply via Bale webhook) and appends them.

  Bugs in the end-to-end flow:

  (a) DUPLICATE-MESSAGE RACE  (LOW-MED)
      ChatSection.tsx:108 sets `setLastPollTs(Date.now())` right after the
      POST returns. The assistant message was already saved server-side
      BEFORE the response was sent (route.ts:192-194), so its `createdAt`
      (server clock) can be > `Date.now()` (client clock) if the client
      clock lags the server by even a few ms. The poll filter at
      src/app/api/chat/messages/route.ts:25 (`createdAt: { gt: sinceDate }`)
      then re-fetches the same assistant message → ChatSection.tsx:65-72
      appends it again → user sees two copies of the reply.
      No dedup by message ID, content-hash, or timestamp is performed
      in `setMessages` (ChatSection.tsx:65-72). `data.messages` is
      mapped straight into the messages array.

  (b) `error` STATE IS DEAD CODE  (LOW)
      ChatSection.tsx:19 declares `const [error, setError] = useState("")`,
      line 86 clears it (`setError("")`), but it is NEVER set to a
      non-empty value anywhere in the component. Errors are instead
      appended as fake assistant messages (lines 115-118, 121-124).
      The `error` state is rendered nowhere in the JSX — pure dead code.

  (c) DEAD IMPORT  (LOW — cosmetic)
      ChatSection.tsx:4 imports `PERSONAL` from `@/lib/content` but
      never references it. (UI and Lang are used; PERSONAL is not.)

  (d) Trailing whitespace on line 44 of ChatSection.tsx (between the
      closing `}` of the `if` and the `}, [lang])` of the effect).
      Cosmetic only.

  (e) POLL ENDPOINT IS UNAUTHENTICATED  (LOW — informational)
      src/app/api/chat/messages/route.ts:9-44 requires NO auth — anyone
      who knows (or guesses) a `sessionId` can read ALL assistant
      messages in that session. sessionId is a 24-char CUID so it
      is not brute-forceable, but if leaked (URL share, referrer
      header, log file) a third party can read the assistant side of
      the conversation. Note: the filter `role: "assistant"` at
      route.ts:24 DOES prevent leaking the visitor's own typed text,
      but LLM replies may quote the visitor's text, so the leak is
      only partially mitigated.

  Verdict: end-to-end "works" for the happy path, but the duplicate
  race (a) and the silent dead-code (b) are real defects.

================================================================================
Q2. Polls for responses?
================================================================================
  ✅ YES — with several caveats
  src/components/ChatSection.tsx:54-78

  Mechanics:
    - `lastPollTs` state holds the watermark  (line 55)
    - `useEffect` creates `setInterval(…, 3000)` polling
      `/api/chat/messages?sessionId=${sessionId}&since=${lastPollTs}`
      (line 62)
    - On new messages: maps them to assistant-role Msg objects and
      appends  (lines 64-72)
    - Updates `lastPollTs` to `data.serverTime || Date.now()`
      (line 73)
    - Cleanup clears the interval  (line 77)

  Caveats / bugs:

  (a) INTERVAL CHURN DUE TO `lastPollTs` IN DEPS  (LOW — perf)
      ChatSection.tsx:78: `}, [sessionId, lastPollTs]);`
      Every successful poll updates `lastPollTs` (line 73), which is
      in the deps array → effect re-runs → clearInterval + new
      setInterval. Net effect: after each successful poll the
      3-second timer is RESET, so the next poll happens 3 seconds
      after the last *successful* poll, not on a steady cadence. If
      admin posts 2 messages 1s apart, the second message may be
      delayed by up to 6s instead of 3s. Should use a ref for the
      watermark and an empty deps array for the interval.

  (b) POLL ENDPOINT NOT RATE-LIMITED  (MED — DoS vector)
      src/middleware.ts:21  `const RATE_LIMIT_PATHS = ["/api/user/login", "/api/contact", "/api/chat"];`
      src/middleware.ts:144 `if (RATE_LIMIT_PATHS.includes(pathname))` — EXACT MATCH.
      So `/api/chat/messages` is NOT in the list → NO rate limit.
      Combined with the unauthenticated nature (Q1.e) and the X-Forwarded-For
      spoofing already documented as F-9 (worklog SEC-02 / Q11), an
      attacker can hammer `/api/chat/messages?sessionId=<guess>` at
      unlimited rate → DB CPU exhaustion.

  (c) SILENT FAILURES  (LOW)
      ChatSection.tsx:75  `} catch {}`  — empty catch.
      Network errors, DNS failures, and 5xx responses are swallowed
      with no UI feedback. Acceptable for a poll loop but means the
      user has no indication that polling has stopped working.

  (d) `res.ok` NOT CHECKED  (LOW)
      ChatSection.tsx:62-63 fetches and parses JSON without checking
      `res.ok`. If the server returns 429/401/500, `data.ok` will be
      falsy and the `if (data.ok && data.messages && …)` guard at
      line 64 silently drops the response. OK in practice but
      silently hides errors.

  (e) POLL RUNS WHILE `sending === true`  (LOW)
      The poll effect does not check `sending` (line 18). When the
      user just hit Enter, the POST is in flight, and a concurrent
      poll could fetch the same assistant message that the POST is
      about to return — amplifying the duplicate-message race (Q1.a).

  Verdict: yes, it polls — but the polling architecture has
  correctness (Q1.a, Q2.e) and security (Q2.b) gaps.

Q3. visitorId forgeable?
================================================================================
  ❌ YES — trivially forgeable (LOW-MED severity for chat, MED if used
       elsewhere for trust decisions)
  src/components/ChatSection.tsx:24-32 (client mint)
  src/app/api/chat/route.ts:89         (server accept)

  Client mint  (ChatSection.tsx:24-32):
    const KEY = "portfolio_visitor_id";
    let v = localStorage.getItem(KEY);
    if (!v) {
      v = "v_" + Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 10) + Date.now().toString(36);
      localStorage.setItem(KEY, v);
    }
    setVisitorId(v);

  Server accept  (route.ts:89):
    const visitorId = String(body.visitorId || "").slice(0, 100) || "anon";

  Problems:
    1. ID is generated entirely client-side with `Math.random()` and
       `Date.now()` — no server signature, no HMAC, no cookie bind.
    2. Server accepts ANY string ≤100 chars from `body.visitorId`
       with no validation, no allowlist, no correlation to the
       requesting IP or session.
    3. Attacker can:
       - Reset localStorage (or use incognito) → unlimited fresh IDs
         → bypass any per-visitorId logic. Note: the route's rate
         limit is keyed on IP (route.ts:11-21), not visitorId, so
         the practical impact here is mostly session-impersonation /
         attribution spoofing rather than rate-limit bypass.
       - Spoof ANOTHER visitor's visitorId by simply copying its
         localStorage value. The server would then attribute the
         attacker's messages to that visitor in the Bale
         notification (route.ts:140-149) and in any admin-side
         audit view that groups by visitorId.
       - Send arbitrary `visitorId` strings up to 100 chars — could
         include HTML/JS-like payloads; they are stored in the DB
         as `String` and may be rendered in the admin panel
         (untested — admin panel not in this audit's scope).
    4. The `visitorId` is sent in the POST body (line 97) — visible
       to anyone reading network traffic (no signing). Over HTTPS it
       is encrypted in transit, but anyone with DevTools can read/
       modify it.
    5. Cross-reference: the prior SEC-02 audit already documented
       that X-Forwarded-For (and thus the IP key) is forgeable
       (worklog Q11 / F-9). So BOTH dimensions of identity used by
       the chat route (IP and visitorId) are attacker-controlled.

  Recommended (advisory only — DO NOT FIX per task instructions):
    - Mint visitorId server-side via an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax
      cookie on first contact, and ignore any client-supplied
      visitorId.
    - Or sign the client-minted visitorId with an HMAC of (IP +
      User-Agent + secret) and verify server-side.

  Verdict: visitorId is forgeable with minimal effort.

Q4. Chat history bounded?
================================================================================
  ❌ NO — neither client-side nor server-side
  src/components/ChatSection.tsx:16         (client messages state)
  src/app/api/chat/route.ts:153-158         (LLM history build)
  src/app/api/chat/messages/route.ts:21-33  (poll query — no limit)
  prisma/schema.prisma:52-74                 (ChatSession / ChatMessage)

  Client-side (ChatSection.tsx:16):
    `const [messages, setMessages] = useState<Msg[]>([]);`
    Grows unbounded. Every user message, every assistant reply,
    every error message (Q7), and every poll-fetched message is
    appended. There is no `.slice(-N)` cap anywhere. A long-running
    conversation will balloon the React state and the rendered DOM
    (one `.chat-msg` div per message, line 158-165).

  Server-side:
    - `ChatMessage` table has NO row-count cap per session
      (schema.prisma:65-74). A single session could accumulate
      thousands of rows.
    - LLM history build (route.ts:151-159): `history = [...session.messages, { user, message }]`
      — passes the ENTIRE message history to the LLM provider with
      no truncation. Long conversations will overflow the LLM context
      window → the provider throws → `callLLMWithFallback` catches
      and returns the canned fallback reply (route.ts:176-185).
      The visitor gets a generic "I'm having trouble connecting"
      message that does NOT reflect the actual cause (context
      overflow), and there is no automatic trimming/retry.
    - Poll query (messages/route.ts:21-33): `findMany` with NO
      `take` limit. A pathological session with millions of
      assistant messages newer than `since` would return them all
      in one response → OOM / huge payload.
    - Admin GET (route.ts:231-240): `take: 100` sessions, but each
      session's `messages` relation has NO `take` limit — if a
      session has 10k messages, all 10k are returned in the admin
      payload.
    - No periodic cleanup cron / TTL on old sessions.

  InteractiveTerminal (cross-reference — also in scope):
    - `lines` state grows unbounded  (InteractiveTerminal.tsx:10).
      Only the `clear`/`cls` command (line 146-148) resets it.
    - `history` state (line 12) grows unbounded — every command
      ever typed is retained for ArrowUp/Down recall.
    - No cap on either. A user who runs 10 000 commands without
      `clear` will eventually see degraded render perf.

  Verdict: chat history is unbounded in 4 places (client state,
  LLM context, poll response, admin response) plus the terminal
  widget has its own unbounded `lines` and `history` arrays.

================================================================================
Q8. Empty state?
================================================================================
  ✅ OK — greeting always present
  src/components/ChatSection.tsx:35-45 (greeting effect)
  src/components/ChatSection.tsx:42    (single assistant greeting message)

  Implementation:
    useEffect(() => {
      const greetings: Record<Lang, string> = { en: …, de: …, fa: … };
      if (messages.length === 0) {
        setMessages([{ role: "assistant", content: greetings[lang], ts: Date.now() }]);
      }
    }, [lang]);

  Positives:
    - On first mount, `messages.length === 0` → greeting is added ✅
    - Greeting is localized in all 3 languages ✅
    - Greeting has the "radio comm" voice (`>> Patched through…`) ✅
    - If the user switches `lang` BEFORE sending any message, the
      greeting is replaced with the new language's greeting ✅
      (because `messages.length === 0` is still true at that point —
      actually wait, see Negatives #1 below)
    - InteractiveTerminal also always shows a welcome line
      (InteractiveTerminal.tsx:18-20) ✅

  Negatives:
    1. GREETING NOT UPDATED ON LANG SWITCH AFTER FIRST MESSAGE  (LOW — UX)
       Once `messages.length > 0`, switching `lang` does NOT update
       the greeting — but more importantly, it doesn't update the
       PRE-EXISTING greeting message either. So if a user starts in
       EN, gets the EN greeting, sends one message, then switches to
       FA, the EN greeting stays in the history forever. The new
       `lang` only affects new messages going forward.
       Actually, re-reading the effect: `if (messages.length === 0)`
       guards against re-greeting. So if the user switches lang while
       `messages.length === 0` (i.e. before sending anything), the
       effect runs and replaces the (single) greeting with the new
       lang's greeting — BUT it does this by calling `setMessages([…
       single greeting …])` which OVERWRITES the array. Since the
       array had exactly one greeting before, this is fine. ✅
       Once `messages.length > 0` the guard skips, so existing
       messages (including the original greeting) are preserved in
       the old language. Minor.
    2. MESSAGE COUNTER INCLUDES GREETING  (LOW — cosmetic)
       The chat-bar shows `{messages.length} msg` (line 154). On
       initial load this shows "1 msg" even though the visitor has
       not sent anything. Misleading.
    3. NO "NO MESSAGES YET" PLACEHOLDER  (LOW — informational)
       The greeting doubles as the empty state, which is fine. But
       there is no separate visual cue that the chat is "fresh /
       empty" vs. "in progress". Acceptable.

  Verdict: empty state is handled — the localized greeting always
  fills the chat body on first render.

================================================================================
Q9. Rate limit feedback?
================================================================================
  ⚠️ PARTIAL — feedback exists but is incomplete and inconsistent
  src/components/ChatSection.tsx:110-114    (client rate-limit handling)
  src/app/api/chat/route.ts:6-21, 72-77      (route-level 1min/8req limit, 429)
  src/middleware.ts:21, 144-154              (middleware 15min/8req limit, 429)
  src/middleware.ts:147                      (`max = … 8 for /api/chat`)

  Two rate-limit layers (INCONSISTENT):
    - MIDDLEWARE  (src/middleware.ts:21,144-154):
        window = 15 min  (RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_MS, line 43)
        max   = 8        (line 147 — `pathname === "/api/user/login" ? 5 : 8`)
        returns 429 with `{ ok: false, error: "rate_limit" }` and
        `Retry-After: 900` header (line 151).
        Keyed on `${pathname}:${ip}` — but `ip` is the spoofable
        X-Forwarded-For (already documented as F-9 in SEC-02 audit).
    - ROUTE  (src/app/api/chat/route.ts:6-21):
        window = 1 min   (RATE_WINDOW_MS, line 7)
        max   = 8         (line 8)
        Bypassed entirely for localhost / "unknown" IPs in non-prod
        (line 12). In production, "unknown" IP is NOT bypassed —
        so if X-Forwarded-For is missing, all "unknown"-IP requests
        share a single bucket → 8/min aggregate cap.
        Returns 429 with `{ ok: false, error: "rate_limit" }` (line 73).

  Client handling  (ChatSection.tsx:110-114):
    const err = data.error || "server_error";
    const msg = err === "rate_limit"
      ? (lang === "fa" ? "... Channel busy. لحظه‌ای صبر کن."
         : lang === "de" ? "... Kanal belegt. Kurz warten."
         : "... Channel busy. Hold a sec.")
      : <generic error>;

  Positives:
    - Both layers return the same `error: "rate_limit"` string ✅
    - Client distinguishes rate-limit from generic errors ✅
    - Feedback message is localized in en/de/fa ✅
    - "Channel busy" fits the radio-comm voice ✅

  Negatives:
    1. NO RETRY-AFTER COUNTDOWN  (MED — UX)
       The middleware returns `Retry-After: 900` (15 minutes!) but
       the client doesn't read this header (the response is JSON-
       parsed for `error`, not for headers). The user sees "Channel
       busy. Hold a sec." with no indication that "a sec" actually
       means up to 15 minutes. They will keep retrying and getting
       the same 429.
    2. INCONSISTENT WINDOWS  (LOW — operational confusion)
       Middleware window = 15min/8req; route window = 1min/8req.
       Middleware triggers first (it runs before the route handler),
       so the effective limit is 8 per 15min — far stricter than
       the route's 8 per 1min. A user having an active conversation
       will hit the middleware 429 after 8 messages in 15 minutes
       (~1 message every 2 minutes), which is far too strict for a
       real chat. The route's 1-min limit is effectively dead code.
    3. NO RATE LIMIT ON POLL ENDPOINT  (MED — DoS, see Q2.b)
       `/api/chat/messages` is NOT in `RATE_LIMIT_PATHS` (exact
       match at line 144) → unlimited polling → DoS vector.
    4. RATE LIMIT BYPASSABLE VIA X-FF SPOOFING  (HIGH — already
       documented as F-9 in prior SEC-02 audit). Attacker can send
       a fresh X-Forwarded-For per request → fresh IP bucket each
       time → 8 messages per 15min PER spoofed IP, effectively
       unlimited.
    5. NO CLIENT-SIDE THROTTLE  (LOW — informational)
       The client disables the submit button only while `sending`
       is true (line 190). Once the POST resolves (even with 429),
       the button re-enables immediately. Nothing stops the user
       from spamming Enter and burning through their 8-req budget
       in 8 seconds.

  Verdict: rate-limit feedback exists and is localized, but the
  UX is misleading (no countdown), the two limit layers are
  inconsistent (15min vs 1min), and the limit itself is bypassable
  via X-Forwarded-For spoofing (F-9).

================================================================================
Q10. AI disabled gracefully?
================================================================================
  ❌ NO — server signals it, client ignores it
  src/app/api/chat/route.ts:99-115  (server-side kill-switch)
  src/lib/settings.ts:44-47         (isApiEnabled reads SiteSetting)
  src/components/ChatSection.tsx:109-118  (client handling — generic fallthrough)

  Server-side  (route.ts:99-115):
    const { isApiEnabled } = await import("@/lib/settings");
    const apiEnabled = await isApiEnabled();
    if (!apiEnabled) {
      return NextResponse.json(
        {
          ok: false,
          error: "api_disabled",
          message: lang === "fa"
            ? "چت موقتاً غیرفعال است. لطفاً بعداً تلاش کنید."
            : lang === "de"
            ? "Chat ist vorübergehend deaktiviert."
            : "Chat is temporarily disabled.",
        },
        { status: 503 }
      );
    }

  `isApiEnabled`  (settings.ts:44-47):
    export async function isApiEnabled(): Promise<boolean> {
      const v = await getSetting("apiEnabled");
      return v === "true";
    }
    // DEFAULTS.apiEnabled = "true" (settings.ts:10) — so by default AI is ON.

  Client-side  (ChatSection.tsx:109-118):
    } else {
      const err = data.error || "server_error";
      const msg =
        err === "rate_limit"
          ? <rate-limit msg>
          : <generic error msg>;   // ← "api_disabled" falls through here
      setMessages((prev) => [...prev, { role: "assistant", content: msg, ts: Date.now() }]);
    }

  Problems:
    1. CLIENT IGNORES `api_disabled`  (HIGH — UX)
       The server explicitly returns `error: "api_disabled"` and a
       translated `message` field, but the client's `if/else` only
       special-cases `rate_limit`. The `api_disabled` case falls
       through to the generic "Error. Try again." message — which
       is misleading: the user is told to retry, but retrying will
       keep returning 503 until the admin re-enables the API. The
       user has no way to know the AI is intentionally offline.
    2. CLIENT IGNORES `data.message`  (MED — UX)
       The translated, server-provided `message` field is never
       read by the client. The client hardcodes its own generic
       message instead of using the server's.
    3. NO PRE-FLIGHT CHECK  (MED — UX)
       The client doesn't call `/api/chat/health` (or similar) on
       mount to check if AI is enabled. The user only discovers AI
       is disabled AFTER typing a message and submitting. A banner
       or disabled input on mount would be better.
    4. INPUT NOT DISABLED ON `api_disabled`  (MED — UX)
       After receiving a 503 with `api_disabled`, the client re-
       enables the input (the `finally` block at line 126 sets
       `setSending(false)`). The user can keep typing and submitting,
       each time getting the same useless "Error. Try again.".
    5. NO BANNER / STATUS INDICATOR  (LOW — UX)
       The chat-bar shows `ONLINE` hardcoded (ChatSection.tsx:132-
       134: `status: "ONLINE" / "آنلاین"`). When AI is disabled,
       the bar still says ONLINE. No correlation with the actual
       server state.
    6. KILL-SWITCH IS DB-BOUND, NOT ENV-BOUND  (LOW — operational)
       `isApiEnabled` reads from the SiteSetting table on EVERY
       request (route.ts:100-101) — no caching. Under load, each
       chat POST triggers a DB round-trip just to read a boolean.
       Minor perf concern.

  Verdict: AI-disabled is NOT graceful. The server correctly
  signals it (503 + translated message), but the client treats it
  identically to a generic server error, ignores the translated
  message, re-enables the input, and shows a misleading "try
  again" prompt.

ADDITIONAL OBSERVATIONS (not in the 10 questions)
================================================================================

A. INTERACTIVE-TERMINAL DOES NOT INTEGRATE WITH CHAT BACKEND
   src/components/InteractiveTerminal.tsx:84-89 (`chat` command)
   The `chat` command merely `scrollIntoView`s the #chat section. It
   does NOT call /api/chat, does NOT display chat messages, does NOT
   share state with ChatSection. So Q1-Q10 (chat-specific) do not
   apply to InteractiveTerminal for chat functionality. The terminal
   IS in scope per the task, but its only chat-related behavior is
   the scroll-to-chat shortcut.

B. INTERACTIVE-TERMINAL — UNBOUNDED `lines` AND `history`
   src/components/InteractiveTerminal.tsx:10 (`lines` state)
   src/components/InteractiveTerminal.tsx:12 (`history` state)
   src/components/InteractiveTerminal.tsx:153 (`history.push(raw)`)
   Both arrays grow without bound. `clear`/`cls` resets `lines` but
   NOT `history`. Should cap at e.g. 100 entries.

C. INTERACTIVE-TERMINAL — `visitor` COMMAND IS FAKE
   src/components/InteractiveTerminal.tsx:123-124
   `case "visitor": return out("you are visitor #" + (Math.floor(Math.random() * 9999) + 1000) + " · welcome 👋");`
   Returns a RANDOM number, not a real count. Misleading — visitors
   may believe it's a real counter. (Cosmetic / honesty issue.)

D. INTERACTIVE-TERMINAL — NO RATE LIMIT / NO ASYNC
   All commands execute synchronously and locally. No rate-limit
   feedback needed. No error state needed (unknown-command is the
   only "error" and it's handled inline at line 135). ✅

E. CHAT INPUT MAXLENGTH MISMATCH
   src/components/ChatSection.tsx:186 (`maxLength={500}` on input)
   src/app/api/chat/route.ts:87 (`.slice(0, 2000)` on server)
   Client caps at 500 chars; server caps at 2000. An attacker
   POSTing directly can submit 4× the client limit. Minor.

F. CHAT INPUT IS SINGLE-LINE
   src/components/ChatSection.tsx:178-189 (`<input type="text">`)
   No multiline support. Enter submits. Users cannot type a multi-
   line message. Acceptable for short chat, may frustrate longer
   questions.

G. POLL RESPONSE PAYLOAD NOT BOUNDED
   src/app/api/chat/messages/route.ts:21-33 — `findMany` has no
   `take` limit. If a session has many assistant messages newer
   than `since`, all are returned. Should `take: 50` and paginate.

H. NO CORS HEADERS ON CHAT ENDPOINTS
   /api/chat and /api/chat/messages return JSON without explicit
   CORS headers. Same-origin by default — fine for the embedded
   ChatSection widget. ✅

I. SESSION CREATION ON EVERY FIRST MESSAGE
   src/app/api/chat/route.ts:118-131
   If `sessionId` is empty or invalid, a new ChatSession row is
   created. An attacker can force the creation of unlimited
   sessions by simply not sending `sessionId` (or sending a random
   one each time) → DB bloat. Combined with F-9 (IP spoofing), the
   rate limit does not help. (Mitigated only by the 1MB body limit
   at middleware.ts:198 and the IP rate limit on /api/chat.)

J. BALE NOTIFICATION IS FIRE-AND-FORGET
   src/app/api/chat/route.ts:140-149
   `import("@/lib/bale").then(...).catch(() => {})` — failures
   are silently swallowed. If Bale is down, the admin never knows
   a visitor messaged. The `baleEnabled` setting (settings.ts:11,
   default "false") is NOT checked here — the notifyNewChat call
   happens regardless. (May be checked inside notifyNewChat itself
   — not in this audit's scope.)

----- 1. Origin check correctness  [PARTIAL, MED] -----
Location: src/middleware.ts:157-177
  157  // --- 2. CSRF protection برای POST/PUT/DELETE به مسیرهای non-public ---
  158  const isPublicApi = PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES.some(p => pathname === p || pathname.startsWith(p + "/"));
  159  if ((method === "POST" || method === "PUT" || method === "DELETE") && !isPublicApi) {
  160    const origin = req.headers.get("origin");
  161    const host   = req.headers.get("host");
  163    if (!origin || !host) { ... 403 missing_origin ... }
  167    try {
  168      const originUrl = new URL(origin);
  169      if (originUrl.host !== host) { ... 403 origin_mismatch ... }
  172    } catch { ... 403 invalid_origin ... }
  175  }

Positives:
  - Strict on missing Origin/Host (returns 403) ✅
  - Uses URL parser for normalization (handles case, trailing slash, default
    ports, subdomain / suffix bypass) ✅
  - SameSite=strict cookie (login route src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:109)
    independently blocks browser-mediated CSRF for cookie-authed routes ✅

Negatives (file:line):
  1.1. PATCH NOT COVERED (LOW-MED) — middleware.ts:159
       CSRF check only fires for POST|PUT|DELETE. PATCH is omitted, even
       though the body-size guard at middleware.ts:196 DOES include PATCH.
       No PATCH routes exist today, but if any future admin route accepts
       PATCH, it will have ZERO CSRF protection. Asymmetry with line 196.

  1.2. NO Sec-Fetch-Site CHECK (LOW-MED) — middleware.ts:160
       Modern browsers send `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin | same-site |
       cross-site | none`. This header is FORBIDDEN to modify from JS
       (cannot be spoofed by browser-mediated attackers), unlike Origin/
       Host which are trivially spoofable by scripts. Adding a strict
       `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin` (or `none` for first-party nav)
       guard would close the script-spoofed-Origin vector for browser-
       issued requests. Does not help against non-browser attackers.

  1.3. SCRIPT-MEDIATED CSRF STILL OPEN (HIGH, prior F-10/F-NEW-10) —
       middleware.ts:160-170. Any HTTP client (curl, Python requests,
       server-to-server) can set both Origin and Host to victim.com.
       Middleware cannot distinguish real browser requests from scripts.
       Defense relies ENTIRELY on SameSite=strict cookie — which DOES NOT
       protect against stolen-cookie attacks (attacker possesses the
       cookie; SameSite only blocks cross-site cookie SENDING from a
       victim's browser context).
       PoC: curl -X POST https://victim.com/api/admin/users \
                -H "Origin: https://victim.com" \
                -H "Host: victim.com" \
                -H "Cookie: access_session=<stolen>" \
                -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
                -d '{"username":"backdoor",...}'
       → 200 OK; Origin matches Host; cookie is valid.

  1.4. HOST HEADER IS CLIENT-CONTROLLED (LOW) — middleware.ts:161
       `req.headers.get("host")` is whatever the client sent. Behind a
       well-behaved proxy (Cloudflare/Vercel/NGINX with
       `proxy_set_header Host $host`), Host reflects the request's true
       Host. But a direct-origin Next.js (no proxy) accepts ANY Host
       value from the client. Combined with Origin spoofing (1.3),
       attacker sets both to victim.com → bypass.
       Mitigation: also compare against a server-side `ALLOWED_HOSTS`
       allowlist.

  1.5. PUBLIC_PREFIX EXEMPTION (MED) — middleware.ts:158
       All paths in PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES (lines 24-37) skip the Origin
       check entirely. Includes:
         /api/user/login   (line 28) — see finding #4 (login CSRF)
         /api/user/logout  (line 30) — see finding #3 (logout CSRF)
         /api/contact      (line 31) — see finding #5
         /api/chat         (line 32) — see finding #6
         /api/track        (line 27) — see finding #9
         /api/bale/webhook     (line 33) — see finding #7 (OK)
         /api/telegram/webhook (line 34) — see finding #7 (OK)
       The /api/messages route is correctly NOT in this list (see #2).

  1.6. CASE-MISMATCH FALSE POSITIVE (LOW) — middleware.ts:169
       URL parser lowercases the host part of Origin. Host header is
       sent as-is by client. If a misconfigured proxy sends
       `Host: Victim.com`, the comparison `originUrl.host ("victim.com")
       !== host ("Victim.com")` is TRUE → 403 false positive.

Severity: MED (script-mediated CSRF is HIGH but is a known inherited
  issue from V17.3-SEC-02 Q5 — the sameSite=strict cookie is the only
  meaningful mitigation, and it doesn't help against stolen cookies).
Cross-reference: V17.3-SEC-02 Q5; F-10, F-NEW-10 in prior audit.

----- 4. /api/user/login CSRF (login CSRF)  [FAIL, MED] -----
Location: src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:36-118 + middleware.ts:28

Issues (file:line):
  4.1. NO ORIGIN CHECK (MED) — middleware.ts:28 (PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES)
       includes /api/user/login → CSRF Origin check skipped.

  4.2. NO CSRF TOKEN / NO REFERER CHECK (MED) — login/route.ts:36-118
       Route accepts any POST with `{username, password}` body. No
       anti-CSRF token, no Origin/Referer check, no per-session nonce.

  4.3. LOGIN CSRF ATTACK VECTOR:
       Attacker hosts page on evil.com:
         <form action="https://victim.com/api/user/login" method="POST"
               enctype="text/plain">
           <input name='{"username":"attacker","password":"attackerpw","ignore":"'
                  value='"}' />
         </form>
       Victim visits evil.com → form auto-submits → victim's browser
       receives `Set-Cookie: access_session=<attacker's_session_token>`.

       Now victim thinks they're logged in as themselves, but their
       browser holds the ATTACKER's session cookie. Any data the victim
       enters (e.g., reply drafts, settings, notes saved server-side)
       is now visible to the attacker via the attacker's session at
       /api/messages, /api/admin/*, etc.

  4.4. SameSite=Strict MITIGATION PARTIAL:
       login/route.ts:106-112 sets the access_session cookie with
       `sameSite: "strict"`. Per RFC 6265bis, a cross-site response
       that sets a SameSite=Strict cookie is REJECTED by modern
       browsers (Chrome 80+, Firefox 69+, Safari 16+). So in modern
       browsers, the login CSRF above is largely mitigated.
       BUT: older browsers (Safari < 16, Chrome < 80, all browsers
       pre-2019) ignore SameSite — login CSRF is fully exploitable
       there.

  4.5. SAME-SITE ATTACK VECTOR STILL OPEN (LOW-MED):
       If the attacker can get the victim to visit a same-site page
       that triggers the login form (e.g., via stored XSS, open
       redirect, or user-uploaded content rendered on victim.com),
       SameSite=Strict does NOT help. Today no such vector is known
       in the codebase, but defense-in-depth gap.

  4.6. POST-CSRF REAUTH CONFUSION (LOW):
       /api/user/verify (route.ts:16-50) returns the logged-in user's
       full profile + permissions. Combined with login CSRF (4.3),
       attacker can fingerprint what data the victim now sees under
       the attacker's account → social-engineering vector.

Severity: MED (login CSRF is real, but largely mitigated by SameSite=
  strict in modern browsers; full exploit requires legacy browser or
  same-site attack vector).
Cross-reference: V17.3-SEC-02 Q5; not explicitly called out before.

       registered site). Cross-origin CSRF that fakes a victim's
       submission will fail reCAPTCHA verification.

       If the attacker themselves solves reCAPTCHA (manually or via

----- 8. CORS preflight  [FAIL, MED] -----
Location:
  - next.config.ts:14-27 (headers block — no CORS)
  - nginx-ehsanmorad.conf:14-63 (no add_header Access-Control-*)
  - Grep across src/: NO `function OPTIONS`, NO `Access-Control-Allow-*`
    headers set anywhere. Confirmed via grep across the entire src/.

Analysis:
  8.1. NO CORS HEADERS SET ANYWHERE (FAIL — but defense-in-depth OK):
       The server NEVER sets:
         - Access-Control-Allow-Origin
         - Access-Control-Allow-Methods
         - Access-Control-Allow-Headers
         - Access-Control-Allow-Credentials
         - Access-Control-Max-Age
       Result: any cross-origin `fetch` with `Content-Type:
       application/json`, custom headers, or non-simple methods
       triggers a preflight OPTIONS request — and the server returns
       no ACAO header → browser blocks the actual request.
       ✅ This is actually GOOD for CSRF defense: it prevents
       cross-origin JSON POSTs from browser scripts.

  8.2. SIMPLE-CONTENT-TYPE BYPASS (MED):
       "Simple" requests (per CORS spec) DON'T trigger preflight if
       they use only:
         - method: GET, HEAD, POST
         - Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded,
           multipart/form-data, or text/plain
         - only CORS-safelisted headers
       For these, the browser sends the request directly. The server
       has no chance to preflight-deny. Combined with the public-prefix
       exemption (findings #4, #5, #6, #9), this is the primary CSRF
       vector: attacker submits cross-origin HTML form with
       `enctype="text/plain"` and a JSON-shaped body. Server's
       `request.json()` parses it as JSON. No preflight ever fires.

  8.3. NO OPTIONS HANDLER (LOW):
       No `export async function OPTIONS` in any route. If a future
       route accidentally sets ACAO (e.g., for a public widget), the
       preflight will fall through to Next.js default OPTIONS handling
       which responds 204 with no CORS headers. Today: not exploitable.

  8.4. NGINX NO CORS DIRECTIVES (OK):
       nginx-ehsanmorad.conf (lines 14-63) has no `add_header
       Access-Control-Allow-*` directives → not adding CORS at proxy
       layer. ✅ Defense-in-depth OK.

Severity: MED (preflight correctly absent → JSON CSRF blocked; but
  simple-content-type bypass exploitable on public POST routes — see
  #6 and #9).

----- 9. Content-Type bypass  [FAIL, MED-HIGH] -----
Location:
  - middleware.ts:157-177 (Origin check only — no Content-Type check)
  - src/app/api/contact/route.ts:57   `await req.json().catch(...)`
  - src/app/api/chat/route.ts:79       `await req.json().catch(...)`
  - src/app/api/track/route.ts:11      `await req.json().catch(...)`
  - src/app/api/messages/route.ts:60   `await req.json().catch(...)`
  - src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:38 `await request.json().catch(...)`
  - src/app/api/bale/webhook/route.ts:31 `await req.json().catch(...)`
  - src/app/api/telegram/webhook/route.ts:19 `await req.json().catch(...)`

Issues (file:line):
  9.1. NO CONTENT-TYPE WHITELIST ANYWHERE (FAIL):
       No route validates `Content-Type: application/json` before
       calling `request.json()`. Next.js's `request.json()` happily
       parses a body sent with `Content-Type: text/plain` or
       `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` as long as the bytes form
       valid JSON.

  9.2. CSRF VIA text/plain FORM POST (MED-HIGH):
       Per CORS spec, `<form enctype="text/plain" method="POST">` is
       a "simple" request — no preflight, browser sends directly.
       Attacker builds:
         <form action="https://victim.com/api/chat" method="POST"
               enctype="text/plain">
           <textarea name='{"message":"hi","lang":"en","visitorId":"x","ignore":"'>
           </textarea>
         </form>
       Browser sends:
         Content-Type: text/plain
         Body: {"message":"hi","lang":"en","visitorId":"x","ignore":"="}
       The trailing `="` is the form-field separator appended by the
       browser (name="..." appends `=value`). The body parses as JSON
       because Next.js's JSON parser is permissive about trailing
       garbage in some Node versions — but the `ignore` field absorbs
       the garbage. Cleaner bypass:
         <form enctype="application/x-www-form-urlencoded">
       with body `{"message":"hi","lang":"en","visitorId":"x"}=x` —
       depending on parser. Most reliable:
         fetch from same-origin after a same-origin XSS, OR use
         `enctype="text/plain"` with carefully crafted body.

       For /api/chat (no reCAPTCHA, no Origin check, no Content-Type
       check): FULL EXPLOIT. See finding #6.4 PoC.

  9.3. /api/contact PARTIALLY MITIGATED (LOW):
       Even though Content-Type bypass works on /api/contact too, the
       reCAPTCHA token is origin-bound — cross-origin form submission
       fails Google's hostname verification. CSRF impact: blocked.

  9.4. /api/messages, /api/admin/* PROTECTED (OK):
       These routes are NOT in PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES, so the CSRF Origin
       check at middleware.ts:159 fires BEFORE the route handler.
       Cross-origin form posts are rejected with `403 missing_origin`
       (Origin is absent on cross-origin form submissions in most
       browsers) or `403 origin_mismatch`.
       BUT script-mediated CSRF (Origin spoofable) still works — see
       finding #1.3.

  9.5. /api/track UNPROTECTED (LOW):
       track/route.ts:11 is in PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES (middleware.ts:27).
       No Origin check, no Content-Type check. Body is just analytics
       fields. Attacker can spam fake page views cross-origin. Low
       impact (analytics pollution).

  9.6. /api/user/login & /api/user/verify (MED):
       login/route.ts:38 — public + no Content-Type check. Login CSRF
       (finding #4) works via text/plain form. SameSite=Strict cookie
       mitigates modern browsers (finding #4.4).
       verify/route.ts:16 is GET — CSRF N/A for GET (no state change).

Severity: MED-HIGH (full exploit chain on /api/chat; mitigated on
  /api/contact by reCAPTCHA; protected on /api/messages by Origin
  check + session).

----- 10. sameSite=strict cookie protection  [PARTIAL, LOW] -----
Location:
  - src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:106-112 (cookie set)
  - src/app/api/user/logout/route.ts:9 (cookie delete)
  - Grep across src/app/: only TWO cookie writes — login (set) and
    logout (delete). No other route touches cookies.

Positives:
  - Login sets `sameSite: "strict"` ✅ — login/route.ts:109
  - Also sets `httpOnly: true` ✅ — login/route.ts:107
  - `secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === "production"` ✅ — login/route.ts:108
  - `path: "/"` ✅ — login/route.ts:110
  - `maxAge: 86400` (24h) ✅ — login/route.ts:111

Issues (file:line):
  10.1. LOGOUT DELETION DOES NOT RE-ASSERT ATTRIBUTES (LOW-MED) —
        logout/route.ts:9:
          response.cookies.delete("access_session");
        Next.js's `cookies.delete(name)` internally calls
        `cookies.set(name, "", { maxAge: 0, expires: epoch, path: "/" })`
        — it does NOT re-specify httpOnly, secure, or sameSite. The
        resulting Set-Cookie header is:
          Set-Cookie: access_session=; Path=/; Max-Age=0; Expires=...
        (no SameSite attribute).

        Implication: per RFC 6265bis, a Set-Cookie with no SameSite
        defaults to `Lax` in modern browsers. Cross-site responses
        that set a `SameSite=Lax` (or unspecified) cookie are
        ACCEPTED by browsers (unlike Strict/None+Secure which have
        different cross-site rules). Therefore:
          - The deletion Set-Cookie from a cross-site response CAN
            delete the victim's SameSite=Strict cookie in some
            browser implementations (e.g., older Safari, embedded
            WebViews that don't follow 6265bis strictly).
        To be safe, logout should explicitly re-assert all
        attributes when clearing:
          response.cookies.set("access_session", "", {
            httpOnly: true,
            secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === "production",
            sameSite: "strict",
            path: "/",
            maxAge: 0,
          });

  10.2. NO COOKIES SET ANYWHERE ELSE (OK — informational):
        Grep across all of src/app/api/** for `cookies.set` returned
        ONLY two matches (login set, logout delete). No other route
        sets state-changing cookies. ✅ minimizes SameSite attack
        surface.

  10.3. ADMIN AUTH USES THE SAME COOKIE ✅ — src/lib/admin-auth.ts:20
        `getSessionFromRequest(request)` reads the same access_session
        cookie. Same SameSite=Strict protection applies to all admin
        routes.

  10.4. NO SETTING OVERRIDES SameSite (OK):
        No code dynamically changes SameSite based on env or feature
        flag. Cookie attribute is hard-coded "strict".

  10.5. PREVIOUS-AUDIT (V17.3-SEC-02 Q5) CORRECTLY NOTED:
        SameSite=strict is the ONLY defense against browser-mediated
        CSRF for non-public routes (admin/*, messages, etc.). It
        DOES NOT defend against:
          (a) stolen-cookie attacks (attacker has the cookie value
              and uses it from any context — finding #1.3)
          (b) same-site attacks (XSS / open-redirect chains — none
              known today)
          (c) legacy browsers that ignore SameSite (pre-2019)

  10.6. SECURE FLAG NOT SET IN DEV (LOW):
        login/route.ts:108 `secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === "production"`
        In dev, secure=false → cookie sent over HTTP. Acceptable for
        localhost; risk if dev env is deployed publicly (e.g.,
        staging.ehsanmorad.ir with NODE_ENV=development).

Severity: LOW (SameSite=Strict is correctly set on the login cookie;
  logout deletion attributes gap is defense-in-depth; no other
  cookie-write paths in codebase).
