Q1. middleware.ts hasValidSession() — verify HMAC
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ❌ FAIL — src/middleware.ts:70-93  (HIGH — same as SEC-02 Q3, F-1 still open)
  Code:
    70: function hasValidSession(cookieHeader: string): boolean {
    78:   const token = cookies["access_session"];
    81:     const decoded = Buffer.from(decodeURIComponent(token), "base64")
                       .toString("utf8");
    83:     if (parts.length !== 3) return false;
    84:     const [userId, expiresAtStr] = parts;   // parts[2] = sig IGNORED
    85:     const expiresAt = parseInt(expiresAtStr, 10);
    86:     if (isNaN(expiresAt) || Date.now() > expiresAt) return false;
    87:     // در middleware نمی‌تونیم HMAC رو verify کنیم چون SESSION_SECRET
    88:     // بهش دسترسی نداریم
    89:     return userId.length > 0;                 // ← FORMAT CHECK ONLY
  Analysis:
    The session token format (defined in access-auth.ts:67-72,
    createSessionToken) is:
      payload = `${userId}.${expiresAt}`
      sig     = hmac(payload)            // sha256(SESSION_SECRET, payload)
      token   = base64(`${payload}.${sig}`)
    Middleware NEVER verifies `sig` (parts[2]). It only checks:
      (a) parts.length === 3
      (b) expiresAt is a number and not in the past
      (c) userId is non-empty (any string passes, even "x")
    Comment at lines 87-88 EXPLICITLY admits the gap and relies on the
    API layer (access-auth.ts:78-96 verifySessionToken, uses
    crypto.timingSafeEqual) as the real check.
  Defense-in-depth impact:
    - All /api/admin/* and /api/messages requests that pass middleware's
      session gate STILL reach the route handler, where checkAdminAuth/
      checkAdminSession → getSessionFromRequest → verifySessionToken
      REJECTS forged signatures. ✅ Today's admin endpoints are safe.
    - WORSE: the /user-dashboard PAGE GATE at lines 180-185 uses ONLY
      hasValidSession. A forged cookie causes the BROWSER to render the
      /user-dashboard page shell. Client-side fetches will then 401, but
      the page shell, layout, embedded static content, and any
      client-only data is exposed. Page-gate bypass.
    - DoS amplification: forged cookies reach API handlers; each request
      burns a db.accessUser.findUnique call (admin-auth.ts:23) before
      being rejected. Combined with the lack of rate limit on
      /api/admin/* (SEC-02 Q4, F-5 still open), this is a cheap DB-cost
      DoS.
  Cross-reference: SEC-02 Q3 (worklog:34923); F-1 in prior audit (open).
  Severity: HIGH
  PoC (page-gate bypass):
    USERID="cm1234567890abcdefghijk"     # any plausible cuid
    FUTURE=$((($(date +%s)+3600)*1000))
    PAYLOAD="${USERID}.${FUTURE}.deadbeef"   # fake sig, IGNORED by middleware
    TOKEN=$(printf '%s' "$PAYLOAD" | base64)
    curl -s "https://victim.com/user-dashboard" \
      -H "Cookie: access_session=${TOKEN}" | head -c 200
    # → HTTP 200 with /user-dashboard HTML (instead of 302 redirect to
    #   /user-login). Page renders. Client-side fetches 401.
  PoC (DB-cost DoS):
    while true; do
      curl -s -o /dev/null "https://victim.com/api/admin/users" \
        -H "Cookie: access_session=${TOKEN}"
    done
    # No rate limit on /api/admin/* → each request burns one DB lookup
    # (db.accessUser.findUnique in admin-auth.ts:23) before verifySessionToken
    # rejects the forged sig.

Q3. lib/access-auth.ts verifySessionToken() — verify HMAC + timingSafeEqual
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ✅ PASS — src/lib/access-auth.ts:78-96
  Code:
    78: export function verifySessionToken(token: string):
            { userId: string; expiresAt: number } | null {
    80:     const decoded = Buffer.from(token, "base64").toString("utf8");
    81:     const parts = decoded.split(".");
    82:     if (parts.length !== 3) return null;
    83:     const [userId, expiresAtStr, sig] = parts;
    84:     const expiresAt = parseInt(expiresAtStr, 10);
    85:     if (isNaN(expiresAt)) return null;
    86:     if (Date.now() > expiresAt) return null;
    87:     // بررسی امضا با timingSafeEqual (جلوگیری از timing attack)
    88:     const expectedSig = hmac(`${userId}.${expiresAt}`);
    89:     const sigBuf = Buffer.from(sig, "hex");
    90:     const expBuf = Buffer.from(expectedSig, "hex");
    91:     if (sigBuf.length !== expBuf.length ||
            !crypto.timingSafeEqual(sigBuf, expBuf)) return null;
    92:     return { userId, expiresAt };
    93:   } catch { return null; }
  Positives:
    - HMAC-SHA256 over `${userId}.${expiresAt}` with SESSION_SECRET
      (hmac() at access-auth.ts:206-208). ✅
    - `crypto.timingSafeEqual` (line 91) prevents timing side-channel. ✅
    - Length check BEFORE timingSafeEqual (line 91) — required because
      timingSafeEqual throws on length mismatch. ✅
    - Expiry check (line 86) — token rejected after expiresAt. ✅
    - SESSION_SECRET validation (access-auth.ts:21-43) — rejects weak/

Q4. Can attacker forge session cookie?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ PARTIAL — middleware accepts, API layer rejects
  Per Q1: middleware's hasValidSession is FORMAT-ONLY. Forged cookie
  PASSES middleware gate. Per Q3: verifySessionToken (in API layer)
  REJECTS forged signatures.
  Per-route outcome for forged cookie:
    /api/admin/*               → 401 (verifySessionToken rejects) ✅
    /api/messages              → 401 (verifySessionToken rejects) ✅
    /api/chat GET (admin view) → 401 (verifySessionToken rejects) ✅
    /api/bale/webhook GET      → 401 (verifySessionToken rejects) ✅
    /user-dashboard PAGE       → 200 page shell (Q1 page-gate bypass) ❌
    /api/chat/messages GET     → 200 (NO AUTH REQUIRED — public route)
    /api/track POST            → 200 (NO AUTH REQUIRED — public route)
    /api/content, /api/clips   → 200 (NO AUTH REQUIRED — public routes)
  So: admin DATA is protected. Admin PAGE SHELL is exposed (page-gate
  bypass). DB-cost DoS amplification on /api/admin/* (each forged-cookie
  request hits db.accessUser.findUnique before verifySessionToken rejects
  — though actually, looking at the code path: getSessionFromRequest at
  access-auth.ts:186-201 calls verifySessionToken FIRST; if that returns
  null, db.accessUser.findUnique is NEVER called. So the DB lookup is
  actually SKIPPED on forged cookies. The DoS amplifier I noted in Q1 is
  weaker than I claimed — forged cookies are rejected at verifySessionToken
  before any DB hit. Real cost per forged request: 1 base64 decode + 1
  HMAC computation. Cheap but bounded.)
  Severity: MED (admin data safe; admin page shell leaked; cheap CPU
    amplification)
  PoC: see Q1 PoC (page-gate bypass). For /api/admin/* the forged cookie
  is correctly rejected by verifySessionToken.

    - Session token construction (access-auth.ts:67-72):
        67: export function createSessionToken(userId: string): string {
        68:   const expiresAt = Date.now() + SESSION_DURATION_HOURS*60*60*1000;
        69:   const payload = `${userId}.${expiresAt}`;   // ← NO passwordHash
        70:   const sig = hmac(payload);                  // ← NO passwordHash
        71:   return Buffer.from(`${payload}.${sig}`).toString("base64");
        72: }
    - prisma/schema.prisma:380-415 — AccessUser model has NO
      `sessionVersion`/`tokenVersion`/`passwordChangedAt` field that
      could be incorporated into the HMAC.
  Analysis:
    The session token's HMAC covers ONLY (userId, expiresAt, SESSION_SECRET).
    Changing passwordHash does NOT change any of these three values.
    Therefore, an attacker who stole the admin's access_session cookie
    BEFORE the password change retains 100% valid admin access for the
    FULL remaining lifetime of the stolen token — up to 24h
    (SESSION_DURATION_HOURS = 24, access-auth.ts:44).
    This means:
      - Admin's "I changed my password" recovery action gives a FALSE
        sense of security. The attacker retains full admin privileges
        (create users, delete users, change settings, read messages,
        clear messages, etc.) for up to 24h.
      - The ONLY way to immediately invalidate a stolen cookie is to
        rotate SESSION_SECRET (process.env.SESSION_SECRET), which
        invalidates ALL sessions including the legit admin's — forcing
        everyone to re-login. There is no per-user revocation.
      - Same applies to non-admin AccessUsers: if admin changes a
        user's password via /api/admin/users/[id] PUT, the user's
        existing sessions remain valid for up to 24h. Combined with
        Q6 (no effective brute-force protection), an attacker who
        steals any user's cookie gets persistent access until natural
        expiry OR until SESSION_SECRET rotation.
    The change_password action does NOT even DELETE/CLEAR the current
    admin's existing cookie from the response (no Set-Cookie with new
    token). So even the admin's own browser keeps using the pre-change
    cookie (which is still valid). The admin has no way to know which
    cookie an attacker may have stolen.
  Severity: CRITICAL
  PoC:

    # 3. Attacker waits 30 min, then performs admin action with the

      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      -d '{"username":"backdoor","password":"pwn3d123","role":"admin"}'
    # → HTTP 200, new admin user created. The stolen cookie is STILL

    # 4. Attacker retains admin access for up to 24h from T0

Q7. Is logout CSRF-protected?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ❌ FAIL — MED (same as F-NEW-6 / F-24, still open)
  Vulnerable code: src/app/api/user/logout/route.ts:7-11
    7: export async function POST() {
    8:   const response = NextResponse.json({ ok: true });
    9:   response.cookies.delete("access_session");
   10:   return response;

  Analysis:
    - POST handler takes NO request argument, performs NO auth check,
      performs NO Origin/CSRF validation.
    - /api/user/logout IS in PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES (middleware.ts:30) →
      EXEMPT from middleware's CSRF Origin check (line 158-159).
    - A cross-site form POSTed to /api/user/logout will:
        (a) Be ALLOWED through middleware (public API exemption)
        (b) Reach the route handler
        (c) Return Set-Cookie: access_session=; Max-Age=0; Path=/
        (d) Browser applies Set-Cookie to victim.com domain
        (e) Victim's existing access_session cookie is CLEARED
    - Cookie attributes on the LOGIN response (login/route.ts:106-112):
      httpOnly: true, secure: NODE_ENV==="production", sameSite: "strict".
      SameSite=strict PREVENTS the browser from SENDING the cookie on
      the cross-site POST, BUT the Set-Cookie from the response is
      applied based on the response's domain (victim.com), NOT on
      whether the cookie was sent. So the attacker's cross-site form
      DOES clear the victim's cookie even though the cookie is not
      included in the request.
    - Impact: nuisance / minor DoS. Victim must re-login. Attacker
      gains NOTHING (no credential exposure, no privilege escalation).

    breaks UX and could be chained with phishing — e.g. force logout,
    then redirect to fake login page to harvest credentials)

Q9. Is middleware matcher complete?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ PARTIAL — LOW-MED (NEW finding, not in SEC-02)
  Matcher (middleware.ts:220-228):
    "/((?!_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|.*\\.(?:png|jpg|jpeg|gif|
       webp|svg|ico|txt|xml|css|js|woff|woff2|ttf|eot)$).*)"
  POSITIVE coverage (confirmed by SEC-02 Q1, Q2):
    - /api/admin/*  ✅
    - /user-dashboard ✅
    - /api/messages ✅
    - /api/chat GET (admin view) ✅
    - /api/bale/webhook GET ✅
  NEGATIVE — matcher EXCLUDES any path ENDING in the listed extensions.
  Intended for static assets, but ALSO matches API paths that happen
  to end in `.css`/`.js`/etc:
    - /api/admin/users/foo.css  → matcher SKIPS middleware
    - /api/admin/clips.css      → matcher SKIPS middleware (but no route
      matches → 404, no harm)
    - /api/admin/users/.css     → matcher SKIPS middleware, route
      /api/admin/users/[id] is invoked with id=".css" → checkAdmin()
      rejects (no session) OR returns 404 user_not_found
  SKIPPED middleware checks on these paths:
    - Session gate (line 188-193)              — route handler catches via checkAdmin
    - CSRF Origin check (line 157-177)        — REAL BYPASS for POST/PUT/DELETE
    - Body-size limit (line 196-205)          — REAL BYPASS (DoS amplification)
    - Rate limit (line 144-155)               — N/A (no .css path is in RATE_LIMIT_PATHS)
    - Security headers (line 209-213)         — defense-in-depth gap
  Mitigating factors:
    - SameSite=strict on the access_session cookie (login/route.ts:109)
      BLOCKS cross-site cookie sending from a browser context. So even
      though CSRF check is skipped on /api/admin/users/foo.css, an
      attacker's cross-site <form> POST will NOT carry the victim's
      cookie. Route handler's checkAdmin rejects the unauthenticated
      request.
    - To exploit the CSRF-bypass, attacker MUST already possess a valid
      cookie (forged or stolen). Forged cookies are rejected by
      verifySessionToken. Stolen cookies already give the attacker full
      admin — CSRF bypass gains them nothing they don't already have.
  Net impact:
    - LOW-MED. SameSite=strict currently saves the day. The matcher
      design is fragile: if SameSite is ever weakened to Lax (e.g. for
      GET requests with top-level navigation), or if a future admin
      route accepts GET for state-changing actions (currently all
      state-changers are POST/PUT/DELETE — safe), the .css bypass
      becomes exploitable for CSRF.
    - Body-size limit bypass IS real: an attacker with a stolen cookie
      can POST huge bodies to /api/admin/users/foo.css, bypassing the
      1MB middleware cap. The route handler doesn't enforce its own
      limit. DoS amplification.
  Severity: LOW-MED (defense-in-depth gap; SameSite=strict saves today)
  PoC (body-size limit bypass — needs valid cookie):
    # Requires attacker to have stolen a valid access_session cookie:
    curl -s -X PUT "https://victim.com/api/admin/users/victim.css" \
      -H "Cookie: access_session=${STOLEN}" \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      --data-binary @huge_payload.bin
    # Middleware SKIPS (path ends in .css) → no 1MB check → request
    # reaches route handler. Route's checkAdmin passes (valid cookie).
    # body.password empty → data.passwordHash not set →
    # db.accessUser.update({where:{id:"victim.css"}}) → Prisma throws
    # "invalid cuid" → 500 server_error. Not exploitable for data
    # corruption, but bypasses body-size limit (DoS amplification).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Q10. Can attacker bypass via path traversal?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ✅ PASS — Next.js App Router normalizes URL paths before matcher applies
  Tested transformations (all normalized, no bypass):
    /api/admin/%2e%2e/user/login   → /api/admin/../user/login → /api/user/login
                                    (matched, public — no harm)
    /api/admin//users              → /api/admin/users (matched, gated)
    /api/admin/users/..%2fpublic   → /api/admin/users/../public → /api/public
                                    (matched, 404)
    /api/admin/users/             → Next.js redirects to /api/admin/users
                                    (canonical)
    /api/admin/users/%2e           → /api/admin/users/. → /api/admin/users
                                    (canonical)
    /%2F%2Fapi/admin/users          → //api/admin/users → /api/admin/users
                                    (matched, gated)
  Next.js internal normalization:
    - URL decoding (%2e → ., %2f → /, %5c → / on POSIX)
    - Redundant slash collapse (//  → /)
    - Dot-segment resolution (/./  → /, /../ → parent)
    - Trailing-slash canonicalization (with redirect)
  The matcher regex itself uses `.*\.(?:ext)$` exclusion which COULD
  match API paths ending in those extensions (see Q9), but this is a
  matcher-design issue, NOT a path-traversal issue. Raw `..` cannot
  reach route handlers — Next.js resolves it before routing.
  Severity: PASS (consistent with SEC-02 Q9)

1) fetchUsers
------------------------------------------------------------
Location: src/components/AccessUserManager.tsx:84-99
Invocation: src/components/AccessUserManager.tsx:81
  useEffect(() => { fetchUsers(); }, []);
Also re-invoked after every create/update/delete success:

Code (lines 84-99):
  async function fetchUsers() {
    setLoading(true);
    try {
      const res = await fetch("/api/admin/users", { cache: "no-store", credentials: "include" });
      const data = await res.json();
      if (data.ok) {
        setUsers(data.users);
      } else {
        setError(data.error || "load_failed");
      }
    } catch (e) {
      setError("network_error");
    } finally {
      setLoading(false);
    }
  }

Findings:
  ✅ POS: setLoading(true) before fetch (line 85), setLoading(false) in
       finally (line 97) — always resets, even on throw.
  ✅ POS: cache: "no-store" (line 87) — admin list is never cached by
       the browser/Next.js fetch layer, so newly created users appear
       immediately on the next call.
  ✅ POS: credentials: "include" present (line 87) — see §10.
  ✅ POS: data.ok branch updates state (line 90); else branch surfaces
       server-provided error string (line 92), falling back to
       "load_failed" if data.error is missing.
  ✅ POS: catch block (lines 94-95) sets error to "network_error" —
       not silently swallowed.

  ❌ NEG (MED — NO res.ok CHECK): Only `data.ok` is inspected (line 89),
       never `res.ok`. If the API returns 401/403/500 with a non-JSON
       body (e.g., Next.js error HTML page), `res.json()` throws → falls
       into catch → user sees the misleading "network_error" message
       even though the network was fine. The actual HTTP status is
       discarded.
  ❌ NEG (LOW — `catch (e)` SHADOWS ERROR): catch parameter `e` is
       declared (line 94) but never used. A 401 from a session-expired
       admin is indistinguishable from a DNS failure. Consider
       `if (e instanceof TypeError)` for true network errors vs.
       res.json() parse failures.
  ❌ NEG (LOW — NO RETRY ON ERROR): After the first load fails,
       `error` is set but no retry button is rendered. The user must
       navigate away and back to trigger another fetchUsers via the
       useEffect at line 80-82.

Verdict: FUNCTIONAL with proper loading + error state, but missing the
        res.ok check (similar antipattern to TextEditor §1).

  async function handleDelete(user: User) {
    if (!confirm(`حذف کاربر "${user.username}"؟ این کار غیرقابل بازگشت است.`)) return;
    try {
      const res = await fetch(`/api/admin/users/${user.id}`, { method: "DELETE", credentials: "include" });
      const data = await res.json();
      if (data.ok) {
        fetchUsers();
      } else {
        const msgs: Record<string, string> = {
          cannot_delete_self: "نمی‌توانید خودتان را حذف کنید.",
          user_not_found: "کاربر یافت نشد.",
          unauthorized: "دسترسی غیرمجاز.",
        };
        alert(msgs[data.error] || data.error);
      }
    } catch {
      alert("خطای شبکه");
    }
  }

Findings:
  ✅ POS: confirm() dialog at line 201 — destructive action is gated.
       Localized warning message.
  ✅ POS: DELETE method with credentials: "include" (line 203).
  ✅ POS: data.ok branch refreshes list (line 205-206).
  ✅ POS: Error code map covers cannot_delete_self, user_not_found,
       unauthorized (lines 208-212).
  ✅ POS: catch block at line 215-217 alerts "خطای شبکه".

  ❌ NEG (HIGH — INCONSISTENT ERROR UX): Uses alert() (lines 213, 216)
       instead of the `error` useState used elsewhere (fetchUsers line
       92, handleSubmit line 193). The error does NOT appear in the
       red error banner (lines 463-472) of the main view. The admin
       sees a browser-native alert dialog and the main view's `error`
       state remains empty. Inconsistent with §1/§2.
  ❌ NEG (HIGH — NO DELETE-LOADING STATE): No `deletingId` state. The
       trash button (line 520) stays clickable during the in-flight
       DELETE. Double-clicking fires two DELETEs in quick succession;
       the second returns "user_not_found" → alerts "کاربر یافت نشد"
       (confusing — the first delete succeeded but the alert implies
       failure).
  ❌ NEG (MED — NO res.ok CHECK, line 204-205): Same antipattern as §1,
       §2, §5.
  ❌ NEG (MED — `confirm()` IS BLOCKING): confirm() at line 201 blocks
       the main thread. In a future SSR/edge migration this would
       break. Also confirm() can be disabled by browser settings
       (rare). Acceptable for an admin tool but worth noting.
  ❌ NEG (LOW): Cannot tell from the UI which row is being deleted

Verdict: FUNCTIONAL but with three real issues: alert()-based error

      const data = await res.json();

Findings:

  ✅ POS: Limit=200 on the query string (line 104) — caps payload size.
  ✅ POS: On success, setShowLogs(true) at line 108 switches the
       component to the logs view (rendered at lines 233-269).

  ❌ NEG (CRITICAL — NO catch BLOCK): The try block at lines 103-109
       has only a `finally` (line 110), NO `catch`. If the fetch
       rejects (network down, DNS failure, CORS) or `res.json()`
       throws (non-JSON 401/500 body), the promise rejects UNHANDLED.
       Browser logs "Unhandled Promise Rejection" to console; user
       sees nothing. The Logs button (line 456) returns to its
       enabled state but the logs view never opens.

       logs view never opens. The admin clicks "Logs" and gets no

  ❌ NEG (HIGH — NO res.ok CHECK): Same antipattern as §1, §2, §4.
  ❌ NEG (MED — NO ERROR STATE FOR LOGS): Unlike fetchUsers (which

Verdict: FAIL — fetchLogs has the WORST error handling in the

       permission selector is only rendered when `form.role === "user"`
       (line 385). If the admin edits an existing user with role=user
       and permissions=["messages","clips"], then changes the Role
       dropdown to "admin" (lines 325-332), the permission UI
       disappears BUT form.permissions state retains ["messages","clips"].
       On submit, body.permissions = "messages,clips" is sent anyway
       (line 161). The server stores it (route.ts:79). The user is
       now an admin (which bypasses permission checks anyway), so

       "text", "nav", "themes". If the server-side permission list
       grows, this list must be manually kept in sync. No
       /api/admin/permissions endpoint to fetch them dynamically.

       a whitelist before submit. The server (route.ts:79) does
       `permissions: string | null` with no enum check, so a
       malicious admin (or XSS-injected form state) could store
       arbitrary strings like "ROOT_FULL_ACCESS" — but the server

       specific known ids, so unknown ids are simply ignored at
       access time. Still, defensive validation would be safer.

Verdict: PASS — permissions are correctly serialized, sent, and
        round-tripped. Caveats: stale permissions on role change,
        hardcoded list, no client-side validation.

7) allowedHours / allowedDays saved
------------------------------------------------------------
Location:
  allowedHourStart:
    Form state:    line 72  `allowedHourStart: "" as string | number`
    UI input:      lines 336-348 (type="number", min=0, max=23)
    Load on edit:  line 122  `allowedHourStart: user.allowedHourStart ?? ""`
    Submit body:   line 158  `allowedHourStart: form.allowedHourStart === "" ? null : Number(form.allowedHourStart)`

  allowedHourEnd:
    Form state:    line 73  `allowedHourEnd: "" as string | number`
    UI input:      lines 349-361 (type="number", min=0, max=23)
    Load on edit:  line 123  `allowedHourEnd: user.allowedHourEnd ?? ""`
    Submit body:   line 159  `allowedHourEnd: form.allowedHourEnd === "" ? null : Number(form.allowedHourEnd)`

  allowedDays:
    Form state:    line 74  `allowedDays: [] as number[]`
    UI buttons:    lines 364-382 (DAY_NAMES toggle, lines 46-54)
    Load on edit:  line 124  `allowedDays: user.allowedDays ? user.allowedDays.split(",").map(d => parseInt(d, 10)) : []`
    Submit body:   line 160  `allowedDays: form.allowedDays.length > 0 ? form.allowedDays.join(",") : null`

Server contract:
  - POST route.ts:76-78 accepts allowedHourStart/End (Number or null)
    and allowedDays (string or null). Range check 0-23 at route.ts:90-95.
  - PUT [id]/route.ts:49-55 same.
  - Both routes return "invalid_hour_start" / "invalid_hour_end" if
    out of range — these are mapped to Persian messages at lines
    186-187.

Findings:
  ✅ PASS (line 158): allowedHourStart coerced via Number() or null
       when empty string. Server validates 0-23 (route.ts:90).
  ✅ PASS (line 159): allowedHourEnd same handling.
  ✅ PASS (line 160): allowedDays joined with "," or null.
  ✅ PASS (lines 336-348, 349-361): HTML number inputs have min=0,
       max=23, so the browser blocks out-of-range values client-side.
  ✅ PASS (lines 367-377): DAY_NAMES toggle uses day.value (0-6),
       form.allowedDays.includes() for highlight state.
  ✅ PASS (line 124): On edit, allowedDays string is split and parsed
       back to numbers.
  ✅ PASS (server contract): Round-trip is symmetric.

  ❌ NEG (HIGH — NaN INJECTION ON EDIT): Line 124
       `user.allowedDays.split(",").map(d => parseInt(d, 10))` does
       NOT filter NaN. If the DB stores "0,abc,2" (e.g., from a
       malicious or corrupt write), parseInt("abc",10) returns NaN,
       and form.allowedDays becomes [0, NaN, 2]. On submit,
       `form.allowedDays.join(",")` (line 160) produces "0,NaN,2" —
       NaN serializes to the literal string "NaN" in JSON. The server
       stores "0,NaN,2" back. The DAY_NAMES toggle (line 372
       `form.allowedDays.includes(day.value)`) will NEVER match NaN
       (NaN !== NaN in JS), so the corrupt day buttons will not
       highlight, but the corrupt data persists in the DB. Data
       integrity leak across edits.
  ❌ NEG (MED — INDEPENDENT START/END ALLOWED): The UI does NOT
       enforce that allowedHourStart and allowedHourEnd are both set
       or both empty. The admin can set start=9 and leave end="",
       which sends `{allowedHourStart: 9, allowedHourEnd: null}` —
       the server stores it as-is. The access-check middleware will
       then likely treat missing end as "no upper bound" or
       "always denied" depending on implementation — undefined
       behavior at this layer.
  ❌ NEG (MED — NO CLIENT-SIDE START ≤ END CHECK): Setting start=20
       and end=8 is accepted by the form. Whether this means
       "20:00-08:00 wraparound" or "never accessible" depends on the
       server enforcement, which is not audited here. The form does
       not warn the user.
  ❌ NEG (LOW — EMPTY STRING vs NULL AMBIGUITY): Form uses "" as the
       "empty" sentinel for hours (lines 72-73), then converts to
       null on submit (lines 158-159). If a future refactor adds a
       "0" hour (midnight), Number("0")=0 ≠ null, so this works —
       but the dual-type `string | number` (line 72-73) is brittle.

Verdict: PASS for the happy path. Two real bugs: NaN injection on
        edit (data corruption risk) and independent start/end allows
        ambiguous state.

  Submit body:   line 162  `expiresAt: form.expiresAt ? new Date(form.expiresAt).toISOString() : null`

Server contract:

      `const expiresAt = body.expiresAt ? new Date(body.expiresAt) : null;`
  - PUT [id]/route.ts:57-59 same.

Findings:
  ✅ PASS (line 162): On submit, the YYYY-MM-DD date string from the
       `<input type="date">` is parsed via `new Date(form.expiresAt)`
       which (for date-only strings) is interpreted as UTC midnight,
       then `.toISOString()` produces e.g. "2026-12-31T00:00:00.000Z".
  ✅ PASS (line 126): On edit, the existing ISO string from the DB
       is converted back to YYYY-MM-DD for the date input. Round-trip
       is symmetric: DB "2026-12-31T00:00:00.000Z" → form "2026-12-31"
       → submit "2026-12-31T00:00:00.000Z".
  ✅ PASS (server contract): Server stores Date object; Prisma
       serializes to ISO string on read. Frontend reads ISO string.
       Round-trip preserved.
  ✅ PASS (lines 422-424): Helper text "خالی = بدون انقضا" makes
       the empty-state semantics explicit to the admin.

  ❌ NEG (MED — TIMEZONE DRIFT IN TABLE DISPLAY): Line 507
       `new Date(user.expiresAt).toLocaleDateString("fa-IR")` uses the
       BROWSER's local timezone. If the admin is in UTC-5 (US Eastern)
       and the DB stored "2026-12-31T00:00:00.000Z" (UTC midnight),
       `toLocaleDateString` displays "12/30/2026" (one day earlier).
       The form (line 126) uses UTC (`.toISOString().slice(0,10)`),
       but the table (line 507) uses local time — INCONSISTENT
       rendering of the same field across the same component.
  ❌ NEG (LOW — `new Date(invalid_string)` THROWS): Line 126 calls
       `new Date(user.expiresAt).toISOString()`. If user.expiresAt
       is somehow a non-ISO string (e.g., a future migration writes
       "Dec 31 2026"), `new Date(...)` returns Invalid Date, and
       `.toISOString()` throws RangeError. This would crash the
       startEdit handler (line 115) — the click on the edit button
       would do nothing visible (error in console). Defensive guard
       missing.
  ❌ NEG (LOW — DATE INPUT NOT BOUNDED): The `<input type="date">`
       at line 416 has no `min` attribute. The admin can set an
       expiry in the past (e.g., 2020-01-01), which would immediately
       deactivate the user upon save. Server (route.ts:80) accepts
       any date. May be intentional ("retroactive deactivation") or
       may be a footgun — no UX guidance either way.
  ❌ NEG (LOW — TIME PORTION LOST): `<input type="date">` only
       captures YYYY-MM-DD, no time. The DB column is a DateTime
       with full ISO timestamps. The form forces all expiries to
       UTC midnight. If an admin wants a user to expire at 5 PM
       tomorrow, they cannot — they must pick "tomorrow" which means
       "tomorrow 00:00 UTC". May be acceptable for an admin tool.

Verdict: PASS — expiresAt is correctly serialized and round-tripped.
        Caveats: timezone display inconsistency in the table,
        Invalid Date crash risk, no min-date guard.

--- Task ID: V17.4-SEC-18 ---
Agent: SEC-18 sub-agent (read-only audit, no fixes applied)
Task: Audit session revocation correctness across the auth surface
Scope: stateless HMAC session token implementation; client + server
  logout/password-change/role-change/deactivation paths; Prisma schema
  for revocation primitives; admin UI for force-logout capability.

================================================================================
ARCHITECTURE SUMMARY (verified by reading the source)
================================================================================
Session implementation: STATELESS HMAC token — there is NO server-side
session table.

Token format (src/lib/access-auth.ts:67-72 createSessionToken):
    base64( userId + "." + expiresAt + "." + HMAC_SHA256(userId + "." + expiresAt) )

verifySessionToken (src/lib/access-auth.ts:78-96) validates only:
  (a) base64 decodability,
  (b) 3-part structure,
  (c) expiresAt not yet reached,
  (d) HMAC signature matches HMAC(userId + "." + expiresAt).

The HMAC input is exclusively userId + expiresAt. There is no
tokenVersion, no passwordChangedAt, no IP/UA, no sessionId, and no
iat (issued-at) embedded in the token. The token is created once at
login (src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:85) and stored in the
`access_session` cookie (httpOnly, secure in prod, sameSite=strict,
maxAge=86400s = 24h, src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:106-112).

Confirmed via grep: NO `Session` model exists in prisma/schema.prisma.
The only `Session`-named model is `ChatSession` (schema.prisma:52-63)
which is the visitor-chat widget's conversation session — UNRELATED
to authentication. NO matches for `tokenVersion`, `passwordChangedAt`,
`sessionVersion`, `revokeAll`, `forceLogout`, `invalidate.*session` in
the src/ tree (the only matches are inside worklog.md from prior
audits — those references document the same gap; they were never acted
upon).

================================================================================
FINDINGS (by checklist item)
================================================================================

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Logout invalidates server-side state?  →  ❌ NO
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
File: src/app/api/user/logout/route.ts:7-11
  export async function POST() {
    const response = NextResponse.json({ ok: true });
    response.cookies.delete("access_session");
    return response;
  }

Logout does TWO things:
  (1) Deletes the `access_session` cookie in the HTTP response.
  (2) Returns {ok:true}.

Logout does NOT do any of the following:
  - Insert into a session-denylist table (no such table exists).
  - Bump a tokenVersion / sessionVersion counter on AccessUser.
  - Call db.accessUser.update(...).
  - Call logAccess(user.id, "logout", ...) — i.e., no audit-trail entry
    is written despite `logout` being a documented AccessLog action
    value (prisma/schema.prisma:424).
  - Touch the DB at all (no `db` import in the file — verified by
    reading the full file).

Consequence: the cookie value (which is a stateless HMAC token) remains
cryptographically valid until `expiresAt` (24h after issuance). If an
attacker captured the cookie value before the user clicked logout
(e.g., via XSS, log injection, proxy/MITM, browser-extension theft,
shared-device shoulder-surfing), the attacker can keep replaying that
cookie value against /api/admin/* endpoints with full privileges for
the remainder of the 24h window.

Severity: CRITICAL (stateless tokens without server-side revocation
make "logout" cosmetic from the perspective of a stolen-token attacker).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Password change invalidates sessions?  →  ❌ NO
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Two password-change code paths; BOTH fail to invalidate sessions.

PATH A — admin self-service (src/app/api/admin/security/route.ts:55-100,
  case "change_password"):
  Lines 87-91:
    const newHash = await hashPassword(newPassword);
    await db.accessUser.update({
      where: { id: adminUser.id },
      data: { passwordHash: newHash },
    });
  Only the `passwordHash` field is updated. No tokenVersion bump,
  no passwordChangedAt write, no session denylist insertion.
  The admin's own session cookie continues to work (good UX, bad
  security — there's no way for the admin to KNOW that all other
  sessions have been killed, because they haven't been).
  logAccess at line 96 writes action "password_changed" but writes
  no per-session revocation record.

PATH B — admin edits another user's password
  (src/app/api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts:67-69):
    if (body.password && body.password.length >= 6) {
      data.passwordHash = await hashPassword(body.password);
    }
  Again only updates `passwordHash`. Same gap as Path A.

PATH C — server-side script (scripts/reset-admin-password.sh:50):
    sqlite3 db/custom.db "UPDATE AccessUser SET passwordHash = '$HASH',
      active = 1 WHERE username = 'admin';"
  Direct DB write; bypasses application layer entirely; no session
  invalidation. (Note: also uses shell-string interpolation of $HASH
  into the SQL — separate SQL-injection risk if HASH ever contained
  a quote; out-of-scope for this audit.)

Consequence: changing the password does NOT log out any existing
session, including the attacker's stolen session. This is the
canonical "stolen cookie survives password change" vulnerability.

Severity: CRITICAL.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. User deactivation invalidates sessions?  →  ⚠️ PARTIAL
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Deactivation DOES stop FUTURE admin-API requests by the deactivated
user — but only via a per-request DB re-fetch, never via token-level
invalidation.

Mechanism (src/lib/admin-auth.ts:23-25 and src/lib/admin-session.ts:
16-18):
    const user = await db.accessUser.findUnique({ where: { id: session.userId } });
    if (!user || !user.active) return { ok: false };

Same check in src/app/api/admin/users/route.ts:25, [id]/route.ts:19,
logs/route.ts:16, and src/app/api/user/verify/route.ts:22-25 (via
checkAccess at access-auth.ts:114).

PUT /api/admin/users/[id] with body.active=false
  (admin/users/[id]/route.ts:60-65):
    if (body.active !== undefined) {
      data.active = Boolean(body.active);
      if (!data.active && body.deactivatedReason) {
        data.deactivatedReason = String(body.deactivatedReason);
      }
    }

What this achieves:
  ✅ The deactivated user's NEXT admin-API request is rejected (401).
  ✅ The verify endpoint returns access.allowed=false with reason
     "access_denied_inactive" (access-auth.ts:114).
  ✅ If the user reloads /user-dashboard, the dashboard's verify call
     (user-dashboard/page.tsx:98-113) will get ok:true but with
     access.allowed=false — the dashboard renders a "restricted"
     banner but does NOT auto-logout (the cookie stays in place).

What this does NOT achieve:
  ❌ The deactivated user's cookie/token remains cryptographically
     valid for the full 24h. Reactivation of the user at any point
     during that window RESURRECTS all previously-stolen cookies.
  ❌ The middleware (src/middleware.ts:70-93 hasValidSession) does
     NOT query the DB at all — it only checks token shape (line 87
     explicitly notes "در middleware نمی‌تونیم HMAC رو verify کنیم"
     / "we can't verify HMAC in middleware"). So a deactivated user
     can still pass middleware for protected routes that don't
     subsequently re-check the DB (though all admin routes DO re-check).
  ❌ The user-dashboard's verify call (user-dashboard/page.tsx:91-113)
     runs ONCE on mount with empty dep array. There is no polling,
     no setInterval, no focus-event re-verify. A user with an open
     dashboard tab when they get deactivated will see NO indication
     until they refresh the page or click a button that hits a
     DB-checking admin route (which will 401, but only then).
  ❌ /api/user/verify returns ok:true even when active=false
     (verify/route.ts:22-49): the user object is returned with
     active:false, but the response is "ok" so the dashboard
     thinks the session is valid. The dashboard's `accessAllowed`
     flag (user-dashboard/page.tsx:106) gates the warning banner,
     but the user's session cookie remains valid.
  ❌ The `access_session` cookie is NOT deleted on deactivation.
  ❌ No `logAccess(user.id, "logout", ...)` or
     `logAccess(user.id, "deactivated", ...)` is written by the
     admin's PUT call — the deactivation itself is unaudited
     (only the user's subsequent failed access attempts get logged
     via checkAccess reason).

Severity: HIGH (deactivation works at the API layer but a stolen
cookie for the deactivated user remains replayable for 24h, and
reactivation silently revives stolen tokens).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Role change invalidates sessions?  →  ❌ NO
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PUT /api/admin/users/[id] with body.role="user"
  (admin/users/[id]/route.ts:48):
    if (body.role !== undefined) data.role = body.role === "admin" ? "admin" : "user";

Only the `role` field is updated. No tokenVersion bump, no session
invalidation, no audit-log entry for the role change itself.

What this means in practice:
  - DEMOTION (admin → user):
    ✅ The demoted admin's NEXT admin-API request is rejected
       (admin-auth.ts:25 returns ok:false because role !== "admin").
    ❌ The demoted user's existing cookie stays valid until 24h
       expiry. Their /user-dashboard tab still shows admin tabs
       (because the dashboard's verify call ran once on mount with
       role:"admin" and is never re-run — user-dashboard/page.tsx:
       91-113 empty-dep-array useEffect).
    ❌ When the demoted user clicks an admin-tab button, the API
       returns 401 — but there's no auto-logout or "your role
       changed, please re-login" UX. The button just fails silently.
    ❌ Reactivation back to admin: previously-issued cookie works
       again with full admin privileges, no re-login needed.

  - PROMOTION (user → admin):
    ❌ The promoted user's existing cookie continues to work; on
       next verify call they'll see admin tabs. No re-login
       needed (this is "convenient" but means an attacker who
       stole a low-priv user's cookie before promotion gets admin
       access for free after promotion, until 24h expiry).

  - PERMISSIONS change (user.permissions field,
       admin/users/[id]/route.ts:56):
    Same story — only the `permissions` field is updated; no
    session invalidation. Dashboard doesn't re-fetch user
    permissions, so the open-tab user keeps seeing the old
    permission set until they reload.

Severity: HIGH.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. tokenVersion column?  →  ❌ NO
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
File: prisma/schema.prisma:380-415 (model AccessUser)

Existing fields on AccessUser:
  id, username, passwordHash, displayName, role, permissions,
  allowedHourStart, allowedHourEnd, allowedDays, expiresAt, active,
  loginCount, lastLoginAt, deactivatedReason, createdAt, updatedAt.

MISSING fields (verified by grep on entire src/ tree and prisma/):
  - tokenVersion
  - sessionVersion
  - tokensValidSince
  - passwordChangedAt
  - passwordUpdatedAt

The token's HMAC payload (access-auth.ts:69 `${userId}.${expiresAt}`)
incorporates NO revocable state. Even if a `tokenVersion` column
existed, the current `createSessionToken` and `verifySessionToken`
functions would not consult it.

Severity: CRITICAL (this is THE root cause of findings #1, #2, #4,
#7, and partially #3 and #10).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. passwordChangedAt column?  →  ❌ NO
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Same AccessUser model (schema.prisma:380-415). No
`passwordChangedAt`, no `passwordUpdatedAt`, no `mustChangePassword`.

The closest existing field is `lastLoginAt` (schema.prisma:404), but
that is updated only on successful LOGIN (login/route.ts:90), never
on password change. So even if verifySessionToken wanted to compare
token-issue-time vs password-change-time, there is no
password-change timestamp to compare against — and the token does
not embed an issue-time (`iat`) anyway (access-auth.ts:69 payload is
only `userId + "." + expiresAt`).

Severity: CRITICAL (root cause of finding #7).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Stolen cookie valid after password change?  →  ❌ YES (for 24h)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Proof by trace:

  Step 1. Attacker exfiltrates victim's `access_session` cookie
          value (via XSS, log injection, MITM, shared device,
          browser extension, etc.).

  Step 2. Victim notices, changes password via
          POST /api/admin/security {action:"change_password",
          currentPassword, newPassword}
          (admin/security/route.ts:55-100).

  Step 3. Server updates only passwordHash
          (admin/security/route.ts:88-91). No tokenVersion bump,
          no passwordChangedAt write, no session denylist insertion.

  Step 4. Attacker replays the captured cookie value against
          /api/admin/users (or any admin route).

  Step 5. Server validates the cookie via getSessionFromRequest
          (access-auth.ts:186-201) → verifySessionToken
          (access-auth.ts:78-96):
            - base64 decodes ✅
            - splits into 3 parts ✅
            - expiresAt not passed ✅ (it's still < 24h old)
            - HMAC matches HMAC(userId + "." + expiresAt) ✅
              (HMAC input is unchanged by password change!)
            → returns { userId, expiresAt } — VALID SESSION.

  Step 6. checkAdminAuth (admin-auth.ts:20-27) re-fetches the user
          from DB. user still exists, user.active is still true,
          user.role is still "admin" — all checks pass.

  Step 7. Attacker receives admin-level response.

The cookie continues to authenticate the attacker for the FULL 24h
window (maxAge: 60*60*24, login/route.ts:111) — i.e., until the
victim's next logout-and-login cycle on the victim's own device, OR
24 hours elapse, whichever comes first.

There is NO way for the victim or any admin to revoke the stolen
cookie before the 24h window expires (see finding #10).

Severity: CRITICAL.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
8. Session bound to IP/UA?  →  ❌ NO
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Token payload (access-auth.ts:69):
    const payload = `${userId}.${expiresAt}`;
That's the entire payload. No IP, no User-Agent, no fingerprint,
no device-id, no `aud` (audience), no `iss` (issuer).

verifySessionToken (access-auth.ts:78-96) does NOT consult
request.headers["x-forwarded-for"], ["x-real-ip"], or
["user-agent"]. Those headers are only read in:
  - logAccess/getClientIp (access-auth.ts:155-181) — for audit
    logging into AccessLog.ip/userAgent columns (schema.prisma:
    425-426). Audit-only; never consulted at auth time.
  - login/route.ts:46-47 — recorded at login time, again for
    audit purposes only.

Consequence: a cookie captured on the victim's home Wi-Fi can be
replayed from a Tor exit node, a VPS in another country, or any
other IP/UA combination without any server-side rejection.

Severity: HIGH (IP binding is a defense-in-depth primitive; without
it, the blast radius of a stolen cookie is global rather than
constrained to the victim's network).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
9. Session rotation?  →  ❌ NO
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
There is NO token rotation during the 24h lifetime.

The token is minted ONCE at login (login/route.ts:85) and never
refreshed. Specifically:
  - verifySessionToken (access-auth.ts:78-96) returns
    {userId, expiresAt} — it does NOT issue a new cookie, does NOT
    extend expiresAt, does NOT call response.cookies.set.
  - /api/user/verify (verify/route.ts:16-50) does NOT set a
    Set-Cookie header on its response. The response is pure JSON.
  - middleware (middleware.ts:138-215) does NOT refresh cookies.
    It reads the cookie, calls hasValidSession (middleware.ts:70-93),
    and either rejects or calls NextResponse.next() with security
    headers — never sets a new access_session cookie.
  - No other code path in src/ writes the access_session cookie
    except login/route.ts:106-112 (verified by grep on
    "cookies.set\(\"access_session\"" across src/ — only 1 match).

Consequence: a token issued at T0 with maxAge=86400 stays
bit-for-bit identical until T0+86400. An attacker who captures it
once has the SAME valid credential for 24h. Even with server-side
session tables, rotation is the standard defense against the
"slow-listening attacker" pattern (passive capture + replay). Here,
rotation does not exist.

Severity: MEDIUM-HIGH (rotation is a defense-in-depth; combined
with the lack of revocation, the practical impact is HIGH).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
10. Admin can force-logout user?  →  ❌ NO
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
There is NO force-logout endpoint. There is NO UI button for it.
There is NO server-side primitive that would enable it.

Searches performed (all returning NO matches):
  - rg "force.logout|forceLogout|force_logout" → 0 matches in src/
  - rg "revoke.*session|terminate.*session|invalidate.*session"
    → 0 matches in src/ (1 match in worklog.md documenting the gap)
  - rg "tokenVersion|passwordChangedAt|password_changed_at|token_version"
    → 0 matches in src/ or prisma/ (matches only in worklog.md)
  - rg "session.*denylist|denylist.*session|sessionBlacklist"
    → 0 matches

Available admin actions on a user (AccessUserManager.tsx:519-520):
    <button onClick={() => startEdit(user)}>✏️</button>
    <button onClick={() => handleDelete(user)}>🗑️</button>

  ✏️ Edit (PUT /api/admin/users/[id]):
    Can change displayName, role, allowedHours, allowedDays,
    permissions, expiresAt, active, password.
    Setting active=false achieves per-request deactivation
    (see finding #3) but does NOT invalidate the user's existing
    access_session cookie.
    Setting password=... only updates passwordHash (see #2).

  🗑️ Delete (DELETE /api/admin/users/[id]):
    Cascades to AccessLog (schema.prisma:423 onDelete:Cascade).
    BUT: the user's access_session cookie remains valid for the
    full 24h! After deletion, getSessionFromRequest still
    returns the userId, but checkAdminAuth
    (admin-auth.ts:23 `if (!user ...)`) returns false because
    findUnique returns null. So delete DOES effectively block
    subsequent admin-API requests. HOWEVER:
      - The deleted user's cookie is still cryptographically
        valid (just happens to point at a non-existent user row).
      - If the admin re-creates a user with the SAME id (cuid
        collisions are astronomically unlikely but possible via
        DB restore from backup), the old cookie "comes back to
        life" with full new-user privileges.
      - There is no audit trail of "admin deleted user X to
        force-logout" — the DELETE route
        (admin/users/[id]/route.ts:100-126) does not call
        logAccess() before or after the delete.

  No "Logout all sessions" / "Revoke tokens" / "Force re-login"
  button exists anywhere in AccessUserManager.tsx (lines 56-578),
  SecurityDashboard.tsx, or SettingsPanel.tsx.

After admin deactivates a user via PUT active=false:
  - The user's open dashboard tab continues to function (the
    dashboard's verify ran once on mount with active:true,
    user-dashboard/page.tsx:91-113, and is never re-run).
  - The user's access_session cookie remains in their browser.
  - On next /api/admin/* call, the request returns 401 — but
    the dashboard's fetch wrappers (e.g., AccessUserManager
    fetchUsers line 87-99) just show an "unauthorized" error,
    they do NOT auto-redirect to /user-login or clear the
    cookie.

Severity: HIGH (no revocation primitive exists; admin cannot
respond to a credential-compromise incident in less than 24h).

================================================================================
EXTRA FINDINGS (outside the 10-item checklist)
================================================================================

E1. MIDDLEWARE SESSION CHECK IS CRYPTOGRAPHICALLY WEAK
    File: src/middleware.ts:70-93 (hasValidSession)
    Lines 87-89 (translated from Persian):
      // In middleware we can't verify HMAC because we don't have
      // access to SESSION_SECRET. We only check the structure —
      // the main API route verifies HMAC itself.
    Consequence: a token with a wrong-but-well-formed HMAC passes
    middleware's session check (line 188 `pathname.startsWith("/api/admin/")`
    gate at middleware.ts:188). The downstream API route
    (verifySessionToken → timingSafeEqual at access-auth.ts:91) then
    rejects it. So security is maintained (defense-in-depth), but
    middleware's "session check" is effectively a structure check,
    not an auth check.

E2. /api/user/verify NEVER DELETES THE COOKIE ON FAILURE
    File: src/app/api/user/verify/route.ts:16-50
    When session is invalid (line 18-20) or user not found (line
    22-25), the response is `{ok:false}` with NO Set-Cookie header.
    The browser keeps the invalid cookie, which it will keep
    sending on subsequent requests until expiry. Minor inefficiency
    and a small fingerprinting leak (server can identify returning
    browsers with stale cookies).

E3. /api/user/verify DOES NOT LOG SUCCESSFUL VERIFICATIONS
    File: src/app/api/user/verify/route.ts:27-31
    logAccess is called only when `!access.allowed` (line 28-30).
    Successful verifications are not audited. So there's no record
    of "user X accessed the dashboard at time T from IP Y". The
    AccessLog table only captures login_success / login_failed /
    access_denied_* / password_changed / password_change_failed
    events — never routine dashboard accesses.

E4. NO LOG ENTRY ON DEACTIVATION OR ROLE CHANGE
    File: src/app/api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts:27-95 (PUT)
    The PUT handler updates active / role / password without
    calling logAccess(). So admin actions against users
    (deactivate, promote, demote, password-reset) are completely
    unaudited. The only audit trail is in the victim's subsequent
    AccessLog rows (which capture the access-denied reason, not
    the admin action that caused it). This makes incident
    forensics very difficult.

E5. NO LOG ENTRY ON DELETE
    File: src/app/api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts:100-126 (DELETE)
    Same problem as E4 — db.accessUser.delete is called without
    a preceding logAccess entry. Once the user row is gone, all
    their AccessLog rows cascade-delete too (schema.prisma:423
    onDelete:Cascade), erasing the audit trail entirely.

E6. ACCESSLOG.LOGOUT ENUM IS DEAD CODE
    File: prisma/schema.prisma:424
    Action enum documents "logout" as a valid value, but the
    logout endpoint (logout/route.ts:7-11) never writes such a
    log entry. The schema documents an audit event that never
    occurs.

E7. SESSION DURATION IS FIXED AT 24H, NOT CONFIGURABLE
    File: src/lib/access-auth.ts:44
      const SESSION_DURATION_HOURS = 24;
    Hard-coded; no env override; no per-role duration (admin vs
    user). Combined with no rotation (#9) and no revocation (#10),
    the 24h window is the ONLY upper bound on stolen-cookie
    lifetime after a compromise.

E8. RESET-ADMIN-PASSWORD.SH DOES NOT INVALIDATE SESSIONS
    File: scripts/reset-admin-password.sh:50
      sqlite3 db/custom.db "UPDATE AccessUser SET passwordHash = '$HASH',
        active = 1 WHERE username = 'admin';"
    Direct DB UPDATE; bypasses application layer; no session
    invalidation. Also re-activates the user (active = 1), which
    resurrects any previously-stolen cookies for the admin account.
    (Side issue: shell-string interpolation of $HASH into SQL is
    a minor SQL-injection risk if HASH ever contained a single
    quote — bcrypt hashes use $ and . and / and A-Za-z0-9, no
    quotes, so practically safe today, but fragile.)

E9. NO CONCURRENT-SESSION LIMIT
    No code path limits the number of valid sessions per user.
    An attacker can log in as the victim an unlimited number of
    times (subject only to the 5-attempts/15-min rate limit at
    login/route.ts:20-34, which is per-IP not per-user). Once in,
    each login issues a fresh 24h cookie — so a successful
    credential-stuffing attack results in unlimited sessions.

E10. NO RE-AUTHENTICATION FOR SENSITIVE ACTIONS
     Password change (admin/security/route.ts:55-100) does
     require `currentPassword` (line 76) — GOOD. But other
     sensitive actions (DELETE user, role change, deactivate)
     do NOT require re-authentication. An attacker who steals
     an admin's session cookie can immediately demote, delete,
     or deactivate other users without any further check.

================================================================================
ROOT-CAUSE CHAIN
================================================================================
All 10 findings trace back to ONE architectural choice: the session
token is a stateless HMAC over (userId, expiresAt) with NO revocable
state embedded in the token and NO server-side session table to
revoke against. Specifically:

  - access-auth.ts:67-72 createSessionToken encodes userId + expiresAt
    + HMAC(userId + expiresAt). No version, no iat, no IP/UA.
  - access-auth.ts:78-96 verifySessionToken validates only signature
    + expiry. No DB lookup, no version check.
  - prisma/schema.prisma:380-415 AccessUser has no tokenVersion /
    passwordChangedAt / tokensValidSince columns.
  - prisma/schema.prisma has no Session model (only ChatSession:52
    which is unrelated visitor-chat data).
  - logout/route.ts:7-11 only deletes the client cookie; never
    touches DB.
  - admin/security/route.ts:88-91 and admin/users/[id]/route.ts:
    67-69 only update passwordHash; never bump any version.
  - middleware.ts:70-93 only checks token shape; cannot verify
    HMAC (no SESSION_SECRET access) and cannot query DB (no db
    import).

================================================================================
TOP-3 MOST IMPACTFUL ISSUES (advisory only — DO NOT FIX per task)
================================================================================
1. CRITICAL (#5 + #6 + #7 + #1): No tokenVersion / passwordChangedAt
   column on AccessUser. The session token is a stateless HMAC over
   immutable inputs, so password change and logout have zero effect
   on stolen cookies. FIX: add `tokenVersion Int @default(0)` AND
   `passwordChangedAt DateTime?` to AccessUser (schema.prisma:380-
   415); embed both in the token payload at access-auth.ts:69; bump
   tokenVersion in admin/security/route.ts:88-91 (password change),
   admin/users/[id]/route.ts:67-69 (password change), and at
   logout/route.ts (logout); reject mismatches in
   verifySessionToken.

2. HIGH (#10): No force-logout endpoint or UI. Admin cannot respond
   to a credential-compromise incident in less than 24h. FIX: add
   PUT /api/admin/users/[id]/force-logout that bumps the user's
   tokenVersion; add a "🚪 Force logout" button in
   AccessUserManager.tsx:519-520 alongside Edit/Delete.

3. HIGH (#3 + #4 + client UX): Even per-request DB re-checks
   (admin-auth.ts:23-25) only take effect on the NEXT API call.
   The dashboard (user-dashboard/page.tsx:91-113) verifies once
   on mount and never re-verifies — so a demoted/deactivated user
   with an open tab sees stale admin UI until they reload. FIX:
   add a setInterval that calls /api/user/verify every 60s and
   force-redirects to /user-login on ok:false or role-change.

Final verdict:
  Of the 10 audit questions: 0 PASS, 1 PARTIAL (#3 — per-request
  DB re-fetch partially mitigates deactivation for admin routes
  only), 9 FAIL. The auth system is functional for the happy path
  (login → use → close tab → cookie expires in 24h) but lacks
  EVERY standard session-revocation primitive: no server-side
  session table, no tokenVersion, no passwordChangedAt, no IP/UA
  binding, no rotation, no force-logout endpoint, no audit trail
  for admin mutations, no re-verification polling on the client.

  Most critically, the documented "logout" and "change password"
  actions are COSMETIC from an attacker's perspective: a stolen
  cookie continues to authenticate for the full 24h lifetime
  regardless of either action. This is the canonical stateless-
  token-without-revocation vulnerability. Prior audits (worklog.md
  lines 796, 801, 804, 878, 891, 1007, 1040, 2241, 6727-6778,
  7322, 7427-7572, 11842-12511) have repeatedly documented this
  exact gap; the gap remains unfixed as of V17.4-SEC-18.

Q4. Touch targets >= 44px?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ❌ NO — virtually every interactive element is below the 44px minimum.

  WCAG 2.5.5 / Apple HIG / Material Design all require ≥44px (or 48dp)
  minimum touch target.

  Buttons:
    - `.btn` (personal.css:267-283): padding 10px 20px, fontSize 0.85rem,
      border 1px → height = 10+10+16.3+2 = ~38px. ❌
    - `.btn-sm` (line 310): padding 6px 12px, fontSize 0.78rem → ~29px. ❌
    - `.dashboard-btn` (line 3167-3183): padding 8px 14px, fontSize 11px,
      border 1px → ~33px. ❌
    - `.dashboard-tab` (line 3248-3261): padding 9px 14px, fontSize 11px,
      border 1px, border-radius 6px → ~35px. ❌
    - `.admin-tab` (line 1661-1672): padding 8px 14px, fontSize 0.78rem,
      border-bottom 2px → ~33px. ❌
    - `.tutorial-filter` (line 1739-1749): padding 5px 12px, fontSize
      0.72rem → ~24px. ❌
    - `.tutorial-modal-close` (line 1067-1076): padding 4px 10px, fontSize
      0.75rem → ~23px. ❌
    - `.lang-toggle button` (line 438-448): padding 5px 9px, fontSize
      inherit (0.72rem) → ~24px. ❌
    - `.theme-switcher button` (line 2064-2076): padding 5px 8px, fontSize
      0.72rem → ~24px. ❌
    - `.signal-waveform-btn` (line 2213-2231): padding 6px 4px, fontSize
      0.68rem → ~22px. ❌
    - `.osc-arrow-btn` (line 2393-2403): padding 5px 10px, fontSize 0.8rem
      → ~25px. ❌
    - `.lab-visualize-btn` (line 2553-2564): padding 6px, fontSize 0.72rem
      → ~22px. ❌
    - `.lab-visualizer-close` (line 2590-2603): width 20px, height 20px
      → 20px×20px. ❌❌ (way below 44px; nearly untappable)
    - `.to-top` (line 1232-1250): width 36px, height 36px → 36×36. ❌
    - `.nav-toggle` (line 456-473): padding 6px 8px, contains 3 spans
      18×1px with 4px gap → total content 11px + padding 12px = ~23px
      tall × ~32px wide. ❌

  Tab buttons:
    - Same as `.dashboard-tab` and `.admin-tab` above. ❌

  Links acting as buttons:
    - `.nav-links a` mobile (line 1378-1382): padding 10px 12px, fontSize
      0.95rem, border 1px → ~38px. ❌ Closest to passing.
    - `.footer-links a` (line 1218-1223): fontSize 0.75rem, no padding
      declared → inherits from `<a>` (line 188-196) which has no padding
      → height = 0.75rem × 1.65 (body line-height) = ~20px. ❌
    - `.brand` (line 384-392): fontSize 1rem, no padding → ~26px tall. ❌

  Toggle switches:
    - `.admin-toggle` (line 2005-2033): width 44px, height 22px → 44×22.
      ❌ (height too small; tap area is 44×22 = barely tappable).

  Severity: HIGH. The entire UI fails WCAG 2.5.5. Users with motor
    impairments, users on cold/foggy touchscreens, and users with phone
    cases will all have frequent mis-taps. Recommended fix: bump every
    button padding to ≥11px vertical (12px ideal) and font-size to 16px
    on inputs to also fix the iOS zoom issue (see Q3).

Q5. Horizontal scroll issues?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ MIXED — body clips overflow, but several internal grids overflow.

  Body-level guard:
    - `body { overflow-x: hidden }` (personal.css:150). ✓
    - Effect: anything wider than viewport is CLIPPED (not scrollable).
      Good for preventing ugly body scroll; BAD for hiding content that
      should be reachable.

  Confirmed overflow / clip issues:
    1. ContentManager admin-tabs (see Q2): 6 tabs × ~85px = 510px in a
       312px-wide container → 2 rightmost tabs ("AI Rules", "Equipment")
       CLIPPED on phones. (src/components/ContentManager.tsx:184;
       personal.css:1655 has no flex-wrap/overflow.)
    2. AccessUserManager logs table (see Q1): 5-col table ~570px wide,
       no overflowX wrapper → Details and IP columns CLIPPED on phones.
       (src/components/AccessUserManager.tsx:240-265)
    3. Navbar right cluster (page.tsx:508-537): `.nav-right` contains
       `.theme-switcher` (7 buttons × ~25px = 175px) + `.lang-toggle`
       (3 buttons × ~30px = 90px) + `.nav-toggle` button (~32px) = ~297px.
       At viewport=360px with container padding 16px×2=32px, available
       width = 328px. The `.nav-inner` is `display: flex; justify-content:
       space-between` (personal.css:378-383) with brand on the left.
       Brand (~80px) + nav-right (~297px) = 377px > 328px → overflow ~50px
       → CLIPPED. The rightmost buttons (theme-switcher's "clean" theme
       + lang-toggle's "DE" button + nav-toggle hamburger) may be cut off
       or wrapped if `flex-wrap: wrap` were set — but it's NOT.
       Severity: HIGH (hamburger menu may be unreachable on phones
       <= 380px, defeating the entire mobile nav).
    4. Status bar (page.tsx:437-461): at 720px breakpoint,
       `.statusbar-item .label` is hidden (personal.css:1358). But the
       values remain: "online" + "-67dBm" + "2.4GHz" (left) + time +
       "/dev/pts/0" (right). At viewport=360px with statusbar padding
       4px 10px (mobile): "online -67dBm 2.4GHz" ~150px + time
       (fa-IR shamsi ~120px) + "/dev/pts/0" ~80px = 350px. Fits 360px
       barely. At 320px viewport → overflows by ~30px → CLIPPED.
       Severity: LOW (rare device widths).
    5. reCAPTCHA on contact form (see Q3): 304px wide in a 240-280px
       container at viewport 320-379px → 24-64px clipped right edge →
       checkbox unreachable.
       Severity: HIGH on small phones.
    6. Hero socials (page.tsx:552-565): `.hero-socials` has `flex-wrap:
       wrap` (personal.css:524-529) → wraps to multiple lines on mobile,
       no overflow. ✓
    7. Hero CTA (page.tsx:548-551): `.hero-cta` is flex with gap 10px,
       `flex-wrap: wrap` (line 521). At 480px breakpoint (personal.css:
       1389) becomes `flex-direction: column` and `.btn { width: 100% }`
       (line 1390). ✓
    8. Oscilloscope / SpectrumAnalyzer canvases: `width: 100%`
       (personal.css:1437-1439, 1803-1807) → no overflow. ✓
    9. Tables in admin (users, logs): users table HAS overflowX:auto
       wrapper (good); logs table DOES NOT (see #2).

  Severity overall: HIGH. The 3 worst cases (#1 admin tabs clipped, #3
    navbar right cluster clipped on phones <= 380px, #5 reCAPTCHA on
    small phones) directly block core admin and contact-form functionality.

Q7. Iframes responsive?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ✅ MOSTLY YES.

  Tutorial modal iframe (PASS):
    - `.tutorial-modal-video { aspect-ratio: 16/9; background: #000 }`
      (personal.css:1081-1086). ✓
    - `.tutorial-modal-video iframe { position: absolute; inset: 0; width:

    - Iframe fills its aspect-ratio:16/9 parent — responsive.
    - src URL is validated to aparat.com / youtube.com / youtu.be /
      player.vimeo.com (page.tsx:853-866). ✓

  Aparat clip iframes (PASS):
    - Parent div inline `style={{ aspectRatio: "16/9", background: "#000"
       }}` (page.tsx:724-727). ✓
    - sanitize-embed.ts:41 emits `<iframe src="..." frameborder="0"
      allowfullscreen style="width:100%;height:100%;border:0;">`. ✓
    - Iframe fills 16/9 parent — responsive.

  reCAPTCHA iframe (PARTIAL FAIL on small phones):
    - Container `.g-recaptcha` (page.tsx:791-795) — Google's script
      injects an iframe at fixed 304×78px.
    - At viewport 320-379px, the contact form's effective inner width is
      240-280px → reCAPTCHA's 304px overflows by 24-64px → CLIPPED by
      body overflow-x:hidden → checkbox unreachable.
    - Severity: HIGH on small phones (≤379px viewport).

  Severity overall: LOW-MED. Embedded iframes are responsive; only
    Google's reCAPTCHA (whose dimensions we don't control) breaks on
    small phones. Mitigation: wrap `.g-recaptcha` in a `transform:
    scale(0.9)` container on small screens, or use the compact
    `data-size="compact"` reCAPTCHA variant (154×74px).

5. SSRF (AI providers, Bale, Telegram, formsubmit, reCAPTCHA)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ MED — AI provider baseUrl is admin-controllable and used in fetch
  without URL scheme/host validation.
  Findings:

    (a) src/lib/providers.ts:99,127,151,171,194  (MED — admin-configurable
        SSRF, host fully attacker-controlled)
        Code (callOpenAI, line 99):
          const baseUrl = provider.baseUrl || "https://api.openai.com/v1";
          const res = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/chat/completions`, { ... });
        Code (callOllama, line 151):
          const baseUrl = provider.baseUrl || "http://localhost:11434";
          const res = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/api/chat`, { ... });
        Code (callGroq, line 171):
          const baseUrl = provider.baseUrl || "https://api.groq.com/openai/v1";
        Code (callCustom, line 194): delegates to callOpenAI.
        Source: `provider.baseUrl` comes from AiProvider table, writable
        via /api/admin/providers POST `action: "create"|"update"` (lines
        60-93 of /api/admin/providers/route.ts).
        POST /api/admin/providers accepts:
          baseUrl: data.baseUrl ? String(data.baseUrl) : null
        with NO URL validation. Admin (or anyone who has compromised
        admin) can set baseUrl to:
          - "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/" (AWS/GCP metadata)
          - "http://internal-service.local:8080/"
          - "http://localhost:6379/" (Redis probe)
        The `/chat/completions` path is appended, so the actual URL is
        e.g. `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/chat/completions`.
        But the attacker can choose the path by setting baseUrl to
        `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` and using the OpenAI
        flow, OR can use a baseUrl ending with `/../../` to manipulate
        the path (e.g. baseUrl = "http://evil.com/api/x/../y" → fetch
        follows to "http://evil.com/api/y").
        The Authorization header is set to `Bearer ${provider.apiKey}` —
        so the attacker's API key would leak in the Authorization header
        to the attacker-controlled host if baseUrl is set to attacker's
        host. Reverse: attacker can use this to capture their own API
        key, but that's a self-attack.
        Impact:
          - Admin-authenticated SSRF. Bypassable only with admin creds
            (which the rest of the audit shows has issues — F-1 etc.).
          - Allows scanning internal network, AWS metadata endpoint,
            localhost services.
          - POST body and Authorization header are sent to the target.
        Severity: MED (admin-gated, but full SSRF if admin is
          compromised or malicious).

    (b) /api/contact/route.ts:163  (LOW — host fixed to formsubmit.co,
        only path is controllable)
        Code:
          await fetch(`https://formsubmit.co/ajax/${forwardEmail}`, { ... });
        Source: `forwardEmail` is read from SiteSetting table. The
        setting is ONLY writable via /api/admin/email POST
        action:"set_email" (line 47-58), which checks `email.includes("@")`
        but does NOT validate against URL path traversal characters.
        If admin sets forwardEmail = "x@y.com/../../attacker.com:8080",
        the URL becomes:
          https://formsubmit.co/ajax/x@y.com/../../attacker.com:8080

7. JSON.parse VALIDATION
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ LOW — All JSON.parse calls are wrapped in try/catch, EXCEPT one
  where the parsed value is re-stringified without validation.
  Findings:
    (a) /api/admin/equipment/route.ts:26-28  (PASS)
        Code:

          catch { specs = null; /* در صورت خرابی، null بده نه 500 */ }
        Wrapped. On failure, sets `specs = null` instead of throwing.
        Response: 200 with null specs. Safe.

    (b) /api/admin/equipment/route.ts:112  (PASS)
        Code (bulk_import, validating string specs):
          try { JSON.parse(item.specs); data.specs = item.specs; }
          catch { failed++; errors.push(`invalid specs JSON for ${data.nameFa || data.nameEn}`); continue; }
        Wrapped. On failure, skips the item with an error message.
        Safe.

    (c) /api/content/route.ts:51-52  (PASS)
        Code:
          try { return JSON.parse(e.specs); }
          catch { return null; /* در صورت خرابی، null بده نه 500 */ }
        Wrapped. Safe.

    (d) /components/ContentManager.tsx:106-119  (PASS — client-side)
        Code:
          try {
            const parsed = JSON.parse(bulkText);
            if (!Array.isArray(parsed)) { alert("Must be JSON array"); return; }
            ...
          } catch { alert("Invalid JSON"); }
        Wrapped + type check. Safe.

    (e) /api/admin/equipment/route.ts:57-58, 67-68  (LOW — unvalidated
        JSON.stringify of arbitrary object into specs column)
        Code (create case, lines 55-59):
          const data = body.data || {};
          if (data.specs && typeof data.specs === "object") {
            data.specs = JSON.stringify(data.specs);
          }
          const created = await db.labEquipment.create({ data });
        Code (update case, lines 65-69): same pattern.
        Impact:
          - `data.specs` is whatever object the admin sends. It's
            stringified and stored. On read-back, JSON.parse is wrapped
            in try/catch (see (a)). So no DoS.
          - But there's no depth/size limit on the JSON.stringify.
            A 1MB JSON body (the middleware limit at middleware.ts:198)
            can produce a ~1MB specs string. Stored in SQLite TEXT
            column. No practical DoS given the 1MB body cap.
        Severity: LOW.

    (f) Middleware body size limit:
        src/middleware.ts:196-204 enforces Content-Length <= 1MB on
        POST/PUT/PATCH. JSON.parse on a 1MB body is well within V8's
        safe envelope (no stack overflow / no OOM).
        But: middleware trusts the Content-Length header (see prior
        SEC-02 audit Q6 — WEAK). Chunked transfer-encoding bypasses
        the check. Then JSON.parse on an attacker-controlled
        unbounded chunked body could cause OOM. This is the prior
        Q6 finding; not a JSON.parse bug per se.
        Severity: LOW (inherits from Q6).

  Net severity: LOW (all parse calls are try/catch-wrapped; the only
    gap is unbounded JSON.stringify, mitigated by 1MB body cap).

8. ReDoS
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ LOW-MED — One regex has O(n²) worst-case behavior.
  Findings:

    (a) /api/contact/route.ts:29  (LOW-MED)
        Code:
          const spamPatterns = [
            /\b(viagra|cialis|casino|lottery|prize|winner|bitcoin investment)\b/,
            /(https?:\/\/[^\s]+){3,}/, // 3+ URLs
            /(.)\1{10,}/, // 11+ of same char in a row
          ];
          return spamPatterns.some((re) => re.test(lower));
        Analysis:
          - Pattern 1: alternation of fixed strings with \b anchors.
            Linear time. Safe.
          - Pattern 2: `(https?:\/\/[^\s]+){3,}` — `[^\s]+` greedy match
            terminates at first whitespace; no overlap with the
            next iteration's `https?://`. Linear time. Safe.
          - Pattern 3: `/(.)\1{10,}/` — captures one char and
            requires 11+ of the SAME char in a row. Worst case:
            input with no match (e.g., "abcdefabcdef...") forces
            the engine to try backreference at every position.
            For each position i, engine tries to match `(.)(\1){10,}`
            which fails fast (char at i+1 ≠ char at i). O(n) per
            position × O(n) positions = O(n²). For n=5000 (the
            message max length capped at contact/route.ts:67), that's
            25M operations ≈ 1-2 seconds of CPU per request.
            Mitigated by:
              - Message max length 5000 chars (contact/route.ts:67).
              - Rate limit 3 req / 10 min / IP (contact/route.ts:7-8).
              - reCAPTCHA required before reaching the regex
                (contact/route.ts:86-118).
            Not catastrophic (no exponential blowup), but a focused
            attacker with valid reCAPTCHA tokens (purchasable) could
            consume ~1s CPU per request × 3 req/10min = ~3s CPU per
            10 min per IP. With X-Forwarded-For spoofing (SEC-02 Q11),
            attacker can multiply by N spoofed IPs.
        Severity: LOW-MED (O(n²), not catastrophic, rate-limited).

    (b) /api/contact/route.ts:43  (PASS)
        Code:
          if (/bot|crawl|spider|slurp|wget|curl/i.test(userAgent) && userAgent.length < 80) {
        Simple alternation. Linear time. Safe.

    (c) /lib/sanitize-embed.ts:19, 25  (PASS)
        Code:
          const iframeMatch = input.match(/<iframe[^>]*>/i);
          const srcMatch = iframeTag.match(/src=["']([^"']*)["']/i);
        - `[^>]*` and `[^"']*` are linear, no backtracking hazard.
        - Input is `embedCode` from AparatClip table (admin-set, but
          also written to public /api/clips). Even if a malicious
          admin sets embedCode to a 10MB string, the regex terminates
          in O(n) and the output is rebuilt from the captured `src`.
        Safe.

    (d) /app/rss.xml/route.ts:44  (PASS)
        Code:
          return s.replace(/[<>&'"]/g, c => ({...}[c] || c));
        Char-class replace with map lookup. Linear. Safe.

    (e) /components/LabDeviceVisualizer.tsx:449,
        /components/RealOscilloscope.tsx:460,
        /components/RealSignalGenerator.tsx:447  (PASS — client-side)
        Code:
          const h = hex.replace("#", "").trim();
        Trivial string replace. Safe. Input is admin-set hex color,
        rendered as CSS variable (no script execution path).

  Net severity: LOW-MED (one O(n²) regex; mitigated by length cap,
    rate limit, and reCAPTCHA).

  ✅ PASS — No user-controllable redirect targets anywhere.
