Q3. Time-trap field actually sent?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ❌ YES it is sent — BUT the implementation is BROKEN (CRITICAL functional bug)

  Render (page.tsx:773):
    <input type="hidden" name="_t" value={mounted ? Date.now() : 0} />

  Send (page.tsx:365):
    _t: (e.target as HTMLFormElement)._t?.value || Date.now()

  Consume (route.ts:77-81):
    const submittedAt = Number(body._t || 0);
    if (submittedAt && Date.now() - submittedAt < 2000) {
      await logSecurityEvent("time_trap_triggered", ip, "Form submitted too fast");
      return NextResponse.json({ ok: false, error: "too_fast" }, { status: 400 });
    }

  THE BUG (CRITICAL):
    `value={mounted ? Date.now() : 0}` is a controlled React value
    expression that is RE-EVALUATED ON EVERY RENDER. The component
    re-renders every 1 second because of the live-clock useEffect at
    page.tsx:216-264:
      const tick = () => { ... setUtcTime(iso + " UTC"); ... setLocalTime(...); };
      const id = setInterval(tick, 1000);   // page.tsx:262
    Every tick updates `utcTime` and `localTime` state → the entire
    `page` component re-renders → the hidden `_t` input's `value` prop
    is re-evaluated → React writes the new `Date.now()` into the DOM
    `input.value`.

    Therefore, by the time the user clicks Submit, the DOM value of `_t`
    is at most ~1 second old (from the most recent setInterval tick — or
    even more recent if the user scrolled, since the scroll listener at
    page.tsx:204-211 calls setScrolled/setToTop on every scroll event,
    triggering more re-renders).

    When handleSubmit reads `(e.target as HTMLFormElement)._t?.value`
    (page.tsx:365), it gets a timestamp from ≤1 second ago. The server
    computes `Date.now() - submittedAt` ≈ 0–1000 ms, which is `< 2000`,
    so the server ALWAYS returns HTTP 400 `{ error: "too_fast" }`.

    Net effect: EVERY LEGITIMATE SUBMISSION IS REJECTED. The contact
    form is functionally broken for human users. The only submissions
    that succeed are:
      (a) Direct API calls where the attacker sends `_t` = a timestamp
          ≥2 seconds in the past (trivial bypass — see below).
      (b) The rare case where the user's client clock is set >2 seconds
          BEHIND the server clock (so `serverNow - clientOldTimestamp`
          exceeds 2000 ms). Unusual; not a reliable UX.

    This is a CRITICAL functional regression — the form appears to work
    (no client-side error) but every submission fails silently with a
    generic "too_fast" / server_error message to the user.

  Files / lines:
    - Root cause: src/app/page.tsx:773 (`value={mounted ? Date.now() : 0}`)
      re-evaluated every render.
    - Trigger: src/app/page.tsx:262 (`setInterval(tick, 1000)`) +
      page.tsx:221,235,245,255,258 (setUtcTime/setLocalTime).
    - Amplifier: src/app/page.tsx:204-211 (scroll listener → setScrolled
      /setToTop on every scroll → re-render → _t refreshed).
    - Server check that always fires: src/app/api/contact/route.ts:78
      (`Date.now() - submittedAt < 2000`).
    - Server rejection: route.ts:80 (returns 400 "too_fast").
    - Client error mapping: page.tsx:383-390 (err === "too_fast" is NOT
      in the switch — falls through to `errs.server` generic message,
      so the user sees a generic "server error" instead of "too fast",
      masking the real cause).

  Additional bypasses (even if the form worked for legit users):
    - Direct API call with `_t` omitted → `Number(body._t || 0)` = 0 →
      the `if (submittedAt && ...)` guard at route.ts:78 short-circuits
      to false → check SKIPPED. So omitting `_t` bypasses the trap
      entirely. (route.ts:77 — `Number(undefined || 0)` = 0; `if (0 && ...)`
      is false.)
    - Direct API call with `_t` = a non-numeric string (e.g. `"abc"`)
      → `Number("abc")` = NaN → `Date.now() - NaN` = NaN →
      `NaN < 2000` is false → check passes. Bypass.
    - Direct API call with `_t` = `Date.now() - 10000` → diff = 10000 ms
      → not < 2000 → check passes. Trivial bypass.

  Verdict: field IS sent (page.tsx:365 ✅) and IS consumed (route.ts:77-81
    ✅), but the client-side implementation is fundamentally broken: the
    `_t` value is refreshed every render, so the time-trap triggers on
    100% of legitimate submissions. The server-side guard is also
    bypassable via NaN, 0, or stale timestamps. CRITICAL.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Q4. Rate limit works?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ PARTIAL — works against naive attackers, fails against IP-rotation

  Two layers:
    Layer 1 (route-local): route.ts:5-21 — in-memory Map `hits`, 3 msgs
      per IP per 10 min. Filtered on each call (line 16) so only recent
      hits remain.
    Layer 2 (middleware): middleware.ts:21,144-147 — `/api/contact` in
      RATE_LIMIT_PATHS, 8 req per IP per 15 min.

  Positives:
    - Two layers (defense in depth). ✅
    - route.ts:16 filters stale hits on each call (window cleanup). ✅
    - 429 response with `error: "rate_limit"` (route.ts:51-54). ✅
    - Client maps to user-friendly message (page.tsx:385). ✅

  Negatives:
    1. X-Forwarded-For spoofing bypasses BOTH layers (HIGH — same as
       prior F11 and worklog Q11).
       - route.ts:36-39: `ip = req.headers.get("x-forwarded-for")
         ?.split(",")[0]?.trim() || req.headers.get("x-real-ip") ||
         "unknown"`. Attacker controls the first XFF entry → unlimited
         fresh buckets → unlimited submissions.
       - middleware.ts:145-146: same pattern, same bypass.
       - Worklog Q11 (line 35439) documents this as still-open HIGH.
    2. route.ts `hits` Map has NO eviction sweep (route.ts:8). Stale
       entries are only filtered at read-time (line 16) but never deleted
       from the Map. Under an IP-rotation attack, the Map grows
       unbounded → memory exhaustion. Same flaw as F15 in prior audit
       (still open). The middleware's `rateLimitMap` (middleware.ts:42-65)
       DOES have a 5-min sweep (per worklog Q10) — better — but the
       route-local `hits` Map does not.
    3. Serverless cold-start resets `hits` Map (route.ts:8) — rate limits
       don't persist across cold starts or across multiple instances
       (no Redis/shared store). Attacker can force a cold start or hit
       a different region. MED.
    4. Default fallback `ip = "unknown"` (route.ts:39) — if a request
       arrives with no XFF/X-Real-IP headers (e.g., behind a misconfigured
       proxy that strips them), all such requests share ONE bucket →
       legit users behind that proxy collectively get 3/10min → effective
       DoS. LOW.
    5. Dev-only bypass (route.ts:12): `if (process.env.NODE_ENV !==
       "production" && (ip === "::1" || ip === "127.0.0.1" || ip ===
       "unknown"))` skips the limit. Fine in prod. But if NODE_ENV is
       unset in a misconfigured deploy (common footgun), the bypass
       applies to `unknown` IPs in production. LOW (same as prior F16).
    6. No identifier other than IP — same user from different networks
       (mobile → wifi) is unlimited. Informational.
    7. The middleware limiter (Layer 2) is checked BEFORE the route
       handler runs (middleware.ts:144-154). On 429 it returns early.
       The route-local limiter (Layer 1) is checked AFTER the bot-UA
       filter (route.ts:43-48) and AFTER IP extraction. A bot-UA request
       gets 403 before consuming a rate-limit slot — fine.

  Verdict: rate limit "works" in the sense that 3-per-10-min per IP is
    enforced against attackers who don't rotate XFF. Against an attacker
    who rotates XFF (trivial), both layers are bypassed. PARTIAL.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Q5. Bot detection bypassable?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ❌ YES, trivially — src/app/api/contact/route.ts:43

  Code (route.ts:42-48):
    if (/bot|crawl|spider|slurp|wget|curl/i.test(userAgent) && userAgent.length < 80) {
      return NextResponse.json({ ok: false, error: "Blocked" }, { status: 403 });
    }

  Bypass methods (all trivial):
    1. Empty User-Agent: `req.headers.get("user-agent") || ""` (route.ts:40)
       → `""`. The regex `/bot|.../i.test("")` is `false` → not blocked.
       A bot that simply omits the UA header passes. ✗
    2. Long UA containing "bot": `userAgent.length < 80` short-circuits
       to false → whole condition false → not blocked. So
       `"Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Googlebot/2.1; +http://www.google.com/bot.html)
       padding-padding-padding-padding-padding-padding"` (≥80 chars) passes
       even though it literally says "bot". ✗
    3. Normal browser UA: `"Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64)
       AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/120.0.0.0 Safari/537.36"`
       → no bot keyword → not blocked. Every scripted bot with a real-
       looking UA passes. ✗
    4. curl with custom UA: `curl -A "Mozilla" https://.../api/contact`
       → UA = "Mozilla" → not blocked. ✗

  False positives (legit users blocked):
    - "Discordbot" (10 chars) → matches `bot` AND length<80 → 403.
      Discord link previews of the contact page are broken.
    - "facebookexternalhit/1.1" (23 chars) → matches `crawl`? No, but
      doesn't match any pattern. Wait — actually "facebookexternalhit"
      contains neither bot|crawl|spider|slurp|wget|curl. So Facebook's
      crawler passes. ✅
    - "Twitterbot/1.0" (14 chars) → matches `bot` AND length<80 → 403.
      Twitter/X card previews broken.
    - "Slackbot-LinkExpanding 1.0" (26 chars) → matches `bot` → 403.
      Slack unfurls broken.
    - "WhatsApp/2.23.21.14" — no match. OK.
    - Any user with a UA containing "bot" <80 chars (some accessibility
      tools, some preview bots) is blocked.

  Verdict: bypassable by any non-trivial attacker; produces false
    positives on social-media link previewers. Security theater. The
    bot-UA check should be removed or replaced with a more sophisticated
    signal (e.g., challenge-response, JS-execution proof, behavioral
    signals). Severity: LOW (reCAPTCHA + honeypot + rate limit are the
    real defenses; this is a no-op layer).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Q6. Spam patterns?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ WEAK — src/app/api/contact/route.ts:23-32

  Code:
    function isSpammy(text: string): boolean {
      const lower = text.toLowerCase();
      const spamPatterns = [
        /\b(viagra|cialis|casino|lottery|prize|winner|bitcoin investment)\b/,
        /(https?:\/\/[^\s]+){3,}/,   // 3+ URLs
        /(.)\1{10,}/,                 // 11+ of same char in a row
      ];
      return spamPatterns.some((re) => re.test(lower));
    }

  Issues:
    1. Pattern 1 (keyword list): English-only. Persian/Arabic/Cyrillic
       spam (very common on this Persian-language site) is NOT caught.
       Synonyms bypass ("ED pills", "crypto deal", "qəza loyrixası").
       Character substitution bypass ("V1agra", "v!agra", "vіagra"
       with Cyrillic і). Trivial evasion.
    2. Pattern 2 (3+ URLs): BROKEN REGEX. `(https?:\/\/[^\s]+){3,}`
       requires 3 CONSECUTIVE matches of the group with NO separator.
       `[^\s]+` is greedy and consumes everything up to whitespace, so
       after the first URL the regex engine needs another `https?://`
       IMMEDIATELY — but there's a space (or punctuation) → no match.
       So "http://a http://b http://c" (URLs separated by spaces, the
       normal case) is NOT caught. Only the impossible case
       "http://ahttp://bhttp://c" (no separators) would match.
       Effectively this pattern is dead code.
    3. Pattern 3 (11+ same char): bypassed by alternating case
       ("aAaAaAaAaAaA") or by varying characters. Only catches very
       dumb flood bots.
    4. isSpammy() only checks `message` (route.ts:140). `name` and
       `email` are NOT checked. An attacker can put spam URLs or spam
       keywords in the `name` field (e.g., name="Visit
       http://casino.example.com") and bypass all spam checks.
    5. No Persian/Arabic spam patterns (no Persian phone-number regex,
       no Persian spam keywords like "تخفیف", "کسب درآمد", "پورن").
    6. No disposable-email-domain check (mailinator, guerrillamail,
       10minutemail, temp-mail.org, etc.).
    7. No link-count via whitespace split (a robust alternative to the
       broken pattern 2 would be: `text.split(/\s+/).filter(w =>
       /^https?:\/\//.test(w)).length >= 3`).
    8. No phone-number pattern (common in Persian spam — "0912xxxxxxx").
    9. The `lower` variable is computed (route.ts:24) but pattern 1 is
       already case-insensitive via the `i` flag (route.ts:27). The
       `.toLowerCase()` is redundant for pattern 1 and a no-op for
       patterns 2 and 3 (no letters). Minor inefficiency.
    10. No machine-learning / heuristic scoring. No Akismet / OOPSpam /
        StopForumSpam integration.

  Severity: LOW. Spam patterns are defense-in-depth on top of
    reCAPTCHA + honeypot + rate limit. The broken URL-count regex
    (pattern 2) is the most concerning because it gives a false sense
    of "we block multiple URLs". Easy to fix.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Q7. Email validation?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ WEAK — src/app/api/contact/route.ts:120 (server);
            src/app/page.tsx:327 (client, identical regex)

  Regex: `/^[^\s@]+@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+$/`

  Positives:
    - Requires exactly one `@`. ✅
    - Requires at least one `.` in the domain part. ✅
    - Rejects whitespace. ✅
    - Same regex on client and server (consistent). ✅

  Negatives:
    1. No TLD validation: `a@b.c` is accepted (single-char TLD — IANA
       requires 2+ char TLDs). `a@b.123` is accepted (numeric TLD —
       invalid).
    2. No local-part length cap: RFC 5321 limits local part to 64 chars
       and total email to 254 chars. The server slices email to 200
       chars (route.ts:66) — close to RFC, but doesn't separately cap
       the local part. An email like
       `aaaaaaaaaa...(200 chars)...@b.com` would be sliced mid-domain
       and might fail the regex differently. Minor.
    3. Allows consecutive dots in local part: `a..b@c.com` (RFC-invalid).
    4. Allows leading dot in local part: `.a@b.com` (RFC-invalid).
    5. Allows trailing dot in local part: `a.@b.com` (RFC-invalid).
    6. Allows dot immediately before/after @: `a.@b.com`, `a@.b.com`
       (the latter would fail the regex because domain is `.[^\s@]+`
       wait — actually `@.` doesn't match `@[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+` because
       `[^\s@]+` requires at least one non-@-non-space char before the
       dot. So `a@.b.com` is rejected. ✓; but `a.@b.com` is accepted
       because local part `a.` matches `[^\s@]+` and domain `b.com`
       matches `[^\s@]+\.[^\s@]+`.)
    7. Allows unicode in local part: `测试@example.com` — could enable
       homograph attacks if the admin later clicks reply and the email
       client resolves to a unicode lookalike domain. Minor.
    8. No disposable-domain blocklist (mailinator.com, guerrillamail.com,
       10minutemail.com, temp-mail.org, throwaway.email, etc.).
    9. No MX-record verification (would catch `a@nonexistent.tld`).
    10. No DNS validation.
    11. Plus-addressing (`a+b@c.com`) is allowed — fine, but no
        normalization (a+b@c.com and a@c.com treated as different).
    12. The 200-char server cap (route.ts:66) is generous; RFC 5321 caps
        total email at 254. 200 is within bounds. ✅
    13. No length check on the client before submit — page.tsx:780 has
        `maxLength={200}` on the input, which is enforced by the
        browser. ✅ But maxLength on `<input type="email">` is a UX
        hint, not a security control — bypassable via direct API call.
        The server cap (route.ts:66) is the real enforcement. ✅

  Severity: LOW. Correct format is enforced; deeper validation
    (disposable domains, MX lookup) is defense-in-depth.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Q8. Length caps?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ MOSTLY OK, with gaps for honeypot / _t / recaptchaToken / userAgent

  Capped fields (server + client):
    - name:      100 chars server (route.ts:65)  + maxLength=100  client (page.tsx:776). ✅
    - email:     200 chars server (route.ts:66)  + maxLength=200  client (page.tsx:780). ✅
    - message:   5000 chars server (route.ts:67) + maxLength=5000 client (page.tsx:784). ✅

  Uncapped fields:
    1. `website` (honeypot): route.ts:69 — `String(body.website || "").trim()`
       has NO length cap before being held in memory. Only the LOG
       entry is sliced to 50 chars (route.ts:72: `website.slice(0, 50)`),
       but the full string is already allocated. Attacker sends a 100 MB
       `website` field → string allocation → memory pressure. Mitigated
       only by Next.js's default body-size cap (~4 MB for App Router,
       or 1 MB per middleware's Content-Length check at middleware.ts —
       but per worklog Q6, chunked Transfer-Encoding bypasses the
       middleware 1 MB check). Severity: LOW-MED.
    2. `_t` (time-trap): route.ts:77 — `Number(body._t || 0)`. The
       `body._t` string is held in memory before `Number()` parses it.
       No cap. Same memory concern as `website`. Severity: LOW.
    3. `recaptchaToken`: route.ts:87 — checks `length < 10` (min) but
       NO upper bound. A 100 MB token would be allocated before the
       fetch to Google's siteverify. Severity: LOW-MED.
    4. `userAgent` (stored in DB): route.ts:148 — `db.contactMessage.create
       ({ data: { ..., userAgent } })`. The UA is taken directly from
       `req.headers.get("user-agent")` (route.ts:40) with NO truncation.
       schema.prisma:40 `userAgent String?` is unbounded (SQLite TEXT,
       no length constraint). Attacker sends a 1 MB UA → stored in DB
       → DB bloat / storage DoS. Severity: LOW-MED. (Compare: the
       middleware's `rateLimitMap` doesn't store UAs, so this is a
       contact-route-specific issue.)
    5. `ip` (stored in DB): route.ts:148 — `ip` from XFF first entry
       (route.ts:36-39). XFF can be up to ~8 KB in practice; the
       first entry is `split(",")[0]`. No length cap. schema.prisma:39
       `ip String?` is unbounded. Severity: LOW.
    6. Slice-then-validate order: route.ts:65-67 slices name/email/
       message BEFORE validation, which is correct. But the FULL
       `body = await req.json()` (route.ts:57) parses the entire JSON
       body into memory FIRST. So a 100 MB JSON body with a 100 MB
       `message` field is fully parsed before `slice(0, 5000)` runs.
       Same as prior F18 (still open). CPU/memory waste. Severity: LOW.
    7. No explicit body-size guard in the route. Relies on Next.js
       default + middleware Content-Length check (per worklog Q6, the
       middleware check is bypassable via chunked encoding).

  Verdict: capped fields are fine; uncapped fields (website, _t,
    recaptchaToken, userAgent, ip) are minor DoS vectors. The JSON
    body is fully parsed before slicing (F18 still open). LOW-MED
    overall.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Q9. IP/UA stored (privacy)?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ YES — both stored in plaintext; no consent notice; no retention policy

  Storage:
    - route.ts:147-149: `db.contactMessage.create({ data: { name, email,
      message, ip, userAgent } })` — both `ip` and `userAgent` are
      persisted in the ContactMessage table.
    - schema.prisma:39-40: `ip String?` and `userAgent String?` columns
      (nullable, unbounded — see Q8).
    - IP is also logged in the SecurityLog table for various events:
      security.ts:22 `logSecurityEvent(type, ip, detail)` writes
      `{ type, ip, detail }` to db.securityLog. Called from:
      route.ts:72 (honeypot), 79 (time-trap), 88 (captcha_missing),
      107 (captcha_failed), 110 (captcha network error).

  Privacy concerns:
    1. NO CONSENT NOTICE to the user that IP and UA are logged. The
       contact form (page.tsx:762-804) has no privacy notice / link to
       privacy policy. Under GDPR (Article 13), data subjects must be
       informed BEFORE data collection. IP addresses ARE personal data
       under GDPR (Recital 30, Court of Justice of the EU Case
       C-582/14 Breyer). Severity: MED (legal/compliance, not a vuln).
    2. NO RETENTION POLICY / auto-deletion. Messages (and their IP/UA)
       persist indefinitely until admin manually deletes them via
       /api/messages POST `action: "set_status"` or via the dashboard
       UI (user-dashboard/page.tsx:478 deleteMessage). GDPR Article 5(1)(e)
       requires storage limitation. Severity: MED.
    3. IP stored in PLAINTEXT (no hashing). Easier for the admin to
       correlate / block, but worse for privacy if the DB leaks.
       schema.prisma:39 is `String?` (not a hash). The `isIpBlocked`
       function (security.ts:8-17) does exact-match lookup, so hashing
       would require a separate `ipHash` column. Severity: LOW-MED.
    4. UA stored in FULL (no truncation — see Q8). UAs can contain
       rare fingerprinting info (custom build IDs, plugin lists in old
       browsers, locale, OS version). Stored indefinitely. Severity: LOW.
    5. IP is also used as the rate-limit key (route.ts:10, middleware.ts:
       145-146) — fine, but the LONG-TERM storage in ContactMessage is
       not necessary for rate-limiting (the in-memory `hits` Map and
       `rateLimitMap` are sufficient for that). The DB storage is for
       admin reference / abuse investigation. Severity: informational.
    6. Third-party data transfer: route.ts:159-176 forwards `name`,
       `email`, `message` to formsubmit.co (a third-party email-
       forwarding service). No DPA mentioned. No consent for this
       transfer. Under GDPR Article 26 (joint controllers) and Article
       46 (transfers to third parties), this requires disclosure.
       Severity: MED.
    7. Bale bot notification (bale.ts:67-85) sends `name`, `email`,
       `message.slice(0, 500)` to the admin's Bale chat. Bale is an
       Iranian messenger service — data transfer to a third country
       (Iran) without safeguards. Severity: LOW (admin-to-admin
       notification; admin presumably consents).
    8. The `forwardEmail` setting (route.ts:161, from DB SiteSetting)
       determines where messages are forwarded. If an admin sets
       `forwardEmail` to a public/shared inbox, all contact messages
       leak there. Severity: LOW (admin-controlled).

  Verdict: IP and UA are both stored in plaintext in the ContactMessage
    table AND in the SecurityLog table. No consent notice, no retention
    policy, no hashing, third-party transfer to formsubmit.co and Bale
    without disclosure. MED privacy/compliance concern (not a vuln).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Q10. HTML injection?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ MOSTLY SAFE — React auto-escaping; minor Markdown-injection in Bale

  Storage-and-render paths:
    1. Admin dashboard render (user-dashboard/page.tsx:451-470):
       - page.tsx:455 `<strong className="dashboard-message-name">{msg.name}</strong>`
       - page.tsx:456 `<span className="dashboard-message-email">{msg.email}</span>`
       - page.tsx:462 `<p className="dashboard-message-text">{msg.message}</p>`
       - page.tsx:465-468 `↳ {r.reply}` (reply text)
       All four are React TEXT CHILDREN (not dangerouslySetInnerHTML).
       React auto-escapes `<`, `>`, `&`, `"`, `'` in text children. ✅
       No HTML injection possible via the admin Messages tab.
    2. Contact form status display (page.tsx:803):
       `<p className={`form-status ${formStatus.kind}`} role="status">{formStatus.text}</p>`
       — formStatus.text is set from `tt.contact.form.errors.*` and
       `tt.contact.form.success` (static i18n strings) OR from
       `errs.server`/`errs.rate`/etc. (also static). NOT user-controlled.
       ✅
    3. Client-side `document.body.innerHTML = \`...\`` (page.tsx:143):
       set with a STATIC template string (no user input). The
       unauthorized-domain block is hardcoded. ✅ No injection.
    4. Anti-clone watermark (page.tsx:418): static string. ✅
    5. The only `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` in page.tsx is at line 726
       (Aparat clip embeds), which uses `sanitizeEmbed(clip.embedCode)`.
       This is OUTSIDE the contact-form scope (clips are admin-managed).
       ✅ (Within contact scope: no dangerouslySetInnerHTML.)

  Forwarding paths (potential injection sinks):
    6. formsubmit.co forward (route.ts:159-176): JSON body with
       `name`, `email`, `message`, `_subject: "📨 New message from ${name}"`
       (route.ts:167). JSON.stringify escapes `<`, `>`, `&`, etc., so the
       HTTP request itself is safe. BUT when formsubmit.co renders the
       email as HTML, the admin's email client may render `<script>`,
       `<img onerror>`, `<a href>` tags contained in the `message`
       field. Email clients typically disable `<script>` but render
       `<img>`, `<a>`, `<b>`, etc. So an attacker could send
       `<img src="https://attacker.com/tracking.png?admin=1" width=0 height=0>`
       to track whether the admin opened the email, or
       `<a href="https://attacker.com/phish">click here</a>` for
       phishing. Severity: LOW (depends on formsubmit.co's escaping,
       which is outside our control; admin should view messages in
       the dashboard, not email).
    7. Bale notification (bale.ts:73-85): `parse_mode: "Markdown"`
       (bale.ts:55). The message is interpolated unescaped:
       bale.ts:76 `*From:* ${msg.name}`
       bale.ts:77 `*Email:* ${msg.email}`
       bale.ts:80 `${msg.message.slice(0, 500)}`
       Markdown injection possible:
       - Attacker sends `name: "*bold*" ` → Bale renders "bold".
       - Attacker sends `name: "[click](http://evil.com)"` → Bale
         renders a clickable link to attacker's site in the admin's
         Bale chat. Phishing vector.
       - Attacker sends `message: "\n\n[reply with /reply ID send-me-money]"`
         → could trick the admin into running a `/reply` command
         (bale.ts:108-233 parses `/reply {id} {text}`).
       - Attacker sends `message: "\n```...code block...```"` → could
         break the Markdown rendering of subsequent fields.
       Severity: LOW-MED (Markdown injection in admin's Bale chat;
       could enable phishing or command-injection-via-social-engineering).
       Fix: use `parse_mode: "MarkdownV2"` and escape special chars,
       OR send as plain text (`parse_mode: ""`).
    8. Server-side console.error (route.ts:184): `console.error("[/api/contact]
       error:", err)` — logs the error object. If `err` contains user
       input (unlikely — most errors are DB connection / JSON parse),
       it could appear in server logs. Low.

  Header injection concerns:
    9. `_subject` for formsubmit.co (route.ts:167): `📨 New message from ${name}`.
       If `name` contains CRLF (`\r\n`), JSON.stringify escapes it to
       `\r\n` literal — no HTTP header injection in the request to
       formsubmit.co. ✅ (And the body is `application/json`, not
       `text/plain`, so even unescaped CRLF wouldn't break the request.)
    10. The formsubmit.co URL (route.ts:163): `https://formsubmit.co/ajax/${forwardEmail}`.
        `forwardEmail` is admin-controlled (from DB SiteSetting, route.ts:161).
        If admin sets `forwardEmail` to something containing `?` or `#`
        or `/`, the URL path changes. But this is admin-controlled, not
        user-controlled. ✅

  Verdict: HTML injection in the React UI is well-mitigated by React's
    auto-escaping (no dangerouslySetInnerHTML on the contact path). The
    main residual risks are (a) Markdown injection in the Bale
    notification and (b) potential HTML rendering in the admin's email
    client via formsubmit.co forwarding. Both LOW/LOW-MED.

SUMMARY TABLE

----+------------+-------------+------------------------------------------------
1   | PASS       | —           | reCAPTCHA mandatory + fail-closed (server+client)
2   | PASS       | —           | honeypot rendered, sent, consumed correctly
3   | FAIL       | CRITICAL    | time-trap: _t re-evaluated every render (1s tick);
    |            |             | server ALWAYS rejects legit submissions as "too_fast";
    |            |             | server guard also bypassable via NaN/0/stale _t

================================================================================
CRITICAL FINDING (Q3) — TIME-TRAP BREAKS THE CONTACT FORM
================================================================================
The time-trap field `_t` (page.tsx:773) is set to `Date.now()` on every
render. The component re-renders every 1 second (setInterval at
page.tsx:262). Therefore the DOM value of `_t` is always ≤1 second old.
On submit, the server computes `Date.now() - submittedAt` ≈ 0–1000 ms,
which is `< 2000`, so the server ALWAYS returns HTTP 400 "too_fast"
(route.ts:80). The contact form is functionally broken for ALL legitimate
users. Only direct API calls (where the attacker controls `_t`) succeed.

PoC (legit user, always fails):
  1. Open https://victim.com/#contact in a browser.
  2. Wait >2 seconds (page.tsx:262 ticks every 1s → _t refreshed).
  3. Fill name, email, message (≥10 chars).
  4. Solve reCAPTCHA.
  5. Click Submit.
  6. Server returns 400 "too_fast" (route.ts:80).
  7. Client shows generic "server error" (page.tsx:390 — "too_fast" is
     NOT in the error-mapping switch, falls through to `errs.server`).
  8. User sees "Server error", no indication of the real cause.

PoC (attacker, always succeeds):
  curl -X POST https://victim.com/api/contact \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{
      "name":"attacker","email":"a@b.com",
      "message":"this is a spam message over 10 chars",
      "recaptchaToken":"<valid token from any site>",
      "website":"",
      "_t":'$(($(date +%s%3N) - 10000))'
    }'
  # _t = 10 sec ago → diff = 10000 ms → not < 2000 → check passes.
  # OR omit _t entirely → Number(0||0)=0 → if(0 && ...) false → passes.

Fix-priority advisory (DO NOT APPLY per task instructions):
  - Q3 CRITICAL: change page.tsx:773 to set _t ONCE on mount using
    useRef + useEffect, or `useState(() => Date.now())`. Do NOT use
    `value={mounted ? Date.now() : 0}` (re-evaluated every render).
  - Q3 CRITICAL: change route.ts:78 to reject NaN/0/_t-missing
    (`if (!Number.isFinite(submittedAt) || submittedAt === 0) return 400;`).
  - Q4 HIGH: replace XFF trust with a trusted-proxy allowlist
    (cross-ref F11 / worklog Q11).
  - Q4 MED: add eviction sweep to `hits` Map (route.ts:8); use a shared
    store (Redis/Upstash) for multi-instance consistency.
  - Q9 MED: add a privacy notice + retention policy to the contact form;
    hash IPs in DB; disclose formsubmit.co + Bale transfers.
  - Q6 LOW: fix the broken URL-count regex (route.ts:28) — replace with
    `text.split(/\s+/).filter(w => /^https?:\/\//.test(w)).length >= 3`;
    add Persian spam keywords; check `name`/`email` too.
  - Q8 LOW-MED: cap `website`, `_t`, `recaptchaToken`, `userAgent` to
    reasonable max lengths on the server.
  - Q10 LOW-MED: escape Markdown special chars in bale.ts before sending
    (or switch to plain text).

Q1. Does the Panel language switcher change ALL UI text?
================================================================================
  ⚠️ PARTIAL — TWO PARALLEL LANGUAGE STATES (HIGH)
  There are TWO independent language systems that do NOT talk to each other:

  (a) Public-site language — `lang` state in src/app/page.tsx:55
      `const [lang, setLang] = useState<Lang>(DEFAULT_LANG);  // DEFAULT_LANG = "en"`
      Switcher: navbar buttons EN/DE/FA at src/app/page.tsx:518-529.
      Affects: hero, about, skills, books, articles, tutorials, chat, contact,
               clips, footer, terminal — all use `tt = UI[lang]` from content.ts.
      Does NOT persist (no localStorage.setItem).

  (b) Panel language — `panelLang` state in src/components/SettingsPanel.tsx:269
      `const savedLang = (localStorage.getItem("panel_lang") as Lang) || "fa";`
      Switcher: dropdown in src/app/user-dashboard/page.tsx:185-194 AND
                buttons in src/components/SettingsPanel.tsx (switchPanelLang).
      Affects: dashboard tabs, dashboard header, SettingsPanel labels, etc.
      Persists to localStorage key `panel_lang`.

  Findings:
    1. Public-site `lang` is NOT synchronized with panel `panelLang`. Selecting
       "فارسی" in the dashboard dropdown does NOT change `page.tsx:lang`, so
       the public homepage content stays in English when admin navigates back
       to "/". (HIGH — split-brain UI.)
    2. Both `useEffect`s write to the SAME `document.documentElement` attributes:
          page.tsx:106-109  → `document.documentElement.lang = lang; dir = tt.dir;`
          SettingsPanel.tsx:271-276 → `document.documentElement.lang = savedLang; dir = savedLang === "fa" ? "rtl" : "ltr";`
          user-dashboard/page.tsx:91-96 → same as SettingsPanel.
       Whichever runs last wins. On dashboard mount, `panel_lang` (default "fa")
       overrides `page.tsx:lang`. On returning to "/", page.tsx's useEffect
       runs again (because `lang` is in deps and effect re-runs on mount) and
       restores it. But the moment the SettingsPanel mounts inside an admin
       tab, the document's lang/dir no longer reflects the public site's lang.
       (MED — affects screen readers, search engines, and CSS selector
       html[dir=rtl] which then mismatches the actual rendered text language.)
    3. Components that take `lang` as a prop but IGNORE it:
       - src/components/AccessUserManager.tsx — no `lang` prop at all; entire
         component is bilingual hardcoded EN/FA strings, never switches
         (see Q3, Q4).
       - src/components/AparatClipManager.tsx — no `lang` prop; Persian-only
         (see Q3).
       - src/components/FontSelector.tsx — no `lang` prop; Persian-only
         descriptions (see Q3).
       - src/components/StatsDashboard.tsx — accepts `lang` but only switches
         between EN/FA; no DE branch (src/components/StatsDashboard.tsx:8
         `const fa = lang === "fa";`).
       - src/components/ContentManager.tsx — accepts `lang` but only switches
         type labels via `lang === "fa" ? typeLabels[t].fa : typeLabels[t].en`
         (src/components/ContentManager.tsx:188). All other strings ("+ add",
         "bulk import", "save", "cancel", "edit", "delete", "loading...",
         "No items yet.", "Must be JSON array", "Invalid JSON") are
         HARDCODED ENGLISH. No DE translations anywhere.
       - src/components/ThemeBuilder.tsx — accepts `lang`, has `const fa = lang === "fa";`
         at line 120 — only EN/FA, no DE.
       - src/components/NavMenuManager.tsx — same pattern; `const fa = lang === "fa";`
         at line 13 — only EN/FA, no DE.
       - src/components/TextEditor.tsx — same pattern; `const fa = lang === "fa";`
         at line 71 — only EN/FA, no DE. e.g. line 161 `{fa ? "ذخیره" : "save"}`,
         line 176 `{fa ? "متن مورد نظر یافت نشد" : "No text found"}`.

       - src/app/user-dashboard/page.tsx — `MessagesPanel` (inline component)

    - line 183:    `html[dir="rtl"] body { font-family: var(--font-fa); }`
    - line 1407:   `html[dir="rtl"] .nav-links { direction: rtl; }`
    - lines 1408-1411: flip pseudo-elements on .about-stats, .skill-card,
      .book-cover, .footer-admin.
    - lines 1413-1419: mobile nav drawer — right→left swap.
    - lines 3460-3463: dashboard flex-direction: row-reverse.

  Negatives:
    1. SSR: src/app/layout.tsx:111 hardcodes
       `<html lang="en" dir="ltr" suppressHydrationWarning>`.
       First paint is ALWAYS en/ltr; JS overrides after mount. Persian users
       see an English/LTR flash before rehydration. No inline script reads
       localStorage `panel_lang` before hydration (compare with the
       `data-font` script at layout.tsx:114-124 which DOES prevent FOUC for
       font). (MED — visual flash + screen-reader announces "English" before
       JS corrects.)
    2. .chat-msg-assistant .chat-msg-text — src/app/personal.css:1597
       `border-left: 2px solid var(--green);`
       Physical `border-left`. In RTL, the "speaker" side should be the right
       (border-right). Not flipped anywhere. (LOW-MED)
    3. .equipment-spec-val — src/app/personal.css:2495
       `text-align: right;`
       Hardcoded right alignment. In RTL, this stays right (which is actually
       the "start" side in RTL, so this happens to work for spec values, but
       it's coincidental — no logical property is used). (LOW)
    4. .oscilloscope-label — src/app/personal.css:1442-1448
       `position: absolute; top: 6px; left: 8px;`
       Physical `left: 8px`. In RTL, the label stays on the left, which is
       the "end" side in RTL. Probably intentional (it's a techy label), but
       inconsistent. (LOW)
    5. .chat-msg-user { align-self: flex-end; align-items: flex-end; }
       (src/app/personal.css:1566-1569). In a flex column, `align-items:
       flex-end` IS direction-aware (cross-axis end flips with `dir=rtl`),
       so user bubbles move to the left in RTL. This is correct convention
       for RTL chat. ✅ (no fix needed, but worth noting that the bubble
       alignment relies on flexbox cross-axis semantics, which IS RTL-aware
       by default.)
    6. .dashboard-message-header — uses `justify-content: space-between` with
       child <div> on left and <span> on right. In RTL, these flip
       automatically. (OK)

  Severity: MED — RTL works at the document level for the public site, but
    a handful of decorative borders / absolute-positioned elements use
    physical properties and don't flip.

    - src/app/personal.css:2496 — `.equipment-spec-val { word-break: break-word; }` ✅

  nowrap elements (potential RTL overflow):
    - src/app/personal.css:906 — `.terminal-prompt { white-space: nowrap; }`
      Terminal prompt `guest@portfolio:~$` is LTR ASCII; in an RTL parent
      it may force horizontal overflow if the container is narrow. (LOW)
    - src/app/personal.css:1856-1858 — `.equipment-name { white-space: nowrap;
      overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis; }` — clips Persian equipment
      names with ellipsis. Acceptable behavior, but no `min-width: 0` on
      parent in RTL (parent .equipment-info has `min-width: 0` at line 1850,
      so OK). ✅
    - src/app/personal.css:1863-1865 — `.equipment-model` same pattern. ✅
    - src/app/personal.css:1633 — `.chat-msg-author { white-space: nowrap; }`
      Author labels like "QRV-7" are short ASCII; OK. ✅
    - src/app/personal.css:1856 — `.chat-bar-meta` etc. — short numeric
      content. ✅
    - src/app/personal.css:3260 — `.dashboard-tab` is `white-space: nowrap`.
      Tab labels include emoji + Persian text (e.g. "📊 داشبورد"). On
      narrow viewports with `overflow-x: auto` (line 3242), tabs scroll
      horizontally — OK. ✅
    - src/app/personal.css:2050 — `.equipment-status-badge { word-break: break-all; }`
      May break Persian words awkwardly mid-character — but acceptable for
      short status words ("online" / "آماده").

  Bidi isolation:
    - No use of Unicode bidi control characters (LRM/RLM) or HTML `dir`
      attribute on inline LTR content (URLs, emails, technical terms)
      embedded in Persian text. The contact form's email and the
      terminal output (`#help` etc.) are LTR ASCII inside an RTL parent.
      Browsers usually handle this via bidi algorithm, but mixed
      direction strings can render incorrectly without explicit
      `dir="ltr"` on the inline span. (LOW-MED)

  Severity: MED — most long-form text wraps correctly; nowrap on labels
    may clip Persian strings on narrow screens; no explicit bidi isolation
    on LTR substrings inside RTL text.

       "LARGER FONTS for readability" block re-declares `.section-title`,
       `.section-subtitle`, `.about-text p`, `.skill-card p`, `.book-body p`,
       `.article-summary`, `.tutorial-body p`, `.tags li`, `.terminal-body`,
       `.chat-body`, `.statusbar`, `.statusbar-item .value` with `!important`.
       These clobber any per-theme overrides and make CSS specificity
       debugging a nightmare. Should be merged into the original rules.
    3. FILE SIZE: 3491 lines / 58.6 KB in one file. Mixes theme tokens,
       layout, components, RF visuals, chat, admin panel, dashboard,
       settings panel, theme-builder. Should be split into 8-10 files
       (tokens.css, base.css, layout.css, components.css, rf.css, chat.css,
       admin.css, dashboard.css, settings.css, themes.css).
    4. Theme token FRAGMENTATION: 8 themes × 18 tokens = 144 hand-typed
       color values. No CSS color-mix(), no HSL derivation. Solarized theme
       (line 2685) sets --text-dim: #586e75 on --bg: #002b36 = ~4.2:1
       contrast (borderline AA failure for normal text). Other themes
       have similar borderline contrast (--text-faint 3-4:1, fails AA).
    5. .stay-alive-warning (line 2745) — vestigial unused class (no JSX
       references it). Same for .anti-clone-watermark (line 1766) and
       .anti-theft-warning (line 2268) — these are referenced by JS but
       the JS may have been removed. Dead CSS.
    6. .dashboard-info-label { font-size: 9px } (line 3300) and other
       9-10px labels — below WCAG minimum readable size (12px). Body text
       at 11-13px throughout the panel — below recommended 16px base.
    7. .settings-toast position: sticky (line 2988) — but the toast is
       rendered as the FIRST child of .settings-root (line 567), so it
       sticks at the top of the scrolling container. However, the
       dashboard-container has `padding: 24px 28px` and no `overflow: auto`,
       so the actual scroll container is the <body>. The sticky toast
       therefore sticks to the top of the viewport, NOT below the navbar —
       OK but can overlap the dashboard tabs if the page is short.
    8. .settings-card-title has text-transform: uppercase + letter-spacing
       0.5px (line 2800) — for Persian text "📝 نام و نام کاربری" the
       uppercase has no effect (Persian has no case) but letter-spacing
       breaks Persian joining behavior. Letter-spacing on RTL text
       visually disconnects joined letters. Should disable letter-spacing
       for fa.
  Severity: CRITICAL (CSS-not-imported) + MED (overlays, dead code, contrast)

       centered text "در حال بارگذاری...". No skeleton, no spinner, no
       shimmer. The user sees a flash of empty page. Same for the 9-card
       layout — each card loads independently but only one loading state.
    2. TOAST DETECTION IS BRITTLE (line 568):
       `className={`settings-toast ${message.startsWith("✅") ? "success"
       : "error"}`}` — relies on the message starting with the ✅ emoji.
       If a success message is reformatted (e.g., to remove emoji, or to
       use a different prefix), it'll silently render as error. Should
       track an explicit `type: "success" | "error"` state.
    3. TOAST POSITION: sticky-top — but since the dashboard-container
       doesn't establish a scroll container, the toast sticks to the
       viewport top, overlapping the page-level navbar (there is none in
       /user-dashboard, so OK). BUT if the user scrolls, the toast
       disappears after 3s anyway. Acceptable.
    4. LAYOUT: 9 cards stacked vertically (Appearance, Name, Tagline,
       Password, Email, Bale, Telegram, AI Providers, Help). Each card
       has its own "Save" button. No tabs/accordions to organize. The
       page is ~3000px tall on desktop — too long. Should use a 2-col
       masonry on desktop OR tabbed sub-navigation OR collapsible cards.
    5. SAVE BUTTON OVERLOAD: 8 separate "Save" buttons (one per card).
       No "Save All" or autosave. User must click 8 times to save all
       settings. The Help card has a list of 6 tips but no save (OK).
    6. THE HELP CARD (lines 953-963) is always-visible at the bottom.
       6 tips clutter the bottom. Should be a collapsible <details>.
    7. AI PROVIDERS LIST (lines 822-847): each provider row has 3 buttons
       (Enable/Disable toggle, Edit, Delete) with English-only labels
       ("Enable", "Disable", "Edit") — NOT translated via t.*. The
       t.deleteProvider is used for delete but Enable/Edit are hardcoded.
    8. AI PROVIDER EDITOR (lines 866-948): a 5-row form inside a
       dashed-border box. The h5 says `"{editingProvider.id ? "Edit" :
       "New"} Provider"` — English-only, not translated. Should use
       t.* labels. The form uses .settings-row 2-col grid which collapses
       to 1-col on mobile (line 2832 @media) — good.
    9. RTL ISSUE: form inputs use dir="ltr" hardcoded (lines 615, 626,
       638, 651, etc.) for English/handle fields — correct. But the
       Persian name input (line 612-616) sets dir="rtl" — good. However,
       the .settings-card-title text-transform: uppercase + letter-spacing
       0.5px (personal.css:2800) breaks Persian joining for titles like
       "📝 نام و نام کاربری". Letter-spacing on RTL Persian text
       visually disconnects joined letters.
    10. NO EMPTY STATE for providers list is "No providers configured."
        (line 845) — English-only, not translated.
    11. NO ERROR RECOVERY: if loadSettings() or loadProviders() fails,
        the catch block is empty (line 341-343 and 353). User sees an
        empty form with no indication of failure. Should show a toast.
    12. FONT SELECTOR (lines 590-600): dropdown lists 5 fonts but no
        preview — user can't see what the font looks like before

Q7. Color consistency?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ PARTIAL — mixed token usage across components
  Analysis:
    Three "primary" naming conventions in simultaneous use (all are
    aliases thanks to personal.css:37-39 aliases, but the inconsistency
    is a code-smell and confusing for future maintainers):
      - --green / --green-dim / --green-bright (original terminal names,
        used in personal.css itself and in ContentManager/ThemeBuilder)
      - --primary / --primary-dim / --primary-bright (alias, used in
        AccessUserManager inline styles and user-login inline styles)
      - Mixed: SettingsPanel uses --green (lines 2794, 2802, 2859, 2888,
        2903, 2913, 2925, 2931, 2951, 2983, 3000, 3006, 3085) but
        NOT --primary. ContentManager uses --green-bright (line 211,
        219, 223) and --text-dim. ThemeBuilder uses --green-bright
        and --text-dim. AccessUserManager uses --primary and
        --primary-bright (lines 230, 237, 255, 275, 468, 548).
    Hard-coded colors that BYPASS theme system (won't adapt to custom
    themes):
      - user-login/page.tsx line 65: `var(--bg-panel, #050505)` —
        fallback is wrong (#050505 is not --bg-panel's terminal value
        of #050d05; also doesn't match the green-tinted panels)
      - user-login line 70: `rgba(0, 255, 65, 0.1)` — hard-coded green
        glow, won't adapt to amber/cyan/purple themes
      - error.tsx line 22: `#ff0040` — hard-coded red (matches --red
        but bypasses the variable)
      - error.tsx line 32: `var(--bg-panel, #050d05)` — OK fallback
      - global-error.tsx lines 16-17: `#000` and `#00ff41` — fully
        hard-coded (this is OK since global-error doesn't load CSS,
        but still bypasses theme)
      - global-error.tsx line 28: `#ff0040` — hard-coded red
      - AccessUserManager line 282: `rgba(255,0,64,0.1)` — hard-coded
        red bg for error (should be `rgba(var(--red-rgb), 0.1)` or
        a CSS class)
      - AccessUserManager line 464: `rgba(255,0,64,0.1)` — same,
        duplicated
      - user-dashboard MessagesPanel line 438: `rgba(255,0,64,0.1)`
        — hard-coded red, bypasses theme
      - ContentManager line 256: `color: "var(--red)"` — OK (uses var)
    SEMANTIC MISUSE: the .dashboard-access-warning class (amber/warning)
      is reused for red errors in MessagesPanel (line 438) with inline
      override. Should be a separate .dashboard-error class.
    THE SOLAR THEME (personal.css:2685-2707): --green: #2aa198 (teal)
      and --text-dim: #586e75 on --bg: #002b36 — contrast ratio ~4.2:1,
      borderline AA failure. Other themes (amber, cyan) have similar
      borderline --text-dim values that may fail WCAG AA on small text.
  Severity: MED (mixed naming, hard-coded colors bypass themes, contrast
    borderline in solar/amber themes)

Q9. Typography hierarchy?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ⚠️ PARTIAL — flat hierarchy, tiny labels, no clear visual scale
  Analysis:
    DASHBOARD (user-dashboard/page.tsx):
      - .dashboard-title: 18px / 700 / uppercase / letter-spacing 2px
      - .dashboard-subtitle: 11px (small)
      - .dashboard-info-label: 9px / uppercase / letter-spacing 1px
        (TOO SMALL — below 12px readable threshold)
      - .dashboard-info-value: 13px
      - .dashboard-help-box: 12px
      - .dashboard-message-name: 13px / 700
      - .dashboard-message-text: 12px
      - .dashboard-empty-state: 13px / italic
      Hierarchy: title(18) > value(13) = empty(13) = name(13) > text(12)
      = help(12) > subtitle(11) > label(9). The 9px label is a
      readability problem and creates a "wall of equal-size text" feel
      since the value (13) and label (9) are visually similar at small
      sizes.
    SETTINGSPANEL:
      - .settings-card-title: 15px / 700 / uppercase / letter-spacing 0.5px
      - .settings-label: 11px / uppercase / letter-spacing 0.5px
      - .settings-input: 13px
      - .settings-hint: 11px
      - .settings-toast: 13px
      - .settings-help-list: 12px
      - .settings-provider-info: 12px
      - .settings-provider-model: 11px
      - .settings-provider-status: 10px
      - .settings-empty: 12px / italic
      Hierarchy: title(15) > input(13) = toast(13) > label(11) = hint(11)
      = model(11) = help(12) > status(10). 9 distinct sizes, mostly
      clustered at 10-13px. No clear primary/secondary/tertiary.
    ACCESSUSERMANAGER (inline):
      - h3 (line 237, 275, 454): default h3 size (browser default ~1.17em
        ≈ 18.7px at 16px base, but base is 15px so ~17.5px)
      - labelStyle: 10px / uppercase / letter-spacing 1px (TOO SMALL)
      - inputStyle: 12px
      - thStyle: 10px / uppercase / letter-spacing 1px (TOO SMALL)
      - tdStyle: 11px
      - small hints: 10px
      Hierarchy: h3(17.5) > input(12) > td(11) > label(10) = th(10) =
      hint(10). All labels are 10px — extremely small, hard to read.
    CONTENTMANAGER (mixed inline + classes):
      - .admin-tab: 0.78rem (~12.5px)
      - Field labels (inline): 0.72rem (~11.5px)
      - .admin-message-head: 0.72rem
      - .admin-message-text: 0.85rem (~13.6px) from CSS — but overridden
        inline at line 246 to 0.78rem (~12.5px) — INCONSISTENT
      - .btn-sm: 0.78rem
      Hierarchy: tab(12.5) = text(12.5) = btn(12.5) > label(11.5) =
      head(11.5). Almost flat — no clear hierarchy.
    THEMEBUILDER (inline):
      - All text 0.68rem-0.8rem (~10.9-12.8px)
      - Live preview h4: 1rem (16px) — only larger element
      - Theme card name: 0.8rem
      - All labels: 0.72rem (~11.5px)
      Hierarchy: preview-h4(16) > card-name(12.8) > labels(11.5) > tiny
      labels(10.9). Mostly flat.
    NO TYPE SCALE: there's no consistent modular scale (e.g., 12/14/16/
      20/28). Sizes are scattered: 9, 10, 11, 11.5, 12, 12.5, 12.8, 13,
      13.6, 15, 16, 17.5, 18 — 13 distinct sizes with no ratio.
    PERSIAN LETTER-SPACING ISSUE: .dashboard-title, .dashboard-info-label,
      .settings-card-title, .settings-label, labelStyle, thStyle all use
      letter-spacing 0.5-2px with text-transform: uppercase. For Persian
      text, uppercase is a no-op (no case), but letter-spacing > 0.5px
      visually breaks Arabic-script joining behavior. Persian letters
      that should connect (ب + ه = به) appear disconnected (ب ه). This
      is a typography bug for the Persian admin.
  Severity: MED (no type scale, 9px labels, letter-spacing breaks Persian)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Q1. Keyboard accessible?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Native <button>, <a>, <input>, <select>, <textarea> elements are keyboard-accessible by default.
FAILURES — clickable <div> elements with onClick but no role="button" / tabIndex / onKeyDown:

1. src/components/GlobalSearch.tsx:103-122
   `<div className="global-search-result" onClick={...}>` for each search result.
   Keyboard users cannot navigate to or activate search results. Should be <button> or
   role="button" tabIndex={0} onKeyDown={Enter/Space}.
   Impact: HIGH — search results entirely inaccessible via keyboard.

2. src/components/GlobalSearch.tsx:87
   `<div className="global-search-overlay" onClick={close}>` — backdrop click closes modal.
   NO Escape key handler. NO focus trap. NO aria-modal. Modal opens, focus leaves
   the page, user has no way to dismiss via keyboard. (page.tsx:305-314 Escape handler
   covers tutorial modal but NOT GlobalSearch.)
   Impact: HIGH — keyboard trap / unusable modal.

3. src/app/page.tsx:841-842
   Tutorial modal: `<div className="tutorial-modal" onClick={close}>` and inner
   `<div onClick={e => e.stopPropagation()}>`. Escape handler exists at page.tsx:305-314 ✅.
   BUT: focus is not moved into the modal when it opens (no focus management), and
   focus is not returned to the trigger button when closed. Tab order may include
   off-screen elements behind the modal.
   Impact: MED — WAI-ARIA dialog pattern (focus management) not followed.

4. src/components/ArchiveGrid.tsx:130, 150, 174 (article/book/tutorial cards)
   `<article ... onClick={() => onItemClick?.(item)} style={{ cursor: "pointer" }}>`
   For tutorials, this opens a video modal — keyboard users cannot activate.
   Impact: HIGH — tutorial grid items are click-only.

5. src/components/InteractiveTerminal.tsx:181
   `<div className="terminal" onClick={() => inputRef.current?.focus()}>`
   Clicking terminal focuses input — keyboard users can still Tab to the input
   directly. Acceptable but not ideal (no role="application" or similar).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Q2. Focus indicators visible?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Global rule:
  src/app/personal.css:3480-3483  `*:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--green, #00ff41); outline-offset: 2px; }`
  This provides a 2px green focus ring for keyboard users on modern browsers. ✅

FAILURES — inline `style={{ outline: "none" }}` overrides the global rule (inline
styles always win the cascade), so keyboard focus is INVISIBLE on these elements:

1. src/app/user-login/page.tsx:110
   `<input type="text" ... style={{ ..., outline: "none", ... }} />` — username input.
   Keyboard focus indicator removed. WCAG 2.4.7 (Focus Visible) violation.

2. src/app/user-login/page.tsx:140
   `<input type="password" ... style={{ ..., outline: "none", ... }} />` — password input.
   Same — focus indicator removed.

3. src/components/AparatClipManager.tsx:292
   `const inputStyle = { ..., outline: "none", ... }` — shared style object applied to
   ALL form inputs in the Aparat clip manager (5 inputs at lines 145, 157, 172, 183, 193).
   Keyboard focus invisible across the entire form.

4. src/components/AccessUserManager.tsx:552
   Same pattern — `inputStyle` with `outline: "none"` applied to ~8 form inputs.

CONCERNS — stylesheet `:focus { outline: none }` rules (these apply to mouse focus
in modern browsers because `:focus-visible` differs from `:focus`; on older browsers
without `:focus-visible` support, keyboard focus is invisible):

5. src/app/personal.css:631       `.field input:focus, .field textarea:focus { outline: 0 }` — but
6. src/app/personal.css:1175-1177  `.field input:focus, .field textarea:focus { outline: none; }` —
   contact-form fields. The global `*:focus-visible` overrides this for keyboard
   users on modern browsers. ⚠️ Brittle on older browsers.

7. src/app/personal.css:1401-1403  `:focus-visible { outline: 1px solid var(--green); outline-offset: 2px; }`
   Only 1px outline. WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.13 (Focus Appearance) recommends ≥2px. The
   later `*:focus-visible` at line 3480 wins by source order and provides 2px. ⚠️ Duplicate
   definition; the 1px version is dead code but misleading.

8. src/app/personal.css:1643       `.chat-input:focus { outline: none; }` — chat input. Same caveat
   as #6 (mouse focus only).
9. src/app/personal.css:1951-1952  `.admin-reply-box textarea:focus { outline: none; }`
10. src/app/personal.css:2001-2002  `.admin-setting-input:focus { outline: none; }`
11. src/app/personal.css:2187       (in another admin style) `outline: none`
12. src/app/personal.css:2308-2310  `.admin-search:focus { outline: none; }`
13. src/app/personal.css:2536-2539  `select.admin-search:focus { outline: none; }`
14. src/app/personal.css:2862-2868  `.settings-input:focus, .settings-select:focus { outline: none; }`
15. src/app/personal.css:3207-3211  `.dashboard-select:focus { outline: none; }`
16. src/app/personal.css:3439-3446  `.dashboard-reply-textarea:focus { outline: none; }`

Net effect on modern browsers (Chrome 86+, Firefox 85+, Safari 15.4+): keyboard focus
is visible via `*:focus-visible` (2px green). Mouse focus is invisible (which is
acceptable per WCAG 2.4.7 since the user's mouse position provides a visual cue).
On older browsers, ALL focus is invisible. The 4 inline-style `outline:none` cases
(Q2.1-4) break keyboard focus EVEN on modern browsers because inline styles override
`:focus-visible`.

FAILURES:

1. src/components/SignalBars.tsx:12-18
   `setInterval(() => { setLevel(3 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 3)); }, 2000 + Math.random() * 2000)`
   Updates the signal-strength bars every ~2-4 seconds. NO `prefers-reduced-motion` check.
   The bars re-render with different heights — a small but constant motion that violates
   WCAG 2.3.3 (Animation from Interactions) for users with vestibular sensitivity.
   Severity: LOW (subtle, slow motion).

2. src/app/page.tsx:299  `window.scrollTo({ top, behavior: "smooth" })` (nav-click smooth scroll)
   Hardcoded `behavior: "smooth"` ignores reduced-motion preference.
   The CSS rule `scroll-behavior: smooth` (personal.css:137) IS overridden by the
   reduced-motion media query at personal.css:1398 (`scroll-behavior: auto !important`),
   but JS-driven scrollTo bypasses this CSS override.
   Severity: MED (scroll motion can trigger motion sensitivity).

3. src/app/page.tsx:834  `window.scrollTo({ top: 0, behavior: "smooth" })` (to-top button)
   Same — hardcoded smooth scroll bypasses reduced-motion preference.

4. src/components/InteractiveTerminal.tsx (terminal typing animation, if any)
   Type-on effect — not verified in this audit; should be checked in a deeper pass.

5. src/app/page.tsx:189  `setInterval(checkDevtools, 1000)` (devtools detection)
   Not a motion animation, but the polling itself is a continuous interval. Acceptable.

Final verdict:
  Of 10 audit categories: 0 PASS, 4 PARTIAL (Q1, Q2, Q4, Q7, Q8, Q9), 3 FAIL (Q3, Q6, Q10),
  and several LOW/informational findings (Q5 — mostly OK).

  Most serious:
    (a) NO <main> landmark on any page (Q10) — every page fails WCAG 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks.
        Screen reader users cannot jump to main content.
    (b) Pervasive low-contrast text (Q6) — `--text-dim` (4.14:1) and `--text-faint` (2.06:1)
        fail AA on small text across navbar, status bar, social chips, section subtitles,
        and admin-panel labels.
    (c) ~40 form labels without `htmlFor` association (Q3) — SettingsPanel, AccessUserManager,
        AparatClipManager, ContentManager, TextEditor all use bare `<label>` next to `<input>`.
    (d) Click-only <div> elements (Q1) — GlobalSearch results, ArchiveGrid tutorial cards,
        search-overlay backdrop — keyboard users cannot activate.
    (e) Inline `outline: none` (Q2) on user-login inputs and admin forms strips keyboard
        focus indicator.

  Cross-references to prior audit findings (open):
    None directly tracked (this is the first a11y audit in the worklog). Future audits
    should reference: A-1 (no <main>), A-2 (low-contrast text-dim/text-faint),
    A-3 (label htmlFor missing), A-4 (click-only divs), A-5 (inline outline:none),
    A-6 (toggle buttons missing aria-pressed), A-7 (icon buttons missing aria-label),
    A-8 (no aria-modal on dialogs), A-9 (canvas elements unlabeled), A-10 (Aparat iframe
    missing title).

9. AI provider apiKey masked?
   (providers/route.ts:27-30; SettingsPanel.tsx:528, 917)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ✅ YES — properly masked end-to-end.
  Audit:
    - Server GET /api/admin/providers (providers/route.ts:27-30):
      `apiKey: p.apiKey ? "••••••••" + p.apiKey.slice(-4) : null`
      Returns null if no key; otherwise 8 bullets + last 4 chars. ✅
    - Client saveProvider (line 528):
      `apiKey: p.apiKey && !p.apiKey.startsWith("••••") ? p.apiKey : undefined`
      Skips sending apiKey if it's still the masked value. ✅
    - Server update (providers/route.ts:87-89):
      `if (data.apiKey && !String(data.apiKey).startsWith("••••")) { updateData.apiKey = ... }`
      Defense-in-depth: server also skips masked values. ✅
    - Editor placeholder (line 917):
      `placeholder={editingProvider.apiKey?.startsWith("••••") ? "(unchanged)" : "sk-..."}`
      Tells admin the existing key is unchanged. ✅
    - apiKey input has type="password" (line 914) — visually masked. ✅
  Negatives:
    1. ⚠️ EDGE CASE — if real apiKey is ≤4 chars long, slice(-4)
       returns the WHOLE key, so the masked value is "••••••••" +
       the entire key (e.g., "••••••••abcd" for a 4-char key "abcd").
       Admin can recover the full key by stripping the 8 bullets.
       LOW (only matters for very short keys — typical API keys are
       40+ chars).
    2. ⚠️ STARTSWITH("••••") CHECK IS LOOSE — any string starting
       with "••••" (4 bullets) is treated as masked. A real API key
       that happens to start with "••••" (extremely unlikely — U+2022
       bullet is not in any standard API key alphabet) would be
       silently dropped on update. LOW.
    3. ⚠️ SECURITY INCONSISTENCY — provider apiKeys are masked, but
       Bale/Telegram bot tokens are returned in plaintext (see #6.1,
       #7.1). Same surface area, different treatment. HIGH.

    treatment. HIGH. (See also #6.1, #7.1, #9 extra.)
    Recommended fix (advisory only): mask bot tokens server-side
    like apiKey, return null on GET, only update on POST if the
    submitted value doesn't start with "••••".

Q1. Login brute-force (5/15min)
================================================================================
  ⚠️ PARTIAL — TWO LAYERS, BOTH SPOOFABLE
  Layer A — middleware:    src/middleware.ts:21,144-154,147
  Layer B — route handler: src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:19-34,46-55

  Layer A code (src/middleware.ts):
    21:  const RATE_LIMIT_PATHS = ["/api/user/login", "/api/contact", "/api/chat"];
    43:  const RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_MS = 15 * 60 * 1000; // 15 دقیقه
    144: if (RATE_LIMIT_PATHS.includes(pathname)) {
    145:   const ip = req.headers.get("x-forwarded-for")?.split(",")[0]?.trim() ||
    146:              req.headers.get("x-real-ip") || "unknown";
    147:   const max = pathname === "/api/user/login" ? 5 : 8;
    148:   if (!checkRateLimit(`${pathname}:${ip}`, max)) {
    149-154: return 429 ...
    }
  ✅ Spec compliant: window=15min, max=5.

  Layer B code (src/app/api/user/login/route.ts):
    20: const RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW = 15 * 60 * 1000;
    21: const RATE_LIMIT_MAX = 5;
    22: const loginAttempts = new Map<string, { count: number; resetAt: number }>();
    24-34: checkRateLimit(ip) — same logic, same 5/15min.
    46:  const ip = getClientIp(request);   // → src/lib/access-auth.ts:175
    50:  const rateLimitKey = ip || "unknown"; if (!checkRateLimit(rateLimitKey)) {
  ✅ Spec compliant: 5/15min.

  Positives:
    - Two independent layers (defense-in-depth). Even if middleware is bypassed
      (e.g., matcher doesn't catch a path), route still enforces 5/15min. ✅
    - Both layers use the same 5/15min spec. ✅
    - Generic "invalid_credentials" message returned for both missing user and
      wrong password (src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:60-70) → no user
      enumeration via response. ✅

  Negatives:
    1. BOTH LAYERS USE THE SAME SPOOFABLE IP SOURCE (HIGH):
       - Middleware:  req.headers.get("x-forwarded-for") → src/middleware.ts:145
       - Route:       getClientIp → src/lib/access-auth.ts:175-181, which also
         reads x-forwarded-for and x-real-ip verbatim.
       - Cross-ref: F-9 (SEC-02 Q11, this worklog line 35441). Still OPEN.
       - Impact: attacker rotates X-Forwarded-For per request → infinite IPs →
         each IP gets its own 5/15min bucket → brute-force unlimited.
       - See Q8 below for full PoC.
    2. ROUTE-LEVEL Map HAS NO CLEANUP (MED — Q7 below):
       - src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:22 `loginAttempts` Map is never swept.
       - Each unique IP key (spoofable) creates a permanent entry. Memory grows
         unbounded over the process lifetime.
       - Cross-ref: F-25 (SEC-02 Q10, line 35392). Still OPEN.
    3. LOCK-OUT IS PER-IP NOT PER-ACCOUNT (MED):
       - An attacker who knows a username can perform 4 attempts from each
         spoofed IP, against the SAME account, with no per-account lockout.
       - Conversely, a victim user behind a NAT (corporate office, campus
         Wi-Fi) gets locked out after 5 attempts across all users behind that
         NAT. Legitimate users DOSed.
    4. NO CAPTCHA / NO PROGRESSIVE BACKOFF:
       - Login has no captcha, no exponential backoff, no MFA, no email
         notification on lockout. 5/15min is a flat limit.
       - Compare: /api/contact enforces reCAPTCHA (src/app/api/contact/
         route.ts:86-118). /api/user/login does not.
    5. RATE LIMIT APPLIES ONLY TO POST /api/user/login (informational):

         RATE_LIMIT_PATHS — middleware.ts:21). GET /api/user/verify and POST
         /api/user/logout are not rate-limited (lower priority but inconsistent).
    6. SPEC SAYS "5/15min" — IMPLEMENTATION MATCHES. ✅ (caveats aside)

    - Middleware runs FIRST (8/15min). Allows up to 8 requests in 15 min.
    - Route runs SECOND (3/10min). Allows only 3 in any 10-min sliding window.
    - The stricter limit (route's 3/10min) is the binding one.

Q3. Chat (8/15min)
================================================================================
  ❌ MISMATCH — MIDDLEWARE SAYS 8/15min, ROUTE SAYS 8/1min (NOT 8/15min)
  Layer A — middleware: src/middleware.ts:21,43,147
  Layer B — route handler: src/app/api/chat/route.ts:6-21,64-77

  Layer A code (src/middleware.ts):
    21: RATE_LIMIT_PATHS includes "/api/chat"
    43: RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_MS = 15 * 60 * 1000  (15 min)
    147: max = pathname === "/api/user/login" ? 5 : 8;  → chat = 8
    → middleware enforces 8 per 15 min. ✅ matches spec.

  Layer B code (src/app/api/chat/route.ts):
    7:  const RATE_WINDOW_MS = 60 * 1000; // 1 min  ❌ NOT 15 min!
    8:  const RATE_MAX = 8;
    9:  const hits = new Map<string, number[]>();
    11: function rateLimit(ip: string): boolean {
    12:   if (process.env.NODE_ENV !== "production" && (...)) return true;
    15:   const arr = (hits.get(ip) || []).filter((t) => now - t < RATE_WINDOW_MS);
    17:   if (arr.length >= RATE_MAX) return false;
    18-21: ...
    }
    → route enforces 8 per 1 MINUTE (NOT 8/15min as spec requires).

  Effective behavior:
    - Middleware (8/15min) allows 8 in 15 min.
    - Route (8/1min) is STRICTER. So the effective cap is 8/1min = 120/15min.
    - Spec says 8/15min. Implementation is 60x stricter than spec.
    - This is NOT a security regression (stricter = safer), but it IS a spec
      mismatch and may frustrate legitimate users (a chatty user gets 429
      after 8 messages in 60 seconds).

  Positives:
    - Stricter than spec (defense-in-depth). ✅
    - Sliding window (filters timestamps). ✅
    - Sliding window more accurate than middleware's fixed window.

  Negatives:
    1. SPEC MISMATCH (LOW):
       - Spec: 8/15min. Code: 8/1min.
       - Either fix the constant or update the spec.
    2. `hits` MAP NEVER CLEANED (MED — Q7):
       - src/app/api/chat/route.ts:9 — same pattern as contact route.
    3. NO RATE LIMIT ON /api/chat/messages (POLLING ENDPOINT) — HIGH:
       - src/app/api/chat/messages/route.ts:9-44 GET handler has NO rate limit.
       - src/middleware.ts:21 RATE_LIMIT_PATHS does NOT include
         "/api/chat/messages" — only "/api/chat".
       - Client polls every 3 seconds (src/components/ChatSection.tsx:60-76).
       - Each connected client = 20 req/min.
       - 100 concurrent clients = 2000 req/min → DB DoS.
       - Per-request DB query: db.chatMessage.findMany (no `take` limit — see
         Q10) returns ALL assistant messages since `since` param. If `since=0`
         (default — src/app/api/chat/messages/route.ts:13) returns ALL messages
         in the session ever.
       - Combined with no `take` limit (Q10) and no rate limit, this is the
         strongest DoS vector in the entire codebase.
    4. BOTH LAYERS USE SPOOFABLE X-Forwarded-For (HIGH — same as Q1):
       - Middleware: src/middleware.ts:145-146.
       - Route: src/app/api/chat/route.ts:66-69.
    5. SESSION-INCLUDE-ALL-MESSAGES GROWTH (MED — Q10):
       - src/app/api/chat/route.ts:120-123 `db.chatSession.findUnique({
           where: { id: sessionId },
           include: { messages: { orderBy: { createdAt: "asc" } } } })`.
       - Each POST to /api/chat fetches ALL messages in the session and sends
         them to the LLM (line 153-159 `history`). As session grows, this
         gets slower and slower and consumes unbounded memory + LLM tokens.
       - No cap on messages per session, no truncation, no sliding context
         window. A long-running session can OOM the process and exceed LLM
         token limits.

  Severity: HIGH (the 8/15min cap is in place but the polling endpoint has
    no cap, and the per-session context grows unbounded — both are DoS vectors).

Q5. Webhook endpoints
================================================================================
  ⚠️ PARTIAL — AUTH BY SECRET, NO RATE LIMIT, NO BODY SIZE CAP BEYOND 1MB
  Endpoints:
    src/app/api/telegram/webhook/route.ts (29 lines, POST only)
    src/app/api/bale/webhook/route.ts     (78 lines, POST + GET helper)

  Code (src/app/api/telegram/webhook/route.ts):
    9:  const secret = url.searchParams.get("secret") || req.headers.get("x-webhook-secret") || "";
    10: const expectedSecret = process.env.TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET;
    11-13: if (!expectedSecret) return 503;
    14-18: const secretBuf = Buffer.from(secret);
           const expBuf = Buffer.from(expectedSecret);
           if (secretBuf.length !== expBuf.length ||
               !crypto.timingSafeEqual(secretBuf, expBuf)) return 403;
    19: const body = await req.json().catch(() => null);
    20: if (!body) return 400;
    21: const result = await processTelegramWebhook(body);
    22: if (result.reply) await sendTelegramMessage(result.reply);

  Code (src/app/api/bale/webhook/route.ts): SAME pattern, lines 16-44.

  Positives:
    - Secret-based auth with `crypto.timingSafeEqual` ✅ (constant-time compare,
      prevents timing attack on secret).
    - Secret read from URL OR `x-webhook-secret` header (flexibility). ✅
    - Returns 503 if env var not set (fail-closed). ✅
    - Body parsed with `.catch(() => null)` — invalid JSON → 400. ✅
    - Webhook routes ARE in PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES (src/middleware.ts:33-34) so
      the middleware's CSRF Origin check is correctly SKIPPED for them
      (webhooks come from external services with no Origin header). ✅

  Negatives:
    1. NO RATE LIMIT ON WEBHOOK ENDPOINTS (HIGH):
       - Middleware RATE_LIMIT_PATHS (src/middleware.ts:21) does NOT include
         /api/telegram/webhook or /api/bale/webhook.
       - An attacker who guesses/leaks the webhook URL (but not the secret)
         can still hammer the endpoint at network speed.
       - Each request:
         • Reads env var (cheap).
         • Buffers secret + calls timingSafeEqual (cheap).
         • Returns 403.
       - Cheap per-request, but at 10k req/s the Buffer.from allocations + JSON
         parse if secret happens to match would still consume CPU. The 403 path
         is fast, but the public endpoint is exposed to amplification-style
         attacks if the secret ever leaks.
    2. SECRET LEAKAGE VIA URL (MED):
       - `url.searchParams.get("secret")` (line 9 of telegram; line 19 of bale)
         means the webhook URL is `https://victim.com/api/bale/webhook?
         secret=XXX`. This URL appears in:
         • Web server access logs (nginx, Caddy).
         • Browser history if anyone visits it.
         • Referrer headers if the webhook service ever redirects.
       - The `x-webhook-secret` HEADER alternative (line 9/19 OR branch) is
         safer. Recommend header-only.
       - Telegram/Bale webhook config stores the URL in their API, which is
         out of our control.
    3. BODY SIZE: NO SEPARATE LIMIT (LOW):
       - Webhooks go through middleware's 1MB Content-Length check
         (src/middleware.ts:196-204). OK.
       - But same chunked-encoding bypass risk as Q6.
    4. NO VALIDATION OF WEBHOOK PAYLOAD SHAPE (MED):
       - src/app/api/bale/webhook/route.ts:36 `processBaleWebhook(body)` — body
         is untyped. processBaleWebhook reads `body?.message?.text`
         (src/lib/bale.ts:108-114). If body is `{}` or `{message: 1}`, no
         crash but also no rate-limit on misformed payloads.
       - Telegram webhook has same issue (src/lib/telegram.ts:66-72).
    5. NO SIGNATURE VERIFICATION (MED):
       - The webhook secret is a SHARED STATIC SECRET, not a per-message HMAC
         signature. Telegram supports `X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token` header
         set via setWebhook `{ secret_token: "..." }` — this code DOES check
         that (line 9 reads header), so OK for Telegram.
       - Bale does NOT support secret tokens in webhooks natively. The
         shared URL secret is the only protection. If the URL leaks, anyone
         can post.
    6. processBaleWebhook / processTelegramWebhook CAN RUN EXPENSIVE DB OPS:
       - src/lib/bale.ts:117-130 `case "/list"` — findMany with take:5 (OK).
       - src/lib/bale.ts:191-208 `case "/stats"` — 3 counts (OK).
       - src/lib/bale.ts:132-149 `case "/reply"` — 1 findUnique + 1 create.
       - src/lib/bale.ts:152-170 `case "/chat"` — findUnique + create + update.
       - All admin-initiated via the bot. An admin (or attacker with the bot
         token) can spam these commands. No rate limit on webhook processing.
       - Telegram: same (src/lib/telegram.ts:74-117).
    7. NO BODY SIZE LIMIT INSIDE processBaleWebhook (LOW):
       - body.message.text is not length-capped before being stored
         (src/lib/bale.ts:143-145 db.messageReply.create — reply text from
         the bot message). If the webhook delivers a 100KB text message,
         it's stored verbatim.
       - Middleware's 1MB cap (Q6) is the only protection.
    8. NO IP ALLOWLIST FOR WEBHOOK SOURCES (informational):
       - Best practice: only accept webhooks from Telegram/Bale API IP ranges.
       - This code accepts from any IP that has the secret.
       - Defense-in-depth missing.

  Severity: MED (auth is solid via timingSafeEqual; main issues are no rate
    limit + URL-secret exposure + no IP allowlist)
