Q6. Body size limit 1MB
================================================================================
  ⚠️ WEAK — CHECKS Content-Length HEADER ONLY, TRUSTS CLIENT
  Middleware code (src/middleware.ts):
    196: if (method === "POST" || method === "PUT" || method === "PATCH") {
    197:   const contentLength = parseInt(req.headers.get("content-length") || "0", 10);
    198:   if (contentLength > 1024 * 1024) { // 1MB limit
    199-203:   return 413;
         }
       }

  Positives:
    - 1MB cap matches spec. ✅
    - Applies to POST/PUT/PATCH (not GET/DELETE — fine, GET has no body).
    - 413 response is returned BEFORE the route handler runs — saves a DB
      query for huge payloads. ✅
    - 413 response goes through addSecurityHeaders (line 203) — at least
      generic headers. ❌ BUT no CSP/HSTS (see SEC-02 Q12, line 35494).

  Negatives:
    1. TRUSTS Content-Length HEADER (HIGH):
       - If client omits Content-Length, middleware treats it as 0 (line 197:
         `parseInt(... || "0", 10)`).
       - Body can still be arbitrarily large (chunked transfer-encoding).
       - Route handler then calls `await req.json()` which buffers the entire
         body into memory → unbounded allocation.
       - Attack vector: `curl -X POST -H "Transfer-Encoding: chunked" --data-
         binary @10GB.bin https://victim.com/api/contact` — bypasses 1MB cap.
       - Cross-ref: SEC-02 Q6 (line 35566). Still OPEN.
    2. NO Transfer-Encoding CHECK (HIGH):
       - Middleware does not inspect `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` header.
       - Next.js's body parser has its own limits (default 1MB on Vercel,
         configurable via `export const config = { api: { bodyParser: { sizeLimit: '1mb' } } }`)
         but NO route in this codebase declares that config.
       - For App Router (which this codebase uses), the body is parsed via
         `Request.json()` / `Request.formData()` etc. — these stream the
         body with no built-in size cap unless the runtime enforces one.
       - Net effect: under Node.js runtime, body can grow until OOM.
    3. NO CHECK ON GET REQUESTS (informational):
       - GET requests can technically carry a body (HTTP/1.1 allows it,
         though discouraged). Middleware does not check GET body size.
       - Most routes don't read GET bodies, so impact is minimal — but
         /api/admin/users/logs uses GET with query params (fine).
    4. NO CHECK ON DELETE REQUESTS (informational):
       - DELETE in /api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts, /api/admin/clips/route.ts,
         /api/admin/themes/route.ts etc. reads `await req.json()`. Middleware
         doesn't check DELETE body size (line 196 only checks POST/PUT/PATCH).
       - Attacker can send a 10GB DELETE body to /api/admin/clips → OOM.
    5. NO REVERSE-PROXY-LEVEL ENFORCEMENT (HIGH):
       - next.config.ts (next.config.ts:14-27) sets headers but not body
         size. No NGINX/Caddy client_max_body_size config checked.
       - Caddyfile exists at /home/z/my-project/Caddyfile (not inspected
         in this audit — outside src/) but should set
         `request_body { max_size 1MB }`.
    6. NO PER-ROUTE OVERRIDE:
       - All routes share the same 1MB cap. Upload endpoints (none exist
         today) would need a higher limit.
    7. 413 RESPONSE MISSING CSP/HSTS (LOW — cross-ref SEC-02 Q12):
       - addSecurityHeaders does not set CSP or HSTS.
       - Minor for a 413 JSON error.

  Severity: HIGH (chunked-encoding bypass makes the 1MB cap trivially
    defeated; no per-route config; DELETE bodies unchecked)

  PoC:
    # Bypass 1MB cap via chunked encoding:
    yes '{' | head -c 100000000 | curl -X POST \
      -H "Transfer-Encoding: chunked" \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      --data-binary @- \
      "https://victim.com/api/contact"
    # → middleware sees no Content-Length → skips 1MB check →
    #   route handler's req.json() tries to parse 100MB → OOM or hang.

    # Bypass via DELETE body (no size check on DELETE):
    yes 'A' | head -c 50000000 | curl -X DELETE \
      -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      --data-binary @- \
      "https://victim.com/api/admin/clips"

================================================================================
  ❌ FAIL — 3 of 4 rate-limit Maps HAVE NO CLEANUP
  Maps in codebase:
    1. middleware rateLimitMap      — HAS cleanup (every 5 min)
    2. /api/user/login loginAttempts — NO cleanup
    3. /api/contact hits             — NO cleanup
    4. /api/chat hits                — NO cleanup

  Map 1 — middleware (src/middleware.ts:42-65):
    42: const rateLimitMap = new Map<string, { count: number; resetAt: number }>();
    57-65: if (typeof setInterval !== "undefined") {
             setInterval(() => {
               const now = Date.now();

               }

           }
  ✅ Cleanup exists. Sweep interval 5 min.
  ⚠️ Edge runtime: `typeof setInterval !== "undefined"` guard means sweep is
     SILENTLY SKIPPED on Edge runtime (Vercel Edge functions don't have
     setInterval). Memory leak on Edge.
  ⚠️ No LRU cap — between sweeps, attacker can grow the Map by sending
     requests with N unique X-Forwarded-For values. At ~100 req/s with random
     IPs, that's 30k entries per 5-min sweep window × ~100 bytes/entry = ~3MB.
     Not catastrophic but grows linearly with attack duration.
  Cross-ref: SEC-02 Q10 (line 35362). Status: SAME.

  Map 2 — loginAttempts (src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:22-34):
    22: const loginAttempts = new Map<string, { count: number; resetAt: number }>();
    24-34: checkRateLimit — sets/increments entries but NEVER deletes.
  ❌ NO cleanup. Each unique IP (spoofable via Q8) creates a permanent entry.
     Over weeks of uptime, Map grows to thousands of entries.
     At ~100 bytes/entry × 10k entries = ~1MB. Not catastrophic but is a
     genuine leak.
  Cross-ref: SEC-02 Q10 (line 35392). Status: STILL OPEN (was F-25).

  Map 3 — hits in /api/contact (src/app/api/contact/route.ts:8-21):
    8:  const hits = new Map<string, number[]>();
    16: const arr = (hits.get(ip) || []).filter((t) => now - t < RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_MS);
    19: hits.set(ip, arr);
  ❌ NO cleanup. Map entries persist forever.
  ⚠️ WORSE THAN loginAttempts: each entry holds an ARRAY of timestamps. The
     array is filtered on each call (line 16) so old timestamps are dropped
     from the array, but the Map KEY persists even when the array becomes
     empty. So `hits.size` grows monotonically.

  Map 4 — hits in /api/chat (src/app/api/chat/route.ts:9-21):
    9:  const hits = new Map<string, number[]>();
    16: const arr = (hits.get(ip) || []).filter((t) => now - t < RATE_WINDOW_MS);
    19: hits.set(ip, arr);
  ❌ NO cleanup. Same pattern as Map 3. Same issue.

  Combined memory exposure:
    - 3 route-level Maps each grow monotonically with unique-IP count.
    - X-Forwarded-For spoofing (Q8) multiplies unique IPs by N×.
    - Each entry ~100-500 bytes (depending on array length).
    - At 10k unique spoofed IPs × 4 Maps × 500 bytes = 20MB. Sustainable.
    - At 1M unique spoofed IPs × 4 Maps × 500 bytes = 2GB. OOM.
    - Serverless cold starts reset the Maps (positive side-effect).

  Negatives:
    1. THREE OF FOUR MAPS HAVE NO CLEANUP (HIGH):
       - Login, contact, chat Maps all leak.
       - The middleware Map is the only one with sweep, and even it's
         silently skipped on Edge runtime.
    2. NO LRU / NO MAX-SIZE CAP ON ANY MAP (MED):
       - All 4 Maps can grow unbounded. Should cap at e.g. 10,000 entries
         and evict oldest.
    3. SWEEP INTERVAL (5 MIN) IS TOO LONG UNDER IP-ROTATION ATTACK (LOW):
       - Between sweeps, attacker can generate millions of unique keys.
       - Cross-ref: SEC-02 Q10 (line 35397). Still applicable.
    4. EDGE RUNTIME SKIPS SETINTERVAL GUARD ENTIRELY (MED):
       - On Vercel Edge, `typeof setInterval !== "undefined"` evaluates to
         `false` → sweep never runs → middleware's Map leaks for the
         lifetime of the Edge worker.
       - Cross-ref: SEC-02 Q10 (line 35403). Still applicable.

  Severity: MED (3 Maps leak; combined with Q8 spoofing, leak rate amplifies;
    serverless cold starts mitigate in practice)

    while true; do
      ip="$RANDOM.$RANDOM.$RANDOM.$RANDOM"

        -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
        -d '{"name":"x","email":"x@x.x","message":"x"}'
      # Hits /api/chat hits Map
      curl -s -o /dev/null -X POST "https://victim.com/api/chat" \
        -H "X-Forwarded-For: $ip" \
        -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
        -d '{"message":"hi","lang":"en","visitorId":"x"}'
    done

  Analysis:
    - ALL 5 sites trust the first comma-separated value of X-Forwarded-For
      WITHOUT validating against a trusted-proxy allowlist.
    - In a legitimate proxy chain (Cloudflare → origin), Cloudflare STRIPS
      client-supplied X-Forwarded-For and sets it to the true client IP →
      first entry IS the client IP → safe.
    - In a typical NGINX/Caddy-fronted deployment WITHOUT explicit stripping,
      the proxy APPENDS to X-Forwarded-For (NGINX default with
      `$proxy_add_x_forwarded_for`), so the first entry remains the
      client-supplied (attacker-controlled) value.
    - Vercel's edge layer sets X-Forwarded-For based on connecting IP but
      does NOT strip client-supplied values → exploitable.
    - The fallback `x-real-ip` is similarly attacker-controlled (NGINX sets
      it but only if configured; otherwise it's a client header).
    - Cross-ref: F-9 (SEC-02 Q11, line 35441). STILL OPEN.

  Impact:
    - Q1 (login brute-force): trivially bypassed.
    - Q2 (contact spam): partially bypassed (reCAPTCHA still gates).
    - Q3 (chat flood): trivially bypassed.
    - Q7 (Map memory leak): amplified (each spoofed IP = permanent Map key).
    - /api/track (uncapped public write): amplified — attacker can spoof
      IPs to fill PageView table with unique rows.
    - db.blockedIp table (src/lib/security.ts:8-17 isIpBlocked): an IP that's
      blocked can simply spoof a new X-Forwarded-For to bypass the block.
      The entire auto-block feature (recordSuspiciousActivity → 3 strikes
      → 24h block) is decorative if attacker rotates IPs.

  Code (src/lib/security.ts:27-57):

    i=0

  Negatives:
    1. NO AbortController / AbortSignal.timeout ON ANY FETCH (HIGH):
       - All 6 fetch call sites can hang indefinitely if the upstream API
         is slow or unresponsive.
       - Node.js's default fetch (undici) has no default timeout.
       - Vercel's edge fetch has a 30s platform timeout, but on Node.js
         standalone (this codebase's deployment mode per next.config.ts:4
         `output: "standalone"`), there's NO default.
       - If OpenAI is slow (10s) and Anthropic is slow (10s) and Groq
         hangs (30s), a single /api/chat request can take 60s+.
    2. NO maxDuration EXPORTED ON ANY ROUTE (MED):
       - Next.js App Router supports `export const maxDuration = 30` per
         route. None of the audited routes declare it.
       - Default on Vercel Hobby: 10s. Pro: 60s. Enterprise: 900s.
       - On Node.js standalone: no default — request can run forever.
       - /api/chat is the worst candidate — LLM calls can be slow.
    3. NO TIMEOUT ON LLM FALLBACK CHAIN (HIGH):
       - src/lib/providers.ts:58-70 loops over providers sequentially.
       - If first provider hangs for 30s, second isn't tried until 30s
         elapsed. User sees a 30s+ response time.
       - Should have per-provider timeout (e.g., 10s) so fallback chain
         completes in <40s total.
    4. NO TIMEOUT ON reCAPTCHA VERIFY (MED):
       - src/app/api/contact/route.ts:96-103.
       - If Google's reCAPTCHA endpoint is slow, /api/contact hangs.
       - reCAPTCHA verify is on the critical path — fail-closed means a
         slow Google = no contact form submissions.
    5. NO TIMEOUT ON FORMSUBMIT.CO FORWARD (LOW):
       - src/app/api/contact/route.ts:159-176 and src/app/api/admin/email/
         route.ts:75-85.
       - These are fire-and-forget (orphan promises) so don't block the
         response. But the orphan promise + its allocated buffer persists
         until GC. Repeated slow calls accumulate memory.
    6. NO TIMEOUT ON TELEGRAM/BALE SENDMESSAGE (LOW):
       - src/lib/telegram.ts:27-38 and src/lib/bale.ts:49-64.
       - These are awaited inside the webhook handler
         (src/app/api/telegram/webhook/route.ts:22, src/app/api/bale/
         webhook/route.ts:41) — so a slow Bale/Telegram API slows the
         webhook response.
       - Telegram/Bale webhooks have a 30s timeout from their side — if
         we don't respond in 30s, they retry → duplicate processing.
    7. NO CACHE DIRECTIVES ON /api/content (informational):
       - src/app/api/content/route.ts is a public GET that fetches 8 tables.
       - No `export const revalidate = 60` or `fetchCache` directive.
       - Every visitor triggers 8 DB queries.
    8. NO TIMEOUT ON RES.JSON() / RES.TEXT() (informational):
       - Even after fetch() resolves, the body stream can be slow to read.
       - No `await res.json()` timeout in any audited file.

  Severity: HIGH (LLM calls + reCAPTCHA + webhook processing all lack

    1. Route-level rate-limit Maps (Q7) — 3 Maps with no cleanup
    2. Client-side polling interval — src/components/ChatSection.tsx:60-78
    3. Orphan fire-and-forget fetches — 5 sites
    4. Session-context fetch growth — src/app/api/chat/route.ts:120-122
    5. Prisma client singleton — src/lib/db.ts:8-22 (no leak, but cold-start cost)

  Finding 1 — Route-level rate-limit Maps (HIGH — see Q7):
    - src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:22 `loginAttempts` Map — NO cleanup.
    - src/app/api/contact/route.ts:8 `hits` Map — NO cleanup.
    - src/app/api/chat/route.ts:9 `hits` Map — NO cleanup.
    - Each unique IP creates a permanent entry. Combined with X-Forwarded-For
      spoofing (Q8), growth is unbounded.
    - Mitigated by serverless cold-starts only.

  Finding 2 — Client-side polling interval never stops on unmount check (MED):
    src/components/ChatSection.tsx:54-78:
      54: const [lastPollTs, setLastPollTs] = useState(Date.now());
      58: useEffect(() => {
      59:   if (!sessionId) return;
      60:   const pollInterval = setInterval(async () => {
      61:     try {
      62:       const res = await fetch(`/api/chat/messages?sessionId=${sessionId}&since=${lastPollTs}`);
      63:       const data = await res.json();
      64:       if (data.ok && data.messages && data.messages.length > 0) {
      65:         setMessages((prev) => { ... });
      73:         setLastPollTs(data.serverTime || Date.now());
                   // ← state change triggers useEffect re-run → interval cleared
                   //   and recreated. OK.
      74:       }
      75:     } catch {}
      76:   }, 3000);
      77:   return () => clearInterval(pollInterval);  // ← cleanup on unmount ✅
      78: }, [sessionId, lastPollTs]);  // ← lastPollTs in deps
    Positives:
      - Cleanup function clears interval on unmount. ✅
      - Effect deps include lastPollTs so interval is reset when new messages
        arrive. ✅
    Negatives:
      - If NO new messages arrive, lastPollTs never updates, interval keeps
        firing every 3s forever (until tab closes or component unmounts).
        A user who leaves the chat section open in a background tab polls
        /api/chat/messages every 3s indefinitely.
      - 100 idle users × 20 polls/min = 2000 polls/min = 2000 DB queries/min
        on /api/chat/messages (which has no take limit — Q10).
      - Polling continues even if browser tab is in background (no Page
        Visibility API check).
      - No exponential backoff on error (catch swallows errors silently).
      - lastPollTs starts at Date.now() — if the user opens the chat, the
        first poll sends since=<current time> → only returns messages
        created AFTER the page loaded. Pre-existing admin replies are missed.

  Finding 3 — Orphan fire-and-forget fetches (LOW):
    5 sites use `.then(...).catch(() => {})` pattern without awaiting:
      a. src/app/api/contact/route.ts:152-156 — import("@/lib/bale").then(...)
      b. src/app/api/contact/route.ts:159-176 — import("@/lib/settings").then(...)
      c. src/app/api/chat/route.ts:140-149 — import("@/lib/bale").then(...)
      d. (implicit) any await import() that's not awaited — but those are
         awaited in this codebase.
    Negatives:
      - Each orphan promise allocates a closure + buffer that persists
        until the fetch resolves or GC. If upstream is slow, memory
        accumulates.
      - The `.catch(() => {})` swallows errors silently — no observability.
      - If the server is shutting down, these orphan promises may prevent
        clean shutdown (Node.js waits for unhandled promises).
      - Mitigated by: each individual allocation is small (a fetch + JSON
        body ~few KB). Need thousands per second to matter.

  Finding 4 — Session-context fetch growth (HIGH — see Q9 Finding 7):
    src/app/api/chat/route.ts:120-122, 153-159:
      - Each /api/chat POST fetches ALL messages in the session.
      - session.messages array grows by 2 per request (user + assistant).
      - The full array is held in memory for the LLM call (line 153-159).
      - 1000-message session = 1000 × ~2KB = 2MB per concurrent request.
      - 100 concurrent users with long sessions = 200MB.
      - NOT a leak per se (memory is freed after request) but a memory
        pressure amplifier under load.
      - Combined with no message-count cap and no sliding window, this is
        an OOM vector.

  Finding 5 — Prisma client singleton (informational — not a leak):
    src/lib/db.ts:8-22:
      const globalForPrisma = globalThis as unknown as { prisma: PrismaClient | undefined }
      export const db = globalForPrisma.prisma ?? new PrismaClient({ ... })
      if (process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production') globalForPrisma.prisma = db
    Analysis:
      - In development: prisma is cached on globalThis to prevent multiple
        clients during hot reload. ✅
      - In production: a new client is created per cold start. The previous
        client is NOT disconnected — but the process is about to die, so
        OS reclaims.
      - No `db.$disconnect()` call anywhere in the codebase. Acceptable for
        long-running servers (Prisma maintains a connection pool). On
        serverless, this can cause connection leaks if the platform
        freezes the process.
      - SQLite (this codebase per src/lib/db.ts:6 `db/custom.db`) uses a
        local file, not a network connection, so no connection-pool leak.

  Finding 6 — setInterval in middleware (LOW — see Q7):
    src/middleware.ts:58-65 — setInterval every 5 min for rateLimitMap sweep.
    - Has `.unref?.()` so doesn't keep process alive. ✅
    - But on Edge runtime, setInterval is undefined → sweep never runs →
      leak (cross-ref SEC-02 Q10).

  Finding 7 — setInterval in client components (informational):
    - src/app/page.tsx:189 — devtools detection interval (1s).
    - src/app/page.tsx:262 — clock tick interval (1s).
    - src/components/SignalBars.tsx:13 — animation interval.
    All have cleanup functions on unmount (verified via typical React
    patterns — these are client components, not audited in depth).

  Severity: HIGH (Finding 1 + Finding 4 are genuine server-side memory
    issues; Finding 2 is a client-side amplification of the server-side
    /api/chat/messages DoS)

Q5. SESSION_SECRET entropy check
================================================================================
  ✅ PRESENT — src/lib/access-auth.ts:19-43
  Code:
    19  // SESSION_SECRET — به‌صورت lazy بارگذاری می‌شه تا build fail نشه
    20  let _SECRET: string | null = null;
    21  function getSecret(): string {
    22    if (_SECRET) return _SECRET;
    23    const s = process.env.SESSION_SECRET;
    24    if (!s) {
    25      throw new Error("SESSION_SECRET env var is required (use: openssl rand -hex 32)");
    26    }
    27    // جلوگیری از placeholder ضعیف
    28    const KNOWN_BAD_SECRETS = new Set([
    29      "build-placeholder",
    30      "change-me",
    31      "secret",
    32      "your-secret-here",
    33      "changeme",
    34      "",
    35    ]);
    36    if (KNOWN_BAD_SECRETS.has(s) || s.length < 32) {
    37      throw new Error(
    38        "SESSION_SECRET is too weak or placeholder. Generate a strong one with: openssl rand -hex 32"
    39      );
    40    }
    41    _SECRET = s;
    42    return _SECRET;
    43  }

  Positives:
    - Rejects known-bad placeholders: build-placeholder, change-me, secret,
      your-secret-here, changeme, "" ✅
    - Rejects length < 32 chars ✅
    - Lazy-load prevents build-time failure when env is missing ✅
    - Module-level cache (`_SECRET`) avoids re-parsing env on every request ✅
    - HMAC uses crypto.timingSafeEqual in verifySessionToken (line 91) ✅
    - HMAC uses SHA-256 via crypto.createHmac (line 207) ✅

  Negatives (LOW-MED):
    1. LENGTH-ONLY CHECK, NO ENTROPY MEASUREMENT (LOW): `s.length < 32` measures
       character count, not byte entropy. A 32-char string of repeated chars
       like "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa" would PASS (32 ≥ 32). A
       predictable-but-long string like "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaab"
       would PASS. Should also compute Shannon entropy or require hex/base64
       format with character-set validation.
    2. NO REJECTION OF COMMON-WORD SECRETS (LOW): blocklist of 6 known-bad
       values is tiny. Common weak values NOT blocked: "test", "default",
       "production", "password", "supersecret", "session-secret", "my-secret",
       "12345678901234567890123456789012" (32-char numeric), "secret-key-..."
       (32+ chars but guessable). Should use a larger denylist or zxcvbn-style
       strength estimator.
    3. NO FORMAT REQUIREMENT (LOW): does not enforce hex/base64 format. A
       32-char ASCII string from a code comment, docstring, or README would
       pass. install.sh:109 uses `openssl rand -hex 32` → 64 hex chars — but
       the entropy check doesn't ENFORCE this format, just hopes for it.
    4. NO WARNING FOR ROTATION (informational): no mechanism to detect that
       the same SESSION_SECRET has been in use for a long time (90+ days)
       and recommend rotation.
    5. CHECK DELAYED UNTIL FIRST USE (LOW): getSecret() throws lazily, so
       `node server.js` boots without error. Health checks (e.g. `curl
       localhost:3000/`) return 200, masking the misconfiguration. A
       boot-time check (in next.config.ts or a server-startup hook) would
       surface the issue earlier.
    6. POSITIVE: V17.3-FINAL worklog claims "✅ SESSION_SECRET — قوی + entropy
       check + lazy-load" (VERSION.txt:124). The implementation matches this
       claim modulo the gaps above.

  Severity: LOW-MED (entropy check is present but shallow; main risk is a
    long-but-predictable secret slipping through).

================================================================================
  ✅ PASS — both webhooks enforce a secret with timingSafeEqual
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  /api/bale/webhook/route.ts:16-29:
    16  export async function POST(req: Request) {
    17    try {
    18      const url = new URL(req.url);
    19      const secret = url.searchParams.get("secret") || req.headers.get("x-webhook-secret") || "";
    20      const expectedSecret = process.env.BALE_WEBHOOK_SECRET;
    21      if (!expectedSecret) {
    22        return NextResponse.json({ ok: false, error: "webhook_not_configured" }, { status: 503 });
    23      }
    24      // Constant-time comparison
    25      const secretBuf = Buffer.from(secret);
    26      const expBuf = Buffer.from(expectedSecret);
    27      if (secretBuf.length !== expBuf.length || !crypto.timingSafeEqual(secretBuf, expBuf)) {
    28        return NextResponse.json({ ok: false, error: "invalid_secret" }, { status: 403 });
    29      }
  /api/telegram/webhook/route.ts:6-18:
    same pattern with `process.env.TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`.

  Positives:
    - Both webhooks REQUIRE a secret env var; return 503 if missing ✅
    - Both return 403 on mismatch ✅
    - Both use crypto.timingSafeEqual (line 27 / line 16) ✅
    - Length-mismatch pre-check (line 27 / line 16) prevents timingSafeEqual
      from throwing on different-length buffers ✅
    - Secret can be passed via URL query (?secret=xxx) OR X-Webhook-Secret
      header (both routes accept both) ✅
    - install.sh:113-125 generates both secrets with `openssl rand -hex 16`
      (64 bits of entropy) and preserves them across re-runs ✅

  Negatives (LOW):
    1. SECRET IN URL QUERY STRING (LOW-MED): the URL-query path means the
       secret appears in:
         - web server access logs (nginx access.log, systemd journal)
         - upstream proxy logs (Cloudflare, Vercel)
         - browser history / referrer headers (if the webhook were ever
           hit from a browser context — not the case today)
       The X-Webhook-Secret header path is safer (not logged by default).
       Bale/Telegram webhook bots always call with query-string secrets
       (Bale/Telegram don't support custom headers on setWebhook), so this
       is unavoidable for the inbound webhook secret model — but the access
       log exposure should be mitigated by:
         a) nginx location /api/bale/webhook { access_log off; }
         b) or: rotate secret + filter $args from access log
       nginx-ehsanmorad.conf does NOT do this today.
    2. 64 BITS OF ENTROPY (LOW): `openssl rand -hex 16` = 16 bytes = 128 bits
       but the hex output is 32 chars representing 128 bits — actually 128
       bits is fine. Wait, install.sh:116/118/122/124 use `openssl rand -hex
       16` which is 16 random bytes → 32 hex chars → 128 bits. ✅ Adequate
       for webhook validation. (Earlier note was wrong — 16 bytes IS 128
       bits, not 64.)
    3. NO RATE LIMIT ON WEBHOOK ENDPOINTS (LOW — informational): a wrong-secret
       attempt returns 403 but is not rate-limited. An attacker could brute-
       force the secret. With 128-bit entropy this is infeasible, but defense-
       in-depth would add a rate limit. middleware.ts:54-56 RATE_LIMIT_PATHS
       does NOT include /api/bale/webhook or /api/telegram/webhook.
    4. NO IP ALLOWLIST (informational): Bale/Telegram webhook IPs are
       well-known (could be allowlisted). Not enforced today.

  Severity: LOW (well-implemented; main concern is access-log leakage of the
    query-string secret).

Q7. AI keys encrypted at rest?
================================================================================
  ❌ FAIL — plaintext storage, schema comment is misleading
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  prisma/schema.prisma:97-110 (AiProvider model):
     97  model AiProvider {
     98    id        String   @id @default(cuid())
     99    name      String   // "openai", "anthropic", "zai", "ollama"
    100    label     String   // Display name
    101    apiKey    String?  // Encrypted API key (or null for local)
    102    baseUrl   String?  // Custom base URL (for Ollama, etc.)
    103    model     String   // Model name to use
    104    enabled   Boolean  @default(false)
    105    priority  Int      @default(0)
    106    createdAt DateTime @default(now())
    107    updatedAt DateTime @updatedAt
    108    @@index([enabled, priority])
    109  }
  The comment on line 101 — "Encrypted API key" — is FALSE. No encryption
  logic exists anywhere in the codebase.

  src/lib/providers.ts (verified lines 1-250):
    - getEnabledProviders (line 24-38): reads apiKey as plaintext string from
      Prisma; returns `apiKey: p.apiKey || undefined` (no decryption call).
    - callOpenAI (line 98-119): uses `Authorization: \`Bearer ${provider.apiKey}\``
      — plaintext key sent directly in HTTP header.
    - callAnthropic (line 122-147): uses `x-api-key: provider.apiKey || ""`
      — plaintext key sent directly in HTTP header.
    - callGroq (line 170-191): same `Bearer ${provider.apiKey}` pattern.
    - callCustom (line 194-196): delegates to callOpenAI → same Bearer pattern.

  src/app/api/admin/providers/route.ts:
    - GET (line 27-30): MASKS apiKey in response as
      `apiKey: p.apiKey ? "••••••••" + p.apiKey.slice(-4) : null` ✅ (this is
      transport-level masking, not at-rest encryption)
    - POST update (line 87-89): only updates apiKey if the submitted value
      does NOT start with "••••" (avoids overwriting real key with the mask)

  Impact:
    - Anyone with read access to db/custom.db (e.g. via the historical git
      blobs — see Q12; or via a misconfigured backup; or via filesystem
      escape on the host) sees ALL AI provider API keys in plaintext.
    - Combined with Q4 (db/custom.db mode 755 on dev box): every local non-
      root user can `sqlite3 /home/z/my-project/db/custom.db "SELECT
      name, apiKey FROM AiProvider"` and steal the keys.
    - The schema comment actively misleads code reviewers into believing
      encryption is in place.

  Severity: HIGH (plaintext storage of high-value long-lived API keys; no
    encryption layer; misleading schema comment).

Q9. Secrets in API responses?
================================================================================
  ⚠️ MIXED — some endpoints mask, some leak
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ✅ GOOD — masked properly:
    - GET /api/admin/users (src/app/api/admin/users/route.ts:38-58):
      Prisma `select` omits passwordHash; comment line 56:
      "// passwordHash هرگز برگردانده نمی‌شه". ✅
    - GET /api/admin/users/[id] PUT response (route.ts:76-92): same `select`
      omits passwordHash. ✅
    - GET /api/admin/providers (route.ts:27-30): masks apiKey as
      `"••••••••" + p.apiKey.slice(-4)`. ✅
    - POST /api/admin/providers update (route.ts:87-89): ignores submitted
      apiKey values that start with "••••" (prevents accidental overwrite
      with the masked display string). ✅

  ❌ FAIL — plaintext secrets in response:
    - GET /api/admin/settings (src/app/api/admin/settings/route.ts:99-137):
      Lines 109-127 return these SiteSetting values in PLAINTEXT in the JSON
      response body:
        - baleBotToken       (full bot token, not masked)
        - baleChatId
        - telegramBotToken   (full bot token, not masked)
        - telegramChatId
      The comment on lines 95-97:
        "Returns current site settings (excluding secrets like API keys /
         bot tokens). Note: Bot tokens are returned so the admin panel
         can populate the form; they are not displayed as plaintext in
         the UI (input type=password)."
      is misleading — the comment claims "excluding secrets" but the code
      DOES include them. The UI uses type=password to hide them visually,
      but the API response is plaintext and visible in:
        - browser dev tools Network tab
        - any client-side JS that fetches the endpoint
        - any MITM/proxy log
        - any XSS that exfiltrates the response
      Even though admin-only, this is unnecessary exposure. Best practice
      is to return hasBaleBotToken: true/false flags and require a separate
      "reveal secret" action with re-authentication.
    - POST /api/admin/settings action="get_telegram" (route.ts:29-41):
      Returns telegramBotToken and telegramChatId in PLAINTEXT. Same issue.
    - GET /api/bale/webhook (route.ts:55-77, the GET handler not the POST
      webhook itself):
      Line 73-75:
        webhookUrl: token
          ? `https://api.bale.ai/v1/bots${token}/setWebhook`
          : null,
      The bot token is interpolated into the webhookUrl string returned in
      the JSON response. Also note the URL is malformed: `bots${token}`
      missing a `/` separator (should be `bots/${token}` per Bale API).
      Admin-only, but again unnecessary exposure — the token is in the
      response body in cleartext.

  Severity: MED-HIGH (admin-only exposure, but plaintext bot tokens in
    API responses violate least-exposure; should return has* flags and
    require re-auth for reveal).

Q10. Secrets in console.error?
================================================================================
  ⚠️ LOW-MED — no explicit secret sanitization; risk is upstream-dependent
  --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  All 35 console.error call sites audited (rg "console\.error" src/):
    - src/lib/providers.ts:63            [LLM] Provider ${provider.label} failed: ${err}
    - src/lib/telegram.ts:35             [telegram] sendMessage error: ${err}
    - src/lib/bale.ts:61                 [bale] sendMessage error: ${err}
    - src/lib/access-auth.ts:168         Failed to log access: ${e}
    - src/app/api/admin/** (16 sites)   generic error: ${err}
    - src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:115  Login error: ${e}
    - src/app/api/chat/route.ts:177     [/api/chat] LLM error: ${llmErr}
    - src/app/api/chat/route.ts:209,248 [/api/chat] error: ${err}
    - src/app/api/messages/route.ts:48,140
    - src/app/api/clips/route.ts:16
    - src/app/api/content/route.ts:60
    - src/app/api/contact/route.ts:184
    - src/app/api/bale/webhook/route.ts:46
    - src/app/api/telegram/webhook/route.ts:25
    - src/app/error.tsx:7
    - src/app/global-error.tsx:7

  Analysis:
    - All 35 sites are inside try/catch error handlers and log `err`/`e`
      (the caught error object) directly.
    - None sanitize the error message before logging.
    - Most error sources (Prisma, fetch, JSON.parse) produce error.message
      strings that DO NOT include secret values:
        * Prisma errors: "Foreign key constraint failed on field: userId"
          → no secret
        * JSON.parse errors: "Unexpected token in JSON" → no secret
        * NextResponse errors: status codes only → no secret
    - POTENTIAL LEAK PATHS (where upstream errors MAY include secrets):
      1. src/lib/providers.ts:63 → logs `err` from callOpenAI/callAnthropic/
         callGroq. If the upstream LLM API (OpenAI, Anthropic, Groq) echoes
         the request headers in its error response (some APIs do for
         debugging), the `Authorization: Bearer <key>` or `x-api-key:
         <key>` header could appear in `err.message`. Empirically OpenAI
         does NOT echo the key, but Anthropic's error responses can include
         the request body (not headers). RISK: LOW but non-zero.
      2. src/lib/telegram.ts:35 → logs `err` from `fetch(\`https://api.telegram.org/bot${token}/sendMessage\`, ...)`.
         If fetch throws (network error, DNS failure), Node's fetch error
         typically does NOT include the URL. But if the error is wrapped
         by a library that includes the request URL, the bot token would
         be in the log. Default Node fetch does not include URL in err.
         RISK: LOW.
      3. src/lib/bale.ts:61 → same pattern as telegram.ts:35. RISK: LOW.
      4. src/app/api/chat/route.ts:177 → logs `llmErr` which is the
         propagated error from callLLMWithFallback (providers.ts:69):
           `throw new Error(\`All providers failed. Last error: ${lastError?.message}\`)`
         This includes the LAST provider's error message — which inherits
         the same LOW risk as #1 above.
    - No CLIENT-FACING secret leak via console.error (the API responses
      always return generic "server_error" — verified across all 35 sites).

  Severity: LOW-MED (defense-in-depth gap; no actual leak observed today,
    but no sanitization layer to prevent future leaks if upstream API
    behavior changes).

  Recommendations (NOT applied — read-only audit):
    - Wrap console.error in a sanitize() helper that strips known patterns:
      /sk-[a-zA-Z0-9]{20,}/ (OpenAI), /Bearer\s+[A-Za-z0-9\-_.]+/,
      /bot[0-9]+:[A-Za-z0-9_-]+/ (Telegram), /x-api-key:\s*[^\s]+/.
    - Or use a structured logger (pino/winston) with redaction rules.

  - 500 server_error:   { ok: false, error: "server_error" } (route.ts:107)
  - Action create  (route.ts:46-72): body.data → { ok: true, theme }

Q1. install.sh: does apply_schema.py run before seeding?
================================================================================
  ✅ YES — order is correct; ⚠️ silent-failure cascade risk
  install.sh ordering:
    - install.sh:166  python3 scripts/apply_schema.py 2>&1 | tail -3   (SCHEMA)
    - install.sh:175  python3 scripts/seed_content.py 2>&1 | tail -2
    - install.sh:176  python3 scripts/seed_equipment.py 2>&1 | tail -2
    - install.sh:177  python3 scripts/seed_texts.py 2>&1 | tail -2
    - install.sh:178  python3 scripts/seed_access_users.py 2>&1 | tail -2  (SEED)
  Gate logic:
    - install.sh:163-169  If sqlite_master count == 0 → run apply_schema.py
    - install.sh:172-182  If AccessUser count == 0 → run seed_*.py
  ✅ SCHEMA precedes SEED in source order.
  ✅ SEED query (line 172) depends on AccessUser table — which only exists
     if apply_schema.py succeeded. Correct dependency.
  ⚠️ SILENT FAILURE CASCADE (MED):
    - Line 166 pipes apply_schema.py output through `tail -3`, hiding all
      but the last 3 lines. If apply_schema.py errors (e.g., bad SQL,
      missing sqlite3, schema mismatch), only the last 3 lines are shown.
    - Line 175-178 each have `|| echo "  ⚠ seed_*.py failed"` which
      converts a Python traceback into a 1-line warning, then proceeds.
    - Net effect: if apply_schema.py fails, seeding silently fails, the
      sqlite3 query at line 172 returns 0 (no such table → caught by
      `|| echo "0"`), seeding runs anyway, fails table-not-exists errors,
      which are also caught by `|| echo "  ⚠ ..."`. The install reports
      "✅ دیتابیس seed شد" (line 179) even though NO seeding happened.
    - PoC: chmod -x scripts/apply_schema.py; rerun install.sh →
      "✅ دیتابیس seed شد" with zero rows in every table.
  Severity: MED (silent failure masquerades as success)

        DATABASE_URL, NODE_ENV, PORT, HOSTNAME, SESSION_SECRET,

      - BALE_BOT_TOKEN, TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN (if configured by user)
      - CONTACT_EMAIL, SMTP_HOST, SMTP_USER, SMTP_PASS (if added)
      - Any NEXT_PUBLIC_* runtime overrides
      - Any custom feature flags
    These would have been added manually by the user between installs.
    `cat > .env` overwrites unconditionally; no merge logic.

    Line 143 `RECAPTCHA_SECRET="$EXISTING_RECAPTCHA_SECRET"` — if user
    had no .env initially, EXISTING_RECAPTCHA_SECRET="" (line 131 fallback
    `|| echo ""`), and the line writes `RECAPTCHA_SECRET=""` to .env.
    Same for NEXT_PUBLIC_RECAPTCHA_SITEKEY (line 144). Empty strings
    overwrite any default the app might fall back to. Not a security
    issue per se, but a regression: if the user previously had the env
    var unset (and the app defaulted to "demo"), after install the var
    is explicitly empty string (and the app treats "" as configured-but-
    empty, which usually means "disabled").

    read/write the top-level db. The standalone/db copy (line 196) is
    unused dead weight. If the user later moves the standalone dir
    elsewhere, the absolute DATABASE_URL breaks silently.

Q5. install.sh: non-root systemd user?
================================================================================
  ✅ YES — ehsansite system user created with hardening
  install.sh:210-211  User creation:
    if ! id -u ehsansite &>/dev/null; then
        useradd -r -s /bin/false -d "$SITE_DIR" ehsansite 2>/dev/null || true
    fi
  ✅ `-r`  — system user (UID < 1000, no /home/ehsansite by default).
  ✅ `-s /bin/false`  — no login shell; cannot SSH in as ehsansite.
  ✅ `-d "$SITE_DIR"`  — home dir set to project dir (for the service).
  ✅ Idempotent: `if ! id -u ehsansite` guards re-creation.
  install.sh:213  Ownership:
    chown -R ehsansite:ehsansite "$SITE_DIR" 2>/dev/null || true
  ✅ Recursive chown to service user.
  install.sh:215-240  systemd unit:
    [Service]
    Type=simple
    User=ehsansite            ← line 222 ✅
    Group=ehsansite           ← line 223 ✅
    WorkingDirectory=$SITE_DIR
    ExecStart=$(which node) server.js
    Restart=always
    RestartSec=10
    Environment=NODE_ENV=production
    Environment=HOSTNAME=0.0.0.0
    Environment=PORT=3000
    # امنیت اضافه
    NoNewPrivileges=true      ← line 232 ✅ (blocks setuid)
    ProtectSystem=full        ← line 233 ✅ (/usr, /boot read-only)
    ProtectHome=true          ← line 234 ✅ (/home, /root, /run/user hidden)
    ReadWritePaths=$SITE_DIR  ← line 235 ✅ (only $SITE_DIR writable)
    PrivateTmp=true           ← line 236 ✅ (isolated /tmp)
  ✅ Hardening is good for a web service.
  ⚠️ ERROR MASKING (LOW):
    - Line 211 `|| true` — if useradd fails (e.g., not root, PAM error),
      script continues. systemd would then fail to start (User=ehsansite
      not found). The `set -e` at line 15 is bypassed.
    - Line 213 `|| true` — if chown fails (e.g., permission denied), the
      service files are still owned by root; ehsansite may not be able
      to read server.js or write to db/. systemd would fail.
    Neither is exploitable; both are silent-failure paths.
  ⚠️ MISSING HARDENING DIRECTIVES (LOW — informational):
    systemd.exec(5) recommends for additional isolation:
      - ProtectKernelTunables=true
      - ProtectKernelModules=true
      - ProtectControlGroups=true
      - RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_INET AF_INET6 AF_UNIX
      - RestrictNamespaces=true
      - RestrictSUIDSGID=true
      - SystemCallArchitectures=native
      - SystemCallFilter=@system-service
      - CapabilityBoundingSet=
      - LockPersonality=true
      - MemoryDenyWriteExecute=true   (would break JIT — Node needs this,
                                       so SKIP)
    Adding the listed ones (except MemoryDenyWriteExecute) would
    further sandbox the service. Not a finding per se, just defense-in-
    depth opportunities.
  ⚠️ WORKINGDIRECTORY RELATIVE TO REASSIGNED $SITE_DIR (LOW):
    In dev mode, line 200 `SITE_DIR="$SITE_DIR/.next/standalone"`
    reassigns BEFORE the systemd unit is written (line 215-240). So
    WorkingDirectory, ReadWritePaths, and `-d "$SITE_DIR"` (useradd)
    all point to the standalone subdir, NOT the project root.
    If useradd ran BEFORE the reassignment (line 210-212 runs before
    line 192's elif), the `-d "$SITE_DIR"` for ehsansite points to the
    TOP-LEVEL dir, while WorkingDirectory points to .next/standalone.
    Inconsistent but not a security issue (home dir is just a default
    for cd if no WorkingDirectory; here WorkingDirectory is explicit).
  ⚠️ PROTECTHOME + WORKINGDIR IN /home (LOW — VERIFY):
    If the project lives under /home (e.g., /home/ehsan/personal-site
    per reset-admin-password.sh:7 docstring), then:
      - ProtectHome=true (line 234) hides /home from the service.
      - ReadWritePaths=$SITE_DIR (line 235) re-exposes /home/ehsan/...
        for read AND write.
    Per systemd docs, ReadWritePaths overrides ProtectHome for the
    listed paths. So the service CAN read/write $SITE_DIR even though
    /home is otherwise hidden. ✅ Functionally correct.
    BUT: any other files in /home (siblings of $SITE_DIR) remain
    hidden — which is the desired behavior.
  Verdict vs. V17.3 claim:
    "✅ install.sh: systemd با user غیر root" — TRUE.
  Severity: PASS (with LOW notes on error masking and missing
    hardening directives)

Q6. install.sh: chmod 600 on .env + db?
================================================================================
  ✅ YES — present on .env, db dir (700), and db/custom.db
  install.sh:148  chmod 600 .env                                 ✅
  install.sh:128  chmod 700 db                                   ✅ (dir)
  install.sh:157  chmod 700 db                                   ✅ (redundant)
  install.sh:158  touch db/custom.db
  install.sh:159  chmod 600 db/custom.db                        ✅
  install.sh:160  rm -f db/custom.db-journal db/custom.db-wal db/custom.db-shm
                                                                  ✅ (clean slate)
  Standalone mode (dev path):
  install.sh:194  cp .env .next/standalone/.env
  install.sh:195  chmod 600 .next/standalone/.env               ✅
  install.sh:196  cp -r db .next/standalone/db 2>/dev/null || true
  install.sh:197  chmod -R 600 .next/standalone/db/*.db 2>/dev/null || true
                                                                  ✅ (redundant -R)
  install.sh:198  cp -r .next/static .next/standalone/.next/ 2>/dev/null || true
  install.sh:199  cp -r public .next/standalone/ 2>/dev/null || true
  ⚠️ RUNTIME SQLite FILE PERMISSIONS (MED — operational, not install):
    SQLite creates auxiliary files during operation:
      - db/custom.db-journal  (rollback journal, default mode)
      - db/custom.db-wal      (write-ahead log, WAL mode)
      - db/custom.db-shm      (shared memory, WAL mode)
    These are created by the Node.js process (running as ehsansite)
    with the process's umask. Default umask is 022 → files are 644
    (world-readable). install.sh:160 removes any pre-existing ones,
    but they get recreated at runtime with 644 perms.
    Impact: a non-ehsansite local user could read db/custom.db-wal
    (which contains uncommitted transaction data) and db/custom.db-shm
    (which contains the WAL index). The main db/custom.db is 600
    (protected), but the WAL/SHM expose the same data while writes are
    in-flight.
    Fix (NOT applied — read-only audit): set `Umask=0077` in the
    systemd unit (line 215-240) to force 600 on newly-created files.
  ⚠️ STANDALONE DB DIRECTORY PERMISSIONS (LOW):
    install.sh:197  `chmod -R 600 .next/standalone/db/*.db`
    - Glob `*.db` matches only .db files, not the db/ dir itself.
      The dir is created by `cp -r db .next/standalone/db` (line 196)
      which inherits source perms (700 from line 128). ✅ OK.
    - `-R` is redundant on a glob of files (no directories matched).
    - `2>/dev/null || true` hides failure if no .db files match.
  ⚠️ DATABASE_URL CROSS-MODE MISMATCH (LOW — see Q2):
    DATABASE_URL (install.sh:137) points to top-level $SITE_DIR/db,
    but in dev mode the standalone server reads .env from
    .next/standalone/.env which still has the top-level path. So the
    standalone server uses the top-level db (not the standalone/db
    copy at line 196). The chmod 600 on standalone/db/*.db (line 197)
    protects a COPY that's never used. The TOP-LEVEL db (the one
    actually used) IS chmod'd at line 159. ✅ Functionally correct,
    just inefficient.
  ⚠️ .env PERMISSIONS NOT RE-VERIFIED AFTER cp (LOW):
    Line 194 `cp .env .next/standalone/.env` — cp may or may not
    preserve source perms depending on flags. Line 195 `chmod 600`
    fixes it explicitly. ✅
  Verdict vs. V17.3 claim:
    "✅ install.sh: chmod 600 روی standalone .env + db" — TRUE.
  Severity: PASS (with MED operational note on runtime SQLite WAL/SHM
    file perms — fixable via UMask=0077 in systemd unit, not an
    install.sh bug per se)

Q7. nginx-ehsanmorad.conf secure?
================================================================================
  ❌ NO — HTTP only, no security headers, no server_tokens off, no body limit
  File: nginx-ehsanmorad.conf (64 lines, 3 identical server blocks)
  Block 1: lines 15-29   (ehsanmorad.ir)
  Block 2: lines 32-46   (ehsan-morad.ir)
  Block 3: lines 49-63   (ehsanmorad.id.ir)
  All three are STRUCTURALLY IDENTICAL — same findings apply to all.
  ❌ HTTP-ONLY (HIGH):
    Line 16  `listen 80;`  (block 1)
    Line 33  `listen 80;`  (block 2)
    Line 50  `listen 80;`  (block 3)
    No `listen 443 ssl;` block. No ssl_certificate / ssl_certificate_key.
    No HTTP→HTTPS redirect.
    The install.sh:284 `certbot --nginx` invocation is supposed to
    auto-modify this file to add an HTTPS server block, but:
      (a) certbot only runs if a domain is found in DNS (install.sh:274-
          279). If no domain resolves, the file stays HTTP-only.
      (b) Even if certbot runs, it modifies the LIVE file at
          /etc/nginx/sites-available/, not the source file in the
          project. The source file (committed to git) remains HTTP-only,
          so a fresh install on a new server starts insecure.
      (c) If certbot fails (e.g., rate limit, DNS not propagated), the
          site stays on HTTP indefinitely.
    Impact: all traffic (including login credentials, session cookies,
    admin operations) flows in plaintext. MITM can steal SESSION_SECRET
    cookie, admin password, reCAPTCHA secrets in transit.
  ❌ NO SECURITY HEADERS (HIGH — defense-in-depth broken):
    No `add_header` directives at all. Missing:
      - Strict-Transport-Security  (HSTS)
      - Content-Security-Policy    (CSP)
      - X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
      - X-Frame-Options: DENY (or SAMEORIGIN)
      - Referrer-Policy
      - Permissions-Policy
    The Next.js middleware sets these (per prior SEC-02 audit Q7), but
    only on NextResponse.next() — NOT on the /user-dashboard 307
    redirect or 4xx/5xx error responses. Nginx-level add_header would
    cover ALL responses uniformly, including Nginx's own error pages
    (502/504 when the backend is down).
  ❌ server_tokens NOT DISABLED (LOW):
    Default `server_tokens on` exposes nginx version in Server header
    and error pages. Helps attackers target known nginx CVEs.
    Fix: `server_tokens off;` in http/server block.
  ❌ NO client_max_body_size (MED — confirms SEC-02 Q6):
    No `client_max_body_size` directive. Defaults to 1MB, which matches
    the middleware's Content-Length check (SEC-02 Q6), but:
      (a) The middleware check trusts Content-Length and is bypassable
          via Transfer-Encoding: chunked (SEC-02 Q6 weakness).
      (b) Nginx enforces client_max_body_size BEFORE forwarding, on
          every request, regardless of Transfer-Encoding. So an
          explicit `client_max_body_size 1m;` at Nginx would close the
          chunked bypass.
    Fix: `client_max_body_size 1m;` in server/location block.
  ❌ CONNECTION HEADER HARDCODED (LOW — functional bug):
    Line 27  `proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";`
    Line 44  `proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";`
    Line 61  `proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";`
    Hardcoded "upgrade" tells the backend to treat every request as a
    WebSocket upgrade. For normal HTTP requests this is incorrect — the
    backend may behave unexpectedly (e.g., hold connections open,
    bypass keepalive pooling).
    Correct pattern:
      map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade {
          default upgrade;
          ''      close;
      }
      # then:
      proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;
    Not a direct security issue, but a known Nginx anti-pattern that
    can cause performance/connection-exhaustion issues.
  ❌ NO RATE LIMITING (MED):
    No `limit_req_zone` / `limit_req` directives. The Next.js
    middleware has in-memory rate limiting (SEC-02 Q4), but:
      - It's per-instance (no shared state across workers).
      - It's bypassable via X-Forwarded-For spoofing (SEC-02 Q11 HIGH).
      - It resets on cold start.
    Nginx rate limiting with `limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr` is
    shared across workers and not spoofable (Nginx uses the actual
    socket peer, not the X-Forwarded-For header). This would close the
    SEC-02 Q11 hole.
  ❌ NO PROXY TIMEOUTS (LOW):
    No `proxy_connect_timeout`, `proxy_read_timeout`, `proxy_send_timeout`.
    Defaults are 60s, which is fine for most requests but could allow
    slow-loris-style attacks on long-running admin operations.
  ❌ NO gzip (LOW — informational):
    No `gzip on;` / `gzip_types` directives. The Caddyfile DOES have
    `encode gzip zstd` (Caddyfile:13). Nginx config is weaker here.
  ❌ NO ACCESS/ERROR LOG CUSTOMIZATION (LOW):
    Uses Nginx defaults. Default access log includes query strings,
    which leaks webhook secrets passed as `?secret=...` (see Q10).
  ❌ NO PROXY BUFFERING SETTINGS (informational):
    No `proxy_buffering on;` / `proxy_buffers` directives.
  ✅ CORRECT proxy_set_header DIRECTIVES (lines 22-25):
    - Host $host                ✅
    - X-Real-IP $remote_addr    ✅
    - X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for  ✅
    - X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme ✅
    All four are standard and correct.
  ✅ WEBSOCKET UPGRADE SUPPORT (lines 26-27):
    - proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade  ✅
    - proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade"   ⚠️ (hardcoded — see above)
  ✅ DEFAULT SITE REMOVED (install.sh:255):
    `rm -f /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/default` — prevents the default
    Nginx welcome page from being served (which leaks nginx version).
  Severity: HIGH (HTTP-only is the dominant issue; no security headers
    and no body limit amplify the risk; no rate limiting leaves the
    app's own (broken) rate limit as the only defense)

================================================================================
Q8. reset-admin-password.sh secure?
================================================================================
  ❌ NO — password echoed 3× to stdout; no root check; weak default; SQL
          interpolation risk
  File: scripts/reset-admin-password.sh (79 lines)
  ❌ HARDCODED WEAK DEFAULT (HIGH — by design, but weak):
    Line 30  `NEW_PASSWORD="admin123"`
    The script's purpose is to reset to this exact password. The user
    is expected to change it after login (per line 68 warning). But:
      (a) "admin123" is in every default password list (rockyou, etc.).
      (b) The script is invokable by anyone with shell access (no auth
          check, just sudo).
      (c) If the operator forgets to change it post-reset, the account
          is wide open.
    No option to randomize: `NEW_PASSWORD="${1:-admin123}"` or
    `NEW_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -base64 12)` would be safer defaults.
  ❌ PASSWORD ECHOED TO STDOUT 3× (HIGH):
    Line 31   `echo "در حال تولید هش برای رمز: $NEW_PASSWORD"`
    Line 61   `echo "  رمز جدید: $NEW_PASSWORD"`
    Line 66   `echo "    password: $NEW_PASSWORD"`
    If stdout is captured (terminal scrollback, tmux capture, CI log,
    shell history if typed interactively, journald if run via systemd
    unit, /var/log/auth.log if sudo logs commands), the password is
    persisted in plaintext.
    Fix: read password via `read -s -p "Password: " NEW_PASSWORD` or
    accept as $1 and NEVER echo it.
  ❌ NO ROOT/SUDO VERIFICATION (MED):
    The docstring (lines 5-11) says to run with `sudo bash`, but the
    script doesn't verify it's running as root. If run without sudo:
      - Line 50  `sqlite3 db/custom.db "UPDATE ..."`  — fails with
        "unable to open database file" if db/ is owned by ehsansite
        with 700 perms (which install.sh:157 enforces).
      - The `2>/dev/null` on line 50 swallows the error. Line 53's
        COUNT query also fails silently, returns "".
      - Line 55 `if [ "$COUNT" = "1" ]` — COUNT is empty, not "1", so
        the else branch (line 71-77) runs: prints "❌ کاربر admin
        پیدا نشد!" — misleading error. The real cause (not root) is
        hidden by `2>/dev/null`.
    Fix: `if [ "$(id -u)" -ne 0 ]; then echo "run as root"; exit 1; fi`
    at the top.
  ❌ SQL INJECTION VIA HASH INTERPOLATION (MED — mitigated in practice):
    Line 50:
      sqlite3 db/custom.db "UPDATE AccessUser SET passwordHash = '$HASH',
       active = 1 WHERE username = 'admin';"
    $HASH is interpolated into the SQL string. If $HASH contained a
    single quote (e.g., `abc'--`), the SQL would become:
      ... SET passwordHash = 'abc'--', active = 1 WHERE username = 'admin';
    which would comment out the rest and update only passwordHash
    (skipping `active = 1`). Or worse, if $HASH were `x'; DROP TABLE
    AccessUser;--`, the table would be dropped.
    Mitigations in practice:
      (a) bcrypt hashes are formatted as `$2a$10$<22-char-salt><31-char-
          hash>` using the alphabet `./A-Za-z0-9` — NO single quotes.
          So today, $HASH is SQL-safe.
      (b) The hash is generated by bcryptjs (line 35), not user input.
    Risk: if bcryptjs ever changes its output format, or if NEW_PASSWORD
    is changed to include shell metacharacters that break the node -e
    command and leak partial output, the SQL could become malformed.
    Fix: use parameterized SQL via sqlite3's `.parameter` or use a
    Python wrapper with proper escaping.
  ❌ SHELL INJECTION VIA NEW_PASSWORD INTERPOLATION (MED):
    Line 33-37:
      HASH=$(node -e "
      const bcrypt = require('./node_modules/bcryptjs');
      const hash = bcrypt.hashSync('$NEW_PASSWORD', 10);
      process.stdout.write(hash);
      " 2>/dev/null)
    $NEW_PASSWORD is interpolated into the JS source via single quotes.
    If NEW_PASSWORD were `'; require('child_process').execSync('rm -rf /')//`,
    the JS would execute arbitrary code. Currently NEW_PASSWORD is
    hardcoded "admin123" (safe), but if a future maintainer changes it
    to accept user input (e.g., `NEW_PASSWORD="$1"`), this becomes
    RCE.
    Fix: pass password via env var: `NEW_PASSWORD="$NEW_PASSWORD" node -e
    "const h=bcrypt.hashSync(process.env.NEW_PASSWORD,10); ..."` or
    via stdin.
  ❌ NO AUDIT LOG (LOW):
    No record of password reset events. If multiple admins have shell
    access, there's no way to tell who reset the password and when.
    Fix: `logger -t reset-admin-password "reset by $(whoami) at $(date)"`
    before the SQL UPDATE.
  ❌ ERROR OUTPUT SUPPRESSED (LOW):
    Line 37  `2>/dev/null`  — hides node error output.
    Line 50  `2>/dev/null`  — hides sqlite3 error output.
    Line 53  `2>/dev/null`  — hides sqlite3 error output.
    If bcryptjs is missing (line 34 `require('./node_modules/bcryptjs')`
    fails), the node process exits non-zero, $HASH is empty, the script
    exits at line 39-43 with "❌ خطا در تولید هش". OK.
    But if sqlite3 fails (line 50), the script proceeds to line 53
    (also fails silently), $COUNT is "", the else branch runs (line 71)
    printing "❌ کاربر admin پیدا نشد!" — WRONG error message. The real
    issue (db not writable, sqlite3 not installed, table missing) is
    hidden.
  ⚠️ PROJECT_DIR DISCOVERY FRAGILE (LOW):
    Line 22  `SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"`
    Line 23  `PROJECT_DIR="$(cd "$SCRIPT_DIR/.." && pwd)"`
    If the script is invoked via symlink (e.g., `ln -s .../reset-admin-
    password.sh /usr/local/bin/reset-admin`), `$0` is the symlink path,
    and SCRIPT_DIR resolves to /usr/local/bin, not the project's scripts/
    dir. `cd "$SCRIPT_DIR/.."` → /usr/local, not the project.
    `db/custom.db` (line 50) would not be found.
    Fix: use `readlink -f "$0"` to resolve symlinks first.
  ✅ set -e (line 14):  aborts on any uncaught error.
  ✅ Exit 1 on hash failure (line 42) and on admin-not-found (line 77).
  Severity: HIGH (password echo is the dominant issue; weak default +
    no root check + no audit log compound it; SQL/shell injection
    mitigated in practice but architecturally unsound)

    redirects to `raw.githubusercontent.com` (also HTTPS). Both are

    Neither install.sh nor the worklog references include a checksum

    before extraction.

    informational on `curl | bash` pattern and missing checksums.

    - Line 335  `http://YOUR_IP:3000/api/bale/webhook?secret=<SEE .env>`
    - Line 336  `http://YOUR_IP:3000/api/telegram/webhook?secret=<SEE .env>`
    Three problems:
      (a) HTTP, not HTTPS — secret in query string is exposed to MITM
          on every webhook delivery.
      (b) Port 3000 — bypasses Nginx (which listens on 80/443). UFW
          (install.sh:87-89) only allows 22/80/443, so port 3000 is
          BLOCKED. The webhook URL won't work at all without manual
          firewall changes.
      (c) "YOUR_IP" literal — user must manually edit. If they forget,
          the URL is unusable. If they substitute a public IP, the
          webhook traffic is unencrypted.
  ❌ SECRET IN QUERY STRING (HIGH — applies to BOTH branches):
    `?secret=<SEE .env>` — the webhook secret is passed as a URL query
    parameter. This is INSECURE because:
      (a) Nginx access logs (default format) include the full URL with
          query string. Anyone with read access to /var/log/nginx/
          access.log (typically root + adm group) can read the secret.
      (b) Bale/Telegram's webhook delivery logs may include the full
          URL. Anyone with access to the Bale/Telegram developer
          dashboard can see the secret.
      (c) Any intermediate proxy (Cloudflare, corporate firewall, ISP)
          logs the URL with query string.
      (d) If the user ever visits the webhook URL in a browser (e.g.,
          to test it), the URL with secret is saved in browser history.
      (e) The Referer header on any subsequent request from the webhook
          handler to a third-party resource would leak the secret.
    Fix: pass secret via header (`X-Webhook-Secret: $BALE_SECRET`) and
    verify server-side. Or use HMAC signing (Telegram's recommended
    approach) instead of a static secret.
    Note: Telegram's official webhook API uses a secret_token parameter
    sent via `X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token` HEADER (not query string).
    So Telegram at least has a header-based option. Bale's API is less
    documented; check if it supports header-based secrets.
  ❌ ONLY ONE DOMAIN PRINTED (LOW — incomplete):
    install.sh:274-279  domain discovery loop:
      for domain in ehsanmorad.ir ehsan-morad.ir ehsanmorad.id.ir; do
          if host "$domain" &>/dev/null; then
              DOMAIN_FOUND="$domain"
              break
          fi
      done
    `break` on first match. If all three domains resolve (which they
    should, per nginx-ehsanmorad.conf which sets up all three), only
    `ehsanmorad.ir` is used for the webhook URL. The user is not told
    that the other two domains ALSO work for webhooks.
    Impact: minor — the user picks the primary domain. But the
    Nginx config serves all three identically, so the webhook works
    on all three; the install output just doesn't mention the others.
  ⚠️ PATH CONSISTENCY (LOW — informational):
    - Bale:     `/api/bale/webhook`      (singular "webhook")
    - Telegram: `/api/telegram/webhook`  (singular "webhook")
    Both use singular. ✅ Consistent.
    Not verified: whether the actual route handlers exist at these
    paths. The Next.js App Router would have:
      - src/app/api/bale/webhook/route.ts
      - src/app/api/telegram/webhook/route.ts
    (Out of scope for this audit — only the 4 listed files inspected.)
  ⚠️ SECRET MASKING IS CORRECT (✅):
    The literal `<SEE .env>` placeholder means the actual secret value
    is NEVER printed to stdout. ✅ (Consistent with Q3 finding.)
    Line 338: "⚠️ Secretها تو فایل .env هستن — با 'sudo cat .env' ببین"
    Instructs user to read .env directly. ✅
  ⚠️ NO WEBHOOK ROUTE VERIFICATION (LOW):
    install.sh doesn't probe `https://$DOMAIN_FOUND/api/bale/webhook`
    to verify the route exists. If the route is misconfigured (e.g.,
    typo in route.ts filename), the user discovers it only when Bale/
    Telegram fail to deliver.
  Severity: HIGH (secret in query string is the dominant issue; HTTP
    fallback compounds it; only mitigated by the fact that the user
    must manually configure Bale/Telegram to use the printed URL, so
    a careful user could swap to a header-based approach — but the
    install output doesn't suggest that)

      name/tagline/status editors). The save actions call
      /api/admin/settings and /api/admin/email which both require
      admin via checkAdminAuth (src/lib/admin-auth.ts:25 —
      `if (user.role !== "admin") return { ok: false };`), so the
      saves will return 401. But the UI is still visible to
      non-admins, which:
        (a) leaks the existence of admin features (Bale bot token,
            Telegram chat ID, admin password change form);
        (b) allows a non-admin to fill the form (form state is
            client-side; submit will silently fail with no visible
            error since SettingsPanel's loadSettings silently
            ignores non-ok responses — see src/components/
            SettingsPanel.tsx:311 `if (settingsData.ok)`).
      Severity: MED — UI leak + misleading UX. Defense-in-depth
        still holds at the API layer.

  6.4 Non-admin with explicit permissions — DEFECT (cross-ref Q1):
      If `user.permissions` includes e.g. "messages", the tab
      button is visible (line 142 returns true) but the panel
      content is gated by `&& isAdmin` (line 265). Clicking the
      tab shows an empty content area. See Q1 for full breakdown.
      Severity: MED for affected users.

  6.5 accessAllowed=false does NOT log user out — INFORMATIONAL:
      src/app/user-dashboard/page.tsx:205-211
        {!accessAllowed && (
          <div className="dashboard-access-warning" role="alert">
            {t.accessWarning}
            <br />
            {t.reason}: <code>{accessReason}</code>
          </div>
        )}
      When `accessAllowed` is false (user is outside allowed
      hour/day window or expired), the page still renders with a
      warning banner. User can still navigate tabs and attempt
      actions — admin API calls will succeed (the API routes do
      NOT call checkAccess — only checkAdminAuth which checks
      role + active + session, not time-of-day). This means:
        - The dashboard's "access schedule" UI is informational.
        - The middleware and /api/user/verify ARE the only
          enforcers of time-based access; once verified, admin
          API routes do NOT re-check time-of-day.
      Not a defect per se (defense-in-depth via verify), but the
      access-schedule restriction is weaker than the UI suggests.

----- 12. Logout button works?  [PARTIAL, LOW] -----
  Button markup:
    src/app/user-dashboard/page.tsx:195-200
      <button onClick={handleLogout} className="dashboard-btn danger">
        {t.logout} →
      </button>

  Handler:
    src/app/user-dashboard/page.tsx:122-125
      async function handleLogout() {
        await fetch("/api/user/logout", { method: "POST",
          credentials: "include" });
        router.replace("/user-login");
      }

  API:
    src/app/api/user/logout/route.ts:7-11
      export async function POST() {
        const response = NextResponse.json({ ok: true });
        response.cookies.delete("access_session");
        return response;
      }
    Cookie deletion via `response.cookies.delete`. ✅

  Middleware protection:
    src/middleware.ts:21 — "/api/user/logout" is in RATE_LIMIT_PATHS.
      Wait: actually "/api/user/logout" is in PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES
      (line 30) which means it skips the Origin/CSRF check. This is
      correct — logout is idempotent and doesn't need CSRF.
    src/middleware.ts:188 — "/api/messages" + "/api/admin/*" require
      session, but /api/user/logout is NOT in ADMIN_API_PREFIX so it
      is not session-checked at middleware. The route handler itself
      does NOT verify session either — it just deletes the cookie
      unconditionally. Safe (deleting a non-existent cookie is a no-op).
      ✅

  Defects:
    12.1 NO try/catch around fetch — page.tsx:123
      If the fetch throws (network error, server down), the await
      will reject, the router.replace on line 124 will NOT execute,
      and the user will see no feedback. The button is also left
      in a clickable state (no `disabled` during pending). User
      can click again and trigger another fetch.

    12.2 NO loading/disabled state on the button — page.tsx:195-200
      No `disabled={isLoggingOut}` guard. Double-click during the
      ~50-200ms fetch window is possible (creates two POSTs to
      /api/user/logout — second one is a no-op, harmless, but
      indicates missing UX polish).

    12.3 NO feedback if /api/user/logout returns non-ok — page.tsx:123
      The handler doesn't check `data.ok` from the response. The
      API always returns ok:true (logout/route.ts:8), so this is
      not exploitable today, but a future API change could break
      silently.

    12.4 Redirect target — PASS:
      router.replace("/user-login") (line 124) uses Next.js
      client-side navigation. /user-login route verified to exist
      (src/app/user-login/page.tsx, 6335 bytes). ✅

  Severity: LOW — logout works end-to-end in the happy path; only
    edge cases (network failure during logout) are mishandled.
    Cookie is cleared and user is redirected in the normal case.

1. Q1/Q6.4 (HIGH for affected users) — Either:

       tabs they're permitted to use. Note: MessagesPanel currently
       relies on checkAdminAuth at the API layer — for non-admin

     (b) bcryptjs is pure JavaScript (~3× slower than native bcrypt).
         Under load, `bcrypt.compare` with rounds=10 ≈ 100 ms per call.
         Combined with F-5 (no rate-limit on /api/admin/*) and F-9
         (X-Forwarded-For spoofing — still open per V17.4-SEC-02 audit),
         an attacker can saturate the event loop with bcrypt work

================================================================================
1. EXPENSIVE SYNC OPS
================================================================================
Findings:

[P18-S-1] HIGH — src/lib/canvas-protect.ts:67 + :79 — watermarkCanvas() calls
  ctx.getImageData(w-20, h-3, 20, 3) AND ctx.putImageData(imageData, w-20, h-3)
  on every invocation. getImageData/putImageData are among the most expensive
  2D canvas operations (they round-trip pixels through the JS heap and disable
  GPU acceleration for the rest of the frame). This function is invoked from
  inside rAF loops in 3 separate components (see [P18-S-2] below), so it runs
  ~60 times/second per visible canvas. That is ~180 expensive pixel-readbacks
  per second when 3 canvases are visible (generator + scope + lab visualizer).
  Steganographic LSB watermarking should run ONCE per canvas on resize / init,
  not every frame.

[P18-S-2] HIGH — dynamic import() called INSIDE requestAnimationFrame loop,
  every frame, in 3 files:
   - src/components/RealSignalGenerator.tsx:225-227
       import("@/lib/canvas-protect").then(({ watermarkCanvas }) => {
         watermarkCanvas(ctx, w, h);
       });
   - src/components/RealOscilloscope.tsx:376-378  (same pattern)
   - src/components/LabDeviceVisualizer.tsx:402-404 (same pattern)
  Although the module is cached after first load, each call allocates a new
  Promise + microtask + then-callback. At 60fps this is 60 wasted Promise
  allocations per canvas per second. The static `import watermarkCanvas from
  "@/lib/canvas-protect"` at module top would eliminate this entirely.

[P18-S-3] MEDIUM — src/app/api/track/route.ts:20-28 — `await
  db.pageView.create(...)` is in the hot path of the response. Every page view
  (if the route were called) blocks the response on a synchronous SQLite write.
  Should be fire-and-forget (no await, return 200 immediately). NOTE: this
  route is currently not called from any client code (grep "/api/track" finds
  only its own definition + middleware whitelist) — so the impact today is
  zero, but the pattern is wrong if re-enabled.

[P18-S-4] LOW — src/lib/db.ts:6 — `path.join(process.cwd(), 'db', 'custom.db')`
  runs once at module load. Cheap (~0.05ms) but happens for every cold start
  of every serverless function. Acceptable.

[P18-S-5] LOW — src/middleware.ts:81 — `Buffer.from(decodeURIComponent(token),
  "base64").toString("utf8")` runs on every request that has a cookie. Cheap
  (cookie is <2KB) but runs on every navigation. Acceptable.

[P18-S-6] LOW — src/components/RealOscilloscope.tsx:92-107 — assigns
  `signalAtTimeRef.current = (t: number) => {...}` DURING RENDER. This is a
  side-effect during the render phase. React 19 strict mode (enabled in
  next.config.ts:12) will call it twice per render in dev. Not a perf bug per
  se but creates a new closure every render and triggers React's "side effect
  in render" warning. Move to useMemo or to a useEffect.

  src/lib/providers.ts:202-249 does `db.aiProvider.count()` (line 203) every

[P18-F-1] HIGH — src/app/layout.tsx:2-4, 9-19 — 6 Google Fonts loaded

    Geist       (line 9)   — subsets: ["latin"]
    Geist_Mono  (line 10)  — subsets: ["latin"]
    Vazirmatn   (line 11-15) — subsets: ["arabic","latin"], display: "swap"
    Inter       (line 17)  — subsets: ["latin"]
    Lora        (line 18)  — subsets: ["latin"]
    Fira_Code   (line 19)  — subsets: ["latin"]
  Issues:
    a. Only Vazirmatn sets `display: "swap"`. The other 5 use next/font's
       default which IS "swap" — but it's inconsistent and fragile.
    b. Only Vazirmatn is actually applied as the default body font (via
       --font-vazirmatn variable, used in personal.css:35
       `--font-fa: "Vazirmatn", var(--font-mono)`). The other 5 are only
       activated when the admin user explicitly selects them via the
       FontSelector component (src/components/FontSelector.tsx).
    c. All 6 woff2 files (often multiple weights each) are preloaded on
       first paint of every page, even though 5 are unused by default.
    d. Body className at line 145 includes all 6 variables:
       `${geistSans.variable} ${geistMono.variable} ${vazirmatn.variable}
         ${inter.variable} ${lora.variable} ${firaCode.variable}`
       This causes Next.js to emit @font-face for all 6.
  Fix: lazy-load 5 non-default fonts via next/dynamic on the FontSelector
  component, or only import Vazirmatn at the layout level and import the
  other 5 inside FontSelector.

[P18-F-3] LOW — No `preload: false` on any font. next/font preloads all

[P18-F-4] NONE — No `@font-face` declarations in CSS files (personal.css

11. MEMORY LEAKS
================================================================================

[P18-ML-1] HIGH — src/app/api/contact/route.ts:8 —
  `const hits = new Map<string, number[]>();`
  In-memory rate limiter Map. Entries are added per-IP (line 19 `hits.set(ip,
  arr)`) but NEVER deleted. Old timestamps are filtered out on subsequent
  hits from the SAME IP (line 16: `.filter((t) => now - t <
  RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_MS)`), but IPs that hit once and never return leave their
  entries in memory FOREVER. Over months of traffic with thousands of
  unique IPs, this Map grows unbounded. Same pattern as [P18-ML-2] and
  [P18-ML-3]. Should have a periodic cleanup interval like middleware.ts:58-
  65 does for rateLimitMap.

[P18-ML-2] HIGH — src/app/api/chat/route.ts:9 —
  `const hits = new Map<string, number[]>();`
  Same pattern as [P18-ML-1]. Same issue.

[P18-ML-3] HIGH — src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:22 —
  `const loginAttempts = new Map<string, { count: number; resetAt: number }>();`
  Same pattern. No cleanup interval. Memory grows with each unique attacking
  IP forever.

[P18-ML-4] PASS — src/middleware.ts:42 — `const rateLimitMap = new Map<...>()`
  HAS cleanup at lines 58-65 via `setInterval(...).unref?.()`. This is the
  correct pattern. The three rate-limiter Maps above should follow this
  pattern.

[P18-ML-5] LOW — src/app/api/chat/route.ts:140-149 — `import("@/lib/bale").
  then(...).catch(() => {})` — fire-and-forget promise. If the component
  unmounts or the serverless function is frozen before the promise resolves,
  the bale notification silently fails. Acceptable (notifications are best-
  effort) but worth noting.

[P18-ML-6] LOW — src/app/api/contact/route.ts:152-176 — Two fire-and-forget
  dynamic imports (bale + settings/email forward). Same acceptable pattern.

[P18-ML-7] NONE — All useEffect cleanups return their teardown functions
  (see Section 12 below for details). No leaked event listeners, intervals,
  or observers in client components.

12. useEffect CLEANUPS
================================================================================

[P18-UE-1] PASS — All useEffect hooks that subscribe to side-effects DO
  return cleanup functions. Verified file-by-file:

  Properly cleaned up (return cleanup fn):
   - src/components/MatrixRain.tsx:74-77          cancelAnimationFrame + removeEventListener
   - src/components/Oscilloscope.tsx:114-118      cancelAnimationFrame + ro.disconnect + removeEventListener
   - src/components/RealOscilloscope.tsx:388-391  cancelAnimationFrame + ro.disconnect
   - src/components/RealSignalGenerator.tsx:237-240  cancelAnimationFrame + ro.disconnect
   - src/components/SpectrumAnalyzer.tsx:147-150  cancelAnimationFrame + ro.disconnect
   - src/components/LabDeviceVisualizer.tsx:415   cancelAnimationFrame
   - src/components/SignalBars.tsx:17             clearInterval
   - src/components/ChatSection.tsx:77           clearInterval
   - src/lib/useContent.ts:68                     cancelled flag (prevents setState after unmount)
   - src/app/page.tsx:194-198  (anti-theft)       removeEventListener x2 + clearInterval
   - src/app/page.tsx:211      (scroll)            removeEventListener
   - src/app/page.tsx:263      (clock)             clearInterval
   - src/app/page.tsx:282      (IntersectionObs)   io.disconnect()
   - src/app/page.tsx:313      (esc key)          removeEventListener
   - src/app/error.tsx:8       (no side effect)    N/A — only console.error, no cleanup needed
   - src/app/global-error.tsx:8 (no side effect)  N/A — same
   - src/components/InteractiveTerminal.tsx:18-20, 23-27 — pure setState, no cleanup needed
   - src/components/FontSelector.tsx:23-26        — pure localStorage read, no cleanup needed

[P18-UE-2] MEDIUM — Fetch-based useEffect hooks WITHOUT cleanup — these
  don't cancel the fetch, so if the component unmounts mid-fetch, React will
  warn "Can't perform a React state update on an unmounted component":
   - src/app/user-dashboard/page.tsx:91-113 (verify fetch)
   - src/app/user-dashboard/page.tsx:365-377 (MessagesPanel fetch)
   - src/app/clips/page.tsx:21-28 (clips fetch)
   - src/components/TextEditor.tsx:29 (loadTexts)
   - src/components/ThemeBuilder.tsx:78 (loadThemes)
   - src/components/ContentManager.tsx:60 (loadItems)
   - src/components/AparatClipManager.tsx:35 (fetchClips)
   - src/components/StatsDashboard.tsx:23 (load)
   - src/components/NavMenuManager.tsx:28 (loadItems)
   - src/components/AccessUserManager.tsx:80 (fetchUsers)
   - src/components/SecurityDashboard.tsx:23 (load)
   - src/components/SettingsPanel.tsx:271-284 (loadSettings + loadProviders)
  None of these use the `let cancelled = false; return () => { cancelled = true; }`
  pattern that useContent.ts:33-68 uses correctly. React 18+ no longer
  warns about this (the warning was removed in React 18), so it's a minor
  issue — but the fetch still completes and the setState call still
  dispatches into a detached fiber, which is wasted work. Use AbortController
  + signal for proper cancellation.

[P18-UE-3] LOW — src/components/ChatSection.tsx:58-78 — polling useEffect
  depends on `[sessionId, lastPollTs]`. Inside, line 73 calls
  `setLastPollTs(data.serverTime || Date.now())` after every successful poll
  that returns messages. This retriggers the useEffect, which clears the
  interval and starts a new one. Net effect: when there are new messages,
  the 3-second interval restarts. When there are none, it persists. The
  pattern works but causes the interval to be torn down and re-created
  unnecessarily. Use a ref for lastPollTs instead of state.
