================================================================
Status: FAIL  | Severity: HIGH
Location: src/lib/providers.ts:99, 104, 151, 171, 176, 127
          prisma/schema.prisma:97-110 (AiProvider model)

Code:
  providers.ts:99:    const baseUrl = provider.baseUrl || "https://api.openai.com/v1";
  providers.ts:100:   const res = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/chat/completions`, {...});
  providers.ts:104:     "Authorization": `Bearer ${provider.apiKey}`,
  providers.ts:151:   const baseUrl = provider.baseUrl || "http://localhost:11434";
  providers.ts:152:   const res = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/api/chat`, {...});
  providers.ts:171:   const baseUrl = provider.baseUrl || "https://api.groq.com/openai/v1";
  providers.ts:172:   const res = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/chat/completions`, {...});
  providers.ts:176:     "Authorization": `Bearer ${provider.apiKey}`,
  providers.ts:127:   const res = await fetch("https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages", {...});
                     // ← HARDCODED, ignores provider.baseUrl (F-F)

Analysis:
  - Three of four provider types (OpenAI, Ollama, Groq) respect
    `provider.baseUrl` from the DB. The AiProvider.baseUrl column
    (schema.prisma:102) is admin-configurable via the admin panel
    with NO validation:
      * No allowlist of hosts.
      * No blocklist for 169.254.169.254 (AWS/GCP/Azure IMDS),
        127.0.0.0/8, ::1, 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, fc00::/7,
        0.0.0.0/8.
      * No DNS-resolution check (DNS rebinding: a domain that
        resolves to a public IP at validation time but to
        169.254.169.254 at fetch time — there is no validation
        today, but even if added naively, rebinding bypasses it).
      * No `redirect: "manual"` — fetch follows 302/301 by
        default. An attacker baseUrl can 302 to an internal URL
        after the initial request.
      * No protocol restriction (http:// allows cleartext MITM
        and interception of the Authorization header).
  - API KEY EXFILTRATION: providers.ts:104 and 176 send
    `Authorization: Bearer ${provider.apiKey}` to whatever host
    the baseUrl points to. If baseUrl is attacker-controlled
    (e.g., admin-compromised via prior audit V17.3-SEC-02 Q4/F-5
    "no rate limit on /api/admin/*"), the attacker receives the
    API key in the Authorization header.
  - RESPONSE INJECTION: an attacker-controlled baseUrl returns
    arbitrary JSON; providers.ts:118 reads
    `data.choices[0]?.message?.content` from it. That string
    becomes the LLM "reply" (route.ts:186) and is stored + served
    to visitors + admin (Q5 amplification). The attacker controls
    the chat-bot output entirely — phishing, misinformation, XSS
    payload delivery.
  - METADATA EXFIL via redirect: an attacker baseUrl that 302s
    to http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-
    credentials/ → fetch follows → response body becomes the
    LLM "reply" → returned to the visitor's chat window. Cloud
    metadata exfil through the chat channel.
  - Anthropic (providers.ts:127) is hardcoded to api.anthropic.com
    — INCONSISTENCY (F-F): admin may set a baseUrl on an
    Anthropic provider expecting it to take effect; it is silently
    ignored. The admin may believe they're routing through a proxy
    when they are not.

  # admin's browser through Q5 stored XSS) creates a "custom"

Q10. visitorId forgeable?
================================================================
Status: FAIL  | Severity: MED
Location: src/app/api/chat/route.ts:101, 139, 152-160
          src/lib/bale.ts:55, 88-105

Code:
  route.ts:101:       const visitorId = String(body.visitorId || "").slice(0, 100) || "anon";
  route.ts:139:       data: { visitorId, ip, userAgent },   // stored at session creation only
  route.ts:152-160:   import("@/lib/bale").then(({ notifyNewChat }) =>
                        notifyNewChat({ sessionId, visitorId, message, isFirst: isFirstMessage })
                      ).catch(() => {});
  bale.ts:55:           parse_mode: "Markdown",
  bale.ts:97:            `*Visitor:* ${msg.visitorId}`,
  bale.ts:100:           `${msg.message.slice(0, 300)}`,
  bale.ts:102:           `_Reply with:_ /chat ${msg.sessionId} your response`,

Analysis:
  - visitorId is read directly from the request body (route.ts:101)
    with only `.slice(0, 100)`. No validation of any kind:
      * Not bound to a cookie / signed token / HMAC.
      * Not bound to the requester's IP.
      * Not bound to the session's existing visitorId (when
        continuing an existing session, the request's visitorId is
        IGNORED for lookups — only used at creation at line 139).
      * No format check (could contain markdown, control chars,
        Unicode zero-width chars, HTML, etc.).
  - Impact #1 — Bale MARKDOWN INJECTION (MED):
      * bale.ts:55 sets `parse_mode: "Markdown"`.
      * bale.ts:97 interpolates `*Visitor:* ${msg.visitorId}` raw.
      * An attacker sets visitorId to `[CEO Ehsan](http://evil.com/phish)`
        → Bale renders "Visitor: CEO Ehsan" as a clickable link
        to evil.com → phishing the admin.
      * An attacker sets visitorId to a victim's known visitorId
        → admin's CRM attribution is corrupted (the admin thinks
        they're talking to the victim).
      * Markdown injection also enables Bale-message structural
        breakage: a visitorId full of unmatched backticks breaks
        the message layout.
  - Impact #2 — message content ALSO injected raw:
      * bale.ts:100 interpolates `${msg.message.slice(0, 300)}`
        raw with parse_mode=Markdown.
      * A user message containing `[click me](javascript:alert(1))`
        or `[x](http://evil.com)` renders as a clickable link in
        the admin's Bale chat. Same phishing / spoofing vector as
        visitorId.
      * A user message containing `*` / `_` / `` ` `` chars
        breaks the Bale markdown structure.
  - Impact #3 — analytics pollution (LOW-MED):
      * The admin GET endpoint (route.ts:243-252) returns sessions
        with their visitorId. An attacker can flood with random
        visitorIds, polluting any analytics keyed on visitorId.
  - Impact #4 — stored visitorId never updated (LOW):
      * When a session is hijacked (Q1), the attacker's visitorId
        is sent in the body but NOT written to the session row
        (line 139 only runs on creation). So the DB keeps the
        original victim's visitorId — good for forensics — BUT
        the Bale notification for the hijacked message uses the
        ATTACKER's visitorId (route.ts:152-160). Inconsistency →
        admin sees a different visitorId in Bale than in the panel
        for the same session.
  - Impact #5 — XSS via visitorId in admin panel (MED, depends
    on client rendering): if the admin panel renders visitorId
    with dangerouslySetInnerHTML or without escaping, a visitorId
    like `<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>` becomes stored XSS in
    the admin panel. The server-side surface is dirty (no
    validation → DB accepts arbitrary strings); whether it
    executes depends on the client code.

PoC (Bale markdown injection — phishing link):
  curl -X POST .../api/chat -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
    "message":"hi",
    "lang":"en",
    "visitorId":"[CEO Ehsan](http://evil.com/phish)"
  }'
  # Admin's Bale chat shows "Visitor: CEO Ehsan" as a clickable
  # link to evil.com.

Cross-reference: V17.4-SEC-12 Q10 — unchanged. V17.4-SEC-04 #6.6
  (visitorId not bound to same-origin, LOW) — extended; this
  audit raises to MED because the message-content markdown
  injection in bale.ts:100 is NEW (was not called out in
  V17.4-SEC-12, which only flagged the visitorId field at
  bale.ts:97).

----- F-A. Rate-limit Map memory leak  [MED → FIXED] -----
Status: ✅ FIXED in V17.4-FINAL sweep (worklog lines 63070-63074).
Location: src/app/api/chat/route.ts:11-21

Code:
  route.ts:11-21: if (typeof setInterval !== "undefined") {
                   setInterval(() => {
                     const now = Date.now();
                     for (const [k, arr] of hits) {
                       const fresh = arr.filter(t => now - t < RATE_WINDOW_MS);
                       if (fresh.length === 0) hits.delete(k);
                       else hits.set(k, fresh);
                     }
                   }, 5 * 60 * 1000).unref?.();
                 }

Analysis:
  - The Map sweep now runs every 5 minutes and deletes empty
    entries. The original F-A memory-leak defect is closed.
  - Caveat: there is still NO upper bound on Map SIZE (an
    attacker rotating X-Forwarded-For can create millions of
    entries between sweep cycles). The 5-minute sweep is
    reactive, not preventive. Memory pressure between sweeps
    remains possible under sustained attack. Mitigation strength:
    MED — better than nothing, not airtight.

Cross-reference: V17.4-SEC-12 F-A — closed. V17.3-SEC-02 Q11/F-9
  (X-Forwarded-For spoofable) — still open; the root cause that
  makes the Map grow unbounded between sweeps is unchanged.

----- F-B. No request-body size limit at route layer  [MED →
        PARTIALLY MITIGATED] -----
Status: ⚠️ PARTIALLY MITIGATED by middleware; route layer still
        does not enforce its own cap.
Location: src/app/api/chat/route.ts:91
          src/middleware.ts:196-205

Code:
  route.ts:91:         const body = await req.json().catch(() => null);
  middleware.ts:196-205: if (method === "POST" || ...) {
                          const contentLength = parseInt(req.headers.get("content-length") || "0", 10);
                          if (contentLength > 1024 * 1024) return 413;
                        }

Analysis:
  - Middleware now caps POST bodies at 1MB based on Content-Length
    header. This stops honest clients.
  - The cap is bypassable (per V17.3-SEC-02 Q6 still open):
      * `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` requests have no Content-
        Length; the middleware check is skipped, and `req.json()`
        in the route buffers the entire chunked body in memory.
      * A client can lie about Content-Length (set 100 bytes in
        the header, send 100MB in the body) — depending on the
        upstream HTTP server (NGINX, Vercel, Node `next start`)
        this may or may not be caught.
  - Defense-in-depth: the route handler (route.ts:91) does NOT
    enforce its own cap. The slice(0, 2000) on `message` (line 99)
    happens AFTER `req.json()` parses the entire body — too late
    to prevent the memory allocation.
  - Mitigation strength: PARTIAL — covers the easy case, leaves
    the chunked-encoding bypass open.

Cross-reference: V17.4-SEC-12 F-B — partially addressed at the
  middleware layer only.

----- F-G. NEW — Dev-mode rate-limit bypass accepts "unknown" IP
        [LOW] -----
Status: ❌ NEW finding (not in V17.4-SEC-12).
Location: src/app/api/chat/route.ts:24

Code:
  route.ts:24: if (process.env.NODE_ENV !== "production" &&
                 (ip === "::1" || ip === "127.0.0.1" || ip === "unknown")) {
                 return true;
               }

Analysis:
  - In non-production environments (NODE_ENV !== "production"),
    the rate limit is bypassed for any request whose IP resolves
    to "unknown" — which is the fallback value at route.ts:81
    when neither x-forwarded-for nor x-real-ip is present.
  - On a self-hosted deployment that runs `next dev` or has
    NODE_ENV mis-set to "development", an attacker can simply
    omit the IP headers to bypass the route-level rate limit
    entirely.
  - Even in production, the bypass for "::1" / "127.0.0.1" is
    suspicious — it allows unlimited requests from localhost,
    which on a containerized deployment may include other
    containers (e.g., sidecar proxies, monitoring agents) that
    can be coerced into issuing requests.
  - Mitigation: this is gated by NODE_ENV, so the production
    blast radius is limited. But the development bypass should
    be explicit (e.g., a separate env var `RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED`)
    rather than implicit on any of three IP strings.

Cross-reference: NEW. V17.3-SEC-02 Q11/F-9 (X-Forwarded-For
  trusted blindly) is the production-side equivalent.

    returns EVERY assistant message in the session — no `take`
    cap. Combined with Q3 (unbounded history) and Q2 (no auth),
    a single GET can return gigabytes of JSON for a long-running
    session.
  - Even an honest client that polls correctly will occasionally
    send `since=0` on first load — but a malicious client can
    always send `since=0` to fetch the entire transcript.
  - No `take` limit means an attacker can DoS the DB + network
    bandwidth with a single request.

Cross-reference: NEW. V17.4-SEC-12 noted "no pagination" but
  did not call out the default-zero behavior.

----- F-I. NEW — Dual rate-limit window mismatch allows burst
        [LOW] -----
Status: ❌ NEW finding.
Location: src/app/api/chat/route.ts:7-8 vs src/middleware.ts:43, 147

Code:
  route.ts:7-8:        const RATE_WINDOW_MS = 60 * 1000;     // 1 minute
                       const RATE_MAX = 8;                  // 8 per minute
  middleware.ts:43:    const RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_MS = 15 * 60 * 1000;  // 15 minutes
  middleware.ts:147:   const max = pathname === "/api/user/login" ? 5 : 8; // 8 per 15 min

Analysis:
  - Two layered rate limits:
      * Middleware: 8 requests / 15 minutes per IP (long window).
      * Route handler: 8 requests / 1 minute per IP (short window).
  - These are INDEPENDENT counters keyed on different things
    (middleware key = `${pathname}:${ip}`, route key = ip only)
    and use different windows.
  - Net effect: the route handler's 8/min limit is the binding
    constraint under normal use. But the windows don't compound
    cleanly — an attacker can send 8 requests in second 0-59,
    then 8 more in second 60-119 (route limit resets), totaling
    16 within 2 minutes — but middleware's 15-min cap of 8
    SHOULD also apply. The interaction depends on timing and
    whether the middleware counter resets at the window boundary
    (it does — middleware.ts:48 `if (!entry || entry.resetAt <
    now)`). So the effective cap is min(8/min, 8/15min) = 8/15min.
  - In practice, this means an attacker can send 8 requests, wait
    15 minutes, send 8 more. This is slower than the route-level
    limit alone would suggest — the middleware limit is the
    binding constraint. But the inconsistency is confusing and
    the route-level 8/min cap is effectively dead code (never
    the binding constraint).
  - Recommendation (advisory only): drop one of the two limits,
    align windows, or document the layering. Not a security
    vulnerability per se, but a maintenance / clarity issue.

Cross-reference: NEW.

     Safari ITP private mode throws on setItem → effect throws → React error
     boundary (if any) catches; otherwise the component tree breaks on first

     Five trailing spaces on the otherwise-empty line 44 between the greeting

Q2. Polls for responses?
================================================================
Status: PARTIAL | Severity: MED

Mechanism:
  - ChatSection.tsx:58-78 — setInterval(3000ms) polling
    GET /api/chat/messages?sessionId=X&since=Y. Returns role:"assistant" msgs
    only (messages/route.ts:24). Polling starts only after first successful
    POST sets sessionId (effect early-returns at line 59 when !sessionId).

Gaps:
  a) **Duplicate-message risk via clock skew** [MED]:
     - ChatSection.tsx:108 `setLastPollTs(Date.now())` after a successful send.
       Uses CLIENT time. messages/route.ts:19,25 filters `createdAt > sinceDate`
       using SERVER time. If client clock is ahead of server (typical), the
       just-saved assistant reply (server-side createdAt ≈ server_now < client
       now) satisfies `createdAt > sinceDate` → re-fetched → DUPLICATE
       assistant bubble appended to chat. No dedup in ChatSection.tsx:64-72.
     - Same hazard on every successful poll: ChatSection.tsx:73
       `setLastPollTs(data.serverTime || Date.now())` — `data.serverTime` is
       route.ts:38 `Date.now()` (server time). If client clock ≠ server clock,
       the next poll's `since` may overlap with already-fetched messages.
     - No `id`-based dedup; client maps messages ignoring their IDs
       (ChatSection.tsx:66-71) so identical content+ts still get appended.

  b) **Polling effect re-creates interval on every state change** [LOW, perf]:
     - Effect dep array `[sessionId, lastPollTs]` (ChatSection.tsx:78).
       Every successful poll calls `setLastPollTs` (line 73), which tears down
       the old interval and sets up a new one. Under steady incoming admin
       messages, polling effectively becomes "3s after the last batch"
       instead of a steady 3s cadence. Minor UX slowdown under load.

  c) **Silent failure** [MED]:
     - ChatSection.tsx:75 `} catch {}` — polling errors swallowed. If the
       polling endpoint goes down (network drop, 500, server restart), the
       user sees no indication; admin replies simply stop arriving. No
       "connection lost" UI for polling (only the send() path shows it at
       line 120-124).
     - Non-200 responses also swallowed (no res.ok check at line 64).

  d) **No auth on /api/chat/messages** [HIGH, already noted V17.4-SEC-12 Q2]:
     - messages/route.ts:9-44 has ZERO auth check. Anyone with a sessionId can
       poll for the session's full assistant-reply history. ChatSection.tsx
       treats it as trusted. Cross-references prior finding.

  e) **Polling never stops on unmount of inactive chat** [LOW]:
     - Effect cleanup (ChatSection.tsx:77) clears the interval on unmount ✅.
       BUT: ChatSection is always mounted (page.tsx:695 — no conditional
       render), so the interval runs forever even when the visitor navigates
       away from the chat section in the DOM (the section is on the same
       page, just scrolled away). 3s × N visitors = steady background load
       on the messages endpoint even when no one is looking at chat.
     - No IntersectionObserver pause when chat is offscreen.

  f) **Polling URL params not encoded** [LOW]:
     - ChatSection.tsx:62 `&sessionId=${sessionId}&since=${lastPollTs}`
       unencoded. sessionId is cuid (safe) and lastPollTs is a number, so
       no real exploit today, but fragrant — should use encodeURIComponent
       for robustness.

Q4. Chat history bounded?
================================================================
Status: FAIL | Severity: HIGH (client side; server side already noted V17.4-SEC-12 Q3)

Client-side (NEW this audit):
  a) **ChatSection.tsx:16 `messages` state is unbounded** [MED]:
     - `useState<Msg[]>([])` — never trimmed, never capped.

     - Polling appends assistant messages (lines 64-72).
     - On error path, MORE assistant messages are appended (lines 115-118,
       121-124). Long error-looping sessions (e.g., rate-limited user
       hammering the form) accumulate error bubbles in DOM forever.
     - No `slice(-N)`, no max-length guard, no virtualisation.
     - Render: every message is a DOM node (ChatSection.tsx:158-165). A 1000-
       message conversation renders 1000 divs on every state change → React
       reconciliation cost grows linearly, scroll jank.
     - `{messages.length} msg` counter at line 154 also unbounded display.

  b) **localStorage used only for visitorId, NOT for chat history** [LOW]:
     - ChatSection.tsx:25 KEY = "portfolio_visitor_id" only.

       greeting effect (line 35-45) re-adds the greeting, BUT the user's
       prior conversation is lost. Server has it (session keyed by
       sessionId), but ChatSection never re-fetches prior history on mount
       — sessionId is also lost on reload (it lives in React state, line 14,
       no persistence). So a refresh = brand new session, brand new greeting,
       prior history orphaned on the server.
     - Effect: server-side chat history grows UNBOUNDED across many
       orphaned sessions per visitor. Combined with route.ts:132-135
       fetching ALL messages per session for LLM context (no take:) and
       route.ts:243-252 admin GET fetching up to 100 sessions each with
       ALL messages (no take: on messages), the cost amplification is

Server-side (cross-ref V17.4-SEC-12 Q3, still applies):

       poll cycle. The visitor has no signal that a reply is incoming.

  b) **Input disabled while sending** [LOW, UX-debatable]:
     - ChatSection.tsx:185 `disabled={sending}`. The visitor can't queue up
       the next message while the LLM is thinking. Combined with possibly-
       long LLM latency (no fetch timeout per V17.4-SEC-12 Q8), this can
       feel like the chat froze.

  c) **No loading state on initial mount** [LOW]:
     - ChatSection.tsx:14-21 initial state: sessionId="", visitorId="", no
       messages, no "Connecting..." indicator. The greeting effect (line 35)
       fills the empty state, but between mount and the visitorId effect
       running (which is synchronous-ish), there's a flash of empty chat
       body with just the chat-bar. Minor.

  d) **No abort/cancel button** [LOW]:
     - While `sending`, the only feedback is the typing dots. If the LLM
       hangs (Q8/cited), the visitor can't cancel the in-flight request.
       They can refresh the page (losing session), or wait indefinitely.

  e) **InteractiveTerminal has no async ops** [N/A]:
     - All commands are synchronous (exec() at InteractiveTerminal.tsx:31-137
       is pure). No loading indicator needed. ✅

================================================================
Q7. Error state?
================================================================
Status: PARTIAL | Severity: MED

Mechanism:
  - ChatSection.tsx:19 `const [error, setError] = useState("");` — declared.
  - ChatSection.tsx:86 `setError("");` — reset at start of send().
  - On error: messages appended with role "assistant" (NOT a dedicated error
    bubble), content is one of:
      - rate_limit → "... Channel busy. Hold a sec." (line 112-113)
      - other server errors → "... Error. Try again." (line 114)
      - network throw → "... Connection lost." (line 123)
  - InteractiveTerminal.tsx:6 has `kind: "error"`. Unknown commands return
    `{kind: "error", text: tt.terminal.unknown(cmd)}` (line 134-135),
    rendered with CSS class `terminal-line error` (line 191). ✅

Gaps:
  a) **`error` state is DEAD CODE** [MED, dead code]:
     - ChatSection.tsx:19 declares `error`, line 86 sets it to "", but THE
       VALUE IS NEVER READ. No `error` reference in the JSX (lines 138-197).
       The intended error-banner UI was never wired up. All errors are
       silently injected as plain assistant messages with no visual
       distinction from real AI replies.
     - Compare: InteractiveTerminal DOES have visual error styling
       (InteractiveTerminal.tsx:6, 191). Inconsistent.

  b) **No retry affordance** [MED, UX]:
     - On error, the assistant-message bubble contains the error text but
       no retry button. The visitor must re-type (or their input was
       already cleared at line 84 — `setInput("")` happens BEFORE the
       fetch at line 89-99). So a failed send LOSES the user's input
       text. No undo, no draft restoration.
     - Workaround: none. The visitor re-types. For a long message that
       failed mid-flight, this is data loss.

  c) **Generic "server_error" lost in translation** [LOW]:
     - route.ts:223 returns `{ok:false, error:"server_error"}` with HTTP
       500. ChatSection.tsx:110 `const err = data.error || "server_error"`
       — falls through to the else at line 114 → "... Error. Try again."
       But the underlying error (DB down, LLM provider 4xx, etc.) is
       opaque. Server logs it (route.ts:189, 221), client sees only generic
       text. Acceptable for security but UX-poor.

  d) **No error escalation** [LOW]:
     - If every send fails (e.g., AI disabled, server down, network
       partition), the visitor accumulates "Error. Try again." bubbles
       in the chat (per Q4, unbounded). No "stop trying after N failures"
       or "switch to contact form" suggestion.

  e) **InteractiveTerminal.exec() has no try/catch** [LOW]:
     - InteractiveTerminal.tsx:31-137 exec() is pure today, but a future
       refactor adding any I/O (e.g., fetching data) would crash the form
       onSubmit handler. No defensive try/catch around `exec(raw)` at
       line 149.

================================================================
Q8. Empty state?
================================================================
Status: PASS | Severity: LOW

Mechanism:
  - ChatSection.tsx:35-45 — on mount or lang-change, if messages is empty,
    seed with a localized greeting ("Patched through. I'm the site's AI
    concierge..."). ✅
  - InteractiveTerminal.tsx:18-20 — on mount or welcome-text change, seed
    `lines` with `[welcome]`. ✅

Gaps:
  a) **Greeting lies when AI is disabled** [MED, UX]:
     - ChatSection.tsx:37-39 greeting says "I'm the site's AI concierge.
       What brings you here today?" — but if the admin has disabled the
       AI (route.ts:114 `api_enabled === false`), the visitor's first
       send returns `api_disabled`. The greeting implies a working chat;
       the response is a generic "Error. Try again." (per Q10). No
       greeting-state-awareness of the kill switch.

  b) **Empty state for polling-only flow** [LOW]:
     - If a visitor opens the page, the chat shows the greeting. If they
       then change language (lang toggle), the greeting effect runs again
       but `messages.length === 0` check fails (greeting already added)
       — so the greeting stays in the OLD language. No re-greeting on
       language change once a message exists. Minor UX inconsistency.

  c) **No "no messages yet" UI distinction** [LOW, informational]:
     - The greeting IS the empty state. There's no separate
       "Start typing below..." placeholder or hint. Acceptable design.

================================================================
Q9. Rate limit feedback?
================================================================
Status: PARTIAL | Severity: LOW

Mechanism:
  - Server: route.ts:84-88 returns HTTP 429 `{ok:false, error:"rate_limit"}`.
  - Client: ChatSection.tsx:101 `if (res.ok && data.ok)` — on 429, res.ok
    is false → else branch (line 109). ChatSection.tsx:112-113 checks
    `err === "rate_limit"` → localized "Channel busy. Hold a sec."
    message appended as assistant bubble. ✅

Gaps:
  a) **Rate-limit feedback is indistinguishable from AI replies** [MED, UX]:
     - The "Channel busy. Hold a sec." text is rendered identically to a
       real AI reply (same `.chat-msg-assistant` styling, same callsign
       author label "QRV-7"). The visitor can't tell it's a system
       throttle vs the bot being snarky. No icon, no color, no separate
       CSS class.

  b) **No retry timer or backoff** [LOW, UX]:
     - Visitor must manually re-submit. No "try again in N seconds"
     countdown, no auto-retry. Combined with input being cleared (line 84)
     and no draft restoration (Q7b), a rate-limited visitor loses their
     message text. Data loss on rate-limit.

  c) **No client-side pre-flight rate awareness** [LOW]:
     - Client has no knowledge of the 8-per-minute-per-IP server cap
     (route.ts:7-8). The send button stays enabled even when the visitor
     is about to be rate-limited. No client-side counter.

  d) **Polling endpoint not rate-limited** [HIGH, security]:
     - /api/chat/messages (messages/route.ts:9-44) is NOT in any rate-
     limit list. Combined with Q2(d) no-auth, an attacker can poll
     /api/chat/messages?sessionId=X&since=0 in a tight loop — DoS on the
     DB reads. ChatSection.tsx polls at 3s, but a malicious client can
     poll at 1ms. Cross-ref prior audit V17.4-SEC-12 Q2.

  e) **Rate-limit on /api/chat trusts X-Forwarded-For** [HIGH, security]:
     - route.ts:78-81 reads `x-forwarded-for` first, splits on comma,
       trims. An attacker rotates X-Forwarded-For to bypass. Already
     noted V17.4-SEC-12 Q7. Client-side: ChatSection has no awareness,
     cannot help.

================================================================
Q10. AI disabled gracefully?
================================================================
Status: FAIL | Severity: MED

Mechanism:
  - Server: route.ts:111-127 checks `isApiEnabled()` (settings.ts:44-47,
    reads `apiEnabled` site setting). When false, returns HTTP 503 with:
        { ok:false, error:"api_disabled", message:<localized string> }
    where `message` is a per-lang "Chat is temporarily disabled..." text
    (route.ts:119-123).

Gaps:
  a) **Client ignores `api_disabled` error code** [MED, primary defect]:
     - ChatSection.tsx:110-114 only checks `err === "rate_limit"` (line 112).
       `api_disabled` falls through to the else branch (line 114) → generic
       "... Error. Try again." message.
     - The server's carefully-localized `data.message` field (route.ts:119-
       123) is NEVER READ by the client. ChatSection.tsx:100 reads only
       `data.error`. The localized "Chat is temporarily disabled." string
       the server prepared is dropped on the floor.
     - Result: visitor sees "Error. Try again." instead of the intended
       "Chat is temporarily disabled." Misleading and not actionable.

  b) **Greeting doesn't reflect disabled state** [MED, UX]:
     - ChatSection.tsx:37-39 greeting always says "I'm the site's AI
       concierge. What brings you here today?" regardless of
       apiEnabled. Visitor is invited to chat with a disabled bot.
     - No client-side fetch of /api/admin/settings or a lightweight
       /api/chat/status to detect disabled state on mount.

  c) **No persistent "AI disabled" banner** [MED, UX]:
     - Visitor can keep submitting. Each submit returns 503 + generic
       error bubble. Chat accumulates "... Error. Try again." bubbles
       (Q4 unbounded). No "stop trying, AI is off" signal, no redirect
       to contact form.

  d) **InteractiveTerminal `chat` command unaware** [LOW, UX]:
     - InteractiveTerminal.tsx:84-89 `chat` command scrolls to #chat
       unconditionally. If AI is disabled, the visitor lands on a
       broken chat. No pre-check.

  e) **Bale notifications still fire when AI disabled** [LOW, logic]:
     - route.ts:111-127 returns 503 BEFORE saving user message (line 146)
       and BEFORE notifyNewChat (line 152-161). ✅ Correctly short-
       circuits. NOT a bug — confirming correct behavior.
     - HOWEVER: if the admin disables AI mid-session, prior messages
       already saved remain in the DB. Visitor polling (Q2) still works
       and may surface old admin replies. Acceptable.

  f) **Kill-switch granularity** [LOW, informational]:
     - `isApiEnabled()` is a single global flag (settings.ts:44-47).
       No per-language, per-visitor, or per-provider granularity. The
       admin can only flip the whole chat on/off.

ADDITIONAL FINDINGS (not in the 10 questions but observed)
================================================================

----- F-A. InteractiveTerminal.tsx history never cleared on `clear`  [LOW] -----
Location: InteractiveTerminal.tsx:146-147, 152-154
Code:
  line 146-147: if (raw.trim().toLowerCase() === "clear" || ...) { setLines([]); }
  line 152-154: if (raw.trim()) { setHistory((h) => [...h, raw]); }
Analysis:
  - `clear`/`cls` empties `lines` but `history` array still gets the
    `clear` command appended (line 152-154 runs unconditionally for any
    non-empty input). ArrowUp after `clear` walks back into pre-clear
    commands. Minor UX inconsistency: "clear" doesn't actually reset
    state, only the visible surface.

----- F-B. InteractiveTerminal input has no maxLength  [LOW] -----
Location: InteractiveTerminal.tsx:195-206
Analysis:
  - No `maxLength` on the terminal input. A user can paste a 1MB string.
    `setInput` (line 200) stores it in React state. `exec()` (line 31)
    trims and lowercases → allocates a new 1MB string. Pushed to `lines`
    state → 1MB rendered in a single `<div>`. DOM bloat, no cap.
  - Compare: ChatSection.tsx:186 has `maxLength={500}` on its input.
    Inconsistent input hygiene between the two components.

----- F-C. ChatSection.tsx input maxLength vs server slice mismatch  [LOW] -----
Location: ChatSection.tsx:186 (maxLength={500}), route.ts:99 (slice(0,2000))
Analysis:
  - Client enforces 500 chars max; server truncates at 2000 chars. If the
    client cap is bypassed (curl, devtools), the server accepts up to
    2000. Inconsistent policy — pick one number, apply on both sides.
  - Also: 500 chars is per-character (JavaScript string length). Multi-
    byte UTF-8 (Persian, emoji) counts as 1-2 chars per JS length but
    1-4 bytes on the wire. Server slices by JS string length too. OK
    consistent on the slicing math, but the 500-vs-2000 mismatch is a
    footgun.

----- F-D. ChatSection greeting useEffect has stale-closure on `messages`  [LOW] -----
Location: ChatSection.tsx:35-45
Analysis:
  - Deps array `[lang]` references `messages.length` inside the body
    (line 41). React's exhaustive-deps lint rule would flag the missing
    `messages` dep. Today benign because the greeting only fires on
    mount or lang-change, and at lang-change time `messages.length` is
    typically > 0 (so the if-guard skips re-seeding). But under React
    Strict Mode in dev (double-invoke of effects on mount), the second
    invoke could see messages.length > 0 from the first invoke's
    setMessages → skip the greeting → user sees empty chat on first
    paint. Hard to reproduce, fragile.

----- F-E. Polling effect doesn't pause on tab-hide / offscreen  [LOW, perf] -----
Location: ChatSection.tsx:58-78
Analysis:
  - No `document.visibilityState` check, no IntersectionObserver. The
    3s poll fires even when the tab is in the background or the chat
    section is scrolled out of view. Wasteful server load: N visitors ×
    (1 / 3s) = constant DB read load even when no one is looking.
  - Browsers throttle background-tab timers (≥1min), but the FIRST poll
    after tab-focus still fires immediately, and the polling is never
    truly paused.

----- F-G. InteractiveTerminal `visitor` command fake number  [LOW, informational] -----
Location: InteractiveTerminal.tsx:123-124
Analysis:
  - Returns `"you are visitor #" + (Math.floor(Math.random()*9999)+1000)`.
    Purely cosmetic, random per call. NOT the real visitorId from
    ChatSection. Two different "visitor" concepts in the same page:
    ChatSection's stable localStorage visitorId vs InteractiveTerminal's
    random per-call number. Confusing if a visitor types `visitor` in
    the terminal expecting their actual session id.

----- F-H. ChatSection chat-bar-meta shows raw count with no cap  [LOW] -----
Location: ChatSection.tsx:154 `{messages.length} msg`
Analysis:
  - Unbounded (per Q4). A 10,000-message session displays "10000 msg"
    in the chat bar. Combined with the unbounded DOM render, this is a
    symptom of Q4.

----- F-I. No XSS sanitisation on rendered chat content  [HIGH, security, cross-ref] -----
Location: ChatSection.tsx:163 `<span className="chat-msg-text">{m.content}</span>`
Analysis:
  - React escapes text by default ✅ — `<script>` in m.content renders
    as text, not as a script tag. So no direct stored XSS in this
    component.
  - HOWEVER: if m.content contains user-controlled HTML and is ever
    later rendered with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` (e.g., in the admin
    panel — cross-ref V17.4-SEC-12 Q5), the stored payload executes
    there. The ChatSection itself is safe; the admin panel may not be.
  - InteractiveTerminal.tsx:191 same pattern (`{l.text}`) — also safe
    via React's default escaping.

================================================================
TOP 5 CRITICAL ISSUES BLOCKING V17.5 RELEASE
================================================================

#1. Default admin password `admin123` shipped + documented publicly
   Location: install.sh:316; scripts/seed_access_users.py:100
   Severity: CRITICAL
   The installer creates the admin account with the hardcoded
   password `admin123` (seed_access_users.py:100) and prints it to
   the install log (install.sh:316). Anyone reading the public
   install.sh on GitHub knows the default admin credentials.
   Combined with the documented username "admin" (install.sh:315),
   the admin panel is one curl away for any attacker who finds an
   unmodified install. The "remember to change it" warning at line
   317 is a UX nudge, not a security control. There is NO force-
   change-on-first-login mechanism. Until either:
     (a) the installer generates a random admin password and prints
         it ONCE (never stored in source), OR
     (b) the first-login flow forces a password change,
   this blocks release.

#2. Middleware session-cookie HMAC NOT verified (format-only check)
   Location: src/middleware.ts:87-89
   Severity: HIGH (defense-in-depth failure)
   hasValidSession() only validates the cookie FORMAT (3 dot-
   separated parts, userId non-empty, expiresAt not expired). It
   explicitly does NOT verify the HMAC signature (line 87 comment:
   "در middleware نمی‌تونیم HMAC رو verify کنیم چون SESSION_SECRET
   بهش دسترسی نداریم"). A forged cookie like
   `YWRtaW4=.<future-ts>.AAAA` (any hex) passes middleware →
   /user-dashboard redirect bypassed (line 180-185), /api/admin/*
   401 bypassed (line 188-193), /api/messages 401 bypassed. API
   route handlers DO call checkAdminAuth (which verifies HMAC via
   access-auth.ts:78-96), so direct API exploitation is contained
   — BUT every middleware-level defense (security headers, CSP,
   body-size, CSRF, rate limit) is bypassable by an attacker who
   forges the cookie shape. Cross-ref V17.3-SEC-02 Q3/F-1 — STILL
   OPEN. Requires either: move HMAC verification into middleware
   (Edge runtime needs access to SESSION_SECRET — currently
   unavailable there), OR add a server-side session table that
   middleware can check.

#3. Webhook secrets leak via URL query string
   Location: src/app/api/bale/webhook/route.ts:19;
             src/app/api/telegram/webhook/route.ts:9
   Severity: HIGH
   Both webhook handlers read `secret` from `?secret=XXX` query
   param FIRST, falling back to x-webhook-secret header. NGINX
   default access_log_format captures the full request URI
   including query string. Vercel/Cloudflare access logs do
   likewise. Anyone with read access to:
     - /var/log/nginx/access.log
     - Vercel project observability
     - Any log shipper (Datadog, Loki, ELK)
     - Any reverse proxy in the chain
   can extract the webhook secret and then replay arbitrary
   webhook bodies, which trigger processBaleWebhook /
   processTelegramWebhook (potentially invoking admin chat
   commands). The header-only path exists at line 19/9 but is
   the secondary fallback, not the primary mechanism. The
   install.sh output (line 332-333) explicitly tells admins to
   use the ?secret= form. Fix: header-only, reject query-param
   secrets.

#4. X-Forwarded-For trusted blindly — all rate limits trivially bypassed
   Location: src/middleware.ts:145 (general rate limiter);
             src/lib/access-auth.ts:175-181 (getClientIp);
             src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:56 (login rate limit);
             src/app/api/contact/route.ts:48-51 (contact rate limit);
             src/app/api/chat/route.ts (chat rate limit, per V17.4-SEC-12)
   Severity: HIGH
   Every IP-based control in the project keys off the first
   value of the x-forwarded-for header. On a self-hosted
   deployment (the project's target per install.sh + systemd),
   this header is attacker-controllable unless NGINX is
   explicitly configured with `proxy_set_header X-Real-IP
   $remote_addr` and `proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For
   $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for` (the install.sh does NOT ship
   the nginx config — it just references nginx-ehsanmorad.conf
   at line 253, which is not audited here). Attacker rotates
   XFF per request → fresh rate-limit bucket each time →
   effectively unlimited login attempts against the documented
   admin account, unlimited contact-form submissions,
   unlimited chat/LLM cost drain. Cross-ref V17.3-SEC-02 Q11/F-9
   — STILL OPEN.

#5. No server-side session invalidation on logout / password change
   Location: src/app/api/user/logout/route.ts:9 (cookies.delete only);
             src/app/api/admin/security/route.ts:88-91 (password
             change does not invalidate existing tokens);
             src/lib/access-auth.ts:44 (SESSION_DURATION_HOURS = 24)
   Severity: HIGH
   Sessions are stateless JWT-like tokens (access-auth.ts:67-72).
   There is NO server-side session table — nothing to revoke.
   On logout: only the browser cookie is cleared. The token
   itself remains cryptographically valid for 24h. If the token
   was intercepted (XSS, MITM on a non-HSTS connection, log leak
   via #3, etc.) before logout, the attacker retains access for
   the full 24h window. On password change: same problem — the
   admin's existing token is not invalidated, so a password reset
   following compromise does NOT evict the attacker. The only
   remediation currently available is rotating SESSION_SECRET
   (which invalidates ALL users' tokens — heavy-handed and
   undocumented in install.sh).

Final verdict:
  3 PASS / 7 FAIL. The V17.5 release is BLOCKED by 5 critical /
  high-severity issues that compound each other:
    (#1 admin/admin123 known default) +
    (#2 middleware HMAC bypass) +
    (#3 webhook secret in URL → log leak) +
    (#4 XFF spoofable rate limits) +
    (#5 no session invalidation on logout/password-change)
  Together these mean: an unauthenticated attacker who knows the
  default admin password (which is public on GitHub) can log in
  as admin; the rate limit will not slow them down (#4); even
  after the admin notices and changes the password, the attacker's
  existing session token remains valid for 24h (#5). Independently,
  the webhook secret leak (#3) gives any log-reader the ability to
  drive the admin chat-reply channel via webhook replay. The
  middleware HMAC bypass (#2) means every middleware-level defense
  (CSP, body-size, CSRF) is also bypassable with a forged cookie.
  Recommended pre-release blockers (in priority order):
    1. Random admin password in installer (no default in source).
    2. Header-only webhook secrets (reject query-param secrets).
    3. Edge-runtime compatible HMAC verification in middleware
       (or move auth gating fully to API layer + add server-side
       session table).
    4. Trust X-Real-IP set by NGINX, ignore client-supplied XFF
       (ship nginx-ehsanmorad.conf in the audit scope).
    5. Server-side session table (or short-lived refresh tokens)
       to enable revocation on logout / password change.

6. Bale bot config save
================================================================
Status: FAIL  | Severity: HIGH
Location: src/components/SettingsPanel.tsx:470-484

Code path:
  - state:  settings.baleBotToken (243), settings.baleChatId (244)
  - UI:     lines 755-778 (token type="password", chatId type="text")
  - load:   line 316: `baleBotToken: s.baleBotToken || ""`
            (s.baleBotToken is the MASKED value "••••••••" +
            last 4 chars, returned by GET /api/admin/settings
            at route.ts:130-131).
  - send:   saveBale() → postJSON("/api/admin/settings",
            { settings: { baleBotToken: settings.baleBotToken,
                          baleChatId: settings.baleChatId,
                          baleEnabled: settings.baleBotToken
                            ? "true" : "false" } })
            (lines 471-477)

CRITICAL BUG (F-A — masked-token round-trip corruption):
  1. GET /api/admin/settings returns:
        settings.baleBotToken = "••••••••" + realToken.slice(-4)
     (settings route.ts:130-131).
  2. SettingsPanel.tsx:316 loads this MASKED value into state
     verbatim: `baleBotToken: s.baleBotToken || ""`.
  3. The UI at line 762 displays it inside an
     `<input type="password" value={settings.baleBotToken}>`.
     Because the input is type=password, the user sees dots —
     indistinguishable from a real token. The placeholder
     "123456789:ABCdef..." only shows when the field is empty,
     not when masked.
  4. The user clicks "Save Bale" (777). saveBale() sends the
     MASKED string "••••••••12ab" back to the server as the new
     baleBotToken (line 473).
  5. The server's POST /api/admin/settings route at
     src/app/api/admin/settings/route.ts:76-80 stores it as-is:
        updates.push(setSetting(key, String(value)));
     There is NO check for the "••••" prefix (contrast with
     /api/admin/providers/route.ts:87 which DOES check).
  6. Result: the DB row SiteSetting["baleBotToken"] now contains
     the literal string "••••••••12ab". Every subsequent Bale
     API call (bale.ts) sends this string as the bot token →
     Bale returns 401 Unauthorized → notifications silently
     fail.
  7. The masked-on-get / unmasked-on-save asymmetry means the
     FIRST time the admin opens Settings and clicks Save (even
     without touching the Bale fields!), the Bale bot token is
     corrupted.

  Cross-reference: worklog V17.4-FINAL (line 63071-63074) claims
    "✅ bot tokens در /api/admin/settings mask می‌شن (قبلا
    plaintext برمی‌گشت!)"
  The masking was added on GET (good), but the matching save-
  side guard was MISSED. The providers API has the guard
  (providers route.ts:87: `if (data.apiKey && !String(data.apiKey).
  startsWith("••••"))`). The settings API does not.

  PoC:
    # 1. Admin logs in, opens Settings tab.
    # 2. settings.baleBotToken = "••••••••12ab" (from GET).
    # 3. Admin clicks "Save Bale" without re-typing the token.
    # 4. POST /api/admin/settings body:
    #      {"settings":{"baleBotToken":"••••••••12ab",
    #                    "baleChatId":"12345",
    #                    "baleEnabled":"true"}}
    # 5. Server stores "••••••••12ab" as the bot token.
    # 6. Next contact-form submission → bale.ts sends
    #    "Authorization: Bot ••••••••12ab" → Bale 401.
    # 7. Admin sees no Bale notification, no error in panel.

Other issues:
  - No token format validation (should match /^\d{6,}:[A-Za-z0-
    9_-]{30,}$/).
  - No chatId format validation (should be numeric or negative
    for group chats).
  - `baleEnabled: settings.baleBotToken ? "true" : "false"`
    (475) — uses the masked value, which is truthy → always
    "true" after first load. The admin has NO checkbox to
    disable Bale without clearing the token. The `baleEnabled`
    field in the Settings type (line 23) is loaded (315) but
    never user-controllable. (See F-F.)
  - `loadProviders()` called after success (480) — wrong
    endpoint reload. Bale is not a provider; should be
    `loadSettings()`. Likely copy-paste from saveProvider (537).
    (See F-D.)
  - No per-action loading state (F-C).
  - Success toast uses generic `t.saved` — no indication that
    Bale was the thing saved.

    "••••••••12ab" is stored as the new token in the DB. The
    next Bale/Telegram API call sends "••••••••12ab" as the
    bot token → 401 Unauthorized → notifications silently
    fail.
  - This is a regression introduced by V17.4-FINAL's masking
    change. Before masking, the GET returned the real token,
    the panel populated the field with the real token, and
    saving it back was a no-op. After masking, the GET
    returns a masked token, the panel populates with the
    masked token, and saving it back CORRUPTS the DB.
  - Severity HIGH: silently breaks Bale + Telegram
    notifications. The admin sees no error in the panel —
    notifications just stop arriving.

Cross-reference: V17.4-FINAL (line 63071-63074). This audit
  identifies the missed save-side guard.

Location: src/components/SettingsPanel.tsx:356-359, 568

============================================================
1. RATE LIMIT LOGIC CORRECTNESS
============================================================
[R1-LOW] middleware.ts:45-55 — Fixed-window algorithm allows burst at window boundary.
  `checkRateLimit()` uses `entry.resetAt < now` to reset. An attacker can fire `max`
  requests at T-1s (just before window end) and another `max` at T+1s (new window),
  yielding 2*max requests within ~2s. Login max=5 (line 147) → 10 logins in 2s possible.

[R2-LOW] middleware.ts:52 — When count >= max, returns false but does NOT extend
  resetAt (no lockout-extension attack) — also does NOT decay the counter, so a
  legitimate user who hit the limit must wait full 15 min. Acceptable trade-off.

[R3-INFO] middleware.ts:147 — `max = pathname === "/api/user/login" ? 5 : 8`.
  Magic numbers inline; should be a per-route config map. Login 5/15min OK,
  chat 8/15min too strict for legit usage IF this were the active limit
  (see NEW-D1 below — middleware's chat limit actually dominates the route's).

[R4-LOW] middleware.ts:21 + login/route.ts:20-22 — Double rate-limit on /api/user/login.
  Both middleware and the route handler independently rate-limit with same params
  (5/15min) but DIFFERENT Maps. Middleware runs first → middleware counter hits 5
  first (route counter never reaches 5 for the rejected requests). Effective limit
  is 5/15min (not 2×5). Redundant but not wrong; the two implementations
  should be unified to avoid drift.

[R5-MED] middleware.ts:148 + 145-146 — Rate-limit key is `${pathname}:${ip}`. If
  `ip === "unknown"` (line 146 fallback), ALL anonymous clients share a single
  bucket keyed `${pathname}:unknown`. On a corporate NAT / Tor exit / proxy that
  strips XFF, legitimate users block each other. Also makes the rate-limit trivially
  DoS-able: send 5 requests with no XFF header to lock out every "unknown" IP user.

  Verdict on correctness: LOGIC IS CORRECT (counter, boundary, return values).
  Algorithm choice is the weakness, not the implementation.

[NEW-D1-MED] middleware.ts:21,144-155 vs chat/route.ts:7-8,23-33 — **Middleware's
  looser 8/15min limit ACCIDENTALLY OVERRIDES the chat route's intended stricter
  8/1min sliding-window limit.** Middleware runs FIRST; it rejects on the 9th
  attempt within 15min (its counter at 8). The chat route's stricter 1-min window
  is effectively neutralized for any single burst: a user can make 8 requests
  within 1 second, then wait 14:59 more minutes, then send 1 more → middleware
  rejects (count still 8 in middleware's 15-min window), even though the chat
  route's sliding-window would have ALLOWED it (all timestamps >1min old).
  Inverse effect on /api/contact: middleware's 8/15min never fires because the
  route's stricter 3/10min (route.ts:6-7) rejects first. Effective limits:
    contact  = 3/10min     (route wins, stricter)   ✅ as intended
    chat     = 8/15min     (middleware wins, LOOSER than route's 8/1min intended) ❌
    login    = 5/15min     (both same, middleware fires first)
  Defense-in-depth here actively WEAKENS the chat route's design.

2. CSRF ORIGIN CHECK
============================================================
[C1-MED] middleware.ts:159 — Only POST / PUT / DELETE are CSRF-checked. PATCH is
  NOT covered, even though the body-size guard at middleware.ts:196 DOES include
  PATCH. No PATCH routes exist today; if a future admin route accepts PATCH, it
  has ZERO CSRF protection. Asymmetry between line 159 (no PATCH) and line 196
  (PATCH included) is a footgun.

[C2-HIGH] middleware.ts:158-176 + 30 — PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES bypass CSRF entirely.
  `/api/user/logout` (line 30) is in the list → CSRF-exempt. Logout CSRF is a
  known attack: an attacker can log the victim out via cross-site POST.
  Combined with logout/route.ts:7-11 (no auth check, no Origin check, no CSRF
  token), the route is fully exposed. SameSite=strict cookie mitigates browser-
  mediated attempts in modern browsers (login/route.ts:106-112) but is rejected
  on older browsers and does not help against server-to-server POSTs.
  Cross-ref: prior F-24/F-NEW-6, still open.

[C3-MED] middleware.ts:169 — `originUrl.host !== host` is case-sensitive.
  `URL.host` is normalized to lowercase, but the `Host` header is case-
  insensitive per HTTP/1.1 spec. If a misconfigured proxy sends
  `Host: EXAMPLE.com` and the Origin is `https://example.com`, comparison fails
  → false-positive 403. Not a bypass, but a correctness bug. Should be
  `originUrl.host.toLowerCase() !== host.toLowerCase()`.

[C4-LOW] middleware.ts:163-176 — Missing Origin is rejected (line 163). Some
  privacy-focused browsers strip Origin on same-origin requests. Strict but
  defensible.

[C5-LOW] middleware.ts:157-177 — No `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin` check. Modern
  browsers send this header, which is FORBIDDEN to modify from JS (unlike
  Origin/Host which are trivially spoofable by scripts). Would close the
  script-spoofed-Origin vector for browser-issued requests.

[C6-INFO] middleware.ts:169 — Origin host comparison IS port-aware (URL.host
  includes port when non-default; Host header does too). Documenting that
  this is NOT a bug.

[C7-HIGH inherited] middleware.ts:160-170 — Script-mediated CSRF still open.
  Any HTTP client (curl, Python requests, server-to-server) can set both
  Origin and Host to victim.com. Middleware cannot distinguish real browser
  requests from scripts. Defense relies ENTIRELY on SameSite=strict cookie,
  which does NOT protect against stolen-cookie attacks. Cross-ref: prior
  F-10/F-NEW-10 from V17.3-SEC-02, still open. Not re-counted in summary
  (already covered by C2+C3 defense gap above; flagged for traceability).

============================================================
3. BODY SIZE LIMIT (1MB)
============================================================
[B1-HIGH] middleware.ts:196 — Only POST / PUT / PATCH are size-checked. DELETE
  is NOT covered. DELETE requests can carry a body (RFC 7231 §4.3.5). If any
  DELETE route reads body, no size limit applies. No DELETE routes today.

[B2-CRITICAL] middleware.ts:197-204 — Trusts `Content-Length` header. A client
  using `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` sends NO Content-Length, so the check at
  line 198 evaluates `0 > 1MB` → false → middleware lets it through. The actual
  body can be arbitrarily large and will be buffered by Next.js / route handler
  until OOM. Real DoS vector. Mitigation requires either rejecting chunked
  encoding or relying on Next.js's `maxBodySize` config (NOT set in
  next.config.ts:3-33). Confirmed unchanged since V17.4-SEC-02.

[B3-LOW] middleware.ts:197 — `parseInt(..., 10)` returns NaN for malformed
  values. `NaN > 1024*1024` is false, so a malformed Content-Length bypasses
  the check. Next.js rejects malformed Content-Length earlier, but middleware
  does not defensively handle this case.

[B4-INFO] middleware.ts:198 — Boundary `> 1024*1024` allows exactly 1048576
  bytes (1 MiB). Comment says "1MB limit" — correct.

4. CSP COMPLETENESS (reCAPTCHA + APARAT + YOUTUBE)
============================================================
[P1-INFO] middleware.ts:111-133 — reCAPTCHA coverage: PASS.
  - script-src includes https://www.google.com + https://www.gstatic.com (line 114).
  - frame-src includes https://www.google.com (line 122) for the challenge iframe.
  - connect-src includes https://www.google.com + https://www.gstatic.com (line 124).
  No gaps for reCAPTCHA v2 or v3.

[P2-INFO] middleware.ts:122 — Aparat coverage: PASS.
  frame-src lists both https://www.aparat.com and https://aparat.com. The standard
  Aparat embed is fully covered.

[P3-INFO] middleware.ts:122 — YouTube coverage: PASS for `youtube.com` /
  `www.youtube.com` / `youtu.be`. NOT covered: `https://www.youtube-nocookie.com`
  — but the app does not use youtube-nocookie embeds (no grep hits). Latent only.

[P4-MED] middleware.ts:114 — script-src contains BOTH `'unsafe-inline'` AND
  `'unsafe-eval'`. `'unsafe-eval'` is needed only for Next.js dev mode. In
  production builds, `'unsafe-eval'` should be removed. `'unsafe-inline'` should
  be replaced with per-request nonces (Next.js 13.4+ supports nonce-based CSP
  via `request.headers.get('x-nonce')`). Current setup allows inline event
  handlers and `eval()` from any same-origin script — XSS amplification surface.
  Cross-ref: prior F-18, still open.

[P5-MED] middleware.ts:111-133 — Missing `upgrade-insecure-requests` directive.
  Without it, any legacy `http://` URL in HTML will be fetched over HTTP,
  breaking the HTTPS-only guarantee and enabling mixed-content passive sniffing.

[P6-MED] middleware.ts:111-133 — Missing `report-uri` / `report-to` directive.
  CSP violations are silently dropped — no visibility into attacks or accidental
  misconfigurations.

[P7-LOW] middleware.ts:111-133 — Missing `media-src` (defaults to default-src
  'self'). If the app ever embeds external `<audio>` / `<video>`, it will be
  blocked. No current usage.

[P8-LOW] middleware.ts:111-133 — Missing `worker-src` (defaults to script-src,
  which includes 'unsafe-eval'). Web Workers can be created from eval'd code.
  Should be `worker-src 'self'`.

[P9-MED] middleware.ts:209 — **CSP is set ONLY on the final pass-through
  NextResponse.next()**. The 6 early-return error responses (429 at line 153,
  403 at lines 165/171/175, 401 at line 191, 413 at line 203) and the redirect
  at line 183 all return WITHOUT CSP. X-Frame-Options:DENY at line 100 (applied
  via addSecurityHeaders to error responses) still blocks clickjacking, but
  script-injection-into-error-JSON is not CSP-protected. Practical impact is
  limited (error responses are JSON not HTML), but the defense-in-depth gap is
  real. Cross-ref: prior V17.3-SEC-02 Q12, still open.

============================================================
5. HSTS ON HTTPS
============================================================
[H1-HIGH] middleware.ts:211 — `req.url.startsWith("https://")` is fragile.
  In Next.js middleware running behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy
  (the project's deployment uses Caddy at line 11 of Caddyfile for HTTPS,
  proxying to Next.js on port 3000 over HTTP), `req.url` reflects the
  proxy→origin connection scheme (http://), NOT the client→proxy scheme.
  → HSTS is NEVER set by middleware, even on HTTPS requests.
  Confirmed by Caddyfile:14-18 (Caddy sets HSTS at the edge with max-age=31536000)
  AND nginx-ehsanmorad.conf:14-29 (nginx listens on port 80 only — no TLS, no HSTS
  at edge). For nginx deployments, middleware is the ONLY HSTS source, and the
  check fails because nginx→Next.js is HTTP.
  nginx DOES set `proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;` (line 25 of
  nginx conf), so the correct middleware check would be
  `req.headers.get("x-forwarded-proto") === "https"` (or
  `req.nextUrl.protocol === "https:"`). Cross-ref: prior F-27, still open.

[H2-LOW] middleware.ts:212 — `includeSubDomains` is set. If any subdomain
  (e.g. dev.example.com, staging.example.com) serves HTTP-only content, HSTS
  will force-HTTPS it and break. Verify all subdomains support HTTPS.
  Note: Caddyfile:14-18 sets `includeSubDomains` too at the edge (without
  `preload`), so middleware's `preload` directive is the project's only
  preload signal — site must be submitted to hstspreload.org to actually
  preload. max-age=63072000 (2 years) meets preload requirement.

[H3-INFO] middleware.ts:212 — `preload` directive present. max-age=63072000
  (2 years) meets preload requirement. Site must be submitted to actually
  be preloaded.

[H4-NEW-LOW] middleware.ts:212 vs Caddyfile:15 — HSTS max-age mismatch.
  Middleware sets `max-age=63072000` (2 years); Caddyfile:15 sets
  `max-age=31536000` (1 year). On Caddy deployments the Caddy header wins
  (edge sets it first; middleware's check at line 211 fails so middleware
  doesn't override). On nginx deployments middleware sets 2-year. Inconsistent
  policy across deployment targets. Not a security issue, but a config
  inconsistency that may confuse audits.

============================================================
6. SECURITY HEADERS
============================================================
[S1-MED] middleware.ts:98-106 — Missing `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` (COOP).
  Should be `same-origin` to prevent cross-origin window attacks
  (Spectre-class side-channel, window.open cross-origin reference).

[S2-MED] middleware.ts:98-106 — Missing `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy` (COEP).
  Should be `require-corp` (with CORP headers on cross-origin resources) to
  enable cross-origin isolation and SharedArrayBuffer.

[S3-MED] middleware.ts:98-106 — Missing `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy` (CORP).
  Should be `same-origin` to prevent cross-origin reads of resources.

[S4-LOW] middleware.ts:104 — `res.headers.set("X-Powered-By", "")` sets the
  header to an empty string instead of deleting it. Most browsers/proxies
  will still transmit an empty header. Better: `res.headers.delete("X-Powered-By")`.
  next.config.ts:6 already sets `poweredByHeader: false`, so this line is
  redundant defense. Not a bug, but a no-op that may give false confidence.

[S5-MED] middleware.ts:208-214 — Same gap as P9: security headers from
  addSecurityHeaders ARE applied to error responses (good), but the CSP and
  HSTS at lines 209/212 are ONLY applied to the final NextResponse.next(). The
  401/403/413/429 responses and the /user-dashboard redirect (line 183) all
  miss CSP and HSTS. The redirect (NextResponse.redirect at line 183) is the
  worst case — it returns NEITHER addSecurityHeaders NOR CSP/HSTS, because it
  returns directly without wrapping in addSecurityHeaders. HIGH severity for
  the redirect path.

[S6-LOW] middleware.ts:98-106 — Missing `Cache-Control` for sensitive
  responses. API responses containing user data could be cached by
  intermediate proxies. Should add `Cache-Control: no-store` to /api/admin/*
  and /api/messages responses. Per-route handling may exist; not enforced at
  middleware level.

[S7-INFO] middleware.ts:99-103 — The 5 headers set (nosniff, DENY, referrer,
  permissions-policy, X-XSS-Protection:0) are all correct and modern.
  X-XSS-Protection:0 is the right choice (disables the buggy IE XSS auditor).
  X-Frame-Options:DENY is redundant with CSP frame-ancestors:none — defense in
  depth, OK.

[S8-INFO] next.config.ts:14-27 — next.config.ts ALSO sets these 5 headers
  via the `headers()` block. Redundant with middleware. Not harmful; if
  middleware is bypassed (matcher exclusion at line 227) the next.config.ts
  headers still apply. Good defense-in-depth. NOTE: next.config.ts does NOT
  set CSP, HSTS, COOP, COEP, CORP, or upgrade-insecure-requests — those are
  middleware-only.

7. RATE LIMIT MAP CLEANUP (V17.4 added cleanup to login/contact/chat)
============================================================
  VERIFICATION TASK — confirmed V17.4 cleanup additions are present in
  all 3 route handlers. The middleware's own rateLimitMap also has cleanup
  (was there before V17.4, flagged M1 in V17.4-SEC-02). All 4 sites use
  the same setInterval(5min sweep) pattern. Details:

  [V1-OK] src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:22-32 — loginAttempts Map,
    fixed-window. Cleanup block at lines 25-32:
      `setInterval(() => { for (const [k, v] of loginAttempts)
        if (v.resetAt < now) loginAttempts.delete(k); }, 5*60*1000).unref?.();`
    Pattern matches middleware's rateLimitMap cleanup (middleware.ts:58-65).
    ✅ Cleanup present. Comment `// V17.4:` confirms V17.4 addition.

  [V2-OK] src/app/api/contact/route.ts:8-20 — hits Map, sliding-window.
    Cleanup block at lines 11-20:
      `setInterval(() => { for (const [k, arr] of hits) {
        const fresh = arr.filter(t => now - t < RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_MS);
        if (fresh.length === 0) hits.delete(k); else hits.set(k, fresh);
      }}, 5*60*1000).unref?.();`
    Pattern DELETES the entry when array becomes empty (better than
    middleware's pattern which only deletes when resetAt < now).
    ✅ Cleanup present.

  [V3-OK] src/app/api/chat/route.ts:9-21 — hits Map, sliding-window.
    Cleanup block at lines 12-21, IDENTICAL pattern to contact/route.ts.
    ✅ Cleanup present.

  [V4-OK] middleware.ts:42 + 58-65 — rateLimitMap, fixed-window.
    Cleanup block at lines 58-65:
      `if (typeof setInterval !== "undefined") {
         setInterval(() => { for (const [k, v] of rateLimitMap)
           if (v.resetAt < now) rateLimitMap.delete(k);
         }, 5*60*1000).unref?.();
       }`
    The `typeof setInterval !== "undefined"` guard is for runtime safety
    (Edge Runtime historically did not expose setInterval — see M1).

[M1-CRITICAL?] middleware.ts:58-65 — **Runtime uncertainty for setInterval
  in Edge Runtime.** Next.js 16.1.1 (package.json:18) middleware runs in
  Edge Runtime by default (no `runtime: 'nodejs'` in config object at
  middleware.ts:220-228). Edge Runtime DOES support `setInterval` (it's in
  the Web Standards supported list), but the guard at line 58 is defensive
  against older Edge versions where it wasn't available. The V17.4-FINAL
  worklog (line 63081) shows "/api/admin/settings: HTTP 200" after login,
  which means middleware's hasValidSession() returns true → Buffer IS
  available in this Edge version (Next.js polyfills Buffer in middleware).
  Conclusion: setInterval likely works in this Next.js version's Edge
  Runtime, but the concern from V17.4-SEC-02 M1 remains a latent risk if
  Next.js changes its Edge polyfills. Recommend explicit verification with
  `console.log(typeof setInterval, typeof Buffer)` in dev. Severity lowered
  from CRITICAL to HIGH given the worklog's working-login evidence.

[M2-HIGH] middleware.ts:42 — No maximum size cap on `rateLimitMap`. An
  attacker rotating `X-Forwarded-For` values (trivial — see X1 below)
  creates one entry per unique value per rate-limited path. At 3 rate-
  limited paths (line 21) × N spoofed IPs, the Map grows linearly with
  attacker effort. Even with the 5-min sweep, the steady-state size is
  bounded by 5min × request_rate × unique_IP_count, which an attacker
  can drive arbitrarily high. Should cap at e.g. 10000 entries with LRU
  eviction. Same defect exists in all 3 route Maps (V1/V2/V3 above) —
  none have a size cap.

[M3-LOW] middleware.ts:59-64 — Cleanup interval is 5 minutes, but the
  rate-limit window is 15 minutes (line 43). An expired entry can persist
  up to 5 minutes past its window before cleanup. Acceptable memory overhead
  (~33% above steady state), not a bug. Same gap in all 3 route Maps.

[M4-LOW] middleware.ts:64 — `.unref?.()` is Node.js-only (Timeout.unref). In
  Edge Runtime it's a no-op (optional chaining skips). Without unref, the
  timer keeps the process alive — but in serverless/Edge this is moot.
  Same in all 3 route handlers (login:31, contact:19, chat:20).

[M5-NEW-MED] middleware.ts:58-65 + login/route.ts:25-32 — **Algorithmic
  inconsistency between Maps.** Middleware and login use fixed-window
  (`{count, resetAt}`), while contact and chat use sliding-window (array
  of timestamps filtered by window). The sliding-window approach is more
  correct (no burst-at-boundary — see R1) but the two algorithms coexist.
  This inconsistency is invisible at runtime but is a maintenance footgun:
  a future dev who "fixes" one Map's algorithm may not realize the other
  three use a different one.

[M6-NEW-LOW] middleware.ts:42 vs route Maps — **Per-path vs per-IP keying
  mismatch.** Middleware keys by `${pathname}:${ip}` (line 148), so the
  same IP gets separate buckets for /api/user/login vs /api/contact vs
  /api/chat. Route Maps key by `ip` only (login:60, contact:line 22 arg,
  chat:line 23 arg). So if an attacker rotates across paths (login →
  contact → chat → login), middleware's per-path keying means each path
  has its own 5/8 budget; route Maps would also be separate (different
  routes entirely). Net effect: an attacker's effective budget is the
  SUM of all per-path limits (5+8+8=21/15min via middleware), not the
  MIN. Not a major issue but worth noting.

============================================================
8. X-FORWARDED-FOR SPOOFING
============================================================
[X1-HIGH] middleware.ts:145-146 — **X-Forwarded-For is trusted blindly.**
  `req.headers.get("x-forwarded-for")?.split(",")[0]?.trim()` takes the
  leftmost value. nginx config sets `proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For
  $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;` (nginx-ehsanmorad.conf:24) which APPENDS
  the client IP to the existing XFF header — it does NOT overwrite. If
  the client sends `X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4`, nginx produces
  `X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4, <real_client_ip>`. The middleware's
  `.split(",")[0].trim()` takes "1.2.3.4" (the client-supplied value,
  not the real client IP). Attacker controls the rate-limit bucket key
  entirely → unlimited login attempts → credential stuffing.
  Cross-ref: prior F-9, still open.
  NOTE: nginx DOES set `X-Real-IP: $remote_addr` (nginx conf:23) which
  OVERWRITES any client-supplied X-Real-IP. So the fallback at line 146
  (`req.headers.get("x-real-ip")`) IS trustworthy IF the deployment uses
  nginx. But the XFF-first ordering means the spoofable XFF wins. Fix
  would be: prefer x-real-ip (nginx-overwritten) over x-forwarded-for,
  OR use the rightmost (last-appended) XFF value, OR strip client-supplied
  XFF at the proxy. Caddy does NOT set X-Real-IP by default (Caddyfile:11-19
  has no header directive for X-Real-IP), so Caddy deployments have NO
  trustworthy IP source — both XFF and X-Real-IP are client-controllable.

[X2-HIGH] middleware.ts:146 — `x-real-ip` fallback is ALSO client-controllable
  on Caddy deployments (Caddyfile does not set X-Real-IP). On nginx
  deployments it's trustworthy (nginx-ehsanmorad.conf:23 sets it from
  $remote_addr). Defense is deployment-dependent.

[X3-MED] middleware.ts:145-146 — Same IP-extraction pattern duplicated in:
    - src/lib/access-auth.ts:175-181 (getClientIp)
    - src/app/api/chat/route.ts:78-81 (own inline extraction)
  Three independent IP-extraction implementations, all with the same
  spoofing flaw. login/route.ts:56 imports getClientIp from access-auth.ts
  (single impl), but chat/route.ts does NOT — it has its own copy.
  Should be unified into a single trusted-proxy-aware helper.

[X4-LOW] middleware.ts:145 — `split(",")[0]` does not validate the IP format.
  An attacker could set `X-Forwarded-For: <long string>` (up to header
  size limit) to bloat the Map key. Combined with M2 (no cap), this
  accelerates OOM. Should validate IPv4/IPv6 format before using as key.

[X5-INFO] middleware.ts:145-146 — No use of `req.ip` (Next.js does not
  expose socket IP in middleware). In API routes, `request.socket.remoteAddress`
  would be authoritative but is not used. Mitigation requires proxy-level
  enforcement (Cloudflare, nginx) of XFF overwrite.

============================================================
9. PATH TRAVERSAL BYPASS
============================================================
[T1-INFO] middleware.ts:138,158,180,188 — Path traversal analysis: NO DIRECT
  BYPASS FOUND. The middleware does not perform file I/O. All prefix checks
  use `pathname === p || pathname.startsWith(p + "/")` (lines 158, 180),
  which correctly prevents prefix confusion (e.g. `/api/content-foo` does
  NOT match the public prefix `/api/content`). Next.js normalizes
  `req.nextUrl.pathname` (URL-decodes, collapses `..`), so
  `/api/admin/../admin/foo` resolves to `/api/admin/foo` before the check
  at line 188.

[T2-LOW] middleware.ts:18 + 188 — `ADMIN_API_PREFIX = "/api/admin/"` includes
  a trailing slash. The check `pathname.startsWith(ADMIN_API_PREFIX)` (line 188)
  means `/api/admin` (no trailing slash) is NOT matched and falls through
  without session check. If a route exists at exactly `/api/admin` (no
  trailing slash), it bypasses the session check. Verified no such route
  exists in src/app/api/admin/ (only sub-directories like /users, /settings,
  /reply, etc.). Latent footgun.
  Recommended: also handle `pathname === "/api/admin"` explicitly or strip
  the trailing slash from the constant.

[T3-LOW] middleware.ts:227 — **Matcher regex extension-exclusion footgun.**
  The matcher `/((?!_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|.*\.(?:png|jpg|jpeg|
  gif|webp|svg|ico|txt|xml|css|js|woff|woff2|ttf|eot)$).*)` excludes any path
  ending in `.js`, `.txt`, `.xml`, etc. from middleware. If a future sensitive
  route is added at e.g. `/api/admin/export.csv` or `/api/admin/logs.txt`, it
  will BYPASS the middleware entirely (no session check, no CSP, no rate limit).
  No such route currently exists (verified via grep on src/app/api/admin/),
  but the matcher is a latent security footgun. Recommended: scope the extension
  exclusion to specific paths (e.g. `/_next/static/.*\.(js|css)$`) rather
  than any path.

[T4-LOW] middleware.ts:158 — `pathname.startsWith(p + "/")` for PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES
  means `/api/content/` (with trailing slash) matches but `/api/content` (exact)
  ALSO matches via the first clause. Both are public. OK. Next.js may serve
  both, redirect, or 308. No security impact.

[T5-INFO] middleware.ts:138-139 — `req.nextUrl.pathname` is used (good).
  URL-encoded slashes (`%2F`) are preserved by Next.js (NOT decoded into
  `/`), so `/api/admin%2Ffoo` does NOT match `startsWith("/api/admin/")`
  and would 404. No bypass via encoded slashes.

[A2-LOW] middleware.ts:24-37 — `/api/user/logout` (line 30) is public,

[A3-INFO] middleware.ts:24-37 — `/api/bale/webhook` and `/api/telegram/webhook`

[A5-LOW] middleware.ts:24-37 — Public prefixes use a MIX of "exact paths" and

[A6-MED] middleware.ts:158 vs 188 — `/api/messages` is NOT in

[A7-INFO] middleware.ts:24-37 — All public prefixes are under `/api/`. No

[A8-NEW-LOW] middleware.ts:24-37 — `/api/track` (line 27) is public. The

  is real.

============================================================
CROSS-CUTTING / DEFENSE-IN-DEPTH NOTES
============================================================
[N1-HIGH] middleware.ts:70-93 — `hasValidSession` is FORMAT-ONLY. It checks
  that the cookie decodes to `userId.expiresAt.signature` (3 parts), the
  expiry is in the future, and userId is non-empty. It does NOT verify the
  HMAC signature — the comment at lines 87-88 admits this. An attacker who
  knows the cookie format can forge a cookie with any userId and a future
  expiry, bypassing the middleware session check at lines 181 and 189.
  Defense-in-depth holds ONLY because each admin API route independently
  calls `checkAdminAuth` / `checkAdminSession` (which DO verify HMAC via
  src/lib/access-auth.ts:78-96). Verified /api/messages uses checkAdminAuth
  at src/app/api/messages/route.ts:14. BUT the `/user-dashboard` page gate
  (line 180-185) is fully bypassable — an attacker can load the dashboard
  HTML, though API calls from there will 401. Cross-ref: prior F-1, still
  open. Recommended: import HMAC verification into middleware (requires
  SESSION_SECRET env access — feasible in Node.js runtime, currently
  Edge Runtime).

[N2-MED] middleware.ts:81 — `Buffer.from(decodeURIComponent(token), "base64")`.
  Buffer is a Node.js global. In Edge Runtime it's undefined unless polyfilled.
  Next.js 16 middleware DOES polyfill Buffer (verified indirectly: worklog
  V17.4-FINAL line 63081 shows /api/admin/settings returning HTTP 200 after
  login, which requires hasValidSession returning true, which requires Buffer
  working). If a future Next.js version removes the Buffer polyfill from Edge,
  middleware breaks silently (all session-protected routes 401, dashboard
  always redirects to login). Risk is real but currently mitigated by Next's
  polyfill.

[N3-LOW] middleware.ts:138 — `export function middleware(req: NextRequest)`.
  Function is NOT async. Fine for current synchronous logic. If HMAC
  verification is added (N1), the function must become async to use `crypto`
  APIs in some runtimes.

[N4-NEW-INFO] middleware.ts:42 + route Maps — All 4 rate-limit Maps (middleware,
  login, contact, chat) are in-memory and per-instance. On Vercel/Edge each
  instance has its own Map → an attacker hitting N instances effectively gets
  N× the rate limit budget. On self-hosted (the project's target per
  install.sh / Caddyfile / nginx conf), the Maps persist for the process
  lifetime. The Caddyfile reverse_proxies to `personal-site:3000` (single
  container) so single-instance — Maps are effective. If scaled horizontally,
  rate limits become per-instance and an attacker can rotate instances.

Q1. try/catch on every route?
================================================================
Status: FAIL  | Severity: HIGH

8 handlers have NO try/catch wrapper at all:

  1. src/app/api/user/verify/route.ts:16 (GET)
     Lines 17–49 — entire handler body unguarded. Includes:
       line 22: await db.accessUser.findUnique(...)
       line 27: await checkAccess(user.id)
       line 30: await logAccess(...)
     A Prisma connection error, an expired-session DB lookup
     failure, or any thrown error from checkAccess/logAccess
     propagates to Next.js's default 500 page (which on Vercel
     returns a generic HTML error, NOT JSON). Caller (frontend
     /verify polling loop) will receive HTML, breaking JSON
     parsing.

     Trivial — only calls response.cookies.delete() (no await,
     no DB). Technically no try/catch needed, but for

     Lines 33–60 — unguarded. Includes:

       line 38: await db.accessUser.findMany({...})
