Q2. Proper status codes?
================================================================
Status: PARTIAL  | Severity: MED

Most status codes are semantically correct (401/400/404/429/
500/503). However, the following are wrong or missing:

  a) MISSING status code entirely (defaults to HTTP 200 OK):
     1. src/app/api/user/verify/route.ts:19
          return NextResponse.json({ ok: false });
        Should be 401 (no valid session). Returning 200 + ok:false
        is misleading; some clients treat any 2xx as success.
     2. src/app/api/user/verify/route.ts:24
          return NextResponse.json({ ok: false });
        Should be 401 (user record vanished — session valid but
        user deleted; treat as auth failure).
     3. src/app/api/admin/text/route.ts:37
          return NextResponse.json({ ok: false, texts: {} });
        Should be 500 (catch block, server error). Returns 200
        with ok:false instead. Caller may not detect failure.
     4. src/app/api/admin/email/route.ts:66
          return NextResponse.json({ ok: false, error: "no_email_set" });
        Should be 400 (bad request — user tried to send without
        configuring email). Returns 200.
     5. src/app/api/admin/email/route.ts:89
          return NextResponse.json({ ok: false, error: "forward_failed" });
        Should be 502 (upstream formsubmit.co failed) or 500.
        Returns 200.
     6. src/app/api/admin/email/route.ts:91
          return NextResponse.json({ ok: false, error: "forward_failed" });
        Should be 502 or 500. Returns 200.

  b) SEMANTICALLY WRONG status code:
     7. src/app/api/admin/security/route.ts:83
          return NextResponse.json(
            { ok: false, error: "wrong_current_password" },
            { status: 403 }
          );
        Should be 401 (authentication failed — current password
        didn't verify). 403 means "authenticated but forbidden",
        which is incorrect here. (Minor — admin IS authed, so 403
        isn't entirely wrong, but 401 is more conventional for
        bad credentials.)

  c) INCONSISTENT 200-OK-for-failure pattern:
     8. src/app/api/contact/route.ts:86
          return NextResponse.json({ ok: true });
        This is the honeypot bait — INTENTIONAL (returns ok:true
        to fool bots). NOT a bug, but documented here for
        completeness.
     9. src/app/api/track/route.ts:17
          return NextResponse.json({ ok: true, tracked: false });
        Bot detection returns 200 + tracked:false. Acceptable
        (the bot is told the request was OK).

  d) UNUSUAL but defensible:
     10. src/app/api/contact/route.ts:155
           return NextResponse.json(
             { ok: false, error: "spam_detected" },
             { status: 422 }
           );
         422 Unprocessable Entity — semantically appropriate
         (well-formed JSON but content rejected). Uncommon but
         defensible. OK.
     11. src/app/api/chat/route.ts:125 (api_disabled) and
         src/app/api/bale/webhook/route.ts:22
         (webhook_not_configured) return 503 — correct.
     12. src/app/api/bale/webhook/route.ts:28 and
         src/app/api/telegram/webhook/route.ts:17 return 403
         for invalid webhook secret — correct.

Q3. JSON error format?
================================================================
Status: PARTIAL  | Severity: MED

Convention observed: `{ ok: false, error: "<snake_case>" }`
with HTTP status. Most routes follow this. Violations:

  1. src/app/api/route.ts:4
       return NextResponse.json({ message: "Hello, world!" });
     No `ok` field, no error code style. This is a smoke-test
     endpoint. Cosmetic inconsistency; not security-relevant.

  2. src/app/api/track/route.ts:32
       return NextResponse.json({ ok: false }, { status: 500 });
     Missing `error` field. Client cannot distinguish failure
     mode (was it DB? JSON? Rate? — only status code 500 helps).

  3. src/app/api/telegram/webhook/route.ts:26
       return NextResponse.json({ ok: false }, { status: 500 });
     Missing `error` field. Same defect as #2.

  4. src/app/api/user/verify/route.ts:19,24
       return NextResponse.json({ ok: false });
     Missing `error` field AND missing status code (defaults 200).
     Double defect.

  5. src/app/api/admin/text/route.ts:37
       return NextResponse.json({ ok: false, texts: {} });
     Missing `error` field. Returns empty texts map on failure —
     client may render empty page on a DB error without realizing
     it was an error.

  6. src/app/api/admin/email/route.ts:66,89,91
       return NextResponse.json({ ok: false, error: "..." });
     Has `error` field — but no status code (defaults 200).
     Inconsistent with all other routes that pair error: with a

Q4. User-friendly messages?
================================================================
Status: FAIL  | Severity: LOW-MED

Across all 47 handlers, error messages sent to the client are
short snake_case machine codes (e.g., "server_error",
"invalid_body", "missing_id", "missing_fields", "unauthorized",
"invalid_action", "rate_limit", "missing_session", "captcha_failed",
"spam_detected", "too_fast", "invalid_email", "username_too_short",
"password_too_short", "invalid_hour_start", "invalid_hour_end",
"username_exists", "user_not_found", "cannot_deactivate_self",
"cannot_delete_self", "wrong_current_password", "current_password_required",
"empty_handle", "empty_name", "invalid_lang", "no_admin_user",
"webhook_not_configured", "invalid_secret", "forward_failed",
"no_email_set", "missing_settings", "missing_ip", "missing_params",
"missing_key", "no_items", "invalid_type", "invalid_target",
"empty_note", "invalid_body", "account_inactive", "account_expired",
"api_disabled", "session_not_found", "message_not_found",
"honeypot_triggered", "time_trap_triggered", "captcha_missing").

NONE of these are end-user friendly. They are intended for the
frontend client to map to localized strings — but there is no
centralized i18n error catalog. The frontend must implement
its own switch statement per code.

The ONLY user-friendly error responses are:
  - src/app/api/chat/route.ts:119-123 — translated (fa/de/en)
    message for `api_disabled` only.
  - src/app/api/admin/security/route.ts:99,114,133 — English
    prose on success only ("Password changed.", "Handle changed.",
    "Name changed.").
  - src/app/api/admin/clear/route.ts:30,37,47,56 — English
    prose on success only ("Chat session deleted", etc.).
  - src/app/api/admin/email/route.ts:87 — English prose on
    success only ("Email forwarded to xxx").

No user-friendly error messages for:
  - 500 server errors (just "server_error" code)
  - 401 unauthorized (just "unauthorized" code)
  - 400 validation errors (just "invalid_body", "missing_id",
    etc.)

This is intentional design (machine codes for client translation)
but it means an unconfigured frontend shows raw snake_case strings
to end users.

Q6. Unhandled promise rejections?
================================================================
Status: FAIL  | Severity: HIGH

  a) NO process-level handlers exist anywhere in the repo:
     - No `process.on('unhandledRejection', ...)` call.
     - No `process.on('uncaughtException', ...)` call.
     - No instrumentation.ts file (Next.js 13+ convention for
       registering such handlers at server startup).
     Verified via grep — only SIGTERM/SIGINT in
     examples/websocket/server.ts (a separate Node script,
       not the Next.js app).
     Cross-ref: prior audit V17.4-SEC-12 worklog.md:6402 already
       flagged this; still not fixed.

  b) FIRE-AND-FORGET promise chains WITHOUT .catch (would
     produce unhandledRejection if they reject):
     None found — all 3 fire-and-forget chains use .then().catch()
       pattern (see Q10 for the silent-catch issue, but they
       do suppress rejection).

  c) AWAIT in non-try/catch handlers (see Q1):
     8 handlers have awaits without surrounding try/catch. Any
     rejection from these awaits propagates to Next.js's error
     handler, which on Vercel returns a generic 500 HTML page
     (not JSON), and on self-hosted Node throws unhandledRejection
     (crashes the process unless Next.js wraps it).
     Files:
       /api/user/verify/route.ts:22,27,30
       /api/admin/users/route.ts:34,38,66,71,98,104,106
       /api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts:31,36,37,40,68,76,104,
         109,117,123
       /api/admin/users/logs/route.ts:22,33,45
       /api/bale/webhook/route.ts:56,61

  d) FLOATING PROMISE in /api/contact/route.ts:171-188:
       import("@/lib/settings")
         .then(async ({ getSetting }) => { ... })
         .catch(() => {});
     The inner `await fetch(...)` (line 175-185) is wrapped
     in its own `.catch(() => {})` (line 185), so a fetch
     failure doesn't reject the outer chain. OK structurally.
     But the outer chain is itself fire-and-forget (no `await`)
     — if the dynamic import fails for any reason other than
     the inner fetch error, the .catch at line 188 catches it.
     OK structurally (but silent — see Q10).

  e) FLOATING PROMISE in /api/chat/route.ts:152-161:
       import("@/lib/bale").then(({ notifyNewChat }) => ...)
         .catch(() => {});
     Same pattern — silent but suppressed.

  f) FLOATING PROMISE in /api/contact/route.ts:164-168:
       import("@/lib/bale").then(({ notifyNewContactMessage }) => ...)
         .catch(() => {});
     Same.

Status: FAIL  | Severity: MED

  Found 5 catch blocks that swallow errors without logging:

  1. src/app/api/admin/content/route.ts:132 (SILENT)

     Inside bulk_import loop — when model.create() fails for an
     item, the error is swallowed. The route returns
       { ok: true, created, total: items.length }
     (line 134) — `created` is incremented only on success

ADDITIONAL FINDINGS (not in the 10 questions but observed)
================================================================

----- F-A. Inconsistent auth helper across admin routes  [LOW] -----
Two different auth patterns are used:

  Pattern 1 (older /api/admin/* routes):
    const authCheck = await checkAdminAuth(req, password);
    if (!authCheck.ok) return 401;
  Used by: equipment, security-dashboard, stats, nav, text,
  settings, content, reply, email, providers, chat-reply,
  themes, security, clear, /api/messages, /api/chat GET,
  /api/bale/webhook GET helper.

  Pattern 2 (newer AccessUser routes):
    const admin = await checkAdmin(request); // local helper
    if (!admin) return 401;
  Used by: /api/admin/users GET/POST, /api/admin/users/[id]
  PUT/DELETE, /api/admin/users/logs GET.

  Pattern 3 (clips only):
    const authCheck = await checkAdminSession(req);
  Used by: /api/admin/clips GET/POST/DELETE.

  The 3 patterns differ in:
    - Whether password query param is supported (Pattern 1)
      vs. session-cookie-only (Pattern 2/3).
    - What gets logged on auth failure (Pattern 1: nothing;
      Pattern 2: nothing; Pattern 3: nothing).
    - What userId is exposed (Pattern 1: authCheck.userId;
      Pattern 2: admin.id; Pattern 3: nothing).

  No auth-failure logging in any pattern (see Q5 g above).

----- F-B. Stale `password` query param  [LOW] -----
Per prior audit V17.4-SEC-12 F-D, /api/chat/route.ts:234 still
reads `url.searchParams.get("password")` and passes it to
checkAdminAuth, which ignores it. Same dead param appears in:
  - /api/admin/equipment/route.ts:13 (GET)
  - /api/admin/security-dashboard/route.ts:12 (GET)
  - /api/admin/stats/route.ts:8
  - /api/admin/nav/route.ts:9
  - /api/admin/text/route.ts:16
  - /api/admin/settings/route.ts:102 (GET)
  - /api/admin/content/route.ts:17 (GET)
  - /api/admin/email/route.ts:23 (GET)
  - /api/admin/providers/route.ts:13 (GET)
  - /api/admin/themes/route.ts:13 (GET)
  - /api/admin/security/route.ts:18 (GET)
  - /api/messages/route.ts:12 (GET)
  - /api/chat/route.ts:234 (GET)

The dead param is logged in NGINX/Vercel access logs — admin
passwords leak via URL if any admin client still sends them.

----- F-C. bot token / API key masking inconsistent  [LOW] -----
  - /api/admin/providers/route.ts:27-30 MASKS apiKeys correctly:
      apiKey: p.apiKey ? "••••••••" + p.apiKey.slice(-4) : null
  - /api/admin/settings/route.ts:130-135 MASKS bale/telegram
    tokens correctly (V17.4 fix).
  - BUT /api/admin/settings/route.ts:35-40 (action: "get_telegram")
    returns `telegramBotToken: token` UNMASKED at line 37!
    Compare to the GET handler at line 99-145 which DOES mask.
    So the admin panel can fetch the raw token via
    POST { action: "get_telegram" } but NOT via GET. Inconsistent
    and a secret-leak vector if the admin panel's request is
    intercepted (no CSP/SSL-only on this response — see prior
    audit V17.3-SEC-02 Q12).
  - Similarly, the bulk settings endpoint (line 75-83) lets an
    admin SET baleBotToken/telegramBotToken to a new value
    (line 65,68 in allowedKeys), but there's no validation that
    the new value matches the expected token format (e.g., bot
    tokens should be digits:xxxx). Allows arbitrary string
    storage.

----- F-D. Rate-limit responses not Vary-by-IP — XFF spoofable  [HIGH] -----
  - /api/contact/route.ts:48-51 — uses x-forwarded-for[0] as
    the rate-limit key. Per prior audit V17.3-SEC-02 Q11/F-9
    (still open), XFF is trivially spoofable.
  - /api/chat/route.ts:78-81 — same defect.
  - /api/user/login/route.ts:56 — uses getClientIp() (in
    access-auth.ts) which may or may not have the same defect.
    Recommend auditing access-auth.ts:getClientIp separately.
  - All three rate-limit Maps now have sweep intervals (V17.4
    fix), but the spoofable key remains the root problem.

----- F-E. No request-size limit on JSON body parse  [MED] -----
Per prior audit V17.4-SEC-12 F-B, all routes that call
  `await req.json().catch(() => null)` (or `() => ({})`)
have NO Content-Length check. The middleware does check body
size, but per V17.3-SEC-02 Q6, the middleware's check trusts
Content-Length (chunked-encoding bypass). Routes that do this:
  - /api/track/route.ts:11
  - /api/contact/route.ts:69
  - /api/chat/route.ts:91
  - /api/messages/route.ts:60 (POST)
  - /api/admin/equipment/route.ts:44 (POST)
  - /api/admin/security-dashboard/route.ts:49 (POST)
  - /api/admin/nav/route.ts:24 (POST)
  - /api/admin/text/route.ts:43 (POST)
  - /api/admin/settings/route.ts:16 (POST)
  - /api/admin/content/route.ts:53 (POST)
  - /api/admin/reply/route.ts:15 (POST)
  - /api/admin/email/route.ts:36 (POST)
  - /api/admin/providers/route.ts:45 (POST)
  - /api/admin/chat-reply/route.ts:14 (POST)
  - /api/admin/themes/route.ts:35 (POST)
  - /api/admin/security/route.ts:41 (POST)
  - /api/admin/clear/route.ts:13 (POST)
  - /api/bale/webhook/route.ts:31 (POST)
  - /api/telegram/webhook/route.ts:19 (POST)
  - /api/admin/users/route.ts:71 (POST) — uses `() => ({})` fallback
  - /api/admin/users/[id]/route.ts:37 (PUT) — uses `() => ({})` fallback

NOT A DEFECT (these use `.catch(() => ({}))` so JSON parse
failure is graceful, returning empty object). The issue is
the upstream allocation: a 100MB JSON body is fully buffered
in memory before .json() rejects or succeeds.

----- F-F. Admin clips POST doesn't use `.catch(() => null)`  [MED] -----
  src/app/api/admin/clips/route.ts:35
    const body = await req.json();  // ← NO .catch()!
  src/app/api/admin/clips/route.ts:82
    const body = await req.json();  // ← same, in DELETE handler

If the request body is not valid JSON (or empty), req.json()
throws SyntaxError. The outer try/catch (line 29-72) catches
it and returns 500 "server_error" — but the correct response
is 400 "invalid_body". Compare with all other POST admin
routes which use `await req.json().catch(() => null)` and
return 400 explicitly. Inconsistent.

----- F-G. Security dashboard POST "block" allows self-DoS  [LOW] -----
  src/app/api/admin/security-dashboard/route.ts:66-75
  Admin can block ANY IP, including their own. No check that
  the IP being blocked isn't the admin's current IP. Admin
  could lock themselves out.

  Also: `attempts: 99` hardcoded at line 70,71 — no validation
  of body.reason length (could be used to dump arbitrary text
  into securityLog.detail — XSS surface if admin panel renders
  detail without escaping).

----- F-H. clear_logs action has no confirmation  [MED] -----
  src/app/api/admin/security-dashboard/route.ts:76-79
    case "clear_logs": {
      await db.securityLog.deleteMany({});
      return NextResponse.json({ ok: true });
    }
  Deletes ALL security logs with no confirmation, no soft-
  delete, no audit trail of who cleared them. If an attacker
  gains admin access, they can wipe the entire security audit
  trail in one request. No logAccess call before deletion.

Q11. aria-labels?
================================================================
Status: PARTIAL | Severity: MED
Location: src/app/user-dashboard/page.tsx:128, 182-184, 189, 195-200,
          206, 214, 218-225, 232, 437, 484-491, 493-494

Analysis:
  - PRESENT aria / role attributes:
      * Line 128: `<div className="dashboard-loading" aria-live="polite">`
        ✅ — SR announces when loading ends.
      * Line 189: `<select aria-label="Language">` ✅ — though the
        label text "Language" is hardcoded English (see Q4).
      * Line 206: `<div className="dashboard-access-warning" role="alert">`
        ✅ — SR announces access-warning banner.
      * Line 214: `<div className="dashboard-tabs" role="tablist">` ✅
      * Line 222: `role="tab"` on each tab button ✅
      * Line 223: `aria-selected={activeTab === tab}` ✅ — reflects
        current tab.
      * Line 437: MessagesPanel error div has `role="alert"` ✅
  - MISSING aria / role attributes:
      * Tablist (line 214): no `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`
        describing what the tabs are for (e.g. "Dashboard sections").
        SR users hear "tablist" with no context.
      * Tab buttons (lines 218-225): no `aria-controls` pointing to
        the tabpanel ID. WAI-ARIA tabs pattern requires each tab
        to control a tabpanel via aria-controls.
      * Content container (line 232 `.dashboard-content`): no
        `role="tabpanel"` and no `aria-labelledby` pointing back
        to the active tab. The WAI-ARIA tabs pattern requires the
        tabpanel to be labelled by its controlling tab.
      * Logout button (lines 195-200): no explicit aria-label, but
        the button text "{t.logout} →" is the accessible name.
        Acceptable per WCAG (button text is the name).
      * Open-site anchor (lines 182-184): no explicit aria-label,
        but the anchor text "{t.openSite}" is the accessible name.
        Acceptable.
      * MessagesPanel reply textarea (lines 484-491): NO aria-label,
        NO <label> association — only a `placeholder` attribute.
        Per WCAG 1.3.3 and 4.1.2, placeholder is NOT a label —
        SR users hear "edit text, blank" with no name. The reply
        textarea needs either a visually-hidden <label> or an
        aria-label.
      * MessagesPanel reply/delete buttons (lines 473-480, 493-494):
        text labels are the accessible names. ✅
      * Language select (line 185-194): has aria-label ✅ but its
        value "Language" is hardcoded English.
  - The tablist/tab/tabpanel triad is INCOMPLETE: tablist +
    tab + aria-selected are present, but tabpanel + aria-controls
    are missing. This is the most common ARIA tabs bug.
  → ARIA is partially implemented. Loading, alerts, tab semantics
    (partial), and the language-select label are present. The
    tabpanel role, aria-controls linkage, tablist aria-label, and
    reply textarea label are MISSING.

Analysis:
  - Button markup (lines 195-200):
      `<button onClick={handleLogout} className="dashboard-btn danger">`
      `{t.logout} →</button>`
      * Has accessible text name (t.logout = "خروج" / "Logout" /
        "Abmelden"). ✅
      * Uses `.dashboard-btn.danger` class for red styling
        (personal.css:3190-3197). ✅
      * No explicit aria-label needed (text is the name).
      * No `type` attribute — defaults to "submit" in forms, but
        this button is NOT inside a <form> so defaults to "button".
        ✅
  - handleLogout (lines 122-125):
      * `await fetch("/api/user/logout", { method: "POST", credentials:
        "include" });` ✅ — POST with credentials.
      * `router.replace("/user-login");` ✅ — redirects to login.
  - Issues:
      * BUG (minor): no try/catch around the await fetch. If the
        fetch throws (network error, server unreachable), the
        await rejects, the function exits, and router.replace
        never runs. User is stuck on the dashboard with no
        feedback. Should wrap in try/catch and call router.replace
        in a finally block.
      * BUG (minor): no loading/disabled state on the button. A
        user can click "Logout" multiple times rapidly before
        navigation commits, firing multiple POST /api/user/logout
        requests. Cosmetic — no functional harm.
      * BUG (minor): no visual feedback during the logout
        request (e.g. button text changes to "Logging out..." or
        spinner). User may think the click didn't register and
        click again (compounding the previous issue).
      * /api/user/logout endpoint verified to exist via LS. ✅
      * No CSRF token sent — relies on same-origin + cookie. The
        logout endpoint must verify session cookie. Not audited
        here (out of scope for page.tsx).
  → Logout WORKS for the happy path. Minor robustness issues:
    no try/catch, no button-loading state, no visual feedback.

Q1. install.sh: apply_schema.py runs?
----------------------------------------------------------------
Status: PASS (with caveats)

Evidence: install.sh:163-169

  163: TABLES=$(sqlite3 db/custom.db "SELECT count(*) FROM sqlite_master
        WHERE type='table';" 2>/dev/null || echo "0")
  164: if [ "$TABLES" = "0" ] || [ -z "$TABLES" ]; then
  165:     echo "  ساخت جداول با apply_schema.py ..."
  166:     python3 scripts/apply_schema.py 2>&1 | tail -3
  167:     TABLES=$(sqlite3 db/custom.db "SELECT count(*) FROM
        sqlite_master WHERE type='table';" 2>/dev/null || echo "0")
  168:     echo "  ✅ $TABLES جدول ساخته شد"
  169: fi

apply_schema.py DOES run, but ONLY when the DB has zero tables
(install.sh:164). Findings:

  (a) ✅ The script is invoked with the right interpreter (python3)
      and the right relative path (scripts/apply_schema.py), but
      ONLY if cwd is $SITE_DIR — which is guaranteed by line 18
      (`cd "$SITE_DIR"`). However, if the standalone branch at
      lines 192-203 reassigns SITE_DIR (line 200:
      `SITE_DIR="$SITE_DIR/.next/standalone"`) BEFORE this block
      is reached... actually this block (line 154-182) is BEFORE
      the standalone branch (line 184-203), so cwd is still the
      original project dir. ✅ Correct.

  (b) ⚠ Gating by "tables == 0" means apply_schema.py NEVER runs
      on subsequent installs even if the schema has been updated
      upstream. This is a schema-migration footgun: schema changes
      shipped in newer apply_schema.py will silently not be applied
      if any table already exists. No migration runner is invoked.
      Severity: MED (operational, not directly exploitable).

  (c) ⚠ Line 166: `python3 scripts/apply_schema.py 2>&1 | tail -3`
      pipes BOTH stdout and stderr through tail. If apply_schema.py
      crashes mid-run, only the last 3 lines of combined output
      are shown to the admin — the failure mode is opaque. The
      exit status of apply_schema.py is MASKED by the pipe (PIPESTATUS
      not checked). The script's `set -e` (line 15) does NOT exit
      on a failed command inside a pipe (only the LAST command in
      the pipeline's status matters to set -e, and `tail` succeeds).
      → apply_schema.py failure is SILENTLY SWALLOWED. Severity:
      MED (install could proceed with an empty/partial schema
      and the service would then crash on first request).

  (d) Line 167-168: re-checks TABLES count after running. If the
      python script failed, TABLES could still be 0, but no error
      is raised; the script prints "✅ 0 جدول ساخته شد". Severity:
      LOW (cosmetic, but misleading).

Verdict: apply_schema.py DOES run, but failure is masked by the
`| tail -3` pipe without PIPESTATUS check. No migration runner.
Schema upgrades are silently skipped on existing DBs.


Q2. install.sh: idempotent?
----------------------------------------------------------------
Status: PARTIAL FAIL

Most blocks ARE idempotent:
  - install.sh:30   swap check via `swapon --show | grep -q swap` ✅
  - install.sh:46   node version check ✅
  - install.sh:66   nginx presence check ✅
  - install.sh:99   .env SESSION_SECRET check ✅
  - install.sh:114  BALE_WEBHOOK_SECRET check ✅
  - install.sh:120  TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET check ✅
  - install.sh:131-132  reCAPTCHA keys preserved ✅
  - install.sh:163  TABLES count check ✅
  - install.sh:172  ADMIN_EXISTS check ✅
  - install.sh:210  ehsansite user check ✅
  - install.sh:211  useradd guarded by `2>/dev/null || true` ✅
  - install.sh:253-255  cp + `ln -sf` + `rm -f` for nginx site ✅
  - install.sh:242-244  daemon-reload/enable/restart — idempotent ✅

BREAKS of idempotency:

  (a) install.sh:135-147  `cat > .env << EOF ... EOF` — TRUNCATES
      and REWRITES the entire .env file on EVERY run. Any custom
      env var the admin has manually added (e.g., SMTP creds,
      custom provider keys, feature flags) is SILENTLY DESTROYED.
      Only the 9 variables explicitly listed in the heredoc are
      preserved (and of those, only SESSION_SECRET, the two
      webhook secrets, and the two reCAPTCHA keys are read back
      from the existing .env before overwrite). Anything else
      (DATABASE_URL, NODE_ENV, PORT, HOSTNAME, NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL)
      is RE-HARDCODED. Severity: HIGH (silent data loss on re-run).

  (b) install.sh:137  `DATABASE_URL="file:$SITE_DIR/db/custom.db"`
      is REWRITTEN on every run — fine if SITE_DIR is stable, but
      if the admin moved the install, the old path is silently
      replaced. Minor.

  (c) install.sh:142  `NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL="https://ehsanmorad.ir"`
      is HARDCODED. Even if the admin previously set a different
      domain, re-running install.sh RESETS this to ehsanmorad.ir.
      Severity: MED (will break OAuth/webhook callbacks on
      multi-domain deployments).

  (d) install.sh:160  `rm -f db/custom.db-journal db/custom.db-wal
      db/custom.db-shm` — DESTRUCTIVE on every run. If the
      personal-site service is currently mid-transaction (WAL
      mode), deleting the WAL/SHM files can CORRUPT the database
      or lose committed-but-uncheckpointed transactions. The
      service is only stopped/restarted LATER (line 244), so
      between line 160 and line 244 the service could be writing.
      Severity: HIGH (potential DB corruption on re-install
      while service is running).

  (e) install.sh:175-178  seeding scripts (`seed_content.py`,
      `seed_equipment.py`, `seed_texts.py`, `seed_access_users.py`)
      run unconditionally whenever `admin` user is missing.
      `seed_access_users.py` could re-create the default `admin`
      user with password "admin123" if it was deleted. Mostly
      idempotent IF the seed scripts themselves are idempotent,
      but not verified by this audit (out of scope).
      Severity: LOW (depends on seed script behavior).

  (f) install.sh:213  `chown -R ehsansite:ehsansite "$SITE_DIR"`
      re-chowns the entire project dir on every run. If the admin
      has files owned by other users (e.g., a deploy key, an
      uploaded asset), they get re-owned. Severity: LOW.

Verdict: PARTIAL FAIL — the .env overwrite (Q2.a) is the biggest
idempotency break: silent destruction of custom env vars on every
re-run. The WAL file deletion (Q2.d) is a corruption risk on
re-install while the service is running.

or RECAPTCHA_SECRET value is ever echoed to stdout. ✅

Webhook URLs at install.sh:332-333 use the literal placeholder
`<SEE .env>` instead of the actual secret value. ✅

LEAKS / RISKS:

  (a) install.sh:316  `echo "    password: admin123"` — the
      DEFAULT ADMIN PASSWORD is printed to stdout in plaintext.
      This is INTENTIONAL (the admin needs to know the initial
      password), but it means:
        - The password is in the terminal scrollback.
        - The password is in shell history IF the install is run
          via `bash install.sh` and any output redirection is
          in place.
        - If the install is run via a CI/CD runner that captures
          stdout, the password leaks into the CI log.
      Severity: MED (intentional but risky; should be replaced
      with a one-time random password printed only once + forced
      change on first login).

  (b) install.sh:166  `python3 scripts/apply_schema.py 2>&1 | tail -3`
      — pipes combined stdout+stderr through tail. If apply_schema.py
      prints DATABASE_URL, SQL statements, or secrets in error
      messages, the last 3 lines leak to stdout.
      Severity: LOW (limited to 3 lines; apply_schema.py would
      need to actively print a secret).

  (c) install.sh:175-178  seeding scripts also piped via
      `2>&1 | tail -2`. Same risk: last 2 lines of seed script
      output could include sensitive content (default admin
      password, default API keys, etc.) if the seed scripts
      print them. Severity: LOW.

  (d) install.sh:284  `certbot --nginx ... 2>&1 | tail -5` —
      certbot output is piped through tail. Certbot does NOT
      print secrets, but it does print domain validation info.
      Severity: LOW.

  (e) install.sh:51,56  `curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/
      setup_22.x | bash -` — the curl output is piped directly
      to bash WITHOUT any output capture. The NodeSource setup
      script's full output goes to the terminal. This is the
      standard pattern but is a supply-chain risk: if the
      NodeSource CDN is compromised, the attacker's script
      runs as root. Severity: MED (supply-chain).

  (f) install.sh:260  `curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}"
      http://localhost:3000/` — only the HTTP code is captured.
      ✅ No leak.

  (g) install.sh:53,58  `echo "  ✅ Node.js نصب شد ($(node -v))"`
      — prints Node.js version. Not sensitive. ✅

  (h) install.sh:338  `echo "    ⚠️ Secretها تو فایل .env هستن —
      با 'sudo cat .env' ببین"` — directs the admin to read .env.
      Not a leak itself, but a UX hint. ✅

  (i) install.sh:311  `echo "    $SITE_URL"` — prints the final
      site URL. If SITE_URL is `http://31.70.76.10:3000` (line 294),
      the public IP is leaked to stdout. Severity: LOW (the IP is
      already in DNS if a domain is configured; otherwise the IP
      being printed is intentional).

Verdict: PARTIAL PASS — no direct secret leak, but:
  (1) Default admin password "admin123" is echoed to stdout
      (install.sh:316). Intentional but risky.
  (2) Subprocess outputs piped through `tail -N` (install.sh:166,
      175-178, 284) could leak indirectly if those scripts print
      secrets.
  (3) Piping curl to bash (install.sh:51, 56) is a supply-chain
      risk that bypasses output review entirely.


Q4. install.sh: openssl check?
----------------------------------------------------------------
Status: PASS

Evidence:
  - install.sh:68  `apt install -y nginx sqlite3 python3 ufw certbot
                   python3-certbot-nginx openssl` — openssl installed.
  - install.sh:73  same package list, `2>/dev/null || true` —
                   attempted silent re-install if nginx already present.
  - install.sh:76-80  EXPLICIT verification:
        76: # بررسی نهایی openssl (مهم برای تولید SESSION_SECRET)
        77: if ! command -v openssl &> /dev/null; then
        78:     echo "  ❌ openssl پیدا نشد! نصب دستی: apt install -y openssl"
        79:     exit 1
        80: fi

The check at line 77 runs AFTER the apt install attempt (line 68/73),
so if apt failed silently (line 73 has `|| true`), the check at line 77
catches it and EXITS 1 before any secret generation happens.

Generation calls that depend on openssl:
  - install.sh:105  `SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 32)`
  - install.sh:109  `SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 32)`
  - install.sh:116  `BALE_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 16)`
  - install.sh:118  `BALE_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 16)`
  - install.sh:122  `TG_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 16)`
  - install.sh:124  `TG_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 16)`

All 6 openssl calls are AFTER the line 77 check. ✅ No code path
reaches openssl generation without the check passing.

Minor note: the apt install at line 73 uses `2>/dev/null || true`
which suppresses errors. If apt fails for a transient reason
(network, lock), the openssl check at line 77 still catches it.
✅ Defense-in-depth correct.

Verdict: PASS — explicit openssl presence check at install.sh:77
before any secret generation.


Q5. install.sh: non-root systemd?
----------------------------------------------------------------
Status: PASS

Evidence:
  - install.sh:210-211  creates dedicated system user:
        210: if ! id -u ehsansite &>/dev/null; then
        211:     useradd -r -s /bin/false -d "$SITE_DIR" ehsansite
                   2>/dev/null || true
        fi
    → `-r` = system user (no home dir, no /etc/skel).
    → `-s /bin/false` = NO LOGIN SHELL — user cannot SSH in or su.
    → `-d "$SITE_DIR"` = home dir set to project (informational).
    → Guarded by `id -u ehsansite` check — idempotent.

  - install.sh:213  `chown -R ehsansite:ehsansite "$SITE_DIR"`
    → entire project dir owned by ehsansite. The service can read
      its own files.

  - install.sh:215-240  systemd unit file:
        222: User=ehsansite
        223: Group=ehsansite
        232: NoNewPrivileges=true       ← blocks setuid escalation
        233: ProtectSystem=full          ← /usr, /boot read-only
        234: ProtectHome=true            ← /home, /root, /run/user hidden
        235: ReadWritePaths=$SITE_DIR    ← service can write its dir
        236: PrivateTmp=true            ← private /tmp

HARDENING GAPS (advisory only):
  - NO `ProtectKernelTunables=true`
  - NO `ProtectKernelModules=true`
  - NO `ProtectKernelLogs=true`
  - NO `ProtectControlGroups=true`
  - NO `ProtectProc=invisible`
  - NO `RestrictNamespaces=true`
  - NO `RestrictRealtime=true`
  - NO `RestrictSUIDSGID=true`
  - NO `LockPersonality=true`
  - NO `MemoryDenyWriteExecute=true`
  - NO `SystemCallFilter=@system-service`
  - NO `CapabilityBoundingSet=` (defaults to all caps retained)
  - NO `AmbientCapabilities=`
  - NO `UMask=0077`
  - NO `LimitNOFILE=`
  - NO `LimitNPROC=`

CRITICAL CONCERN:
  - install.sh:234  `ProtectHome=true` + install.sh:235
    `ReadWritePaths=$SITE_DIR`. If $SITE_DIR is under /home
    (which it is, per reset-admin-password.sh:7:
    `cd /home/ehsan/personal-site`), then:
      ProtectHome=true hides /home
      ReadWritePaths=/home/ehsan/personal-site re-exposes it
    systemd semantics: ReadWritePaths TAKES PRECEDENCE over
    ProtectHome, so the service CAN access /home/ehsan/personal-site.
    ✅ Functionally correct.
    ⚠ FRAGILE: if the admin relocates the install to e.g.
    /opt/personal-site, ProtectHome no longer applies and the
    service silently gains different filesystem semantics.
    Severity: LOW (works as-shipped, but brittle).

  - install.sh:211  `useradd ... 2>/dev/null || true` — silently
    swallows useradd failures. If useradd fails for a real reason
    (e.g., disk full, /etc/passwd locked), the script continues
    and `chown -R ehsansite:ehsansite` at line 213 fails too
    (silently via `2>/dev/null || true`). The systemd unit at
    line 222 then references a non-existent user → systemd
    fails to start the service → install reports "⚠ نصب انجام
    شد ولی سایت بالا نیومد" (line 305). Severity: LOW (the
    failure is visible, but the root cause is hidden by the
    error suppression).

Verdict: PASS — non-root systemd user is created and used, with
basic hardening (NoNewPrivileges, ProtectSystem=full, ProtectHome,
PrivateTmp). Missing many recommended systemd hardening directives
(see list above) but the essentials are present.


Q6. install.sh: chmod 600?
----------------------------------------------------------------
Status: PASS

Evidence:
  - install.sh:32   `chmod 600 /swapfile`                       ✅
  - install.sh:128  `chmod 700 db`                              ✅ (dir)
  - install.sh:148  `chmod 600 .env`                           ✅ (sensitive)
  - install.sh:157  `chmod 700 db` (redundant w/ line 128)      ✅
  - install.sh:159  `chmod 600 db/custom.db`                    ✅ (database)
  - install.sh:195  `chmod 600 .next/standalone/.env`           ✅
  - install.sh:197  `chmod -R 600 .next/standalone/db/*.db
                    2>/dev/null || true`                        ✅

Sensitive files with 600: .env (line 148, 195), db/custom.db (159,
197), /swapfile (32). Sensitive dirs with 700: db/ (128, 157).

MINOR NOTES:

  (a) install.sh:197  `chmod -R 600 .next/standalone/db/*.db`
      — `chmod -R` on a glob that matches only files (no dirs) is
      functionally equivalent to `chmod 600`. The `-R` is harmless
      but misleading. If the glob ever matched a directory (e.g.,
      a subdir ending in `.db`, unlikely), `chmod -R 600` on a dir
      makes it 600 = `rw-------` for owner, NO execute bit →
      directory becomes un-listable. Severity: LOW (globs in
      practice match only files).

  (b) install.sh:213  `chown -R ehsansite:ehsansite "$SITE_DIR"`
      — combined with the chmod 600 on .env (line 148) and
      db/custom.db (line 159), the ehsansite user is owner and
      can read them. ✅ Correct.

  (c) ⚠ install.sh:160  `rm -f db/custom.db-journal db/custom.db-wal
      db/custom.db-shm` — the WAL/SHM files (if they existed) are
      DELETED rather than chmod'd. Their previous permissions are
      irrelevant after deletion. But if a WAL file existed with
      world-readable permissions BEFORE this line ran (e.g., from
      a prior insecure install), it would have been readable up
      until this line. Severity: LOW (transient exposure window
      only matters if a multi-user system has untrusted local
      users).

  (d) install.sh:253  `cp nginx-ehsanmorad.conf /etc/nginx/sites-
      available/nginx-ehsanmorad.conf` — the nginx config file is
      copied with the DEFAULT umask (typically 644). The nginx
      config has NO secrets (just proxy_pass to localhost:3000),
      so 644 is acceptable. ✅ Not flagged.

  (e) ⚠ install.sh:215-240  systemd unit file written via
      `cat > /etc/systemd/system/personal-site.service << EOF`
      with NO explicit chmod afterward. The file inherits the
      default umask (644 typically). systemd unit files contain
      no secrets here (User=ehsansite, ExecStart=node server.js,
      etc.). ✅ Acceptable, but if the unit ever embeds an
      `Environment=SECRET=...` line, the 644 perms would leak.
      Severity: LOW (no secrets currently embedded).

  (f) install.sh:175-178  seeding scripts write to db/custom.db.
      The DB file is already chmod 600 (line 159), so any new rows
      inherit the file's permissions. ✅ Correct.

Verdict: PASS — all sensitive files (.env, db/custom.db, /swapfile)
have chmod 600. Sensitive dirs (db/) have chmod 700. No world-
readable secrets on disk after install.


Q7. Nginx secure?
----------------------------------------------------------------
Status: FAIL

Evidence (nginx-ehsanmorad.conf):
  - lines 16, 33, 50: `listen 80;` — ALL THREE server blocks listen
    on HTTP ONLY. No `listen 443 ssl;`, no `http2`, no SSL config.
    The install.sh delegates HTTPS to certbot (install.sh:284)
    which modifies the nginx config post-hoc, but the SOURCE conf
    shipped in the repo is HTTP-only.
    Severity: HIGH (in transit, until certbot runs and succeeds,
    ALL traffic including admin login, session cookies, webhook
    secrets is over plaintext HTTP).

FINDINGS (all in nginx-ehsanmorad.conf unless noted):

  (a) lines 16, 33, 50  NO TLS. Plaintext HTTP only.
      Severity: HIGH.

  (b) NO HTTP→HTTPS redirect server block. Even after certbot
      adds a 443 listener, the 80 listeners (lines 16, 33, 50)
      continue to proxy plaintext traffic to localhost:3000
      instead of 301-redirecting to HTTPS. Severity: HIGH.

  (c) NO `server_tokens off;` — nginx version leaked in HTTP
      Server header and on error pages. Severity: LOW (info leak).

  (d) NO security headers anywhere:
        - NO `add_header X-Frame-Options DENY` (clickjacking)
        - NO `add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff` (MIME sniffing)
        - NO `add_header Referrer-Policy strict-origin-when-cross-origin`
        - NO `add_header Content-Security-Policy ...`
        - NO `add_header Strict-Transport-Security ...` (HSTS)
        - NO `add_header Permissions-Policy ...`
        - NO `add_header X-XSS-Protection` (deprecated but harmless)
      Severity: HIGH (defense-in-depth absent; HSTS absent means
      the first HTTP request can be MITM'd even after HTTPS is
      set up — see prior audit V17.3-SEC-02 Q8).

  (e) NO `client_max_body_size` — defaults to 1MB, but explicit
      setting is recommended to prevent oversized POST DoS.
      Severity: LOW.

  (f) NO rate limiting (`limit_req_zone`, `limit_req`). The
      application has its own rate limiting (per prior audit
      V17.4-SEC-12 Q7), but defense-in-depth at nginx is absent.
      Severity: MED.

  (g) NO access restrictions on sensitive paths:
        - NO `location ~ /\. { deny all; }` (blocks .env, .git,
          .htaccess — currently .env is in $SITE_DIR which nginx
          proxies as `/`, so `GET /.env` would be proxied to the
          Node server which presumably 404s, but a misrouted
          static handler could leak it).
        - NO `location = /db/ { deny all; }` (the db/ dir is in
          $SITE_DIR; if nginx ever serves static files from
          $SITE_DIR it could leak the SQLite DB).
      Severity: MED (depends on Next.js routing).

  (h) line 24 (and 41, 58): `proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For
      $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;` — trusts the upstream XFF
      header chain. The application's rate limiter (per prior
      audit V17.3-SEC-02 Q11/F-9) blindly trusts XFF → rate-limit
      bypass. nginx here UNCONDITIONALLY forwards any client-set
      XFF. Severity: HIGH (rate-limit bypass — confirms and
      extends V17.3-SEC-02 Q11/F-9 at the proxy layer).

  (i) NO `proxy_read_timeout` / `proxy_connect_timeout` /
      `proxy_send_timeout` — defaults to 60s. Long-running LLM
      requests (per prior audit V17.4-SEC-12 Q8: no fetch timeout
      in providers.ts) could exceed 60s and nginx would 504
      while the upstream Node process is still hung → no backpressure
      → worker starvation. Severity: MED.

  (j) line 27 (and 44, 61): `proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";`
      — UNCONDITIONALLY sets Connection: upgrade. This forces
      WebSocket semantics on EVERY request, even non-WebSocket
      HTTP requests. For non-WS requests this is mostly harmless
      (nginx handles it) but it's incorrect. The standard pattern
      is `map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade { default upgrade;
      '' close; }` and `proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;`.
      Severity: LOW (functional oddity, not a security bug per se).

  (k) NO `ssl_protocols`, `ssl_ciphers`, `ssl_prefer_server_ciphers`
      — N/A until TLS is added, but their absence means certbot
      will use its defaults (typically acceptable). Severity: LOW.

  (l) NO `access_log` / `error_log` customization — uses nginx
      defaults. Combined with `server_tokens off` missing, error
      pages leak nginx version. Severity: LOW.

  (m) NO `gzip` / `gzip_types` — performance, not security. ✅ Not
      flagged.

  (n) Three near-identical server blocks (lines 15-29, 32-46,
      49-63) — code duplication. If one is patched, the others
      must be patched too. Severity: LOW (maintainability risk
      that leads to security drift).

  (o) NO `default_server` directive on any listener — the
      default_server falls to the first server block (or to
      /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/default, which install.sh:255
      removes). After `rm -f default`, the FIRST server block
      (ehsanmorad.ir) becomes the catch-all for ANY Host header
      including bare IPs. Severity: LOW (host-header injection
      surface, though limited since all three blocks proxy to
      the same upstream).

Verdict: FAIL — nginx config is HTTP-only, has zero security
headers, no rate limiting, no access restrictions on sensitive
paths, blindly trusts X-Forwarded-For (extending V17.3-SEC-02
Q11/F-9 to the proxy layer), and no timeouts. Many HIGH-severity
gaps.


Q8. reset-admin-password.sh secure?
----------------------------------------------------------------
Status: FAIL

Evidence (scripts/reset-admin-password.sh):

  (a) line 30  `NEW_PASSWORD="admin123"` — HARDCODED WEAK DEFAULT
      PASSWORD. No option to specify a custom password via flag
      or interactive prompt. Every reset produces the same
      password. Severity: HIGH (known-credential attack: anyone
      who knows an admin reset was performed can try admin123).

  (b) line 31  `echo "در حال تولید هش برای رمز: $NEW_PASSWORD"` —
      PRINTS THE PASSWORD TO STDOUT. The password is now in:
        - Terminal scrollback
        - Shell history IF stdout was redirected
        - Any CI/deploy log capturing stdout
        - The systemd journal IF run via a systemd unit
      Severity: HIGH (credential exposure to anyone with log
      access).

  (c) line 61  `echo "  رمز جدید: $NEW_PASSWORD"` — SECOND print
      of the password to stdout. Same risk as (b).

  (d) line 66  `echo "    password: $NEW_PASSWORD"` — THIRD print
      of the password to stdout. Same risk as (b).

  (e) lines 33-37  Node.js bcrypt invocation:
        33: HASH=$(node -e "
        34: const bcrypt = require('./node_modules/bcryptjs');
        35: const hash = bcrypt.hashSync('$NEW_PASSWORD', 10);
        36: process.stdout.write(hash);
        37: " 2>/dev/null)
      The bash variable `$NEW_PASSWORD` is expanded INSIDE a
      double-quoted node -e string, which is then inserted into
      a single-quoted JS string. If $NEW_PASSWORD contained a
      single quote `'`, the JS string would terminate early and
      the rest of the password would be parsed as JS code →
      arbitrary code execution in the node process.
      Currently safe because $NEW_PASSWORD is hardcoded to
      "admin123" (no quotes), but the PATTERN IS INSECURE — any
      future edit that introduces a quote (or, worse, accepts
      user input) would create an RCE.
      Severity: MED (latent injection; not currently exploitable
      but pattern is unsafe).

  (f) line 35  `bcrypt.hashSync('$NEW_PASSWORD', 10)` — bcrypt
      cost factor 10 is the MINIMUM acceptable in 2024+; 12 is
      recommended for production. Severity: LOW.

  (g) line 50  sqlite3 SQL UPDATE:
        sqlite3 db/custom.db "UPDATE AccessUser SET passwordHash
        = '$HASH', active = 1 WHERE username = 'admin';" 2>/dev/null
      The bash variable `$HASH` is expanded INSIDE a double-quoted
      SQL string, which is then inserted into a single-quoted SQL
      literal. bcrypt hashes are constrained to the alphabet
      `$./A-Za-z0-9` (22 chars + cost prefix), so they CANNOT
      contain a single quote → no SQL injection is currently
      possible. BUT the PATTERN IS INSECURE — if $HASH were ever
      sourced from user input, or if the hash algorithm changed to
      one whose output includes quotes, this would be SQLi.
      Severity: MED (latent injection; not currently exploitable
      but pattern is unsafe — should use parameterized queries
      via sqlite3's `.param set` or via a Python helper).

  (h) line 50  `2>/dev/null` — SUPPRESSES sqlite3 errors. If the
      UPDATE fails (e.g., db is locked, schema mismatch, db file
      missing), the script continues to line 53. The COUNT query
      at line 53 then returns 1 (the admin row exists from before,
      just with the OLD password), and the script reports
      "✅ رمز ادمین ریست شد!" (line 58) — FALSE SUCCESS.
      Severity: HIGH (silent failure; admin believes password
      was reset but it wasn't).

  (i) line 53  `COUNT=$(sqlite3 db/custom.db "SELECT count(*) FROM
      AccessUser WHERE username = 'admin';" 2>/dev/null)` — same
      error suppression. If the db file is missing, sqlite3
      would create an EMPTY db file (sqlite3 default behavior)
      and COUNT would be 0. The script would then take the
      else-branch at line 71 ("❌ کاربر admin پیدا نشد!") —
      accidentally correct failure mode. But if the db file
      EXISTS but is locked, COUNT could be empty (sqlite3 returns
      error to stderr, stdout is empty) → `COUNT=""` → `[ "$COUNT"
      = "1" ]` is false → also takes the else-branch. OK.
      Severity: LOW (the failure mode is correct, but for the
      wrong reasons).

  (j) line 37  `2>/dev/null` on the node command — suppresses
      node errors. If bcryptjs is missing (line 34: `require
      ('./node_modules/bcryptjs')` fails), node prints to stderr
      "Cannot find module" — suppressed. The `HASH` variable
      would then be empty → caught by line 39 `if [ -z "$HASH" ]`
      → exits 1 with a helpful message. ✅ This error path is
      handled correctly.

  (k) NO sudo / root check. The script does NOT verify it's
      running as root (or as the ehsansite user with write access
      to db/custom.db). If run as a non-privileged user, the
      sqlite3 UPDATE at line 50 silently fails (suppressed by
      2>/dev/null) and the false-success path in (h) is taken.
      Severity: MED.

  (l) line 22-24  SCRIPT_DIR / PROJECT_DIR resolution:
        22: SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
        23: PROJECT_DIR="$(cd "$SCRIPT_DIR/.." && pwd)"
        24: cd "$PROJECT_DIR"
      If the script is invoked via a symlink (e.g.,
      `/usr/local/bin/reset-admin -> /home/ehsan/personal-site/
      scripts/reset-admin-password.sh`), then `$0` is the symlink
      path, `dirname "$0"` is `/usr/local/bin`, and `cd ... &&
      pwd` returns `/usr/local/bin`. Then `cd "$SCRIPT_DIR/.."
      && pwd` returns `/usr/local`. The script then tries to
      `cd /usr/local` and run `sqlite3 db/custom.db` — which
      doesn't exist there → silent failure.
      Severity: LOW (install.sh:347 directs admins to run via
      `sudo bash scripts/reset-admin-password.sh` from the
      project dir, so symlink invocation is unlikely; but the
      pattern is fragile).

  (m) NO audit log. The script does not log WHO reset the
      password and WHEN. If multiple sysadmins have sudo access,
      a password reset is unattributable. Severity: MED.

  (n) NO lockout after reset. The script does NOT invalidate
      existing sessions, does NOT force a password change on
      next login, does NOT notify the admin via email/Bale that
      a reset occurred. Severity: MED.

  (o) NO cleanup of the bash variable. After the script exits,
      `$NEW_PASSWORD`, `$HASH` remain in the bash process's
      environment until the shell terminates. If the script is
      sourced (`. scripts/reset-admin-password.sh`) instead of
      executed, the variables persist in the caller's shell.
      Severity: LOW.

  (p) line 50  `active = 1` is set unconditionally. If the admin
      was intentionally deactivated (e.g., compromised account),
      running this script REACTIVATES them. Severity: LOW
      (intentional behavior, but undocumented).

  (q) line 34  `require('./node_modules/bcryptjs')` — assumes
      the node_modules dir is at PROJECT_DIR/node_modules. If
      the install is the STANDALONE build (per install.sh:189
      `if [ -f server.js ]`), there may be NO node_modules dir
      in PROJECT_DIR. The script would then fail at line 39
      (HASH empty) with a misleading "npm install --legacy-peer-
      deps" hint (line 41) — which is WRONG for a standalone
      build. Severity: MED (the reset script doesn't work on
      standalone installs).

Verdict: FAIL — multiple HIGH-severity issues:
  (1) Hardcoded weak password "admin123" (line 30).
  (2) Password printed to stdout THREE TIMES (lines 31, 61, 66).
  (3) Silent sqlite3 failure with false-success reporting
      (line 50 `2>/dev/null`).
  (4) No sudo/root check.
  (5) Latent JS injection in node -e (line 35) and latent SQLi
      in sqlite3 (line 50) — not currently exploitable but
      patterns are unsafe.
  (6) Doesn't work on standalone builds (line 34 require path).
Plus MED/LOW: no audit log, no session invalidation, bcrypt
cost 10, symlink fragility, no env-var cleanup, undocumented
`active=1` reactivation.

Status: PARTIAL PASS

Evidence (install.sh):

        334: else

        336:   echo "    Telegram: http://YOUR_IP:3000/api/telegram/webhook?secret=<SEE .env>"
        337: fi

  (a) ✅ GOOD: The literal placeholder `<SEE .env>` is used INSTEAD
      of the actual secret value. No webhook secret is leaked to
      stdout. This is the correct pattern.

  (b) ✅ GOOD: install.sh:338  `echo "    ⚠️ Secretها تو فایل .env
      هستن — با 'sudo cat .env' ببین"` — directs the admin to
      read .env (which is chmod 600) via sudo. No leak.

  (c) ✅ GOOD: install.sh:339  `echo "    ⚠️ این URL رو با کسی به
      اشتراک نذار!"` — explicit warning.

  (d) ⚠ install.sh:335-336  HTTP webhook URLs (no-domain branch):
      - `http://YOUR_IP:3000/api/bale/webhook?secret=<SEE .env>`
      - `http://YOUR_IP:3000/api/telegram/webhook?secret=<SEE .env>`
      Bale (per Bale's bot API) and Telegram (per Telegram's bot
      API) BOTH REQUIRE HTTPS for webhook endpoints. These URLs
      are FUNCTIONALLY UNUSABLE. The install script prints them
      without warning that they won't work.
      Severity: HIGH (functional failure + admin misinformed).

  (e) ⚠ install.sh:335-336  Placeholder `YOUR_IP` — the install
      script does NOT substitute the actual server IP. The admin
      must manually replace `YOUR_IP` with the server's public IP.
      Contrast with install.sh:294 which HARDCODES `31.70.76.10`
      — inconsistent. Either approach is suboptimal.
      Severity: LOW (UX inconsistency).

  (f) ⚠ Webhook URLs reference `/api/bale/webhook` and `/api/
      telegram/webhook` — these endpoints are NOT verified to
      exist by the install script. If the route files are missing
      (e.g., standalone build doesn't include them), the webhook
      POST would 404 and Bale/Telegram would disable the webhook
      silently. Severity: LOW (out of scope for install audit,
      but flagged).

  (g) ⚠ Webhook URL uses `?secret=<SEE .env>` query parameter.
      This means the webhook secret is passed in the URL, which:
        - Ends up in nginx access logs (default combined format
          includes the query string).
        - Ends up in Bale/Telegram's request logs.
        - Could be leaked via Referer header if the webhook
          endpoint ever issues a redirect (it shouldn't, but
          defense-in-depth).
      A more secure pattern is HMAC signing of the request body
      with the secret, or a header-based secret. Severity: MED
      (design weakness; secret in URL is common but discouraged).

  (h) ⚠ NO webhook secret rotation. The install script preserves
      the existing BALE_WEBHOOK_SECRET and TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET
      on re-runs (install.sh:114-125), but provides NO mechanism
      to rotate them. If a secret is compromised, the admin must
      manually edit .env and restart the service. Severity: LOW.

  (i) ⚠ The webhook secret length is `openssl rand -hex 16` =
      16 bytes → 32 hex chars → 128 bits of entropy. ✅ Sufficient
      entropy. (Compare SESSION_SECRET at install.sh:105/109:
      `openssl rand -hex 32` = 256 bits — also sufficient.)

  (j) ⚠ The webhook URLs are NOT tested by the install script.
      After printing them, the script does NOT make a test POST
      to verify the endpoint is reachable and the secret is
      accepted. Severity: LOW (admin discovers breakage only
      when configuring Bale/Telegram).

Verdict: PARTIAL PASS — webhook secrets are NOT leaked to
stdout (placeholder `<SEE .env>` used correctly, install.sh:332-
333). However:
  (1) HTTP fallback URLs (install.sh:335-336) are functionally
      unusable — Bale and Telegram REQUIRE HTTPS webhooks.
  (2) Webhook secret is passed in URL query string (design
      weakness; logged in nginx access logs).
  (3) No webhook secret rotation mechanism.
  (4) No end-to-end webhook test.

================================================================
ROOT-CAUSE ANALYSIS
================================================================

The deployment scripts ship TWO HIGH-SEVERITY patterns that compound
each other:

  (1) HTTP-EVERYWHERE UNTIL CERTBOT (Q7 + Q9): the nginx config
      ships as HTTP-only. The install script runs certbot
      (install.sh:284) AFTER the site is already serving traffic
      over HTTP. Between line 244 (systemctl restart personal-site
      → site goes live on HTTP) and line 284 (certbot succeeds →
      HTTPS), the site is serving the admin login page over
      plaintext HTTP. If certbot fails (line 287-291), the site
      STAYS on HTTP permanently. The admin is then told (line 290)
      to use `http://$DOMAIN_FOUND/user-login` — admin password
      sent in plaintext.
      Compounded by reset-admin-password.sh:64 which ALWAYS prints
      `http://YOUR_IP:3000/user-login` regardless of TLS state.

  (2) HARDCODED DEFAULT CREDENTIALS (Q3 + Q8): the install script
      seeds the admin user with username `admin` and password
      `admin123` (per seed_access_users.py, not directly audited
      but referenced at install.sh:178). The reset script
      (Q8) resets back to `admin123`. The password is printed
      to stdout 3 times by reset-admin-password.sh (lines 31,
      61, 66) and once by install.sh (line 316). Combined with
      HTTP-by-default (Q7+Q9), an attacker on the network path
      between admin and server can:
        (a) Sniff the HTTP login (Q9 HTTP fallback).
        (b) Capture `password: admin123` from stdout (Q3+Q8
            leak) if any CI/deploy log captures output.
        (c) Login as admin immediately.
      The only barrier is the time window between install
      completion and the admin's first manual password change.
      install.sh:317 warns the admin to change the password,
      but does NOT enforce it (no force-change-on-first-login
      flag in the DB or in the login route).

  (3) SILENT FAILURE PROPAGATION (Q1 + Q2 + Q8): the install
      script and the reset script both liberally use `2>/dev/null`
      and `|| true` (install.sh:73, 90, 160, 197, 211, 213, 253-
      255; reset-admin-password.sh:37, 50, 53) which suppresses
      real errors. Combined with `| tail -N` pipes (install.sh:
      166, 175-178, 284) that mask PIPESTATUS, this means:
        - apply_schema.py failure is silent (Q1).
        - sqlite3 UPDATE failure is silent (Q8.h).
        - apt install failure is silent (install.sh:73).
        - chown failure is silent (install.sh:213).
      The install reports "✅ نصب کامل شد!" (install.sh:303)
      even when the underlying steps failed. The admin only
      discovers breakage when the site doesn't load (and even
      then, the journalctl hint at install.sh:264 doesn't reveal
      the suppressed errors).

  (4) .ENV OVERWRITE ON EVERY INSTALL (Q2.a): the `cat > .env`
      at install.sh:135 destroys custom env vars. If the admin
      previously added custom env vars (e.g., custom LLM provider
      API keys, SMTP creds, feature flags), they are silently
      lost on the next install.sh run. Combined with Q3.c
      (subprocess output piped through tail), the admin has no
      log of what was lost.

  (5) NGINX TRUSTS X-FORWARDED-FOR (Q7.h): confirms and extends
      prior audit V17.3-SEC-02 Q11/F-9. The application's rate
      limiter blindly trusts XFF (per V17.4-SEC-12 Q7) AND the
      nginx proxy here UNCONDITIONALLY forwards any client-set
      XFF via `$proxy_add_x_forwarded_for` (nginx-ehsanmorad.conf
      lines 24, 41, 58). An attacker can:
        - Set `X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4` to bypass per-IP rate
          limits (V17.4-SEC-12 Q7).
        - Set `X-Forwarded-For: <victim-IP>` to frame the victim
          in logs.
      The fix would be `proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For
      $remote_addr;` (overwrite, not append) at the nginx layer
      — but per task instructions, NO FIX APPLIED.

Q1. Origin check correctness
================================================================
Status: PARTIAL  | Severity: MED
Location: src/middleware.ts:157-177

Code:
  middleware.ts:158:   const isPublicApi = PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES.some(p => pathname === p || pathname.startsWith(p + "/"));
  middleware.ts:159:   if ((method === "POST" || method === "PUT" || method === "DELETE") && !isPublicApi) {
  middleware.ts:160:     const origin = req.headers.get("origin");
  middleware.ts:161:     const host = req.headers.get("host");
  middleware.ts:163:     if (!origin || !host) { /* 403 missing_origin */ }
  middleware.ts:168-172: const originUrl = new URL(origin);
                       if (originUrl.host !== host) { /* 403 origin_mismatch */ }

Analysis:
  - The check is method-gated to POST/PUT/DELETE only (line 159).
    GET/HEAD/OPTIONS bypass entirely — correct for CSRF semantics
    (safe methods don't change state). PATCH is NOT in the list →
    any future PATCH handler would be CSRF-exposed (no PATCH routes
    exist today; defense-in-depth gap).
  - Origin is compared ONLY to the raw `host` header (line 169).
    Scheme is NOT verified. URL.host normalizes away default ports
    (443/80), so `https://victim.com` → host = "victim.com". If
    a reverse proxy preserves a non-canonical Host header like
    "victim.com:443" (rare but possible), originUrl.host="victim.com"
    !== host="victim.com:443" → false rejection. NOT a security
    issue (fails closed), but a correctness footgun.
  - Host-header spoofing: if an attacker can control the Host
    header (via HTTP request smuggling or a misconfigured proxy),
    they can set Host: "evil.com" + Origin: "https://evil.com" →
    match → CSRF bypass. Out-of-scope of pure CSRF, but worth
    noting as a chain vector.
  - `null` Origin (sandboxed iframes, data: URLs, redirects):
    req.headers.get("origin") returns the string "null", which is
    truthy → enters try block → new URL("null") throws → caught
    → 403 invalid_origin. ✅ Fails closed.
  - Empty Origin: `if (!origin)` → 403 missing_origin. ✅ Fails closed.
  - Missing Sec-Fetch-Site validation (modern defense-in-depth).
    Browsers now send `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin/cross-origin/
    same-site/none`. Not checked. Could be used as an additional
    CSRF signal (e.g., reject if `cross-site`).
  - The check is COMPLETELY SKIPPED for PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES
    (see Q3, Q4, Q5, Q6 below) — by design, but creates CSRF gaps
    for login and logout.

Verdict: Implementation is correct for the routes it covers
         (/api/admin/*, /api/messages). The MED rating is for the
         systemic gap that PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES bypass it (Q3+Q4).

Q3. /api/user/logout CSRF (Logout CSRF)
================================================================
Status: FAIL  | Severity: LOW
Location: src/middleware.ts:30 (PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES includes
                                "/api/user/logout")
          src/app/api/user/logout/route.ts:7-11

Code:
  middleware.ts:30:  "/api/user/logout",
  logout/route.ts:7:  export async function POST() {
  logout/route.ts:8:    const response = NextResponse.json({ ok: true });
  logout/route.ts:9:    response.cookies.delete("access_session");
  logout/route.ts:10:   return response;
  logout/route.ts:11: }

Analysis:
  - /api/user/logout is in PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES (line 30) →
    isPublicApi=true → Origin check SKIPPED (middleware.ts:159).
  - The route handler takes no body, performs no auth check,
    does not call logAccess, and just deletes the cookie.
  - SameSite=strict on the access_session cookie does NOT
    mitigate this: the CSRF attack surface is the Set-Cookie
    response that expires the cookie. Set-Cookie is processed
    by the browser regardless of whether the request was same-
    site. The cookie was already sent on the CSRF request
    (or not — doesn't matter); the response Set-Cookie with
    Max-Age=0 unconditionally expires the victim's cookie.
  - Logout CSRF PoC (works from any origin):
      <!-- attacker.com/csrf.html -->
      <form action="https://victim.com/api/user/logout" method="POST">
        <input type="submit" value="Click me">
      </form>
      <!-- Or auto-submit: -->
      <script>document.forms[0].submit()</script>
  - Impact: victim is silently logged out → next /api/user/verify
    returns { ok: false } → admin panel kicks them to /user-login.
    Annoyance/DoS only. No data leak, no privilege escalation.
  - Cross-ref: prior audit V17.4-SEC-04 F-7 (line 840 of worklog)
    flagged this as LOW and recommended: "Require a CSRF token or
    Origin header on POST /api/user/logout, validate that a session
    exists, and log the logout event." NONE of these were applied.
  - Additional issue: `response.cookies.delete("access_session")`
    (line 9) does NOT pass `path: "/"` or `sameSite: "strict"` —
    it uses Next.js defaults. The original cookie was set with
    `path: "/"` (login/route.ts:120). If Next's default path for
    delete is not "/", the browser may not match the cookie and
    fail to delete it. (In practice Next.js 14/15 sets path="/"
    by default for cookies.delete, so this works — but it's a
    latent footgun if Next ever changes defaults.)

Verdict: FAIL (LOW). Same finding as V17.4-SEC-04 F-7, unmitigated.

Q4. /api/user/login CSRF (Login CSRF)
================================================================
Status: FAIL  | Severity: MED
Location: src/middleware.ts:28 (PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES includes

          src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:46-128

Code:
  middleware.ts:28:  "/api/user/login",
  login/route.ts:46:  export async function POST(request: NextRequest) {
  login/route.ts:48:    const body = await request.json().catch(() => ({}));
  login/route.ts:49:    const username: string = (body.username || "").trim().toLowerCase();
  login/route.ts:50:    const password: string = body.password || "";
  login/route.ts:95:    const token = createSessionToken(user.id);
  login/route.ts:116:   response.cookies.set("access_session", token, {
  login/route.ts:117:     httpOnly: true,
  login/route.ts:118:     secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === "production",
  login/route.ts:119:     sameSite: "strict",
  login/route.ts:120:     path: "/",
  login/route.ts:121:     maxAge: 60 * 60 * 24, // 24 ساعت
  login/route.ts:122:   });

Analysis:
  - /api/user/login is in PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES (line 28) →
    isPublicApi=true → Origin check SKIPPED. Intentional (login
    form is reachable cross-origin) but creates Login CSRF.
  - SameSite=strict on the access_session cookie does NOT mitigate
    Login CSRF: the attack is that the SERVER sets the victim's
    cookie to the ATTACKER's session token. Set-Cookie is on the
    response, processed by the browser regardless of the request's
    sameSite context.
  - The handler parses body via `request.json()` (line 48) —
    `request.json()` parses the body as JSON regardless of the
    request's Content-Type header. A CSRF form with
    `enctype="text/plain"` posting a crafted JSON body succeeds:
        <!-- attacker.com/login-csrf.html -->
        <form action="https://victim.com/api/user/login"
              method="POST"
              enctype="text/plain">
          <input name='{"username":"attacker","password":"attacker_pass","x":"'
                 value='"}'>
        </form>
        <script>document.forms[0].submit()</script>
      Browser sends body like:
        {"username":"attacker","password":"attacker_pass","x":"="}
      request.json() parses this successfully → login succeeds →
      victim's browser now holds attacker's session cookie.
  - Impact: victim is logged into the attacker's account. If the
    victim then enters sensitive data into the dashboard (e.g.,
    changes their password, enters personal notes via /api/admin/*
    — wait, they're logged in as "attacker", not as admin, so
    they can't access /api/admin/* unless the attacker's account
    is admin role). The realistic attack:
      * Attacker creates an AccessUser with role=user.
      * Attacker CSRF-logs the victim into that account.
      * Victim sees the dashboard and may enter personal notes,
        contact details, etc. thinking it's their own account.
      * Attacker logs in to the same account later and reads
        the victim's data.
    Severity MED (depends on what data the dashboard accepts;
    the dashboard exposes ContentManager, ThemeBuilder, etc.
    only to admin role — but the user-dashboard page may have
    user-writable fields).
  - Cross-ref: prior audit V17.4-SEC-04 (line 2061 of worklog)
    flagged this as MED. UNMITIGATED.

Verdict: FAIL (MED). Login CSRF confirmed working PoC.

Status: PASS (defense-in-depth)  | Severity: LOW

  contact/route.ts:95-130:  // reCAPTCHA VERIFICATION — mandatory + fail-closed
  contact/route.ts:98:    const recaptchaToken = body.recaptchaToken;
  contact/route.ts:99:    if (!recaptchaToken || typeof recaptchaToken !== "string" || recaptchaToken.length < 10) {
  contact/route.ts:100:    ... return 400 captcha_required
  contact/route.ts:121-124: } catch (e) { ... // fail-closed
  contact/route.ts:125:    if (!captchaOk) { return 400 captcha_failed }

Analysis:
  - /api/contact is in PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES (line 31) → Origin
    check SKIPPED. By design — contact form is reachable from
    any page.
  - The route DOES require a valid reCAPTCHA token (lines 98-130)
    and is fail-closed (network errors reject, line 121-124).
  - reCAPTCHA tokens are bound to the registered domain (set in
    the Google reCAPTCHA admin console via RECAPTCHA_SECRET).
    A CSRF from attacker.com with a token minted for attacker.com
    will FAIL Google's siteverify (hostname mismatch). ✅
  - BUT: the defense relies entirely on reCAPTCHA. If:
      * RECAPTCHA_SECRET is empty/leaked, OR
      * Google's siteverify has a flaw, OR
      * The attacker can mint a valid token for victim.com
        (e.g., by solving the captcha on victim.com manually
        and reusing the token — reCAPTCHA tokens are single-use
        and expire in ~2 min, so this is hard)
    then CSRF succeeds.
  - The text/plain CSRF PoC from V17.4-SEC-04 (line 3071-3075 of
    worklog) NO LONGER WORKS because reCAPTCHA is now mandatory
    (V17.4 change). The PoC's body would have `recaptchaToken:""`
    → line 99 catches it (length < 10) → 400 captcha_required. ✅
  - Cross-ref: V17.4-SEC-04 finding #2 (CRITICAL) was about
    OPTIONAL reCAPTCHA. V17.4 made it mandatory (contact/route.ts
    comment: "V17.4: پاکسازی دوره‌ای Map..." — actually that's
    the rate-limit cleanup comment; the mandatory reCAPTCHA change
    is implicit in the current code at lines 98-130). The CSRF
    PoC from V17.4-SEC-04 is now blocked. ✅ Fixed.
  - Other contact-route mitigations:
      * Per-IP rate limit (3 per 10 min, contact/route.ts:6-7) —
        weak (bypassable via X-Forwarded-For per V17.3-SEC-02 Q11).
      * Honeypot `website` field (line 81-87).
      * Time-trap `_t` field (line 89-93).
      * Spam-pattern regex (line 35-44).

Verdict: PASS (with caveat: relies on reCAPTCHA as sole CSRF
         defense for this endpoint). LOW severity if reCAPTCHA
         is ever weakened.

      * Use the victim's IP for rate-limit accounting (chat/
        route.ts:23-33 — per-IP rate limit, 8 per minute).

        cap, X-Forwarded-For bypass).
      * Result is returned to the VICTIM's browser (same-origin
        CORS would block the attacker from reading it, but the
        server-side side effects — DB writes, LLM calls, Bale

    assistant messages by sessionId. Cross-ref V17.4-SEC-12 Q2

    Not a CSRF issue per se — it's an unauthenticated IDOR.

      * Amplify LLM cost attacks via victim browsers (each victim
        contributes 8 req/min, multiplied across many victims).
      * Pollute chat sessions with attacker-chosen messages
        attributed to victim IPs (Bale notifications sent to
        admin with victim's IP/UA — see V17.4-SEC-12 Q10).

    and IP pollution.

Q8. CORS preflight
================================================================
Status: PASS (default-deny)  | Severity: —
Location: src/middleware.ts (no OPTIONS handler)
          src/app/api/**/route.ts (grep for OPTIONS = 0 hits)
          next.config.ts:14-27 (headers() block — no CORS)
          Caddyfile (no CORS directives)
          nginx-ehsanmorad.conf (no CORS directives)

Analysis:
  - No OPTIONS handler anywhere in src/ (grep confirmed 0 hits).
  - No Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods,
    Access-Control-Allow-Headers, or Access-Control-Allow-
    Credentials headers set anywhere (middleware, next.config,
    Caddyfile, nginx).
  - Result: cross-origin XHR/fetch from browsers is BLOCKED by
    default — no ACAO header in any response → browser's same-
    origin policy denies the response.
  - This incidentally mitigates CSRF for protected routes that
    would otherwise be subject to cross-origin JSON POSTs:
      * Cross-origin fetch with `Content-Type: application/json`
        triggers a CORS preflight (OPTIONS) → no ACAO in response
        → preflight fails → browser never sends the actual POST.
      * So /api/admin/* and /api/messages are protected by CORS
        default-deny EVEN IF the Origin check in middleware were
        bypassed. ✅ Defense-in-depth.
  - HOWEVER: "simple requests" (form-encoded, text/plain, no
    custom headers) do NOT trigger preflight. Browser sends them
    directly. The Origin header is sent automatically. For:
      * Protected routes: middleware Origin check rejects. ✅
      * Public routes (login/logout/contact/chat): middleware
        skips Origin check → text/plain CSRF works (see Q3, Q4).
  - The CORS default-deny does NOT block cross-origin <form>
    submissions — those are subject to the same-origin policy on
    the RESPONSE side (attacker can submit but can't read the
    response). For state-changing endpoints, the submission
    itself is the attack (response reading not needed).

Verdict: PASS for CORS posture (default-deny is correct).
         The CSRF mitigation it provides is incidental, not
         intentional — relying on it as a CSRF defense is fragile
         (any future addition of an OPTIONS handler or CORS
         header would weaken it).

Q9. Content-Type bypass
================================================================
Status: PARTIAL  | Severity: MED
Location: src/middleware.ts:157-177 (Origin check)
          src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:48 (request.json())
          src/app/api/user/logout/route.ts:7-11 (no body)
          src/app/api/contact/route.ts:69 (req.json())
          src/app/api/chat/route.ts:91 (req.json())
          src/app/api/messages/route.ts:60 (req.json())
          src/app/api/admin/**/route.ts (all use req.json())

Analysis:
  - The middleware Origin check (line 159) is gated on HTTP
    method (POST/PUT/DELETE), NOT on Content-Type. So a POST
    with Content-Type: text/plain, application/x-www-form-
    urlencoded, or even no Content-Type is subject to the
    Origin check on protected routes. ✅ Good — no Content-Type
    bypass on protected routes.
  - The CSRF risk is on PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES routes, where the
    Origin check is skipped regardless of Content-Type:
      * /api/user/login (login/route.ts:48): `request.json()`
        parses the body as JSON regardless of Content-Type
        header. A text/plain CSRF form posting crafted JSON
        succeeds. → Login CSRF (see Q4).
      * /api/user/logout (logout/route.ts:7-11): takes no body.
        A form-encoded POST is enough. → Logout CSRF (see Q3).
      * /api/contact (contact/route.ts:69): `req.json()` parses
        regardless of Content-Type. A text/plain CSRF form
        would be parsed — BUT reCAPTCHA blocks it (line 98-130).
        → CSRF blocked by reCAPTCHA, not by Content-Type check.
      * /api/chat (chat/route.ts:91): `req.json()` parses
        regardless of Content-Type. A text/plain CSRF would be
        parsed. → No auth, no CSRF concern.
  - The classic CSRF Content-Type bypass (text/plain to evade
    CORS preflight + craft JSON body) DOES NOT bypass the
    middleware Origin check on protected routes (because the
    check is method-gated, not Content-Type-gated). ✅
  - For /api/messages POST (line 60: `req.json()`): not in
    PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES → Origin check applies → text/plain
    CSRF blocked at middleware. ✅
  - For /api/admin/** POST: same as /api/messages. ✅
  - The "JSON Content-Type enforces preflight → CORS default-
    deny blocks it" defense (see Q8) is NOT relied upon — the
    middleware Origin check is the primary defense. ✅ Robust.

Verdict: PARTIAL. No Content-Type bypass on protected routes.
         The MED rating is for the systemic gap that PUBLIC_API_
         PREFIXES routes accept text/plain CSRF bodies (Q3+Q4).
