Q10. sameSite=strict
================================================================
Status: PASS  | Severity: —
Location: src/app/api/user/login/route.ts:116-122 (cookie set)
          src/app/api/user/logout/route.ts:9 (cookie delete)
          src/lib/access-auth.ts:67-72 (createSessionToken)

Code:
  login/route.ts:116:   response.cookies.set("access_session", token, {
  login/route.ts:117:     httpOnly: true,
  login/route.ts:118:     secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === "production",
  login/route.ts:119:     sameSite: "strict",
  login/route.ts:120:     path: "/",
  login/route.ts:121:     maxAge: 60 * 60 * 24, // 24 ساعت
  login/route.ts:122:   });
  logout/route.ts:9:    response.cookies.delete("access_session");

Analysis:
  - access_session cookie attributes (login/route.ts:116-122):
      * httpOnly: true  ✅ — XSS cannot steal the cookie via
        document.cookie.
      * secure: NODE_ENV === "production"  ✅ — HTTPS-only in
        prod (prevents cookie leak over HTTP MITM).
      * sameSite: "strict"  ✅ — STRONGEST setting. Cross-site
        requests (including top-level navigation GETs) do NOT
        send the cookie. This is the strongest sameSite value.
      * path: "/"  ✅ — site-wide.
      * maxAge: 86400  ✅ — 24h.
  - sameSite=strict mitigates CSRF for state-changing requests
    that rely on the session cookie (admin POSTs, /api/messages,
    /api/admin/*, /api/admin/users/[id] PUT/DELETE):
      * Cross-site POST without cookie → checkAdminAuth fails →
        401. ✅ Defense-in-depth (in addition to Origin check).
  - sameSite=strict does NOT mitigate:
      * Login CSRF (Q4): the cookie is being SET, not read.
        Set-Cookie response is processed regardless of request
        sameSite context.
      * Logout CSRF (Q3): the cookie is being DELETED via
        Set-Cookie response. Same reason.
      * /api/contact, /api/chat: no auth, no cookie dependency.
  - Trade-off of sameSite=strict: breaks SSO-style flows and
    deep-linking. If a user clicks a link to /user-dashboard
    from an external site (e.g., email), the access_session
    cookie is NOT sent → user appears logged out → must
    re-authenticate. For this app's UX (single-user admin
    dashboard), strict is appropriate.
  - Cookie deletion (logout/route.ts:9): `response.cookies.
    delete("access_session")` uses Next.js defaults — does NOT
    explicitly pass path:"/" or sameSite:"strict". Next.js 14/15
    cookies.delete defaults to path="/" (verified empirically),
    so this works correctly today. Latent footgun if Next ever
    changes the default.
  - No other cookies are set anywhere in src/ (grep confirmed:
    only login/route.ts:116 sets a cookie; logout/route.ts:9
    deletes it).

Verdict: PASS. Cookie attributes are best-practice.
         sameSite=strict is the correct setting for this app.

Location: src/middleware.ts:159

Analysis:
  - OPTIONS is not in the CSRF gate. This is CORRECT — OPTIONS
    is a preflight method, not state-changing. Browser sends
    OPTIONS preflight automatically; rejecting it would break
    legit cross-origin API access (if any future CORS config
    is added).

----- F-D. No CSRF token anywhere in the codebase  [INFO] -----
Location: grep for `csrf|CSRF|csrfToken` → only middleware
          comments at src/middleware.ts:8, 157.

Analysis:
  - The app relies entirely on:
      1. sameSite=strict cookie (primary defense for state-
         changing requests that depend on the session cookie).
      2. Origin header check in middleware (defense for state-
         changing requests that don't require a cookie but
         mutate server state, e.g., admin POSTs if the cookie
         were ever relaxed to sameSite=lax).
      3. reCAPTCHA (defense for /api/contact).
      4. CORS default-deny (incidental defense for cross-origin
         JSON POSTs).
  - No synchronizer-token or double-submit-cookie CSRF defense.
  - This is acceptable given sameSite=strict + Origin check +
    httpOnly + secure. Modern guidance (OWASP Cheat Sheet)
    considers sameSite=strict + Origin/Referer check sufficient
    for first-party apps without cross-origin API consumers.
  - IF the app ever needs to expose an API to third-party
    consumers (e.g., mobile app, browser extension, or another
    domain), sameSite=strict would block them and a CSRF token
    scheme would be required.

Q2. apply_schema.py matches schema.prisma?
================================================================
Status: FAIL  | Severity: LOW (correctness, not directly exploitable)

DIVERGENCE 1 — ContactMessage.updatedAt:
  - schema.prisma:34-50 — ContactMessage model has `createdAt DateTime
    @default(now())` (line 42) but NO `updatedAt` field.
  - apply_schema.py:41-51 — ContactMessage table includes BOTH:
        createdAt DATETIME NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP  (line 49)
        updatedAt DATETIME NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP  (line 50)
  - The extra `updatedAt` column in SQL is invisible to Prisma client
    (Prisma SELECTs only known columns; INSERTs only known columns), so
    the field silently defaults to CURRENT_TIMESTAMP on INSERT and is
    never updated thereafter (Prisma UPDATEs don't touch unknown columns).
  - Per worklog V17.4-FINAL note "✅ apply_schema.py: تمام updatedAt ها
    DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP دارن", this column was added to ALL tables
    during V17.4 to fix NOT-NULL crashes — but ContactMessage has no
    Prisma counterpart, so the divergence was introduced.

DIVERGENCE 2 — @updatedAt semantics:
  - schema.prisma declares `updatedAt DateTime @updatedAt` on 19 models
    (User, Post, ChatSession, SiteSetting, AiProvider, LabEquipment, Book,
    Article, Tutorial, Skill, AiInstruction, EmailConfig, TelegramConfig,
    CustomTheme, SiteText, NavItem, AccessUser, BlockedIp, AparatClip).
  - apply_schema.py implements each as `updatedAt DATETIME NOT NULL
    DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`.
  - SQLite's `DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` only fires on INSERT. Prisma
    client sets `updatedAt = NOW()` explicitly in its UPDATE SQL because
    it understands `@updatedAt`, so Prisma-driven updates DO refresh the
    field. BUT raw SQL / python sqlite3 updates (as in seed_access_users.py,
    reset-admin-password.sh:37, list_messages.py) will NOT refresh
    `updatedAt`. So audit timestamps drift when scripts mutate rows.
  - This is a correctness gap, not a security gap.

DIVERGENCE 3 — SiteSetting.value default:
  - schema.prisma:90-94 — `value String` (NOT NULL, no default).
  - apply_schema.py:117-121 — `value TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT ''`.
  - In practice harmless (Prisma always passes a value), but the schema
    and SQL disagree on whether empty-string is implicit.

Cross-reference: prior audit worklog V17.4-FINAL claimed "apply_schema.py
  matches schema.prisma". The ContactMessage divergence refutes that.

Q5. DB path secure?
================================================================
Status: FAIL  | Severity: HIGH

ISSUE 5.1 — db.ts:6 cwd-relative path:
  Code (src/lib/db.ts:6):
    const dbPath = path.join(process.cwd(), 'db', 'custom.db')
  - `process.cwd()` is the directory from which the Node process was
    launched, NOT the project root. If systemd unit's WorkingDirectory
    is misconfigured (e.g., a deploy script `cd`s elsewhere), or a
    maintainer runs `node server.js` from /tmp, Prisma will silently
    create an EMPTY db/custom.db in that cwd, then re-seed admin with
    the default "admin123" password. The original DB is abandoned
    silently.
  - Inconsistent with apply_schema.py:14 which uses
    `Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "db" / "custom.db"`
    (absolute, file-relative — robust).
  - Inconsistent with .env: `DATABASE_URL=file:/home/z/my-project/db/custom.db`
    (absolute). The .env value is IGNORED by db.ts (see ISSUE 5.2).

ISSUE 5.2 — db.ts:14-20 OVERRIDES DATABASE_URL env:
  Code (src/lib/db.ts:14-20):
    new PrismaClient({
      datasources: { db: { url: `file:${dbPath}` } },
    })
  - Explicitly passing `datasources.db.url` overrides the `DATABASE_URL`
    env var. This is a documented Prisma anti-pattern (https://pris.ly/d/datasources-inline)
    — the .env file becomes a no-op for runtime DB selection.
  - Result: changing `.env`'s `DATABASE_URL` has NO EFFECT on which DB
    Prisma uses. Operators who rotate DB paths by editing .env will
    believe they've moved the DB; in reality the old path is still in
    use.
  - An operator who wants to point the app at a different DB (e.g., a
    read replica, a snapshot for forensic analysis, a SQLCipher-encrypted
    DB on a different mount) cannot do so via env — must edit source.

ISSUE 5.3 — File permissions:
  - `stat -c "%a %U:%G %n"` on dev box:
        755 z:z db/custom.db
        755 z:z .next/standalone/db/custom.db
        755 z:z .next/standalone/.env
        755 z:z db/  (parent dir)
  - VERSION.txt:144 claims "✅ db با chmod 600" — FALSE on dev box. The
    install.sh:159 `chmod 600 db/custom.db` only runs at install time
    on the target machine; the dev repo's tracked file is 0755.
  - Anyone with shell access on a shared dev box can:
      sqlite3 /home/z/my-project/db/custom.db
      sqlite> SELECT username, passwordHash FROM AccessUser;
      sqlite> SELECT name, apiKey FROM AiProvider;
      sqlite> SELECT botToken FROM TelegramConfig;
      sqlite> SELECT smtpPass FROM EmailConfig;
      sqlite> SELECT ip, message FROM ContactMessage;
    All plaintext (see Q4).
  - install.sh:128 `chmod 700 db` and install.sh:157 `chmod 700 db`
    set the parent dir to 0700, but only at install time on target.

ISSUE 5.4 — No encryption at rest:
  - SQLite raw file, no SQLCipher, no SEE, no ATTACH KEY (see Q4).
  - Backups (auto-backup.sh exists in /scripts) capture the raw .db
    file. If backup storage is shared/leaked, all secrets leak.
  - Container escape / volume mount exposure on Kubernetes/Docker
    deployments exposes the raw DB.

ISSUE 5.5 — Path traversal in apply_schema.py:
  - apply_schema.py:14 — `DB_PATH = str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "db" / "custom.db")`
    Path is constructed from __file__, not from user input. Safe.
  - apply_schema.py:458-459 — `open(DB_PATH, "a").close()` — opens with
    mode "a" (append), no O_EXCL, no O_CREAT flags. If an attacker can
    pre-create a symlink at db/custom.db → /etc/passwd, the open will
    follow the symlink. Then sqlite3.connect() would try to write SQLite
    format to /etc/passwd, but on most systems /etc/passwd is root-owned
    and the write would fail. Theoretical risk only; mitigated by
    filesystem perms.
  - seed_access_users.py:24-25 — `PROJECT_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent`
    then `DB_PATH = str(PROJECT_ROOT / "db" / "custom.db")`. Same
    pattern as apply_schema.py. Safe.

        const bcrypt = require('./node_modules/bcryptjs');
        const hash = bcrypt.hashSync('$NEW_PASSWORD', 10);
        process.stdout.write(hash);
        " 2>/dev/null)
        sqlite3 db/custom.db "UPDATE AccessUser SET passwordHash = '$HASH',
        active = 1 WHERE username = 'admin';" 2>/dev/null
    Two layers of injection risk:
      * JS injection: `'$NEW_PASSWORD'` is bash-interpolated into a JS
        single-quoted string. If NEW_PASSWORD contains a single quote
        (currently doesn't — hardcoded "admin123"), breaks JS.
      * SQL injection: `'$HASH'` is bash-interpolated into SQL. bcrypt
        output charset is `[./A-Za-z0-9$]` (no single quotes), so
        currently not exploitable. Pattern is unsafe.

  - scripts/seed_access_users.py:91-96 — `if existing: print(...); return`
    Idempotent on admin user existence. But does NOT verify the
    existing admin's password is not the default "admin123" — if the
    admin row exists with the default password, the script silently
    exits without warning.

  - scripts/seed_content.py — only `SELECT name FROM sqlite_master`,
    no INSERTs. Safe.
  - scripts/seed_equipment.py — same. Safe.
  - scripts/seed_texts.py:34-41 — parameterized INSERT with `?`
    placeholder. Safe.

  - All seed scripts use the same hardcoded DB path `db/custom.db`:
      * seed_texts.py:10
      * seed_content.py:10
      * seed_equipment.py:9
      * seed_access_users.py:25
    No env override, no `--db` flag. If an operator accidentally runs
    `python3 scripts/seed_access_users.py` from a different cwd, the
    script will try to open `./db/custom.db` relative to cwd (or fail
    with "Database not found" — see seed_access_users.py:60-63). No
    guard against running on the wrong DB.

  - install.sh:172-179 — runs all 4 seed scripts UNCONDITIONALLY when
    `ADMIN_EXISTS = 0`. If the DB is fresh but already has data in
    other tables (e.g., from a partial restore), seed_texts.py will
    skip duplicates via `WHERE key = ?` check (idempotent), but
    seed_access_users.py creates admin with "admin123" silently.

Q9. Transactions?
================================================================
Status: FAIL  | Severity: HIGH

EVIDENCE:
  - Grep for `db\.\$transaction` across /home/z/my-project/src → ZERO
    matches. (All matches in worklog.md are historical references to
    prior audits, not actual code.)
  - Grep for `\$transaction|\$queryRaw.*BEGIN|db\.transaction` →
    ZERO matches in /src.

MULTI-STEP ADMIN OPERATIONS LACKING ATOMICITY:
  1. POST /api/admin/clear (clear/route.ts:43-46) — 4 sequential
     `deleteMany` (replies, notes, tags, message). If process crashes
     after reply delete but before message delete, orphans remain.
     Also: should be wrapped in $transaction AND redundant given
     `onDelete: Cascade` (schema.prisma:71, 83, 125, 137).
  2. POST /api/admin/content `bulk_import` (content/route.ts:123-133) —
     for-loop of `create()` per item with try/catch swallowing errors.
     N sequential creates. Partial failure → partial import with no
     rollback.
  3. POST /api/admin/text `bulk_set` (text/route.ts:79-94) — for-loop
     of `upsert()` per item. N sequential upserts = 2N queries. Partial
     failure → partial update.
  4. POST /api/admin/settings (settings/route.ts:45-49) — 3 parallel
     `setSetting()` calls = 3 separate upserts. If site name succeeds
     but bale token fails, settings are inconsistent.
  5. POST /api/admin/users (route.ts:104+) — `accessUser.update` then
     `accessLog.create` (in user/login/route.ts:86-93). Should be
     atomic — if update succeeds but log fails, login count drifts
     from log.
  6. POST /api/admin/reply (route.ts) — `messageReply.create` +
     `contactMessage.update({status: 'replied'})`. If reply creates but
     status update fails, message appears unreplied in admin UI but
     reply exists in DB.
  7. POST /api/admin/chat-reply — `chatMessage.create` +
     `chatSession.update`. Same issue.
  8. POST /api/admin/security-dashboard action="clear_logs" —
     iterates and deletes security logs in batches; no transaction
     around the loop.

IMPACT:
  - Partial failures leave DB in inconsistent state (orphans, status
    mismatches, missing audit records).
  - An attacker who can race the API (e.g., send a flood of bulk_import
    requests) can amplify inconsistency — though no known exploit
    chain currently depends on this.
  - Recovery: a maintainer who notices inconsistent state has no
    transaction log to replay.

Cross-reference: prior audits V17.3-SEC-02 Q12 (worklog:7577), V17.4-SEC-04
  (worklog:8494, 8506, 8507, 8508), V17.4-SEC-12 Q3, V17.4-SEC-14 Q9 all

ADDITIONAL FINDINGS (not in the 10 questions but observed)
================================================================

----- F-A. apply_schema.py:462-469 error handling swallows details  [LOW] -----
  Code (apply_schema.py:461-472):
    try:
        conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
        conn.executescript(SCHEMA_SQL)
        conn.commit()
        ...
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"ERROR: {e}")
        sys.exit(1)
  - Generic exception catch. If schema application partially fails
    (e.g., one CREATE TABLE fails due to a syntax error), the partial
    state is committed (Python sqlite3 autocommit is off, but
    executescript may have already applied some statements before the
    failure). No transaction wrapper around executescript.
  - Error message goes to stdout, not stderr. systemd journal capture
    depends on StandardOutput= configuration.
  - No retry logic, no transaction rollback on partial failure.

----- F-B. apply_schema.py:458-459 race condition on DB creation  [LOW] -----
  Code:
    if not os.path.exists(DB_PATH):
        open(DB_PATH, "a").close()
  - TOCTOU race: between `os.path.exists()` check and `open()` call,
    another process could create the file (or a symlink). The open()
    follows symlinks. Mitigated by the fact that apply_schema.py is
    typically run as root during install (install.sh:1 has `set -e`,
    install.sh typically runs with sudo).
  - `open(DB_PATH, "a")` mode is "append" — does not truncate. If the
    file exists as a non-SQLite file (e.g., a logfile), sqlite3.connect
    will fail on first query with "file is not a database".

----- F-C. db.ts:8-10 global singleton unsafe in serverless  [LOW] -----
  Code (db.ts:8-10):
    const globalForPrisma = globalThis as unknown as {
      prisma: PrismaClient | undefined
    }
  - The singleton pattern is correct for long-lived Node servers, but
    in serverless/edge runtimes (Vercel, Cloudflare Workers), each
    invocation may get a fresh isolate, so the cache is useless. Each
    cold start pays the PrismaClient connection cost. Combined with
    the cwd-relative path (Q5), each cold start may also pick a
    different DB if cwd changes between invocations.
  - In production with `output: "standalone"` (next.config.ts:4) and
    systemd unit (install.sh:215-229), the singleton works correctly.
    So this is a future-deployment risk, not a current one.

----- F-D. seed_access_users.py:50-56 subprocess.run security  [LOW] -----
  Code:
    result = subprocess.run(
        ["node", "-e", f"""
        const bcrypt = require({json.dumps(bcrypt_path)});
        console.log(JSON.stringify(bcrypt.hashSync({json.dumps(password)}, 10)));
        """],
        capture_output=True, text=True, check=True, cwd=str(PROJECT_ROOT)
    )
  - Uses subprocess.run with a list (not shell=True), so no shell
    injection. Good.
  - json.dumps escapes strings safely for embedding in JS string
    literals. Good for the current hardcoded inputs.
  - `check=True` raises CalledProcessError if node exits non-zero —
    caught by no try/except in main(), so script crashes. Acceptable.
  - If `bcryptjs` is not found (find_bcryptjs returns None), the script
    sys.exit(1)s — see lines 41-47. Hard fail, no graceful degradation
    to a weaker hash. Good (avoids accidental weak hash).

----- F-E. .env file permissions  [LOW] -----
  - `.env` at /home/z/my-project/.env — `stat` not run, but install.sh:148
    `chmod 600 .env` only runs at install time. Dev box state unverified
    but likely 0644 (default umask) since the file isn't chmod'd at
    creation. Contains DATABASE_URL only (no SESSION_SECRET visible) —
    though SESSION_SECRET is required at runtime per access-auth.ts:23.
    Where SESSION_SECRET is stored is unclear from this audit scope —
    may be in .env.local (not present), or environment-only.
  - .next/standalone/.env — 755 (per `stat` above). install.sh:195
    chmod 600 runs at install time on target, but the LEAKED file in
    the build artifact is 755.

  L14 — FINDING (cosmetic/formatting): Two statements on a single
         line. `const [savedKey, setSavedKey] = useState<string |
         null>(null);` and `const loadTexts = async () => {` are
         on the SAME physical line. Hurts readability/grep-ability;
         not a runtime bug.
  L15 — PASS: setLoading(true) before fetch (loading flag flipped
         on).
  L17 — PASS: credentials: "include" set on GET (see criterion 4).
  L18 — FINDING (MEDIUM): No HTTP-status check (`res.ok`). If the
         server returns 401/403/500 with a non-JSON body (HTML
         error page, empty body), `res.json()` throws → caught by
         empty catch on L20 → user never sees an error.
  L19 — FINDING (HIGH): `if (data.ok) setTexts(data.texts || {})`
         silently discards the failure branch. If the API returns
         `{ ok: false, texts: {} }` (which is EXACTLY what route.ts
         GET returns on internal error — see route.ts:37), the
         `texts` state stays as the initial `{}` and the UI later
         shows "No text found" (TextEditor.tsx:174-178), which is
         misleading: the user thinks there are no texts when

  L20 — FINDING (HIGH): `catch {}` — empty catch block. NO error
         state, NO user-visible error message, NO logging. All
         fetch/json errors are silently swallowed. Criterion 6
         ("errors shown") FAILS for loadTexts.
  L21 — PASS: setLoading(false) is OUTSIDE the try/catch, so it
         always runs (loading state is correctly reset even on

Latent data-shape bug (cross-file):
  route.ts GET (lines 18-26) returns `{ ok: true, texts:
  Record<string, string> }` (single-string values) when the caller
  is NOT an admin (public fallback). TextEditor.tsx:11 declares
  state as `Record<string, { en: string; fa: string; de: string }>`
  and accesses `texts[key]?.en`, `texts[k].en.includes(...)`, etc.
  If TextEditor.tsx is ever rendered WITHOUT an admin session, the
  shape mismatch causes:
    - Line 68: `texts[k].en.includes(filter)` — `texts[k]` is a
      string `"hello"`, so `"hello".en` is `undefined`, and
      `undefined.includes(...)` throws TypeError.
    - Line 117/130/144: `value={texts[key]?.en || ""}` — `texts[key]`
      is a string; `"hello"?.en` is `undefined`; `""` fallback
      kicks in → all textareas render empty.
  Currently masked because the admin page is gated by auth, but
  this is a brittle contract between client and server.

Findings:
  L68   — FINDING (HIGH — bug): `texts[k].en.includes(filter)` —
          NO optional chaining on `texts[k]` and `.en`. If
          `texts[k]` is undefined (shouldn't happen in normal flow
          since groups were derived from Object.keys(texts), but
          becomes possible during the data-shape mismatch
          described in STEP 1 — `texts[k]` would be a STRING, not
          an object), `"hello".en` is `undefined`, and
          `undefined.includes(filter)` throws TypeError. Also
          note: uses raw `filter` (case-sensitive) instead of
          `filter.toLowerCase()` — inconsistent with the
          `k.includes(filter.toLowerCase())` half of the same
          expression.
  L68   — FINDING (MEDIUM — bug): Section-level filter does NOT
          search FA or DE values, only EN. Item-level filter
          (L100-101) searches both EN and FA but also not DE.
          Inconsistent: searching for a German-only string in
          any field returns no results.
  L99   — PASS: `key.includes(filter.toLowerCase())` — keys are
          typically lowercase, so this works for case-insensitive
          key matching.
  L100  — FINDING (MEDIUM — bug): `(texts[key]?.en || "").includes(filter)`
          uses RAW `filter` (case-sensitive). If user types
          "Hello" in the search box, it will NOT match "hello"
          in the EN value. Should be `.includes(filter.toLowerCase())`
          OR the EN value should be lowercased before comparison.
  L101  — Same as L100 for FA value.
  L102  — FINDING (LOW — missing feature): DE value is never
          searched at the item level (only EN and FA).
  L97-102 — FINDING (MEDIUM — UX bug): The item-level filter
          (L97-102) is INSIDE the section that already passed
          the section-level filter (L65-69). If the section
          matches the filter (e.g., section name contains the
          query) but NO individual keys match the filter, the
          section header is rendered (L88-96) with NO items
          underneath. This renders an empty section block —
          looks like a broken UI (header with no content).

Criterion 3 ("filter working") — PARTIAL: The filter mechanism
  does SOME filtering, but has 5 bugs:
    (a) TypeError risk on data-shape mismatch (L68)
    (b) Case-sensitivity inconsistency (L68, L100, L101)
    (c) DE values never searched at any level
    (d) FA not searched at section level (only at item level)
    (e) Empty-section rendering when section matches but no items

STEP 6 — Errors shown audit
================================================================
Findings:
  L20   — `catch {}` in loadTexts — empty. No error UI, no toast,
          no banner. Network errors and JSON parse failures are
          silently swallowed.
  L19   — When API returns `{ ok: false, texts: {} }`
          (route.ts:37 server-error GET case), loadTexts treats
          it the same as "no texts" — UI shows "No text found"
          (L174-178) which is misleading.
  L43-47 — saveText has NO try/catch and NO error branch. If the
          server returns 401 (route.ts:48), 400 (route.ts:56/77),
          500 (route.ts:103), or if fetch/json throws, NOTHING
          happens in the UI. No error message, no red indicator,
          no banner. The user clicks "save", sees nothing, and
          has no way to know whether it worked or failed (the
          only feedback is the green ✓ — its ABSENCE is the only
          failure signal, which is easy to miss).
  No error state declared. The component has exactly 4 useState
  hooks: texts (L11), loading (L12), filter (L13), savedKey (L14).
  There is NO `error` state, NO `saveError` state, NO `lastError`
  state. Errors have nowhere to go even if they were caught.

Criterion 6 ("errors shown") — FAILS. NO errors are shown to the
  user for either loadTexts or saveText failures.

[Q1] KEYBOARD ACCESSIBILITY                                    SC 2.1.1
================================================================
STATUS: PARTIAL — 4 CRITICAL VIOLATIONS

Q1-A. CRITICAL — Clickable <div>/<article> with onClick but no
       keyboard handler, no role, no tabIndex.
       -------------------------------------------------------------------
       Files / lines:
         - src/components/ArchiveGrid.tsx:130-148
             <article className="article-row"
               style={{ cursor: onItemClick ? "pointer" : "default" }}
               onClick={() => onItemClick?.(item)}>
             No onKeyDown, no role="button", no tabIndex.
             → Keyboard users CANNOT open article cards.
         - src/components/ArchiveGrid.tsx:150-172  (book card — same defect)
         - src/components/ArchiveGrid.tsx:174-190  (tutorial card — same
             defect; opens tutorial modal in page.tsx)
         - src/components/LabEquipmentRack.tsx:50-55
             <div className="equipment-item ..."
               onClick={() => setExpanded(isExpanded ? null : eq.id)}
               style={{ cursor: "pointer", ... }}>
             No onKeyDown, no role, no tabIndex.
             → Keyboard users CANNOT expand lab equipment details.
         - src/components/GlobalSearch.tsx:103-122
             <div className="global-search-result"
               onClick={() => { onNavigate(item.href); close(); setQuery(""); }}>
             No onKeyDown, no role, no tabIndex.
             → Keyboard users CANNOT select search results (only mouse).
             Note: the input itself is keyboard-accessible (line 89-96
             has autoFocus), but the result list is mouse-only.

Q1-B. CRITICAL — Anti-theft keyboard shortcut blocker interferes with
       assistive tech and standard browser shortcuts.
       -------------------------------------------------------------------
       File: src/app/page.tsx:171-181
         Code:
           if (
             e.key === "F12" ||
             (e.ctrlKey && e.shiftKey && (e.key === "I" || ... )) ||
             (e.ctrlKey && (e.key === "u" || ... "s" ...))
           ) { e.preventDefault(); return false; }
       Effect:
         - Ctrl+U (view source), Ctrl+S (save page) are standard browser
           features used by some screen-reader users to inspect content
           offline. Blocked with no alternative.
         - F12 / Ctrl+Shift+I/J blocked — disables browser DevTools,
           which screen-reader testers and keyboard-only users rely on
           for accessibility inspection. (WCAG 2.1.1 does not strictly
           require this, but it interferes with assistive workflows.)
         - devtoolsInterval polls window.outerWidth - window.innerWidth
           every 1 second (line 193); if the user has the browser
           zoomed or uses a screen-reader helper toolbar, the 160px
           threshold trips and the anti-theft warning covers the page
           (line 427-438), blocking all interaction. This is a
           documented false-positive class for a11y tools.

Q1-C. CRITICAL — Tutorial modal: no focus trap, no initial focus,
       no focus restoration to triggering card.
       -------------------------------------------------------------------
       File: src/app/page.tsx:843-878
         - Modal opens on click of tutorial card (Q1-A above).
         - ESC closes (handled at page.tsx:310-318) ✓ — keyboard
           DISMISS works.
         - BUT: on open, focus stays on the clicked card; Tab cycles
           through the entire page behind the modal overlay → focus
           escapes the dialog. Violates WAI-ARIA Dialog Pattern.
         - On close, focus is NOT returned to the triggering card
           (line 851 setActiveTutorial(null)) → focus drops to body
           → keyboard users lose their place.
         - Modal has no role="dialog", no aria-modal="true",
           no aria-labelledby (see Q10-D below).

Q1-D. CRITICAL — global-search modal: same defect.

         - No role="dialog", no aria-modal, no aria-labelledby.

           - Line 2188:       (input:focus { outline: none; }) — generic
           - Line 2309-2311:  .admin-search:focus { outline: none; }
           - Line 2537-2540:  select.admin-search:focus { outline: none; }
           - Line 2863-2869:  .settings-input:focus,
                             .settings-select:focus { outline: none; }
           - Line 3208-3212:  .dashboard-select:focus { outline: none; }
           - Line 3440-3447:  .dashboard-reply-textarea:focus { outline: none; }

       Specificity math:
         `.field input:focus`           → (0,1,2)
         `*:focus-visible`               → (0,0,1)
         → per-element rule wins. outline:none applies for BOTH :focus
         and :focus-visible (since :focus-visible ⊂ :focus). The visible
         focus indicator is REMOVED for keyboard users on:
           - Contact form name/email/message inputs (page.tsx:780,784,788)
           - All admin panel inputs (every component)
           - Chat input (ChatSection.tsx:178-189)
           - Settings panel inputs (SettingsPanel.tsx, ~30 inputs)
           - Dashboard select (user-dashboard/page.tsx:185-194)
           - Reply textarea (user-dashboard/page.tsx:484-491)
           - Search/sort inputs (ArchiveGrid.tsx:86-115)
           - Text editor textareas (TextEditor.tsx:116-152)

       Also user-login/page.tsx inputs use inline `outline: "none"`
       (lines 110, 140) and AccessUserManager.tsx `inputStyle.outline`
       is set to "none" (line 552), and AparatClipManager.tsx
       `inputStyle.outline` is "none" (line 292). Same defect.

Q2-B. CRITICAL — Earlier `:focus-visible` rule at line 1402-1405
       specifies only `outline: 1px solid var(--green)`. 1px outline
       FAILS WCAG 1.4.11 (Non-text Contrast: 3:1) and 2.4.13 (Target
       Size — pointer-area alternatives). The 2px rule at line 3481
       is later in the file and wins, so this rule is effectively
       dead, but if the file order ever changes the 1px would reapply.

Q2-C. POSITIVE — Native <button> elements without `:focus { outline:
       none }` overrides will use the global `*:focus-visible` 2px
       solid green indicator. Buttons in nav, hero CTAs, theme switcher,
       to-top, tutorial modal close, lab-visualizer close all use
       native <button> and DO get a visible keyboard focus indicator.

================================================================
Q1. Secret required?
================================================================
Status: PASS (conditional)  | Severity: -

Code:
  bale route.ts:19-23:
    const secret = url.searchParams.get("secret") || req.headers.get("x-webhook-secret") || "";
    const expectedSecret = process.env.BALE_WEBHOOK_SECRET;
    if (!expectedSecret) {
      return NextResponse.json({ ok: false, error: "webhook_not_configured" }, { status: 503 });
    }
  telegram route.ts:9-13: identical pattern with TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET.

Analysis:
  - Both routes refuse to operate if env var is unset → 503. OK.
  - If env var is set, request MUST supply matching secret (else 403 at
    timingSafeEqual check). Effectively required.
  - No default/hardcoded secret.
  - Edge case: if env var is "" (empty), `!expectedSecret` is true → 503.
    Fails closed.
  - Caveat (INFO): request-side default is `""` (bale route.ts:19,
    telegram route.ts:9). If both URL and header absent → secret="" →
    fails length check → 403. Effectively required.
  - Caveat (INFO): "required" is contingent on operator setting the env
    var. No startup warning, no admin-panel indicator that the webhook
    is unconfigured. The 503 only fires when a request arrives.

================================================================
Q2. timingSafeEqual used?
================================================================
Status: PASS*  | Severity: LOW

Code:
  bale route.ts:25-29:
    const secretBuf = Buffer.from(secret);
    const expBuf = Buffer.from(expectedSecret);
    if (secretBuf.length !== expBuf.length || !crypto.timingSafeEqual(secretBuf, expBuf)) {
      return NextResponse.json({ ok: false, error: "invalid_secret" }, { status: 403 });
    }
  telegram route.ts:14-18: identical pattern.

Analysis:
  - crypto.timingSafeEqual IS used. OK.
  - Caveat 1 (LOW — bale route.ts:27 / telegram route.ts:16): the length
    pre-check `secretBuf.length !== expBuf.length` returns BEFORE
    timingSafeEqual. This is a timing oracle that leaks the secret's
    byte-length: "wrong length" → fast early-return; "right length,
    wrong bytes" → full timingSafeEqual. Practical exploitability is
    very low (network jitter dominates, and DB operations downstream
    dominate timing anyway), but it is a textbook constant-time
    comparison defect. Fix (DO NOT APPLY): hash both sides with
    SHA-256 to fixed 32-byte digests, then compare digests with
    timingSafeEqual (no length check needed).
  - Caveat 2 (INFO): `Buffer.from("")` produces zero-length buffer.
    crypto.timingSafeEqual throws RangeError on zero-length buffers,
    but the length check guards this.
  - Caveat 3 (INFO): `Buffer.from(secret)` defaults to UTF-8. If env
    var contains multi-byte chars, byte comparison is still correct.

Q3. Rate limit on secret?
================================================================
Status: FAIL  | Severity: HIGH

Code:
  middleware.ts:21: const RATE_LIMIT_PATHS = ["/api/user/login", "/api/contact", "/api/chat"];
  middleware.ts:33: "/api/bale/webhook",
  middleware.ts:34: "/api/telegram/webhook",
  (Both webhook paths in PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES — NOT in RATE_LIMIT_PATHS.)
  bale route.ts:16-49: full POST handler — no internal rate limit.
  telegram route.ts:6-28: full POST handler — no internal rate limit.

Analysis:
  - Neither webhook route is in RATE_LIMIT_PATHS (middleware.ts:21).
    Only /api/user/login, /api/contact, /api/chat are rate-limited at
    the middleware.
  - No per-route rate limit inside either handler.
  - Impact:
      * Brute-force: attacker can POST unlimited
        /api/bale/webhook?secret=GUESS requests. If secret is short
        or weak (dictionary word, date, "admin123"), brute-force is
        feasible. timingSafeEqual + DB calls limit throughput to
        ~100 req/s per Vercel Edge instance, but attacker can fan
        out across instances/IPs.
      * CPU DoS: each request parses JSON, allocates Buffers, calls
        timingSafeEqual, and (if secret matches) hits DB. Without a
        rate limit, attacker can saturate worker concurrency.
      * Log injection: each request produces an access-log entry.
        Flooding pollutes logs and may push out legitimate entries.
  - Cross-ref: V17.3-SEC-02 Q4/F-5 (/api/admin/* not rate-limited,
    still open). Same class of defect.

================================================================
Q4. Secret in URL?
================================================================
Status: FAIL  | Severity: HIGH

Code:
  bale route.ts:8 (comment):  POST /api/bale/webhook?secret=XXX
  bale route.ts:19:           const secret = url.searchParams.get("secret") || ...
  telegram route.ts:5 (cmt):  POST /api/telegram/webhook?secret=XXX
  telegram route.ts:9:        const secret = url.searchParams.get("secret") || ...

Analysis:
  - Both routes accept the secret from URL query string as the
    PRIMARY source. The `x-webhook-secret` header is only a fallback.
  - Code comments (bale route.ts:8, telegram route.ts:5) document
    the URL form as the supported way to call the webhook.
  - URL query strings are logged in MANY places:
      * NGINX access logs (combined format includes query string).
      * Vercel / serverless-platform invocation logs.
      * CDN edge logs (Cloudflare, Fastly, AWS CloudFront).
      * Bale's own webhook config storage — setWebhook stores the
        URL with the secret. Any compromise of Bale infrastructure
        or Bale insider exposes the secret.
      * Any HTTP proxy, observability layer (Datadog, NewRelic,
        Sentry), or APM between Bale and origin.
      * Browser history / referer — less applicable for server-to-
        server, but if URL is ever pasted into Slack/email/commit,
        it leaks.
  - Bale's setWebhook API does NOT support custom headers — URL is
    the only way to convey the secret. For Bale, the URL form is
    structurally MANDATORY. This is a platform limitation, not a
    code defect, but the code embraces it without mitigation.
  - Telegram DOES support a header-based mechanism: configure
    `secret_token` in setWebhook → Telegram echoes it back as
    `X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token` header on each webhook call.
    This code does NOT read that header — it reads `x-webhook-secret`
    (custom name, telegram route.ts:9). So admin is FORCED to use
    the leaky URL form even for Telegram. See F-F.
  - Practical leak vector: if a single access log line containing
    `?secret=XXX` is exposed (log file leaked to pastebin,
    observability vendor breach, support engineer copies logs),
    attacker has the secret and can forge webhook calls (Q8
    replay + Q9/F-C /chat content injection).

================================================================
Q5. Header accepted?
================================================================
Status: PARTIAL  | Severity: MED

Code:
  bale route.ts:19:     req.headers.get("x-webhook-secret")
  telegram route.ts:9:  req.headers.get("x-webhook-secret")

Analysis:
  - A custom `x-webhook-secret` header IS accepted as fallback. OK.
  - Caveat 1 (INFO): header is FALLBACK only — URL takes precedence
    via `||`. Not exploitable in practice for webhooks (Bale/Telegram
    don't let callers set both URL and headers simultaneously in a
    way that would cause conflict).
  - Caveat 2 (MED — telegram-specific): Telegram's OFFICIAL secret-
    token mechanism uses `X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token` header
    (Telegram sends this when you configure `secret_token` in
    setWebhook). This code reads `x-webhook-secret` (custom name)
    INSTEAD — so the official mechanism is NOT used. Admin must
    fall back to URL `?secret=XXX` pattern (Q4 leak). Fix (DO NOT
    APPLY): also read `x-telegram-bot-api-secret-token` and document
    as preferred mechanism for Telegram.
  - Bale has no official signed-header mechanism — only the URL.

Q6. Body validated?
================================================================
Status: FAIL  | Severity: MED

Code:
  bale route.ts:31-34:
    const body = await req.json().catch(() => null);
    if (!body) {
      return NextResponse.json({ ok: false, error: "invalid_body" }, { status: 400 });
    }
  telegram route.ts:19-20: similar (single-line).
  bale.ts:108-114 (processBaleWebhook):
    const message = body?.message;
    if (!message || !message.text) return { ok: false };
    const text: string = message.text.trim();
    const parts = text.split(/\s+/);
  telegram.ts:66-71: similar.

Analysis:
  - Only a null/truthy check on parsed body (bale route.ts:32,
    telegram route.ts:20). No schema validation (zod, ajv, etc.).
  - No type check on `body.message.text`. The line
    `const text: string = message.text.trim()` (bale.ts:112,
    telegram.ts:69) ASSUMES `message.text` is a string. If attacker
    sends `{"message":{"text":123}}` or `{"message":{"text":{"foo":"bar"}}}`,
    `.trim()` throws TypeError → caught at route.ts:45 → 500
    "server_error". Minor DoS (CPU for stack unwinding) + log noise.
  - No length cap on `text` before `text.split(/\s+/)` (bale.ts:113,
    telegram.ts:70). Middleware caps body at 1MB (middleware.ts:198),
    so `text` can be ~1MB. `split(/\s+/)` on a 1MB string of all
    spaces produces ~500k empty-string entries → array allocation.
    `parts.slice(2).join(" ")` then allocates another ~1MB string.
    Per-request memory amplification.
  - `messageId = parts[1]` (bale.ts:134, telegram.ts:84) — no format
    validation. Passed to Prisma `findUnique({ where: { id } })`.
    Prisma parameterizes → no SQL injection. But if `messageId`
    isn't a valid cuid (24-char base36), Prisma throws → 500.
  - `replyText = parts.slice(2).join(" ")` (bale.ts:135,
    telegram.ts:84/92) — no length cap before DB write. Up to ~1MB
    per ChatMessage.content / MessageReply.reply row. DB bloat DoS.
  - Middleware 1MB body cap (middleware.ts:198) trusts Content-Length
    header — chunked-encoding bypass noted in V17.3-SEC-02 Q6. So
    effective body cap may be higher.
  - `processBaleWebhook` returns `{ ok: false, reply: "..." }` for
    various shape errors (e.g., "Usage: /reply {id} {your reply}").
    The route at bale route.ts:39-42 then SENDS this reply back to
    admin's Bale chat via sendBaleMessage. If caller is attacker
    with forged secret, attacker receives these usage/error messages
    — minor info disclosure about command syntax (already public
    in /help, so negligible).

================================================================
Q7. CSRF-exempt?
================================================================
Status: PASS (intentional)  | Severity: -

Code:
  middleware.ts:24-37: PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES includes
    "/api/bale/webhook" and "/api/telegram/webhook".
  middleware.ts:158: isPublicApi = PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES.some(...)
  middleware.ts:159: CSRF check only runs when `!isPublicApi`.

Analysis:
  - Both webhook routes ARE in PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES (middleware.ts:33-34)
    → they bypass the Origin/Host CSRF check at middleware.ts:159-177.
  - This is CORRECT for webhooks: Bale/Telegram servers call these
    endpoints server-to-server and do NOT send an `Origin` header
    (Origin is a browser-only concept). If CSRF check applied,
    legitimate webhook calls would be rejected.
  - Risk note (LOW): the exemption means the ONLY protection on
    these endpoints is the webhook secret. If secret is compromised
    (Q4 URL leak, Q3 brute-force, Q8 replay), endpoint is fully
    open from any origin. Defense-in-depth: consider IP allowlist
    for Bale/Telegram egress ranges (F-H).

================================================================
Q8. Replay protection?
================================================================
Status: FAIL  | Severity: HIGH

Code:
  bale route.ts:25-29, telegram route.ts:14-18: only a static-secret
    comparison. No nonce, no timestamp, no HMAC over request body.
  No call to `crypto.createHmac` anywhere in either route or in
    bale.ts / telegram.ts.

Analysis:
  - The static BALE_WEBHOOK_SECRET / TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET env var
    is the same for every request and is NOT bound to:
      * The request body (no HMAC over body).
      * A timestamp (no freshness check — no Date header validation).
      * A per-request nonce (no nonce storage / cache).
  - An attacker who captures ONE legitimate webhook call can replay
    it indefinitely. Capture vectors:
      * Server access log containing URL with `?secret=XXX` (Q4) —
        gives the secret, enabling arbitrary forging (not just replay).
      * Network MITM if HTTPS is improperly terminated (V17.3-SEC-02
        Q8 — HSTS missing behind TLS proxy).
      * Server compromise / log-service breach / observability
        vendor breach.
      * Bale's or Telegram's own infrastructure compromise (they
        store the webhook URL with the secret).
  - Impact of replay:
      * /disable — takes down AI chat API. DoS.
      * /enable — re-enables a disabled API (less impact).
      * /list — leaks recent contact messages (PII: name + message
        preview).
      * /stats — leaks DB counts.
      * /reply {id} {text} — injects a reply into a contact message
        thread. If admin later emails the contact, attacker's text
        is sent.
      * /chat {sessionId} {text} — injects ARBITRARY content as an
        assistant message into any chat session. Per V17.4-SEC-12
        Q5, this content is rendered to visitors without
        sanitization → stored XSS. See F-C.
  - Telegram's official `secret_token` mechanism is ALSO a static
    secret — same replay weakness. Telegram does NOT sign request
    bodies. So even using the official header (Q5) would not add
    replay protection. Bale has no signing mechanism at all.
  - True replay protection would require HMAC over body+timestamp+
    nonce, which neither Bale nor Telegram supports at the protocol
    level. Mitigation: rotate secrets frequently, restrict by source
    IP (F-H), log/alert on unexpected webhook payloads.

================================================================
Q9. Command injection?
================================================================
Status: PASS (no shell exec)  | Severity: -

Code:
  bale.ts:116-231: switch (cmd) over known commands.
  telegram.ts:73-117: switch (cmd) over known commands.
  No imports of `child_process`, no `exec`, no `eval`, no `Function()`,
    no dynamic template-string evaluation.

Analysis:
  - The "commands" (/list, /reply, /chat, /disable, /enable, /stats,
    /start, /help) are application-level routing via a `switch`. The
    `default` branch (bale.ts:229-231, telegram.ts:115-117) returns
    "Unknown command" — does NOT execute arbitrary input.
  - `messageId`, `sessionId`, `replyText` are passed to Prisma
    (`db.contactMessage.findUnique`, `db.chatMessage.create`, etc.).
    Prisma parameterizes queries → no SQL injection.
  - No string is interpolated into a shell command, file path, or
    URL-with-eval.
  - PASS on traditional command injection.
  - HOWEVER (related finding — see F-C, HIGH): /chat injects
    attacker-controlled `replyText` as an assistant message into
    chat sessions. Combined with Q3 (no rate limit) + Q4 (URL leak)
    + Q8 (no replay protection), an attacker who forges a webhook
    call can inject arbitrary content (including HTML/script tags)
    into any chat session. Per V17.4-SEC-12 Q5, this content is
    served to visitors without sanitization → stored XSS. This is
    content injection with XSS-equivalent impact, not command
    injection, but worth flagging in the same breath.

================================================================
Q10. Info leak?
================================================================
Status: FAIL  | Severity: HIGH (bot-token leak); MED/LOW for the rest.

Code — HIGH (bot-token leak via GET /api/bale/webhook):
  bale route.ts:55-77 (GET handler):
    export async function GET(req: Request) {
      const authCheck = await checkAdminAuth(req, "");
      ...
      const [token, chatId, enabled] = await Promise.all([
        getSetting("baleBotToken"), ...]);
      return NextResponse.json({
        ...
        webhookUrl: token
          ? `https://api.bale.ai/v1/bots${token}/setWebhook`
          : null,
      });
    }
  bale route.ts:73-75: the bot token is embedded in the returned URL.

Code — MED (logs include full err objects, possibly URLs with tokens):
  bale route.ts:46:     console.error("[/api/bale/webhook] error:", err);
  telegram route.ts:25: console.error("[/api/telegram/webhook]", err);
  bale.ts:61:           console.error("[bale] sendMessage error:", err);
  telegram.ts:35:       console.error("[telegram] sendMessage error:", err);
  bale.ts:48:           const url = `${BALE_API_BASE}${config.token}/sendMessage`;
  telegram.ts:26:       const url = `https://api.telegram.org/bot${config.token}/sendMessage`;

Code — LOW (status-code distinguishability + enumeration):
  bale route.ts:22, telegram route.ts:12: 503 "webhook_not_configured"
  bale route.ts:28, telegram route.ts:17: 403 "invalid_secret"
  bale route.ts:33, telegram route.ts:20: 400 "invalid_body"
  bale route.ts:47:                     500 "server_error"
  bale.ts:140-141: "Message ${messageId} not found." (enumeration)
  bale.ts:148:      "Reply saved for ${original.name}." (PII: visitor name)
  bale.ts:160-161: "Session ${sessionId} not found." (enumeration)
  telegram.ts:87, 89, 95, 99: same patterns.

Analysis:

  HIGH — bot-token leak via GET /api/bale/webhook (bale route.ts:73-75):
    - GET handler returns `webhookUrl: \`https://api.bale.ai/v1/bots
      ${token}/setWebhook\`` — the BOT TOKEN is embedded in the URL,
      returned in the JSON response body in PLAINTEXT.
    - V17.4-FINAL supposedly masked bot tokens in /api/admin/settings
      ("bot tokens در /api/admin/settings mask می‌شن"), but this GET
      endpoint at /api/bale/webhook was NOT masked.
    - Auth via `checkAdminAuth(req, "")` (bale route.ts:56). Per
      V17.3-SEC-02 Q3/F-1, middleware session validation is
      FORMAT-ONLY — a forged `access_session` cookie with correct
      shape bypasses middleware. The API layer (admin-auth.ts:17-31
      → access-auth.ts:78-96) DOES verify the HMAC, so direct API
      access requires a real admin session. BUT: if admin session
      is hijacked (via V17.4-SEC-12 Q1 session-hijack chain, or
      V17.3-SEC-02 Q12 missing-CSP XSS risk, or admin-password
      brute-force V17.3-SEC-02 Q4/F-5 — all still open), attacker
      gets the raw bot token → full bot takeover (read all incoming
      Bale messages, impersonate admin via bot, delete messages, etc.).
    - The token is ALREADY in admin's possession (they configured
      it). Returning it in plaintext is unnecessary disclosure —
      endpoint should return only a boolean `hasToken` and a URL
      template `https://api.bale.ai/v1/bots<TOKEN>/setWebhook` (with
      a placeholder), letting admin substitute the token they
      already know.
    - Asymmetry: Telegram route has NO equivalent GET handler
      (telegram route.ts:1-28 is POST-only). Bale-only defect.

  MED — error logs may include URLs with bot tokens (bale.ts:61,
       telegram.ts:35):
    - `sendBaleMessage` constructs `url = \`${BALE_API_BASE}${config.
      token}/sendMessage\`` (bale.ts:48) — bot token is in URL.
    - If `fetch(url, ...)` throws (network error, DNS failure, TLS
      error, connection reset), the thrown Error object commonly
      includes `err.url`, `err.message`, or the URL in stack trace.
      `console.error("[bale] sendMessage error:", err)` then logs
      the token to server logs.
    - Same pattern in telegram.ts:26 + telegram.ts:35.
    - Note: Bale's and Telegram's APIs REQUIRE the token in URL
      path (it's how their bot APIs authenticate). So removing the
      token from the URL is not possible — only redacting it from
      logs is.

  MED — server logs include full error objects (bale route.ts:46,
       telegram route.ts:25):
    - `console.error("[/api/bale/webhook] error:", err)` logs the
      entire err object. If Prisma throws (e.g., invalid cuid
      format for messageId at bale.ts:139), the error includes
      query params, Prisma client version, and stack trace with
      file paths. Visible to anyone with log access.
    - The 500 response itself returns only generic "server_error"
      (bale route.ts:47) or `{ ok: false }` (telegram route.ts:26)
      — no stack trace leaks to the CLIENT.

  LOW — status-code distinguishability:
    - 503 "webhook_not_configured" (bale route.ts:22, telegram
      route.ts:12) leaks that env var is unset.
    - 403 "invalid_secret" (bale route.ts:28, telegram route.ts:17)
      leaks that env var IS set but supplied secret was wrong.
    - 400 "invalid_body" (bale route.ts:33, telegram route.ts:20)
      leaks that JSON parsing failed.
    - An attacker can probe the endpoint to determine configuration
      state WITHOUT ever guessing the secret — just send an empty
      POST and see whether response is 503 (not configured) or 403
      (configured but wrong/missing secret). Useful for
      reconnaissance before mounting a brute-force (Q3).

  LOW — enumeration via /reply and /chat (bale.ts:139-148, 159-170;
       telegram.ts:86-99):
    - "Message ${messageId} not found." (bale.ts:141, telegram.ts:87)
      confirms a messageId does NOT exist.
    - "Reply saved for ${original.name}." (bale.ts:148, telegram.ts:89)
      confirms a messageId DOES exist AND leaks the visitor's name
      (PII).
    - "Session ${sessionId} not found." (bale.ts:161, telegram.ts:95)
      confirms a sessionId does NOT exist.
    - "Reply injected into chat ${sessionId}." (bale.ts:170,
      telegram.ts:98) confirms a sessionId DOES exist.
    - These responses are sent BACK via sendBaleMessage (bale
      route.ts:39-42, telegram route.ts:22) to whoever called the
      webhook. If caller is legit admin, fine. If caller is attacker
      with forged/stolen secret, they can enumerate valid
      message/session IDs and learn visitor names.
    - Cross-ref: V17.4-SEC-12 Q10 — visitorId is forgeable and
      reflected in Bale notifications. Combined: an attacker who
      forges a webhook call can enumerate sessions AND learn which
      visitorId each session belongs to (via admin's prior Bale
      notifications).

  PASS — no secret returned in any response.
  PASS — 500 responses don't leak stack traces to the client.

ADDITIONAL FINDINGS (not in the 10 questions but observed)
================================================================

----- F-A. Bot token in URL passed to fetch  [HIGH, info leak via logs] -----
Location: bale.ts:43-64 (sendBaleMessage), bale.ts:48;
          telegram.ts:22-38 (sendTelegramMessage), telegram.ts:26.

Code:
  bale.ts:48:     const url = `${BALE_API_BASE}${config.token}/sendMessage`;
  telegram.ts:26: const url = `https://api.telegram.org/bot${config.token}/sendMessage`;

Analysis:
  - Bot token is in the URL path (Bale/Telegram API design — token
    is the auth mechanism, no header alternative).
  - If fetch throws, the error commonly includes the URL → token
    leaks to server logs via console.error at bale.ts:61 /
    telegram.ts:35.
  - Cannot be fixed at the URL level (API requires it). Can only
    be mitigated by redacting the URL in error logs.

----- F-B. No body-size cap inside the route  [MED] -----
Location: bale route.ts:31, telegram route.ts:19.

Code:
  bale route.ts:31:  const body = await req.json().catch(() => null);

Analysis:
  - Middleware caps body at 1MB (middleware.ts:198), but:
      * The middleware check trusts `Content-Length` (V17.3-SEC-02
        Q6 — chunked-encoding bypass). Effective cap may be higher.
      * The route doesn't independently enforce a smaller cap.
        Bale/Telegram webhook payloads are typically <10KB. A 1MB
        payload is suspicious and should be rejected.
      * `await req.json()` buffers the entire body in memory
        before any validation.
  - Combined with Q3 (no rate limit), an attacker can flood the
    endpoint with 1MB bodies → worker memory exhaustion.

----- F-C. /chat command allows arbitrary assistant-message injection
       [HIGH, content injection → stored XSS] -----
Location: bale.ts:152-171, telegram.ts:91-98.

Code:
  bale.ts:163-165:
    await db.chatMessage.create({
      data: { sessionId, role: "assistant", content: replyText },
    });
  telegram.ts:96: same pattern.

Analysis:
  - `/chat {sessionId} {replyText}` creates a ChatMessage with
    `role: "assistant"` and `content: replyText` (attacker-
    controlled, up to ~1MB per middleware body cap).
  - Per V17.4-SEC-12 Q5, /api/chat serves assistant messages to
    visitors WITHOUT sanitization → stored XSS.
  - An attacker who forges a webhook call (via Q3 brute-force +
    Q4 URL leak + Q8 no replay protection) can:
      * Inject `<img src=x onerror=alert(document.cookie)>` as
        an assistant message into any chat session.
      * When visitor opens /api/chat/messages (per V17.4-SEC-12
        Q2: ZERO auth on that endpoint), the XSS fires in the
        visitor's browser.
      * Combined with V17.4-SEC-12 Q1 (session hijack via sessionId
        — cuid, no auth binding), this is a full visitor-session-
        takeover chain.
  - Note: the LEGITIMATE use of /chat is for admin to reply to a
    chat session via Bale. So the command itself is not a defect —
    the defect is that an attacker can reach it without strong auth
    (Q3+Q4+Q8).
  - Mitigation (DO NOT APPLY): add HMAC signature verification
    over request body (requires Bale/Telegram cooperation, which
    they don't provide). Failing that, IP-allowlist Bale/Telegram
    egress ranges (F-H) + rate-limit invalid_secret responses (Q3).

----- F-D. Reply text not length-capped before DB write  [LOW, DoS] -----
Location: bale.ts:143-145 (messageReply.create), bale.ts:163-165
          (chatMessage.create), telegram.ts:88, telegram.ts:96.

Analysis:
  - `replyText = parts.slice(2).join(" ")` (bale.ts:135,
    telegram.ts:84/92) — no length cap. Up to ~1MB per write (per
    middleware body limit, which itself is bypassable per
    V17.3-SEC-02 Q6).
  - An attacker (or even legit admin pasting a huge reply) can
    bloat the DB. ChatMessage.content has no DB-level length cap
    (per prisma schema, text type).
  - Mitigation: cap replyText to e.g. 4000 chars before DB write.

----- F-E. Timing-safe comparison length-leak  [LOW] -----
Location: bale route.ts:27, telegram route.ts:16.

Code:
  if (secretBuf.length !== expBuf.length || !crypto.timingSafeEqual(secretBuf, expBuf)) {

Analysis:
  - The length check returns BEFORE timingSafeEqual, leaking the
    secret's byte-length via response-time difference.
  - Practical exploitability: very low (network jitter dominates,
    and DB operations downstream dominate timing anyway).
  - Trivially fixable: hash both sides with SHA-256 (fixed 32-byte
    digests) before comparing — eliminates the length check.

----- F-F. Telegram doesn't use official secret-token header  [MED] -----
Location: telegram route.ts:9.

Code:
  const secret = url.searchParams.get("secret") || req.headers.get("x-webhook-secret") || "";

Analysis:
  - Telegram's official mechanism: configure `secret_token` in
    setWebhook → Telegram sends
    `X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token: <token>` header on each
    webhook call.
  - This code reads `x-webhook-secret` (custom name) instead.
  - Consequence: admin cannot use Telegram's official header-based
    secret mechanism. They MUST use the URL `?secret=XXX` pattern
    (Q4 leak), because Telegram's setWebhook doesn't let you set
    arbitrary headers — it sets `secret_token`, which Telegram
    echoes back as `X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token`.
  - Fix (DO NOT APPLY): also read `x-telegram-bot-api-secret-token`
    header; document it as the preferred mechanism for Telegram.
    This eliminates the URL-form leak for Telegram (Bale still
    has no header alternative).

----- F-G. Bale GET endpoint exposed at webhook path  [MED] -----
Location: bale route.ts:55-77.

Analysis:
  - GET handler exists at the SAME path as the webhook POST
    (/api/bale/webhook).
  - Authenticated via `checkAdminAuth(req, "")` (bale route.ts:56).
    The empty-string password is the legacy pattern noted in
    V17.4-SEC-12 F-D — checkAdminAuth ignores the password param
    (V17.2 change). Auth falls back to session-cookie verification
    only.
  - Returns config status AND the raw bot token via `webhookUrl`
    (see Q10 HIGH finding).
  - The Telegram route has NO equivalent GET — asymmetric.
  - Mitigation: remove the GET handler, or move it to
    /api/admin/bale/status (under ADMIN_API_PREFIX, gets middleware
    session check), and mask the token in the response.

----- F-H. No source-IP allowlist  [LOW] -----
Location: middleware.ts:21, 24-37 (webhooks in PUBLIC_API_PREFIXES
          but no IP allowlist).

Analysis:
  - Webhooks should only be called from Bale's and Telegram's
    egress IP ranges (documented ranges, relatively stable).
  - No IP allowlist at the route or middleware level.
  - Combined with Q3 (no rate limit) and Q8 (no replay protection),
    this means anyone from any IP can hit the endpoint (subject
    only to the static secret).
  - Mitigation: add an IP allowlist for Bale/Telegram egress
    ranges. This is the strongest defense-in-depth available
    given that neither platform signs request bodies.

Final verdict:
  Of 10 audit questions: 5 FAIL (Q3, Q4, Q6, Q8, Q10), 1 PARTIAL
  (Q5), 2 PASS-with-caveats (Q1, Q2), 2 clean PASS (Q7, Q9).
  Severity breakdown: 4 HIGH (Q3, Q4, Q8, Q10), 2 MED (Q5, Q6),
  1 LOW (Q2), 3 PASS (Q1, Q7, Q9).
  Plus 8 additional findings: 3 HIGH (F-A, F-C, plus Q10/F-G token
  leak), 3 MED (F-B, F-F, F-G), 3 LOW (F-D, F-E, F-H).

  The most severe SINGLE finding is the BOT TOKEN LEAK via
  GET /api/bale/webhook (Q10 + F-G) — bale route.ts:73-75 returns
  the raw bot token in the JSON response. V17.4-FINAL masked bot
  tokens in /api/admin/settings but MISSED this endpoint. Anyone
  with admin access (or who bypasses middleware per V17.3-SEC-02
  Q3/F-1) gets the raw bot token → full bot takeover.

  The most severe CHAIN is:
    Q3 (no rate limit) +
    Q4 (secret in URL → logs) +
    Q8 (no replay protection) +
    F-C (/chat injects assistant messages) +
    V17.4-SEC-12 Q5 (assistant messages served without sanitization
      → stored XSS) +
    V17.4-SEC-12 Q2 (/api/chat/messages has ZERO auth → IDOR)
    = an attacker who obtains the webhook secret (via log leak,
      brute-force, or Bale infrastructure compromise) can inject
      arbitrary HTML/script into ANY chat session, which then
      executes in any visitor's browser when they view the chat
      history. Full visitor-side XSS, no admin interaction required

Q1. middleware.ts hasValidSession() — HMAC verification?
================================================================
Status: FAIL  | Severity: HIGH
Location: src/middleware.ts:70-93 (function hasValidSession)
          src/middleware.ts:87-89 — explicit comment + return statement

Code (verbatim):
  line 70:  function hasValidSession(cookieHeader: string): boolean {
  line 71:    if (!cookieHeader) return false;
  line 72-77: // parse cookies into {k: v} map
  line 78:    const token = cookies["access_session"];
  line 79:    if (!token) return false;
  line 80:    try {
  line 81:      const decoded = Buffer.from(
                  decodeURIComponent(token), "base64").toString("utf8");
  line 82:      const parts = decoded.split(".");
  line 83:      if (parts.length !== 3) return false;
  line 84:      const [userId, expiresAtStr] = parts;  // ← parts[2] (sig) discarded
  line 85:      const expiresAt = parseInt(expiresAtStr, 10);
  line 86:      if (isNaN(expiresAt) || Date.now() > expiresAt) return false;
  line 87:      // در middleware نمی‌تونیم HMAC رو verify کنیم چون SESSION_SECRET
                  بهش دسترسی نداریم
  line 88:      // فقط ساختار رو چک می‌کنیم — API route اصلی خودش HMAC رو
                  verify می‌کنه
  line 89:      return userId.length > 0;       // ← ONLY structural check
  line 90-92: } catch { return false; }
  line 93:  }

Analysis:
  - The third part of the token (HMAC signature, parts[2]) is destructured
    on line 84 but NEVER compared against an expected HMAC. It is silently
    discarded.
  - The function returns true iff:
      (a) the cookie value is valid base64
      (b) the decoded payload has 3 dot-separated parts
      (c) parts[1] parses as an integer (expiresAt)
      (d) Date.now() <= expiresAt (not yet expired)
      (e) parts[0] (userId) is non-empty (any non-empty string)
  - The author's own comment (lines 87-88) admits the omission: middleware
    "can't verify HMAC because SESSION_SECRET is unavailable". This is
    incorrect — process.env IS available in Next.js middleware (Edge runtime
    has access to env vars exposed to the runtime). The reason given is
    a misunderstanding of Edge-runtime env access.
  - Defense-in-depth assumption "API route verifies HMAC anyway" holds
    ONLY for routes that call checkAdminAuth / getSessionFromRequest.
    Middleware-only gates (e.g. /user-dashboard page rendering at
    middleware.ts:180-185) rely SOLELY on this structural check.

PoC:
  # Forge a cookie that passes middleware (no HMAC needed):
  PAYLOAD="anyuserX.$(($(date +%s%3N) + 86400000)).fakesig"
  COOKIE=$(printf '%s' "$PAYLOAD" | base64)
  # Access /user-dashboard:
  curl -sI "https://victim.com/user-dashboard" \
       -H "Cookie: access_session=$COOKIE"
  # → HTTP 200 (page renders). The page then client-side fetches
  # /api/user/verify which DOES verify HMAC → {ok:false} → router.replace
  # to /user-login. So functional compromise is limited, but middleware
  # is bypassed (an attacker need NOT know SESSION_SECRET to clear the
  # /user-dashboard redirect gate, nor to clear the 401 gate at line 188
  # for /api/admin/* — those still 401 because the routes re-verify).
  #
  # The dangerous implication: an attacker who has STOLEN a real cookie
  # whose expiresAt has been deliberately extended (e.g. by a buggy
  # client that stored expiresAt = +10y) can use it indefinitely past
  # the legitimate 24h — because middleware never checks the HMAC, and
  # if ANY downstream admin route fails to call checkAdminAuth, the
  # gate is open. (See Q8 — currently no such downstream gap found.)

Cross-reference:

Q3. lib/access-auth.ts — HMAC + timingSafeEqual correctness?
================================================================
Status: PASS (with notes)  | Severity: LOW
Location: src/lib/access-auth.ts:67-96 (createSessionToken / verifySessionToken),
          206-208 (hmac)

Code:
  line 67-72: createSessionToken(userId):
                expiresAt = now + 24h
                payload  = `${userId}.${expiresAt}`
                sig      = hmac(payload)         // SHA-256-HMAC, hex digest
                return base64(`${payload}.${sig}`)
  line 78-96: verifySessionToken(token):
                decoded = base64decode(token).toString("utf8")
                parts   = decoded.split(".")
                if (parts.length !== 3) return null
                [userId, expiresAtStr, sig] = parts
                expiresAt = parseInt(expiresAtStr, 10)
                if (isNaN(expiresAt)) return null
                if (Date.now() > expiresAt) return null
                expectedSig = hmac(`${userId}.${expiresAt}`)
                sigBuf = Buffer.from(sig, "hex")
                expBuf = Buffer.from(expectedSig, "hex")
                if (sigBuf.length !== expBuf.length ||
                    !crypto.timingSafeEqual(sigBuf, expBuf)) return null
                return { userId, expiresAt }
  line 206-208: hmac(message) = crypto.createHmac("sha256",
                                  getSecret()).update(message).digest("hex")

Notes (all LOW — no actual exploit, but worth flagging):
  - The length check `sigBuf.length !== expBuf.length` on line 91 happens
    BEFORE timingSafeEqual — this is the correct idiom (timingSafeEqual
    throws on length mismatch). ✅
  - The early-return checks (lines 85-86: NaN, expiry) happen BEFORE
    the HMAC comparison, which leaks timing information about whether
    the token is expired (cheap reject) vs signature-invalid (slightly
    more expensive reject). For an attacker who does NOT know
    SESSION_SECRET, this distinction is not useful. For an attacker
    who DOES know SESSION_SECRET, the token is already fully forgeable.
    → no exploitable timing channel.
  - The HMAC is computed over `${userId}.${expiresAt}` — NOT over the
    raw cookie (which would include `sig` itself, impossible). ✅
  - SHA-256 is the correct HMAC algorithm; hex encoding makes the sig
    a fixed 64-char string. ✅
  - getSecret() (lines 21-43) rejects placeholder secrets
    (build-placeholder, change-me, etc.) and secrets <32 chars. ✅
  - The token format `base64(payload.sig)` means the signature is
    NOT URL-safe by default (base64 uses + and /). The cookie is set
    via response.cookies.set (login/route.ts:116) which URL-encodes
    values, and getSessionFromRequest (line 198) decodes via
    decodeURIComponent — so the round-trip is correct. ✅
  - One minor concern: if a deployed instance is missing SESSION_SECRET
    env var, getSecret() throws → verifySessionToken catches via the
    try/catch on line 79 and returns null → all sessions invalidated.
    Fail-closed behavior. ✅

Cross-reference:
  - V17.4-SEC-02 audit covered IP/rate-limit concerns; this audit
    confirms the HMAC implementation itself is sound.
  - Q5 (below) shows the real auth-chain weakness is NOT in the HMAC
    crypto but in the LACK of server-side session state.

Q4. Can session cookie be forged?
================================================================
Status: PARTIAL  | Severity: MED
Location: src/middleware.ts:70-93 (structural-only gate)
          src/lib/access-auth.ts:78-96 (true HMAC gate — not forgeable)

Analysis:
  - The CRYPTOGRAPHIC token (parts[2] = HMAC) is NOT forgeable without
    SESSION_SECRET — Q3 confirms the implementation is sound.
  - HOWEVER, the middleware gate (Q1) IS forgeable: an attacker who
    constructs any payload matching `<non-empty>.<future-int>.<any>`
    base64-encoded and sets it as `access_session` will pass
    middleware's hasValidSession() check (line 89).
  - Functional impact analysis (what does this forged cookie unlock?):
    A. /user-dashboard page (middleware.ts:180-185):
       → Forged cookie passes middleware → page HTML rendered.
       → Page immediately calls /api/user/verify (page.tsx:98) which
         DOES verify HMAC → returns {ok:false} → router.replace
         to /user-login. Net effect: attacker briefly sees "Loading"
         div, then redirect. Severity: INFO LEAK (UI labels, tab
         names visible in HTML source).
    B. /api/admin/* (middleware.ts:188-193):
       → Forged cookie passes middleware → request reaches route
         handler → handler calls checkAdminAuth → getSessionFromRequest
         → verifySessionToken fails HMAC → returns 401.
       Net effect: 401 same as if cookie were absent. Severity: NONE.
    C. /api/messages (middleware.ts:188-193, exact match):
       → Same as (B). 401 from checkAdminAuth. Severity: NONE.
  - Conclusion: cookie forging yields a denial-of-service AMPLIFIER
    (forged cookies pass cheap middleware check then trigger DB-bound
    API calls that all reject at HMAC verification — but the DB query
    for accessUser happens AFTER HMAC check inside checkAdminAuth at
    line 23, so actually only the cheap HMAC check runs).
    More importantly: forged cookies can be used in CSRF-style attacks
    to make an admin's browser think they have a session — but since
    the admin already has a valid session, this is moot.
  - The CRITICAL impact: if any FUTURE admin route is added that
    trusts middleware's check and does NOT call checkAdminAuth, it
    becomes immediately accessible. The middleware's structural-only
    check is a latent security debt — it currently works only because
    every admin route has defense-in-depth via checkAdminAuth.

PoC:
  # Forge a cookie to pass middleware (does not grant API access):
  PAYLOAD="forged_user_id.$(($(date +%s%3N) + 86400000)).INVALID_SIG"
  COOKIE=$(printf '%s' "$PAYLOAD" | base64 -w0)
  curl -sI "https://victim.com/user-dashboard" \
       -H "Cookie: access_session=$COOKIE"
  # Expected: HTTP 200 (page renders) → JS bounce to /user-login.
  curl -s "https://victim.com/api/messages" \
       -H "Cookie: access_session=$COOKIE"
  # Expected: {"ok":false,"error":"unauthorized"}  ← HMAC fails

Cross-reference:
  - NEW finding. Latent risk — flagged for fix recommendation.

Q5. Can attacker reuse stolen cookie after password change?
================================================================
Status: FAIL  | Severity: HIGH
Location: src/app/api/admin/security/route.ts:56-99 (change_password action)
          src/lib/access-auth.ts:67-72 (token = HMAC(userId.expiresAt),
                                        NO passwordHash binding)

Code:
  security/route.ts:86-91:
    const newHash = await hashPassword(newPassword);
    await db.accessUser.update({
      where: { id: adminUser.id },
      data: { passwordHash: newHash },
    });

  access-auth.ts:67-72:
    export function createSessionToken(userId: string): string {
      const expiresAt = Date.now() + 24h;
      const payload = `${userId}.${expiresAt}`;
      const sig = hmac(payload);           // ← hmac depends ONLY on
                                            //   SESSION_SECRET + userId + expiresAt
      return Buffer.from(`${payload}.${sig}`).toString("base64");
    }

Analysis:
  - The session token's HMAC is computed over `userId.expiresAt` only.
    It does NOT bind to:
      * passwordHash (changing the password leaves old tokens valid)
      * user.active (deactivating the user leaves old tokens valid
        AT MIDDLEWARE LEVEL — see Q4. Per-request auth catches active
        via checkAdminAuth, but middleware still passes)
      * user.expiresAt (account-expiry change leaves old tokens valid
        AT MIDDLEWARE LEVEL — checkAdminAuth also does NOT check
        user.expiresAt; only checkAccess() does, and admin routes
        don't call checkAccess)
      * any per-session token id (no DB-side session table)
      * any password-changed-at timestamp
      * any session-rotation counter
  - The change_password handler (security/route.ts:56-99) updates
    ONLY the passwordHash column. It does NOT:
      * bump a `tokenVersion` field (no such column exists)
      * delete/expire existing sessions (no server-side session store)
      * rotate SESSION_SECRET (would invalidate ALL users)
      * set a `passwordChangedAt` timestamp for later comparison
      * log out the changer's other devices
      * blacklist the old cookie
  - Therefore, an attacker who has exfiltrated a valid access_session
    cookie (via XSS, network sniffing, log leak, screenshot, proxy
    compromise, etc.) can continue to use it for up to 24 hours AFTER
    the admin notices the compromise and changes their password.
  - The ONLY ways to invalidate the stolen cookie are:
      (a) Wait 24h for natural expiry (access-auth.ts:44
          SESSION_DURATION_HOURS = 24; cookie maxAge = 86400s
          at login/route.ts:121).
      (b) Rotate SESSION_SECRET env var — invalidates ALL users
          (disruptive; admin would also lose their session).
      (c) Deactivate the admin account — but middleware still passes
          the cookie (Q1), and checkAdminAuth catches it; non-admin
          actions that bypass checkAdminAuth (currently none, per Q8)
          would still be reachable.
  - In the current architecture, there is NO mechanism to perform a
    targeted revocation of a SINGLE stolen session.

PoC:
  # 1. Attacker steals admin cookie via XSS (hypothetical — no XSS
  #    found in this audit but see V17.4-SEC-12 Q5 stored-XSS in chat).
  STOLEN=$(curl -s -X POST "https://victim.com/api/user/login" \
           -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
           -d '{"username":"admin","password":"adminpw"}' \
           -c - | grep access_session | awk '{print $NF}')
  # 2. Admin notices and changes password:
  curl -X POST "https://victim.com/api/admin/security" \
       -H "Cookie: access_session=$STOLEN" \
       -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
       -d '{"action":"change_password","currentPassword":"adminpw",\
            "newPassword":"newstrongpw"}'
  # → server returns { ok: true, message: "Password changed." }
  # 3. Attacker uses the OLD stolen cookie:
  curl "https://victim.com/api/messages" \
       -H "Cookie: access_session=$STOLEN"
  # → STILL RETURNS 200 with full messages list — old cookie still valid
  #    for up to 24h after the password change.

Cross-reference:
  - NEW finding. No prior audit covered post-incident session
    revocation. V17.4-SEC-04 touched password change but only for
